🏗️ Directory Skeleton — anihpj / jobpost

This document uses the real-world anihpj project as the reference environment, deploying the jobpost Django application on Kubernetes with Cilium for networking and security. All examples, paths, and context use this directory structure.

PROJECT ROOT: /lpj — Django app + REST API + K8s/Cilium + ops artifacts (logs, systemd, backups, cron). Built for daily Linux mastery and LFCS exam practice.

📋 LFCS Exam Coverage

This document covers all LFCS (Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator) exam domains with hands-on examples using the anihpj/jobpost environment. Each domain below maps to the relevant sections in this document.

Domain 1: Essential Commands (25%)
ls, cd, pwd, find, locate, cp, mv, rm, mkdir, touch, ln, grep, sed, awk, cut, sort, uniq, wc, tar, gzip, bzip2, xz, zip, I/O redirection
Domain 2: Operation of Running Systems (20%)
ps, top, kill, nice, bg, fg, free, df, du, uptime, vmstat, iostat, systemctl, journalctl, GRUB, kernel params, cron, crontab, at, systemd timers
Domain 3: User & Group Management (10%)
useradd, usermod, userdel, passwd, groupadd, groupmod, groupdel, chmod, chown, chgrp, umask, ACLs, SUID/SGID, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group, /etc/skel
Domain 4: Networking (12%)
ip, ifconfig, nmcli, /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, ping, traceroute, netstat, ss, dig, nslookup, iptables, firewalld, ufw, ssh, scp, rsync, curl, wget
Domain 5: Service Configuration (20%)
Nginx, Apache, PostgreSQL, MySQL, DNS, chronyd, timedatectl, rsyslog, journalctl, logrotate, virtual hosts, database backup/restore
Domain 6: Storage Management (13%)
fdisk, parted, gdisk, mkfs.ext4, mkfs.xfs, mount, umount, /etc/fstab, pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate, lvextend, resize2fs, mdadm, mkswap, swapon, fsck, xfs_repair
🎯 LFCS Exam Tip: The exam is performance-based — you'll be given tasks on a live system. Practice every command in this document hands-on. Don't just read — type them out. The anihpj directory skeleton gives you a realistic environment to practice in.

🔀 Redirection & Pipes

I/O redirection operators and pipes — the shell's plumbing system for connecting commands, files, and streams. These operators are fundamental to shell scripting and daily CLI productivity. Every command in this document can be combined using these operators in the anihpj/jobpost environment.

> — Redirect stdout (Overwrite)

WRITE Redirection I/O LFCS Domain 1

Redirect standard output to a file, overwriting any existing content

> is the most fundamental I/O redirection operator. It takes the stdout of a command and writes it to a file, creating the file if it doesn't exist or truncating it to zero before writing. Use set -o noclobber to prevent accidental overwrites.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, this operator is used for:

  • Capturing ls -la /lpj/k8s/base/ output to /lpj/ops/reports/k8s_snapshot.txt for audit trails
  • Writing version info with echo "v2.0" > /lpj/ops/reports/current_version.txt for CI/CD pipelines
  • Truncating logs safely with cat /dev/null > /lpj/ops/logs/app.log on production servers
  • Using set -o noclobber to protect critical report files in /lpj/ops/reports/
  • Combining command output with { ... } > /lpj/ops/reports/deployment_audit.txt

Syntax

CMD > FILE

# Common patterns:
ls -la > listing.txt          # Save directory listing to file
echo "v2.0" > version.txt     # Write a single value (overwrites)
cat /dev/null > app.log       # Truncate/empty a log file

Parameters

FlagDescription
> FILERedirect stdout to FILE (overwrite if exists)
>| FILEForce overwrite even with noclobber set
1> FILEExplicit form — redirect stdout (fd 1)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — stdout redirected and written
1Permission denied or noclobber prevented overwrite

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Redirect stdout (Overwrite)

Daily Workflow: Carol uses > to capture command output for deployment reports and audit snapshots. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical > usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls -la /lpj/ops/reports/

# Carol uses > to capture command output for deployment reports
# The anihpj team generates daily snapshots with > redirection
# All output files go to /lpj/ops/reports/ for audit trails
Example 1: Save Directory Listing

Scenario:

📄 Context — First Morning Check:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/
# Carol saves a snapshot of the k8s manifests directory
Carol wants a permanent record of what's in the k8s base directory at this moment.

Command:

ls -la /lpj/k8s/base/ > /lpj/ops/reports/k8s_snapshot.txt && head -5 /lpj/ops/reports/k8s_snapshot.txt

Output:

total 36 drwxr-xr-x 2 carol developers 4096 Jun 5 08:00 . drwxr-xr-x 6 carol developers 4096 Jun 5 08:00 .. -rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 320 Jun 5 08:00 api-deployment.yaml -rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 280 Jun 5 08:00 configmap.yaml

📝 What happened: The ls output was captured into a file instead of printing to the terminal. head -5 verified the first lines. If k8s_snapshot.txt already existed, it was truncated first. This is the standard pattern for generating deployment manifests or audit snapshots.

Example 2: Write Configuration Value

Scenario:

📄 Context — Version Tracking:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/
# Carol records the current deployment version
Carol writes the current app version to a file that the CI/CD pipeline reads.

Command:

echo "jobpost-v3.2.1-$(date +%Y%m%d)" > /lpj/ops/reports/current_version.txt && cat /lpj/ops/reports/current_version.txt

Output:

jobpost-v3.2.1-20260605

📝 What happened: A single line was written — any previous version info was overwritten. The $(date +%Y%m%d) command substitution embedded today's date. CI/CD scripts read this file to know which version is deployed.

Example 3: Truncate a Log File

Scenario:

📄 Context — Log Rotation:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log
# Carol empties a growing log without deleting it (preserves inode/permissions)
app.log has grown to 5GB and Carol needs to reset it without breaking the open file handle.

Command:

ls -lh /lpj/ops/logs/app.log && cat /dev/null > /lpj/ops/logs/app.log && ls -lh /lpj/ops/logs/app.log

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 5.2G Jun 5 08:00 /lpj/ops/logs/app.log -rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 0 Jun 5 08:01 /lpj/ops/logs/app.log

📝 What happened: The file was truncated from 5.2G to 0 bytes. Unlike rm && touch, this preserves the inode — any process with the file open continues writing to the same file. This is the safe way to empty logs on running systems.

Example 4: noclobber Protection

Scenario:

📄 Context — Safety Guard:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/
# Carol prevents accidental overwrites of important report files
Carol has an important report and wants to ensure she never accidentally overwrites it.

Command:

set -o noclobber && echo "new data" > /lpj/ops/reports/k8s_snapshot.txt 2>&1; echo "Exit: $?"

Output:

bash: /lpj/ops/reports/k8s_snapshot.txt: cannot overwrite existing file Exit: 1

📝 What happened: noclobber prevented the overwrite! The shell returned exit code 1. Use >| to force overwrite when you really mean it. set +o noclobber turns it off. Essential safety net in production environments.

Example 5: Redirect Multiple Commands

Scenario:

📄 Context — Deployment Audit:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/
# Carol creates a comprehensive deployment audit file
Carol combines output from multiple commands into a single audit report.

Command:

{ echo "=== K8s Manifests ==="; ls /lpj/k8s/base/; echo ""; echo "=== Python Version ==="; python3 --version; } > /lpj/ops/reports/deployment_audit.txt && cat /lpj/ops/reports/deployment_audit.txt

Output:

=== K8s Manifests === api-deployment.yaml configmap.yaml namespace.yaml secrets.yaml web-deployment.yaml === Python Version === Python 3.12.3

📝 What happened: A command group { ...; } combined multiple commands into a single stdout stream, all redirected to one file. The file starts with the header, lists manifests, then shows the Python version. Grouping + redirection is how deployment reports are built.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: > truncates first, then writes. Use >> to append. set -o noclobber prevents accidental overwrites (use >| to override). cat /dev/null > file safely empties a file without changing its inode — critical for log rotation on live services.

>> — Redirect stdout (Append)

APPEND Redirection I/O LFCS Domain 1

Append standard output to a file without overwriting existing content

>> appends stdout to the end of a file. If the file doesn't exist, it's created. Unlike >, existing content is preserved. This is the operator for building log files, accumulating command output, and adding to existing reports.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, this operator is used for:

  • Appending timestamped entries to /lpj/ops/logs/deploy.log for compliance audit trails
  • Building health check timelines in /lpj/ops/logs/health.log via 5-minute cron jobs
  • Merging status reports from /lpj/ops/reports/web_status.txt and api_status.txt into full report
  • Documenting project structure by appending tree output to /lpj/README.md
  • Appending to privileged files with echo ... | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts pattern

Syntax

CMD >> FILE

# Common patterns:
echo "new entry" >> log.txt        # Append a line to a log
uptime >> /lpj/ops/reports/uptime.log  # Accumulate uptime records

Parameters

FlagDescription
>> FILEAppend stdout to FILE (create if not exists)
1>> FILEExplicit form — append stdout (fd 1)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — data appended
1Permission denied or filesystem error

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Redirect stdout (Append)

Example 1: Build a Deployment Log

Scenario:

📄 Context — Deployment Trail:

📁 Directory Snippet:

└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/

# Carol appends timestamped deployment entries
Carol runs a deployment and wants to log every step with timestamps.

echo "$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') - Starting deployment v3.2" >> /lpj/ops/logs/deploy.log && echo "$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') - kubectl apply -f k8s/" >> /lpj/ops/logs/deploy.log && tail -2 /lpj/ops/logs/deploy.log

2026-06-05 08:00:00 - Starting deployment v3.2 2026-06-05 08:00:01 - kubectl apply -f k8s/

📝 What happened: Two timestamped lines were appended to deploy.log. Each echo >> adds a line without touching previous entries. Over days, this builds a complete deployment history. Eve (auditor) reviews this file for compliance.

Example 5: Append with sudo (Privileged Write)

Scenario:

📄 Context — System Config:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/
├── 📁 jobpost/

# Carol appends a DNS entry to /etc/hosts with elevated privileges
Carol needs to add a host entry but redirects don't inherit sudo.

Command:

echo "192.168.10.50  monitoring-01" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts > /dev/null && grep monitoring /etc/hosts

Output:

192.168.10.50 monitoring-01

📝 What happened: sudo echo >> /etc/hosts would fail — the >> runs as the current user, not sudo. The fix: pipe to sudo tee -a. This is the standard pattern for privileged file writes. Critical knowledge for the LFCS exam.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: >> appends (creates if missing), > overwrites. For privileged files, use echo "line" | sudo tee -a /etc/file because sudo echo >> /etc/file doesn't work — the redirection happens in the current shell, not under sudo. set -o noclobber does NOT prevent >> — it only affects >.

< — Redirect stdin

READ Redirection I/O LFCS Domain 1

Redirect a file's contents as standard input to a command

< feeds a file's contents to a command's stdin instead of the keyboard. While many commands accept filenames directly (e.g., grep pattern file), < is essential for commands that only read stdin, for loop constructs, and for controlling exactly which input stream a command receives.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, this operator is used for:

  • Getting clean line counts without filenames from /lpj/ops/logs/app.log for script variables
  • Processing /lpj/ops/deploy_manifest.txt line-by-line with while-read loops for deployment validation
  • Transforming /lpj/k8s/base/configmap.yaml content with tr for legacy API integration
  • Feeding /lpj/ops/backups/migration_v4.sql to psql for automated database migrations
  • Comparing directory listings with process substitution diff <(ls dir1) <(ls dir2)

Syntax

CMD < FILE

# Common patterns:
wc -l < /lpj/ops/logs/app.log     # Count lines — only line count, no filename
while read line; do ... done < file  # Process file line-by-line
tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' < input.txt        # Uppercase conversion from file

Parameters

FlagDescription
< FILEUse FILE contents as stdin
0< FILEExplicit form — redirect stdin (fd 0)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1File not found or permission denied

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Redirect stdin

8472 /lpj/ops/logs/app.log
carol@prod-api-01:~$ wc -l < /lpj/ops/logs/app.log
8472

carol@prod-api-01:~$ cat /lpj/ops/deploy_manifest.txt
namespace.yaml
web-deployment.yaml
api-deployment.yaml
configmap.yaml
secrets.yaml
ingress.yaml

# Essential for while-read loops in deployment scripts

Example 1: Count Lines Without Filename

Scenario:

📄 Context — Pure Numeric Output:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log
# Carol needs just the line count, not the filename
Carol wants only the number of lines in a file for a script variable — no filename in the output.

Command:

wc -l /lpj/ops/logs/app.log && echo "---" && wc -l < /lpj/ops/logs/app.log

Output:

8472 /lpj/ops/logs/app.log --- 8472

📝 What happened: With the filename argument, wc prints the count AND the filename. With <, wc only sees the count — cleaner for script variables. LINES=$(wc -l < file) captures just the number. This is the standard pattern for numeric-only output.

Example 2: Process File Line by Line

Scenario:

📄 Context — Deployment Validation:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/
# Carol validates each YAML file listed in a manifest index
Carol has a list of YAML files and needs to check each one exists before deployment.

Command:

while read file; do
  if [ -f "/lpj/k8s/base/$file" ]; then
    echo "✓ $file exists"
  else
    echo "✗ $file MISSING"
  fi
done < /lpj/ops/deploy_manifest.txt

Output:

✓ namespace.yaml exists ✓ web-deployment.yaml exists ✓ api-deployment.yaml exists ✗ ingress.yaml MISSING

📝 What happened: The while-read loop processed each line from deploy_manifest.txt via stdin redirection. Three files were confirmed, one was flagged missing. This pattern is the foundation of deployment validation scripts — read a list, check each item, report status.

Scenario:

📁 Directory Snippet:

└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml

Alice needs an uppercase version of a config file for a legacy API integration.

tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' < /lpj/k8s/base/configmap.yaml | head -3

Output:

APIVERSION: V1 KIND: CONFIGMAP METADATA:

📝 What happened: tr reads from stdin (not a filename argument), so < is required to feed it a file. All lowercase letters became uppercase. The pipe to head limits output. Without <, you would need cat file | tr ... — the redirect form avoids a useless cat process.

Dave has a SQL file with migration commands and wants to run it against prod-db-01.

Example 5: Compare Two Commands with Process Substitution

Scenario:

📄 Context — Diff Without Temp Files:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml
# Carol compares directory listings without creating temporary files
Carol wants to diff the output of ls on two servers without creating temp files.

Command:

diff <(ls /lpj/k8s/base/) <(ssh prod-web-02 "ls /lpj/k8s/base/")

Output:

4d3 < configmap.yaml 6a6 > ingress.yaml

📝 What happened: Process substitution <(cmd) makes command output look like a file — diff sees two "files" but they're actually live command output. configmap.yaml exists on web-01 but not web-02; ingress.yaml is the reverse. This is pure shell magic — no temp files needed.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: < feeds a file as stdin. Use it when: (1) the command only reads stdin (tr, while read), (2) you want output without filenames (wc -l < file), (3) process substitution <(cmd) to treat command output as a file. cmd < file is preferred over cat file | cmd — it avoids a useless cat process.

<< — Here-Document

MULTILINE Redirection I/O LFCS Domain 1

Feed a multi-line inline block of text as stdin to a command

<<DELIMITER (here-document) lets you embed multi-line text directly in a script or command line. Everything between the delimiters becomes stdin. Essential for embedding configuration files in scripts, writing SQL directly in shell, and generating multi-line output without echo chains.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, this operator is used for:

  • Generating /lpj/k8s/base/dynamic-config.yaml inline with environment-specific values in deploy scripts
  • Embedding SQL migrations directly in shell scripts for psql against prod-db-01
  • Creating /lpj/scripts/health_check.sh with quoted delimiter to preserve literal $variables
  • Running multi-command remote sessions on prod-web-02 via ssh host << REMOTE pattern
  • Using here-strings <<< for quick single-line processing without echo+pipe overhead

Syntax

CMD << DELIMITER
line 1
line 2
...
DELIMITER

# Common patterns:
cat << EOF > config.yaml     # Write inline config to file
mysql -u root << SQL           # Run inline SQL statements
ssh host << 'EOF'              # Quote delimiter disables variable expansion

Parameters

FlagDescription
<< EOFHere-doc with EOF delimiter (variables expanded)
<< 'EOF'Quoted delimiter — no variable/command expansion
<<- EOFStrip leading tabs from content (not spaces)
<<< STRINGHere-string — feed a single line as stdin

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Command receiving stdin failed

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Here-Document

Daily Workflow: Carol and Alice use here-documents to embed multi-line configs, SQL, and scripts inline. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls /lpj/k8s/base/dynamic-config.yaml
/lpj/k8s/base/dynamic-config.yaml

carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls /lpj/scripts/health_check.sh

alice@dev-01:~$ psql -U anihpj -d jobpost << SQL
SELECT * FROM deployment_log;
 id | version |        deployed_at
----+---------+----------------------------
  1 | v3.2.1  | 2026-06-05 08:00:00
# Key locations where << is used daily:
#  /lpj/k8s/base/dynamic-config.yaml
#  /lpj/ops/
#  /lpj/scripts/health_check.sh

Example 1: Generate a YAML Config Inline

Carol's deploy script needs to create a new configmap with environment-specific values.

Scenario:

Dave writes a migration script that creates a table and inserts seed data.

Example 3: Suppress Variable Expansion

Scenario:

📄 Context — Template Generation:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh
    ├── 📄 connectivity-test.sh
    └── 📄 deploy.sh
# Alice writes a script template with literal $variables that must not expand
Alice generates a script that itself contains shell variables — they must stay as literal $VAR, not be expanded now.

Command:

cat << 'SCRIPT' > /lpj/scripts/health_check.sh
#!/bin/bash
# Auto-generated health check — DO NOT EDIT
SERVER=${1:-localhost}
PORT=${2:-8000}
curl -s "http://$SERVER:$PORT/health/" || echo "Health check FAILED for $SERVER:$PORT"
SCRIPT
cat /lpj/scripts/health_check.sh

Output:

#!/bin/bash # Auto-generated health check — DO NOT EDIT SERVER=${1:-localhost} PORT=${2:-8000} curl -s "http://$SERVER:$PORT/health/" || echo "Health check FAILED for $SERVER:$PORT"

📝 What happened: Because the delimiter 'SCRIPT' was quoted, all $SERVER, $PORT variables stayed literal. If SCRIPT were unquoted, they would have expanded to empty strings (or whatever values existed in the current shell). Quoted delimiters are essential for generating scripts and templates.

Scenario:

📄 Context — Remote Execution:

📁 Directory Snippet:

├── 📁 anihpj/

echo "=== Disk Usage ==="

Example 5: Here-String for Single-Line Input

Scenario:

📄 Context — Quick Processing:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/
├── 📁 jobpost/
├── 📁 api/
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml

├── 📁 k8s/
├── 📁 ops/
└── 📁 scripts/
# Carol uses here-strings for quick single-line processing
Carol wants to quickly count words in a string without echo and pipe.

Command:

wc -w <<< "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" && echo "---" && tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' <<< "hello world"

Output:

9 --- HELLO WORLD

📝 What happened: <<< (here-string) feeds a single string as stdin. It's shorthand for echo "string" | cmd. The first counted 9 words; the second uppercased "hello world". Here-strings are cleaner than echo+pipe for single-line input — no subshell overhead.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: <<EOF expands variables and commands inside the heredoc. <<'EOF' (quoted delimiter) treats everything literally — essential for generating scripts and templates. <<-EOF strips leading tabs. <<< "string" is a here-string for single-line stdin. The delimiter word must appear alone on its own line to end the heredoc.

| — Pipe

CHAIN Redirection I/O LFCS Domain 1

Connect stdout of one command to stdin of another — the foundation of shell composition

| (pipe) is the most powerful operator in Unix/Linux. It chains commands together by connecting the stdout of the left command to the stdin of the right command. Pipes enable the Unix philosophy: small, focused tools that combine to solve complex problems. The anihpj team builds entire deployment pipelines from pipes.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, this operator is used for:

  • Chaining grep | awk | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head to find top error sources in app.log
  • Extracting PIDs with ps aux | grep [g]unicorn | awk for process management
  • Calculating total YAML file sizes with find | stat | awk pipeline for storage monitoring
  • Live monitoring with tail -f | grep --line-buffered during database migrations
  • Using set -o pipefail in deployment scripts for correct exit code propagation

Syntax

CMD1 | CMD2 | CMD3 ...

# Common patterns:
cat app.log | grep ERROR | wc -l       # Count errors
ps aux | grep nginx | awk '{print $2}'  # Get Nginx PID
find /lpj -name "*.yaml" | xargs grep "version"  # Search all YAML files

Parameters

FlagDescription
|Connect stdout (fd 1) of CMD1 to stdin (fd 0) of CMD2
|&Pipe both stdout AND stderr (bash 4+)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
$?Exit code of the LAST command in the pipe (by default)
set -o pipefailExit code is first non-zero in pipe (recommended)

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Pipe

Daily Workflow: Carol builds complex queries by piping simple commands together — the Unix philosophy in action. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical | usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ grep ERROR /lpj/ops/logs/app.log | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
    127 jobpost.views
     89 api.views
     34 celery.tasks

carol@prod-api-01:~$ ps aux | grep "[g]unicorn.*master"
anihpj   12845  0.5  2.3 456780 92340 ?  Ss   Jun04  12:34 gunicorn: master [jobpost]

carol@prod-api-01:~$ find /lpj/k8s/ -name "*.yaml" | wc -l
15
# Key locations where | is used daily:
#  /lpj/ops/
#  /lpj/ops/
#  /lpj/ops/

📄 Context — Command Composition:

# Carol builds complex queries by piping simple commands together
# The anihpj deployment pipeline chains grep, sort, wc, and awk
# Every log investigation starts with cat | grep | sort | uniq -c
Example 1: Find Top Error Sources

Scenario:

📄 Context — Log Analysis:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log
# Carol investigates which components generate the most errors
Carol wants to know which application component has the most ERROR entries in the log.

Command:

grep ERROR /lpj/ops/logs/app.log | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

Output:

127 jobpost.views 89 api.views 34 celery.tasks

📝 What happened: A 6-command pipe chain: grep filtered ERROR lines → awk extracted the component name (5th field) → sort prepared for counting → uniq -c counted occurrences → sort -rn sorted by count descending → head -3 showed top 3. jobpost.views has 127 errors — needs attention. Each command does one thing; together they answer a complex question.

Example 2: Get Process ID by Name

Scenario:

📄 Context — Process Management:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/
├── 📁 jobpost/
├── 📁 api/
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml
├── 📄 requirements.txt
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/
├── 📁 ops/
└── 📁 scripts/
# Carol finds the PID of the Django gunicorn process
Carol needs the PID of the gunicorn master process to send a reload signal.

Command:

ps aux | grep "[g]unicorn.*master" | awk '{print $2}'

Output:

12845

📝 What happened: ps listed all processes → grep filtered for gunicorn master (the [g] trick prevents grep from matching itself) → awk extracted PID (column 2). The result is a clean PID ready for kill -HUP 12845. This pipe chain is one of the most common patterns in system administration.

Example 3: Calculate Total Disk Usage

Scenario:

📄 Context — Storage Monitoring:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
    ├── 📁 base/
    ├── 📁 cilium/
    ├── 📁 ingress/
    └── 📁 monitoring/
# Carol calculates total disk usage of all YAML files
Carol wants to know the total size of all YAML files in the k8s directory.

Command:

find /lpj/k8s/ -name "*.yaml" -exec stat -c "%s" {} \; | awk '{sum+=$1} END {printf "Total: %d bytes (%.1f KB)
", sum, sum/1024}'

Output:

Total: 28470 bytes (27.8 KB)

📝 What happened: find located all .yaml files → stat extracted each file's size in bytes → awk accumulated the sum and formatted the output. The pipe converted a list of sizes into a single total. Without the pipe, you would need a loop and manual addition.

Example 4: Monitor Real-Time Logs

Scenario:

📄 Context — Live Monitoring:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log
# Carol watches for database errors in real time during a migration
During a database migration, Carol wants to see only connection errors as they happen.

Command:

tail -f /lpj/ops/logs/app.log | grep --line-buffered "database" | grep -i "error\|timeout\|refused"

Output:

Jun 5 08:00:05 prod-api-01 jobpost[12845]: database connection timeout after 30s Jun 5 08:00:12 prod-api-01 jobpost[12845]: database error: too many connections

📝 What happened: tail -f streams new log lines → first grep filters for "database" → second grep filters for error keywords. --line-buffered ensures grep outputs immediately instead of buffering. This live pipe is how operators watch for specific issues during deployments — the output scrolls in real time as events occur.

Example 5: pipefail for Correct Exit Codes

Scenario:

📄 Context — Script Reliability:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log
# Carol ensures her deployment script catches failures in any pipe stage
Carol's deployment script has a pipe, and she needs the script to fail if any part of the pipe fails.

Command:

set -o pipefail
grep "DEPLOY_SUCCESS" /lpj/ops/logs/deploy.log | wc -l
echo "Exit code: $?"
set +o pipefail

Output:

1 Exit code: 1

📝 What happened: Without pipefail, the pipe would return 0 (wc -l succeeded even though grep found nothing). With pipefail, it returns 1 because grep failed. This is critical in scripts — without pipefail, grep pattern file | wc -l silently succeeds even if the file doesn't exist.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: Pipes connect stdout to stdin. Always use set -o pipefail in scripts — without it, only the last command's exit code is checked. grep pattern file | wc -l returns 0 even if file doesn't exist, because wc succeeds (counting 0). The [g]rep trick in ps | grep [p]attern prevents grep from matching its own process line.

2> — Redirect stderr

ERROR Redirection I/O LFCS Domain 1

Redirect standard error (file descriptor 2) to a file, separating errors from normal output

2> captures stderr separately from stdout. Every process has three default file descriptors: 0 (stdin), 1 (stdout), 2 (stderr). By default, both stdout and stderr go to the terminal. 2> lets you capture errors to a file while normal output continues to the terminal — or vice versa.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, this operator is used for:

  • Suppressing permission errors with find / -name "*.yaml" 2> /dev/null for clean system-wide searches
  • Capturing Django test failures to /lpj/ops/logs/test_errors.log for CI/CD pipeline analysis
  • Merging stderr into stdout with 2>&1 for complete deployment logs in /lpj/ops/logs/full_deploy.log
  • Silent cron health checks with curl ... > /dev/null 2>&1 — only checking exit code
  • Separating stdout and stderr to check_ok.log and check_err.log for parallel analysis

Syntax

CMD 2> ERROR_FILE

# Common patterns:
find / -name "*.log" 2> /dev/null          # Hide permission errors
python3 manage.py test 2> test_errors.log  # Capture only test errors
tar -czf backup.tar.gz /data 2> tar.log    # Log tar warnings separately

Parameters

FlagDescription
2> FILERedirect stderr to FILE (overwrite)
2>> FILEAppend stderr to FILE
2> /dev/nullDiscard stderr entirely
2>&1Merge stderr into stdout (redirect fd 2 to fd 1)
1>&2Merge stdout into stderr

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Permission denied or write error

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Redirect stderr

Daily Workflow: Carol separates error output from normal output during builds, tests, and system searches. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical 2> usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ find / -name "*.yaml" 2>/dev/null | head -5
/lpj/k8s/base/api-deployment.yaml
/lpj/k8s/base/configmap.yaml
/lpj/k8s/base/namespace.yaml
/lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml
/lpj/k8s/base/web-deployment.yaml

carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls -la /lpj/ops/logs/test_errors.log /lpj/ops/logs/full_deploy.log /lpj/ops/logs/check_ok.log /lpj/ops/logs/check_err.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers    0 Jun  5 08:00 /lpj/ops/logs/check_err.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers  345 Jun  5 08:00 /lpj/ops/logs/check_ok.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 2150 Jun  5 08:01 /lpj/ops/logs/full_deploy.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers    0 Jun  5 08:00 /lpj/ops/logs/test_errors.log
# Key locations where 2> is used daily:
#  /lpj/ops/
#  /lpj/ops/logs/test_errors.log
#  /lpj/ops/logs/full_deploy.log

📄 Context — Error Isolation:

# Carol separates errors from normal output during deployment scripts
# The CI/CD pipeline captures stderr to alert on failures
# Error logs go to /lpj/ops/logs/ for post-mortem analysis
Example 1: Hide Permission Denied Errors

Scenario:

📄 Context — Clean Output:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml
# Carol suppresses permission errors when searching the entire filesystem
Carol searches for all .yaml files system-wide but doesn't want permission errors cluttering the output.

Command:

find / -name "*.yaml" 2> /dev/null | head -5

Output:

/lpj/k8s/base/api-deployment.yaml /lpj/k8s/base/configmap.yaml /lpj/k8s/base/namespace.yaml /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml /lpj/k8s/base/web-deployment.yaml

📝 What happened: Only the actual YAML file paths were shown — all the "Permission denied" errors for /root, /etc/ssl, and other restricted directories were sent to /dev/null (discarded). Without 2> /dev/null, the output would be 90% error messages and nearly unreadable.

Example 2: Capture Test Failures Separately

Scenario:

📄 Context — CI/CD Pipeline:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log
# Alice runs Django tests and captures errors for the CI dashboard
Alice runs the test suite and wants stdout (test progress) on screen but stderr (failures) saved to a file.

Command:

cd /lpj && python3 manage.py test 2> /lpj/ops/logs/test_errors.log && echo "--- Errors captured ---" && cat /lpj/ops/logs/test_errors.log

Output:

Creating test database... ................ Ran 16 tests in 2.3s OK --- Errors captured ---

📝 What happened: The test progress (stdout) displayed on screen while any stderr output went to test_errors.log. Since all tests passed, the error file is empty. If tests fail, the CI pipeline reads test_errors.log for the failure details without parsing through the progress output.

Example 3: Merge stderr into stdout

Scenario:

📄 Context — Combined Logging:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log
# Carol wants both stdout and stderr in the same log file for complete context
Carol runs a deployment script and wants ALL output (both normal and errors) in one log file.

Command:

bash /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh > /lpj/ops/logs/full_deploy.log 2>&1 && tail -5 /lpj/ops/logs/full_deploy.log

Output:

Applying k8s/base/namespace.yaml... Applying k8s/base/configmap.yaml... Applying k8s/base/secrets.yaml... Deployment complete: 9 resources applied Warning: secret "api-key" already exists, skipping

📝 What happened: 2>&1 merged stderr into stdout, then > captured the combined stream to a file. The log now shows both normal messages AND the warning about the pre-existing secret — complete context for debugging. Order matters: 2>&1 > file does NOT work — the redirects are processed left to right.

Example 4: Discard All Output

Scenario:

📄 Context — Silent Operation:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/
├── 📁 jobpost/
├── 📁 api/
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml
├── 📄 requirements.txt
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/
├── 📁 ops/
└── 📁 scripts/
# Carol runs a command where she only cares about the exit code
Carol's cron job runs a curl health check — she only needs the exit code, not the output.

Command:

curl -s http://prod-api-01:8000/health/ > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo "API is UP" || echo "API is DOWN"

Output:

API is UP

📝 What happened: Both stdout and stderr from curl were discarded to /dev/null. The && / || chain checked only the exit code. This is the standard pattern for health checks in cron — silent on success, alert on failure. No log clutter when everything is working.

Example 5: Separate stdout and stderr to Different Files

Scenario:

📄 Context — Parallel Logging:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log
# Carol sends normal output and errors to separate files for analysis
Carol runs a build and wants success messages in one file and errors in another.

Command:

(python3 /lpj/manage.py check --deploy > /lpj/ops/logs/check_ok.log) 2> /lpj/ops/logs/check_err.log && echo "OK log:" && cat /lpj/ops/logs/check_ok.log && echo "ERR log:" && cat /lpj/ops/logs/check_err.log

Output:

OK log: System check identified no issues (0 silenced). ERR log:

📝 What happened: Stdout went to check_ok.log, stderr to check_err.log. The subshell (...) was needed so the stdout redirect only applied to the command, not the entire line. Django found no issues — the error file is empty. This pattern lets you monitor successes and failures independently.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: File descriptors: 0=stdin, 1=stdout, 2=stderr. 2> file redirects stderr, 2>&1 merges stderr into stdout. Order matters: cmd 2>&1 > file sends stderr to the ORIGINAL stdout (terminal) then stdout to file — not what you want. Use cmd > file 2>&1 for combined capture. 2> /dev/null discards errors silently.

&> — Redirect stdout + stderr

COMBINE Redirection I/O LFCS Domain 1

Redirect both standard output and standard error to a file in one operator

&> is a bash shorthand that captures both stdout and stderr to the same file. It's equivalent to > file 2>&1 but shorter and clearer. Use it when you want a complete record of everything a command produced — both normal output and errors.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, this operator is used for:

  • Capturing complete deployment output with bash deploy.sh &> /lpj/ops/logs/deploy_$(date).log for audit
  • Running silent cron jobs with cleanup.sh &> /dev/null — no cron mail spam
  • Benchmarking database migrations with time python3 manage.py migrate &> /lpj/ops/logs/migrate_timing.log
  • Appending cumulative health checks with &>> /lpj/ops/logs/health_full.log for complete history
  • Understanding &> vs > file 2>&1 — bash shorthand vs POSIX compatibility

Syntax

CMD &> FILE

# Common patterns:
./deploy.sh &> deploy_full.log           # Capture everything
python3 script.py &> /dev/null           # Run silently
time tar -czf backup.tar.gz /lpj &> timing.log  # Time + all output

Parameters

FlagDescription
&> FILERedirect stdout AND stderr to FILE (bash shorthand)
>& FILEAlternate form (also works in bash)
&>> FILEAppend both stdout and stderr to FILE

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Write error or permission denied

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Redirect stdout + stderr

Daily Workflow: Carol uses &> to capture complete command output — both normal and error streams together. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

Example 5: Compare with Separate Redirects

Scenario:

📄 Context — Teaching Moment:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/
├── 📁 jobpost/
├── 📁 api/
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml
├── 📄 requirements.txt
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/
├── 📁 ops/
└── 📁 scripts/
# Carol demonstrates the difference between &> and separate redirects
Alice (junior dev) needs to understand when to use &> vs separate redirects.

Command:

echo "With &>:" && (echo "normal output" && echo "error output" >&2) &> /tmp/test_and.txt && cat /tmp/test_and.txt && echo "Without &>:" && (echo "normal output" && echo "error output" >&2) > /tmp/test_no.txt && cat /tmp/test_no.txt

Output:

With &>: normal output error output Without &>: normal output error output

📝 What happened: With &>, both lines were captured in the file. Without &>, only stdout was captured — "error output" appeared on the terminal instead (>&2 sent it to stderr). This demonstrates that > alone only captures stdout, while &> captures everything.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: &> file is bash-specific shorthand for > file 2>&1. For POSIX compatibility (exam scripts), use the longer form. &>> file appends both streams. Use &> when you need a complete record — stdout and stderr together. Use separate redirects (> out 2> err) when you need to process normal output and errors independently.

tee — Write to File and stdout

SPLIT Redirection I/O LFCS Domain 1

Read from stdin and write to both stdout and one or more files simultaneously

tee splits the data stream — like a plumbing T-junction. Input from stdin is copied to stdout (so the pipe continues) AND written to file(s). It's essential when you need to both see output and save it, or when you need to write to a privileged file while preserving the pipe.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, this operator is used for:

  • Watching deployment live while saving to /lpj/ops/logs/deploy_TIMESTAMP.log with 2>&1 | tee
  • Writing to privileged files with echo "line" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts — the exam-critical sudo+tee pattern
  • Teeing status reports to both /lpj/ops/reports/status.txt and /mnt/backup-nas/reports/status.txt
  • Live log monitoring with tail -f | tee full.log | grep ERROR for simultaneous archive and alerting
  • Building timestamped monitoring logs with tee -a /lpj/ops/logs/health_tee.log from cron jobs

Syntax

CMD | tee [OPTIONS] FILE...

# Common patterns:
./deploy.sh | tee deploy.log                    # See output AND save it
echo "line" | sudo tee -a /etc/config          # Write to privileged file
cmd | tee file1 file2                           # Write to multiple files
cmd | tee >(grep ERROR > errors.log)            # Tee into process substitution

Parameters

FlagDescription
-a, --appendAppend to file(s) instead of overwriting
-i, --ignore-interruptsIgnore interrupt signals (Ctrl+C)
-pDiagnose errors writing to non-pipe outputs

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — data written to all outputs
1Write error to one or more files

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Write to File and stdout

Daily Workflow: Carol uses tee to watch deployment output while saving it — the split-stream operator. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical tee usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls -la /lpj/ops/logs/deploy_0830.log

carol@prod-api-01:~$ grep monitoring /etc/hosts

Example 1: Watch and Save Deployment

Scenario:

📄 Context — Live + Archived:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log
# Carol wants to see deployment progress AND save it for audit
Carol runs a deployment and wants to watch the output in real time while also saving it to a log file.

Command:

bash /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh 2>&1 | tee /lpj/ops/logs/deploy_$(date +%H%M).log

Output:

Applying k8s/base/namespace.yaml... Applying k8s/base/configmap.yaml... Applying k8s/base/secrets.yaml... Applying k8s/base/web-deployment.yaml... Deployment complete: 4 resources applied

📝 What happened: The deployment output appeared on Carol's terminal AND was simultaneously written to a timestamped log file. 2>&1 first merged stderr into stdout, then tee split it. Without tee, Carol would have to choose: see it OR save it. With tee, she gets both.

Example 2: Write to Privileged File

Scenario:

📄 Context — System Config:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/
├── 📁 jobpost/
├── 📁 api/
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml

├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/
├── 📁 ops/
└── 📁 scripts/
# Carol adds a line to /etc/hosts — redirection runs as user, tee runs as root
Carol needs to append a host entry to /etc/hosts, which requires sudo.

Command:

echo "192.168.10.50  monitoring-01  # Prometheus+Grafana" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts > /dev/null && grep monitoring /etc/hosts

Output:

192.168.10.50 monitoring-01 # Prometheus+Grafana

📝 What happened: echo | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts is the standard pattern for writing to privileged files. The echo runs as carol, the pipe runs as carol, but tee runs as root via sudo — so it can write to /etc/hosts. > /dev/null suppressed tee's stdout since we only needed the file write. This is the exam-critical sudo+tee pattern.

Example 3: Tee to Multiple Files

Carol generates a status report and wants it saved locally AND copied to the backup NAS.

Output:

Report saved to 2 locations

📝 What happened: tee wrote the same report to two files simultaneously — local and network storage. The terminal output was suppressed with > /dev/null since we only needed the file copies. tee can write to any number of files — they all get identical copies of stdin.

Scenario:

Carol wants to save all logs to a file while simultaneously scanning for ERROR lines to display.

tail -f /lpj/ops/logs/app.log | tee /lpj/ops/logs/app_full.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR" &

Output:

[1] 29451 ERROR 2026-06-05 08:00:05 database connection timeout ERROR 2026-06-05 08:00:12 too many connections

Example 5: Append with Timestamps

Scenario:

📄 Context — Timestamped Monitoring:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log
# Carol builds a timestamped monitoring log from periodic checks
A cron job runs every 5 minutes and appends timestamped output to a log while also displaying it.

Command:

{ echo "=== $(date) ==="; curl -s http://prod-api-01:8000/health/; echo ""; } | tee -a /lpj/ops/logs/health_tee.log

Output:

=== Thu Jun 5 08:00:00 UTC 2026 === {"status":"healthy","database":"connected"}

📝 What happened: tee -a appended the timestamped health check to the log AND displayed it. Each cron run adds a new entry. The -a flag is critical — without it, each run would overwrite the previous check. Over days, this builds a complete health timeline.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: tee is the ONLY way to write to a privileged file from a pipe: echo "data" | sudo tee /etc/file. The -a flag appends (like >>). tee /dev/null just passes through stdin — useful for sudo elevation. cmd 2>&1 | tee log captures both stdout and stderr. tee is named after the T-splitter in plumbing — one input, two outputs.

&& — Logical AND (Conditional Chain)

CONDITION Redirection Control Flow LFCS Domain 1

Run the next command only if the previous command succeeds (exit code 0)

&& creates a conditional chain: CMD2 runs only if CMD1 exits with status 0 (success). It's the shell's logical AND operator. Use it to sequence dependent operations — don't deploy if the build fails, don't restart if the config check fails. Essential for safe automation.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, this operator is used for:

  • Chaining kubectl dry-run && python3 test && kubectl apply — three-stage deployment pipeline
  • Ensuring backup directory exists before copying: mkdir -p /lpj/ops/backups/$(date) && cp
  • Validating Nginx config before restart: nginx -t && systemctl restart nginx — the gold standard
  • Pre-flight infrastructure check: ping web-01 && ping api-01 && ping db-01 before deployment
  • Smart git automation: only commit if there are staged changes using git diff --cached --quiet || { ... }

Syntax

CMD1 && CMD2 && CMD3 ...

# Common patterns:
./build.sh && ./deploy.sh                    # Only deploy if build succeeds
mkdir -p /lpj/backups && cp file /lpj/backups/  # Only copy if dir exists
cd /lpj && python3 manage.py test            # Only test if cd succeeds

Parameters

FlagDescription
&&Run CMD2 only if CMD1 exits with code 0
CMD1 && CMD2 && CMD3Chain — stops at first failure

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0All commands in chain succeeded
NExit code of first failing command in chain

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Logical AND (Conditional Chain)

Daily Workflow: Carol chains operations with && — each step a safety gate before the next. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical && usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-web-01:~$ kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f /lpj/k8s/base/ && echo "DRY-RUN OK" || echo "DRY-RUN FAILED"
configmap/jobpost-config created (dry run)
namespace/production created (dry run)
DRY-RUN OK

carol@prod-web-01:~$ nginx -t && systemctl restart nginx && echo "RESTART OK"
nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf syntax is ok
RESTART OK

alice@dev-01:~$ cd /lpj && git add -A && git diff --cached --quiet || { git commit -m "Auto" && git push; }
# Key locations where && is used daily:
#  /lpj/ops/
#  /lpj/ops/backups/$(date) && cp
#  /lpj/ops/

📄 Context — Safe Deployment Chains:

# Carol uses && to create safe, sequential deployment pipelines
# Each step must succeed before the next runs
# The anihpj CI/CD pipeline is built on && chains
Example 1: Safe Deployment Pipeline

Scenario:

📄 Context — Production Deploy:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/
├── 📁 jobpost/
├── 📁 api/
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml
├── 📄 requirements.txt
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/
├── 📁 ops/
└── 📁 scripts/
# Carol chains build, test, and deploy — any failure stops the process
Carol runs a three-stage deployment: validate configs → run tests → apply to Kubernetes.

Command:

kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f /lpj/k8s/base/ && python3 /lpj/manage.py test && kubectl apply -f /lpj/k8s/base/ && echo "✅ Deployment successful"

Output:

configmap/jobpost-config created (dry run) namespace/production created (dry run) Creating test database... ................ Ran 16 tests in 2.3s OK configmap/jobpost-config unchanged namespace/production unchanged ✅ Deployment successful

📝 What happened: Four commands ran in sequence: dry-run validated the YAML → tests passed → actual apply to K8s → success message. If dry-run had failed (invalid YAML), tests and apply would have been skipped entirely. Each && is a safety gate — no step runs unless the previous one succeeded.

Carol wants to copy deployment logs to a backup directory, but only if the directory can be created/accessed.

Output:

Backup: OK

📝 What happened: mkdir -p created the monthly backup directory (or confirmed it exists) → cp copied the log with a daily suffix → echo confirmed success. If the disk were full, mkdir would succeed but cp would fail — the || echo "Backup: FAILED" at the end catches any failure in the chain.

Carol edited the Nginx config and must validate it before restarting the service.

Command:

Output:

nginx: the configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf syntax is ok nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf test is successful Nginx restarted successfully

📝 What happened: nginx -t tested the config syntax → exit 0 meant valid → systemctl restart ran. If the config had an error, nginx -t would exit non-zero and systemctl restart would be SKIPPED — preventing an outage. This && pattern is the gold standard for service restarts.

Carol's pre-deployment checklist verifies connectivity to all 6 production servers.

Command:

ping -c 1 -W 2 prod-web-01 && ping -c 1 -W 2 prod-api-01 && ping -c 1 -W 2 prod-db-01 && echo "✅ All servers reachable" || echo "❌ One or more servers unreachable"

Output:

PING prod-web-01 (192.168.10.10) 56(84) bytes of data. 64 bytes from prod-web-01: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 PING prod-api-01 (192.168.10.20) 56(84) bytes of data. 64 bytes from prod-api-01: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 PING prod-db-01 (192.168.10.30) 56(84) bytes of data. 64 bytes from prod-db-01: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 ✅ All servers reachable

📝 What happened: Three ping commands ran sequentially. Each ping must succeed (exit 0) for the next to run. If prod-db-01 were down, the chain would stop at the second ping — prod-db-01 wouldn't even be pinged, and the failure message would display. This is a pre-flight check pattern.

Example 5: Git Workflow Automation

Scenario:

📄 Context — Development Workflow:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/
├── 📁 jobpost/
├── 📁 api/
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml
├── 📄 requirements.txt
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/
├── 📁 ops/
└── 📁 scripts/
# Alice automates her git workflow with conditional chaining
Alice wants to add all changes, commit, and push — but only if there are actual changes to commit.

Command:

cd /lpj && git add -A && git diff --cached --quiet || { git commit -m "Auto-commit: $(date)" && git push origin main && echo "✅ Pushed"; }

Output:

[main a1b2c3d] Auto-commit: Thu Jun 5 08:00:00 UTC 2026 3 files changed, 45 insertions(+) ✅ Pushed

📝 What happened: git add staged everything → git diff --cached --quiet checked if there are staged changes (exit 0 = no changes, exit 1 = changes). The || after --quiet means: if NO changes (exit 0), skip the commit block. If changes exist (exit 1), run the commit+push. This prevents empty commits — a clever use of exit codes.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: && runs the next command ONLY if the previous succeeds (exit 0). It stops at the first failure — perfect for deployment pipelines. Common pattern: cmd1 && cmd2 && cmd3 || handle_error. The || catches failure from ANY command in the chain. For services: always configtest && restart — never restart with a broken config.

|| — Logical OR (Fallback Chain)

FALLBACK Redirection Control Flow LFCS Domain 1

Run the next command only if the previous command fails (exit code non-zero)

|| creates a fallback chain: CMD2 runs only if CMD1 fails (exits non-zero). It's the shell's logical OR operator. Use it for error handling, providing default values, attempting alternative approaches, and creating robust scripts that handle failure gracefully.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, this operator is used for:

  • Logging deployment failures with kubectl apply || { echo "FAILED" | tee -a errors.log; exit 1; }
  • Trying multiple package managers: apt install tree || dnf install tree || pacman -S tree
  • Providing default values: DEPLOY_ENV=$(cat file) || DEPLOY_ENV="production" — the classic pattern
  • Pass/fail reporting in CI/CD: python3 test && echo "PASSED" || echo "FAILED"
  • Retry pattern with for loop: for i in 1 2 3; do cmd && break || sleep 2; done for flaky operations

Syntax

CMD1 || CMD2

# Common patterns:
ping -c 1 host || echo "Host unreachable"     # Error message on failure
mkdir dir || exit 1                            # Exit script if mkdir fails
cmd1 || cmd2 || cmd3                           # Try commands until one succeeds

Parameters

FlagDescription
||Run CMD2 only if CMD1 exits with non-zero code
CMD1 || CMD2 || CMD3Chain — runs until one succeeds

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0At least one command in chain succeeded
NExit code of last command (all failed)

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Logical OR (Fallback Chain)

Daily Workflow: Carol uses || for error handling, fallbacks, and graceful failure recovery in scripts. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical || usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-web-01:~$ kubectl apply -f /lpj/k8s/base/ || echo "DEPLOY FAILED at $(date)" >> /lpj/ops/logs/deploy_errors.log

alice@dev-01:~$ DEPLOY_ENV=$(cat /lpj/ops/deploy_env.txt 2>/dev/null) || DEPLOY_ENV="production" && echo "Deploying to: $DEPLOY_ENV"
Deploying to: production

jenkins@ci-runner-01:~$ python3 /lpj/manage.py test && echo "✅ TESTS PASSED" || echo "❌ TESTS FAILED"
✅ TESTS PASSED
# Key locations where || is used daily:
#  /lpj/ops/
#  /lpj/ops/
#  /lpj/ops/

📄 Context — Error Recovery:

# Carol uses || for error handling and fallback logic in scripts
# The anihpj deployment scripts have || fallbacks at every critical step
# Combined with &&, this creates robust, self-healing automation
Example 1: Error Notification on Failure

Scenario:

📄 Context — Deployment Alert:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log

Carol runs a critical deployment and wants immediate notification if it fails.

kubectl apply -f /lpj/k8s/base/ || { echo "❌ DEPLOY FAILED at $(date)" | tee -a /lpj/ops/logs/deploy_errors.log; exit 1; }

❌ DEPLOY FAILED at Thu Jun 5 08:00:00 UTC 2026

📝 What happened: kubectl apply failed → the || triggered the error block → a timestamped error was logged AND displayed via tee → the script exited with code 1. The { ... } group ran multiple commands as the fallback: log the error, then exit. Without the group, only echo would run as the fallback.

Scenario:

Alice writes a setup script that should work on any Linux distribution.

Reading package lists... Done Building dependency tree... Done tree is already the newest version (2.1.0-1).

📝 What happened: The chain checks for apt → if found, install with apt. If apt fails or doesn't exist, try dnf → then pacman → then give up. This is a portable installation pattern. Note the combination of && (check then install) nested within || (try alternative).

Example 5: Retry Pattern with ||

Scenario:

📄 Context — Resilient Operations:

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/
├── 📁 jobpost/
├── 📁 api/
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml
├── 📄 requirements.txt
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/
├── 📁 ops/
└── 📁 scripts/
# Carol retries a flaky network operation up to 3 times
Carol's script pulls a Docker image from a sometimes-flaky registry — she wants to retry on failure.

Command:

for i in 1 2 3; do docker pull registry.anihpj.io/jobpost:latest && break || echo "Attempt $i failed, retrying..."; sleep 2; done && echo "✅ Image pulled" || echo "❌ All attempts failed"

Output:

Attempt 1 failed, retrying... latest: Pulling from jobpost Digest: sha256:abc123... ✅ Image pulled

📝 What happened: Loop tried docker pull → first attempt failed (|| triggered retry message) → sleep 2 → second attempt succeeded → && break exited the loop → final success message. The && break exits on success; || echo handles each failure. After the loop, &&/|| reports overall result.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: || is the error handler: CMD2 runs only if CMD1 fails. cmd1 && cmd2 || cmd3 is the most common shell conditional — if cmd1 succeeds, run cmd2; otherwise run cmd3. Caveat: if cmd2 itself fails, cmd3 also runs! For complex logic, use if/then/else instead. command || DEFAULT is the standard default-value pattern.

📂 File System Navigation

Commands for browsing directories, locating files, and understanding the filesystem layout. These are the most-used commands in daily Linux work for the anihpj environment.

ls

LIST Navigation Core LFCS Domain 1

List directory contents — the most frequently used command in any Linux session

The ls command lists files and directories, displaying names, permissions, ownership, sizes, and timestamps. It's the first command every Linux user learns and the one used most often — dozens of times daily in any sysadmin workflow.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, ls is essential for:

  • Checking what's deployed in /lpj/ before running scripts
  • Verifying log files exist in /lpj/jobpost/
  • Inspecting Kubernetes manifests in /lpj/k8s/
  • Checking permissions on K8s secrets and configmaps in /lpj/k8s/base/
  • Listing Dockerfiles before building images

Syntax

ls [OPTIONS]... [FILE]...

# Common patterns:
ls                    # List current directory
ls -la                # Long format with hidden files
ls -ltr               # Long format, sorted by time, reversed (newest last)
ls -lh                # Human-readable sizes
ls -d */              # List only directories

Parameters

FlagDescription
-a, --allShow all entries including hidden files (starting with .)
-lLong listing format — permissions, owner, size, date, filename
-h, --human-readablePrint sizes in human readable format (1K, 234M, 2G)
-tSort by modification time, newest first
-r, --reverseReverse order while sorting
-R, --recursiveList subdirectories recursively
-SSort by file size, largest first
-i, --inodePrint the index number (inode) of each file
-d, --directoryList directories themselves, not their contents
-1List one file per line
--color[=WHEN]Colorize output: always, never, auto
-F, --classifyAppend indicator: /=dir, *=exec, @=symlink, |=fifo
-ZPrint SELinux security context of each file

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — directory contents listed
2Error — file or directory not found, or permission denied

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Directory Exploration

Daily Workflow: Carol (DevOps lead) uses ls dozens of times daily while managing the anihpj deployment. Here's the real directory layout she works with on prod-api-01.

carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls -la /lpj/
total 48

Command:

ls -R /lpj/api/ | grep "\.py$"

Output:

📝 What happened: Four Python files in the API app. The recursive search (-R) found them inside /lpj/api/, and grep filtered for .py files only. This confirms the API app has the expected structure.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: Know ls -l output cold — you'll need to interpret permissions strings like -rwxr-xr--, identify file types from the first character (-=file, d=dir, l=symlink), and understand the permission triplet (owner-group-others). The LFCS exam frequently tests permission interpretation.

cd

NAVIGATE Navigation Shell Builtin LFCS Domain 1

Change directory — navigate the filesystem tree

cd is a shell builtin (not an external binary) that changes the current working directory. It's the second-most-used command after ls. Unlike most commands, cd has no man page — use help cd in bash.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, cd is essential for:

  • Navigating between /lpj/jobpost/, /lpj/k8s/, and /lpj/ops/logs/
  • Quickly jumping to the project root with cd /lpj
  • Returning to the previous directory with cd - when bouncing between code and ops
  • Using cd ~ to jump home from deep in the project tree
  • Scripting with cd /lpj/scripts && ./deploy.sh to ensure correct working directory

Syntax

cd [DIRECTORY]

# Common patterns:
cd /lpj                     # Absolute path
cd ../..                    # Relative path (up two levels)
cd -                        # Previous directory
cd ~                        # Home directory
cd ~/scripts                # From home
cd                          # Home (no argument)
cd -P /symlink/path         # Follow physical path (resolve symlinks)

Parameters

ArgumentDescription
DIRECTORYTarget directory (absolute or relative). If omitted, goes to $HOME
-Switch to the previous working directory (stored in $OLDPWD)
~Shorthand for $HOME. ~user goes to user's home
..Parent directory. Can chain: ../../..
-PUse physical directory structure (resolve all symlinks)
-LUse logical directory structure (follow symlinks, default)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — directory changed
1Error — directory not found, permission denied, or too many symlink levels

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Directory Navigation Patterns

Daily Workflow: Carol (DevOps lead) navigates the anihpj project tree constantly — jumping from logs to configs to Kubernetes manifests. Here are the real paths she traverses on prod-api-01.
# Carol's typical navigation flow on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ cd /lpj
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj$ ls

# Check logs first thing in the morning:
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj$ cd ops/logs
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/ops/logs$ ls -lt
-rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj anihpj 524288 Jun  3 14:23 error.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj anihpj 196542 Jun  3 14:23 app.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj anihpj  89432 Jun  3 14:20 access.log

# Jump back to root, then to Kubernetes manifests:
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/ops/logs$ cd /lpj/k8s
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/k8s$ ls
base  cilium  ingress  monitoring

carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/k8s$ cd /lpj/k8s/cilium

# DNS policy allowing kube-dns egress on port 53

Example 1: Absolute Path to Project Root

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: cd is tested implicitly throughout the LFCS exam — you'll navigate directories constantly. Know these cold: cd - (previous dir), cd .. (parent), cd ~ (home), and the difference between absolute (/lpj/k8s) and relative (../ops) paths. Also know that cd is a shell builtin, not a binary — which cd returns nothing, use help cd.

pwd

INFO Navigation Scripting LFCS Domain 1

Print Working Directory — show the absolute path of the current directory

pwd outputs the full path of the current working directory. Invaluable for scripts that need to know their execution context, and for orienting yourself when deep in nested directory trees.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, pwd is used for:

  • Confirming you're in the correct directory before running destructive commands
  • Setting SCRIPT_DIR=$(pwd) in deployment scripts
  • Verifying symlink resolution with pwd -P vs pwd -L
  • Embedding the current path in log messages: echo "[$(date)] Running from $(pwd)"

Syntax

pwd [-LP]

# Common patterns:
pwd             # Show current directory (logical, default)
pwd -P          # Show physical path (resolve all symlinks)
pwd -L          # Show logical path (preserve symlinks, default)
SCRIPT_DIR="$(pwd)"   # Store in variable for scripts

Parameters

FlagDescription
-LLogical path — use $PWD from environment, preserving symlinks. Default.
-PPhysical path — resolve all symlinks to their real locations

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — path printed to stdout
1Error — cannot determine current directory (rare: deleted directory)

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Path Verification Patterns

Why pwd matters: When Carol runs a deployment script, she always starts with pwd to make sure she's in /lpj/scripts, not accidentally in /home/carol. A misplaced rm -rf * in the wrong directory is an SRE's nightmare.
# Carol's deployment pre-flight check on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ cd /lpj/scripts
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/scripts$ pwd
/lpj/scripts
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/scripts$ ls deploy.sh
deploy.sh
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/scripts$ bash deploy.sh

# Physical vs Logical — the /lpj symlink scenario:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls -l /lpj
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 18 Jun  1 09:00 /lpj -> /mnt/data/lpj
carol@prod-api-01:~$ cd /lpj/k8s
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/k8s$ pwd -L
/lpj/k8s                 # Logical: shows the symlink path
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/k8s$ pwd -P
/mnt/data/lpj/k8s        # Physical: shows the real path

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Print Working Directory

Daily Workflow: Carol uses pwd constantly to confirm her location in the anihpj project tree before running commands. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical pwd usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ pwd
/home/carol
carol@prod-api-01:~$ cd /lpj/k8s/base/ && pwd
/lpj/k8s/base
# Key locations where pwd is used daily:
#  /lpj/k8s/base/        — Kubernetes manifests
#  /lpj/ops/logs/         — Application logs
#  /lpj/scripts/          — Deployment scripts

Examples

Example 1: Confirm Directory Before Destructive Action

Scenario: Carol is about to run a script that deletes old log files. She ALWAYS checks pwd first.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh              # Cilium installation + verification
    ├── 📄 connectivity-test.sh         # End-to-end connectivity checks
    └── 📄 deploy.sh                    # Full deployment script

📄 Context — Safety Check:

# if [ "$(pwd)" != "/lpj/ops/logs" ]; then
#     echo "ERROR: Must run from /lpj/ops/logs"
#     exit 1
# fi

Command:

cd /lpj/ops/logs && pwd

Output:

/lpj/ops/logs
Example 2: Capture pwd in a Script Variable

Scenario: Alice's Django migration script needs to know its own location to find the manage.py file.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh              # Cilium installation + verification
    ├── 📄 connectivity-test.sh         # End-to-end connectivity checks
    └── 📄 deploy.sh                    # Full deployment script

📄 Context — Script Self-Awareness:

# /lpj/scripts/migrate.sh:
# SCRIPT_DIR="$(pwd)"
# cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/../jobpost"
# python manage.py migrate

Command:

cd /lpj/scripts && SCRIPT_DIR="$(pwd)" && echo "Script running from: $SCRIPT_DIR"

Output:

Script running from: /lpj/scripts

📝 What happened: The script captured its own location using SCRIPT_DIR="$(pwd)". This pattern is essential for scripts that need to find files relative to their own location, regardless of where they are invoked from.

    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:

cd /lpj/api && pwd && ls -l

Output:

/lpj/api -rw-r--r-- 1 bob bob 1542 Jun 3 12:00 __init__.py -rw-r--r-- 1 bob bob 3847 Jun 3 12:00 views.py -rw-r--r-- 1 bob bob 2145 Jun 3 12:00 urls.py -rw-r--r-- 1 bob bob 4096 Jun 3 12:00 serializers.py

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: Know the difference between pwd -L (logical/default, preserves symlinks) and pwd -P (physical, resolves symlinks). The LFCS exam may use symlinked directories — pwd -P reveals the real location. Also: echo $PWD is not always the same as pwd if you've changed directories via symlinks.

tree

INFO Navigation Visualization LFCS Domain 1

Display directory structure as a visual tree hierarchy

tree recursively lists directories and files in a tree-like format. It's the fastest way to understand a directory structure at a glance. May need installation: apt install tree or brew install tree.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, tree is used for:

  • Documenting the project structure in /lpj/README.md
  • Quickly understanding what's inside /lpj/k8s/ without cd/ls cycles
  • Auditing directory depth with tree -L 2
  • Checking directory permissions with tree -pu

Syntax

tree [OPTIONS] [DIRECTORY]

# Common patterns:
tree                    # Show tree from current directory
tree -d                 # Directories only
tree -L 2               # Limit depth to 2 levels
tree -a                 # Show hidden files too
tree -h                 # Show human-readable file sizes
tree -pug               # Show permissions, user, group
tree -J                 # JSON output for scripts

Parameters

FlagDescription
-aAll files — include hidden files (dotfiles)
-dDirectories only — suppress file listing
-L NMax display depth — descend at most N levels
-hHuman-readable — print file sizes in K, M, G
-P PATTERNFilter — list only files matching shell pattern
-I PATTERNExclude — do not list files matching pattern
-JJSON output — machine-parseable tree
-pPrint file permissions (e.g., drwxr-xr-x)
-uPrint file owner username
-gPrint file group name
-sPrint file size in bytes
-FAppend indicator: / for dirs, * for executables, @ for symlinks

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — tree displayed
1Error — directory not found or permission denied

find

SEARCH Navigation File Search Scripting LFCS Domain 1

Search for files and directories in a directory hierarchy — the most powerful filesystem search tool

find recursively searches a directory tree for files matching criteria like name, type, size, modification time, permissions, ownership, and more. It's an SRE's swiss army knife for file discovery, cleanup, and batch operations.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, find is used for:

  • Finding all .py files modified today: find /lpj/ -name "*.py" -mtime -1
  • Cleaning old log files: find /lpj/ops/logs -name "*.log" -mtime +30 -delete
  • Locating files with insecure permissions: find /lpj -perm /o+w -type f
  • Finding large files consuming disk: find /lpj -type f -size +100M
  • Batch-executing commands on matched files with -exec

Syntax

find [PATH...] [EXPRESSION]

# Common patterns:
find . -name "*.py"                     # Find by name (case sensitive)
find . -iname "*.log"                   # Find by name (case insensitive)
find . -type f                          # Files only
find . -type d                          # Directories only
find . -type f -size +100M              # Files larger than 100MB
find . -type f -mtime -7               # Modified in last 7 days
find . -type f -mtime +30 -delete       # Older than 30 days → delete
find . -user alice -type f              # Files owned by alice
find . -perm 0777                       # Files with 777 permissions
find . -empty                           # Empty files/directories
find . -name "*.pyc" -exec rm {} \;     # Delete all .pyc files
find . -maxdepth 2 -name "Dockerfile"   # Limit search depth

Parameters

ExpressionDescription
-name PATTERNFile name (case sensitive, supports *, ?, [])
-iname PATTERNFile name (case insensitive)
-type fRegular files only
-type dDirectories only
-type lSymbolic links only
-size +N[c/k/M/G]Size: +100M (over 100MB), -10k (under 10KB), 0 (empty)
-mtime NModified exactly N*24h ago: -7 (last 7d), +30 (older than 30d)
-atime NAccessed N*24h ago
-ctime NMetadata changed N*24h ago
-mmin NModified N minutes ago
-user NAMEOwned by user NAME
-group NAMEOwned by group NAME
-perm MODEPermission bits: 0777 (exact), /o+w (any world-writable)
-emptyFile or directory is empty
-newer FILEModified more recently than FILE
-maxdepth NDescend at most N levels (must come before other tests)
-mindepth NDescend at least N levels
-exec CMD {} \;Execute CMD on each matched file ({} = placeholder)
-exec CMD {} +Execute CMD with all matches at once (more efficient)
-deleteDelete matched files (use with extreme caution!)
-print0Null-delimited output (for xargs -0)
-not or !Negate the following expression
-o or -orOR between expressions

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — all paths traversed (may have zero matches)
1Error — some paths could not be traversed (permissions, etc.)

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — SRE Find Patterns

# Carol's daily find operations on prod-api-01:

# 1. Find all Django migrations created today:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ find /lpj/jobpost -name "*.py" -path "*/migrations/*" -mtime -1

# 2. Find world-writable files (security risk):
carol@prod-api-01:~$ find /lpj -type f -perm /o+w 2>/dev/null

# 3. Find files larger than 50MB eating disk space:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ find /lpj/ops/backups/ -type f -size +50M -exec ls -lh {} \;

# 4. Clean log files older than 7 days:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ find /lpj/ops/logs -name "*.log" -mtime +7 -delete

# 5. Find all empty directories (orphaned structure):
carol@prod-api-01:~$ find /lpj -type d -empty

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: find is one of the most heavily tested commands. Know: -name vs -iname, -mtime with + and - prefixes, -type f vs -type d, -perm with / and - prefixes, -exec {} \; (backslash-semicolon is required!), -maxdepth placement, and -delete. The most common exam task: "Find all files owned by user X modified in the last 7 days and change their permissions."

locate

SEARCH Navigation Fast Search LFCS Domain 1

Find files by name using a pre-built database — much faster than find

locate searches a pre-built index (/var/lib/mlocate/mlocate.db) for file paths matching a pattern. It's orders of magnitude faster than find for simple name searches, but depends on updatedb running regularly (usually via cron). Install with apt install mlocate.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, locate is used for:

  • Instantly finding all settings.py files across the system
  • Quickly locating where a specific binary or config file lives
  • Searching for files by partial name when you can't remember the full path
  • Counting how many of a certain file type exist: locate -c "*.conf"

Syntax

locate [OPTIONS] PATTERN

# Common patterns:
locate "*.py"               # Find all Python files
locate -i "anihpj"          # Case-insensitive search
locate -l 20 "jobpost"      # Limit to 20 results
locate -c "*.log"           # Count matching entries
locate -e "settings.py"     # Only existing files (not deleted)
sudo updatedb               # Rebuild the locate database

Parameters

FlagDescription
-iCase-insensitive search
-l N, --limit NLimit output to N entries
-c, --countPrint number of matches instead of filenames
-e, --existingPrint only entries that exist right now (files may have been deleted since last updatedb)
-r, --regexpSearch with basic regular expressions
--regexSearch with extended regular expressions

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription

which

INFO Navigation PATH Resolution LFCS Domain 1

Show the full path of shell commands — which executable would run?

which searches $PATH and returns the first matching executable. It answers "Which binary will execute if I type this command?" Essential for debugging when multiple versions of a tool are installed.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, which is used for:

  • Confirming the correct Python version is active: which python3
  • Debugging CI/CD pipelines when tools can't be found
  • Checking if kubectl, docker, helm are installed
  • Finding all installed versions: which -a python

Syntax

which [OPTIONS] PROGRAM...

# Common patterns:
which python3               # Where is python3?
which -a python             # Show ALL python executables in PATH
which python node npm       # Check multiple commands at once
which docker kubectl helm   # Verify DevOps tools are installed

Parameters

FlagDescription
-a, --allPrint all matching executables in PATH, not just the first one found

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — all specified programs found
1One or more programs not found in PATH

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — DevOps Tool Verification

/usr/local/bin/kubectl
/usr/local/bin/helm
/usr/bin/python3
/usr/bin/node
/usr/sbin/nginx

# Jenkins pipeline debug — which python is the CI using?
jenkins@ci-runner-01:~$ which -a python3
/usr/local/bin/python3       # Custom install
/usr/bin/python3              # System default

# Check if a command is NOT installed:

whereis

INFO Navigation Binary Locator LFCS Domain 1

Locate the binary, source, and manual page files for a command

whereis searches standard Linux directories (not $PATH) for a command's binary, source code, and man pages. Unlike which, it searches a broader set of standard locations and shows all three file types at once.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, whereis is used for:

  • Finding man pages for installed tools: whereis -m nginx
  • Locating source code for open-source packages
  • Discovering all locations of a tool's binary: whereis -b docker

Syntax

whereis [OPTIONS] COMMAND...

# Common patterns:
whereis nginx               # Find binary, source, and man for nginx
whereis -b python3          # Show only binary paths
whereis -m ls               # Show only manual pages
whereis python node docker  # Locate multiple commands at once

Parameters

FlagDescription
-bSearch only for binaries
-mSearch only for manual sections
-sSearch only for source files
-B DIRSLimit binary search to specified directories
-M DIRSLimit manual search to specified directories
-S DIRSLimit source search to specified directories

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — at least one match found for all commands
1Nothing found for one or more commands

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Tool Documentation Discovery

# Find man pages for tools used in the anihpj stack:
carol@prod-web-01:~$ whereis -m nginx gunicorn postgres redis
nginx: /usr/share/man/man8/nginx.8.gz
gunicorn: /usr/share/man/man1/gunicorn.1.gz
postgres: /usr/share/man/man1/postgres.1.gz
redis: /usr/share/man/man1/redis-cli.1.gz /usr/share/man/man5/redis.conf.5.gz
