type

INFO Shell Builtin Command Resolution LFCS Domain 1

Display how a command name would be interpreted by the shell — the ultimate "what is this?" tool

type is a shell builtin that reveals how the shell would interpret a given command name — whether it's a builtin, an alias, a function, an external binary, or a keyword. Unlike which, it sees everything the shell sees.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, type is used for:

  • Debugging why a command behaves unexpectedly (alias shadowing)
  • Checking if cd, echo, alias are builtins (they are!)
  • Discovering all definitions: type -a python
  • CI/CD debugging when scripts behave differently than interactive shells

Syntax

type [OPTIONS] NAME...

# Common patterns:
type cd                     # "cd is a shell builtin"
type -t cd                  # Just the type word: "builtin"
type -a python              # All definitions (alias, function, binary)
type grep                   # "grep is /usr/bin/grep"
type -t ls                  # "file" (external binary)

Parameters

FlagDescription
-aShow all locations containing the command (not just the first)
-tPrint a single word: alias, keyword, function, builtin, file — or nothing if not found
-pForce PATH search even for builtins (returns external binary or nothing)
-PForce PATH search for each name, even if it's an alias/builtin/function

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — command found (any type)
1Command not found

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Command Classification

# Carol audits all key commands in the anihpj toolchain:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ type cd pwd ls grep echo [ alias
cd is a shell builtin
pwd is a shell builtin
ls is aliased to `ls --color=auto'
grep is /usr/bin/grep
echo is a shell builtin
[ is a shell builtin
alias is a shell builtin

# Check the full chain for python:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ type -a python3
python3 is /lpj/venv/bin/python3
python3 is /usr/bin/python3

# The -t flag for scripts:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ type -t docker && echo "docker is available" || echo "docker MISSING"
file
docker is available

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Command Type

Daily Workflow: Carol uses type to distinguish shell builtins from external binaries. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

carol@prod-api-01:~$ type python3 systemctl
# Key locations where type is used daily:
#  Shell diagnostics    — Command resolution
#  Script debugging      — Verifying availability

Examples

Example 1: Identify Builtins vs External Commands

Scenario: Alice is learning bash and wants to know which commands are builtins.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

type cd echo alias source export pwd

Output:

cd is a shell builtin echo is a shell builtin alias is a shell builtin source is a shell builtin export is a shell builtin pwd is a shell builtin

📝 What happened: Six commands are all shell builtins — they are part of bash itself, not separate binaries. This means they have no man pages and which won't find them. Use help <cmd> for documentation.

Output:

ls is aliased to `ls --color=auto -h'

📝 What happened: The ls command is not running the raw binary — it is aliased with --color=auto -h. This explains why ls always shows colors and human-readable sizes. Aliases can shadow the original command — type reveals the truth.

Example 3: Show All Definitions of a Command

Scenario: A custom function shadows the system grep. type -a shows both.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml
├── 📄 requirements.txt
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

type -a grep

Output:

grep is a function grep () { /usr/bin/grep --color=auto "$@" } grep is /usr/bin/grep

📝 What happened: A function AND a binary both named grep exist. The function (defined first) takes priority — it wraps the binary with --color=auto. type -a shows the full resolution chain: function → binary.

Example 4: Script-Friendly Type Check

Scenario: A deployment script uses type -t to check if a command exists before using it.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml
├── 📄 requirements.txt
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

type -t kubectl >/dev/null && echo "kubectl ready" || echo "kubectl NOT installed"

Output:

kubectl ready

📝 What happened: The type -t flag outputs a single word — "file" means an external binary was found. Redirecting to /dev/null suppresses that word, and the exit code drives the conditional. This pattern is cleaner than which for scripts.

Example 5: which vs type — The Real Difference

Scenario: Bob asks why which cd returns nothing. Carol shows why.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml
├── 📄 requirements.txt
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

which cd; echo "Exit: $?" && type cd; echo "Exit: $?"

Output:

Exit: 1 cd is a shell builtin Exit: 0

📝 What happened: which cd failed (exit 1) because cd is not an external binary. type cd succeeded (exit 0) and correctly identified it as a shell builtin. This is the definitive demonstration: type sees what the shell sees.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: type is the definitive way to determine what a command is: builtin, alias, function, keyword, or external binary. Use it instead of which for builtins and aliases. type -t is perfect for scripts: if type -t docker >/dev/null; then .... The LFCS exam expects you to know that cd, echo, pwd, alias, and [ are all shell builtins.

dirs

INFO Shell Builtin Directory Stack LFCS Domain 1

Display the directory stack — see where you've been

dirs is a shell builtin that displays the current directory stack — the list of directories saved by pushd. Think of it as a breadcrumb trail through your filesystem navigation.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, dirs helps Carol quickly orient herself during incident response when she's pushed through multiple directories — dirs -v shows her the full trail at a glance.

Syntax

dirs [-clpv] [+N | -N]

# Common patterns:
dirs            # Show stack (space-separated, left=top)
dirs -v         # Show numbered stack (0=current)
dirs -c         # Clear the entire stack
dirs -l         # Expand ~ to full paths
dirs -p         # One entry per line (script-friendly)

Parameters

FlagDescription
-cClear the directory stack (remove all entries)
-lLong listing — expand ~ to full home path
-pPrint one entry per line (script-parsable)
-vPrint with index numbers — best for interactive use

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — stack displayed

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Stack Inspection

# Alice checks her directory stack while debugging across multiple apps:
alice@dev-01:/lpj$ pushd /lpj/jobpost >/dev/null
alice@dev-01:/lpj$ pushd /lpj/jobpost/templates >/dev/null
alice@dev-01:/lpj$ pushd /lpj/api >/dev/null

alice@dev-01:/lpj$ dirs -v
 0  /lpj/api
 1  /lpj/jobpost/templates
 2  /lpj/jobpost
 3  /lpj

# Clear after done:
alice@dev-01:/lpj$ dirs -c && dirs -v
 0  /lpj

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Directory Stack

Daily Workflow: Carol uses dirs to view the pushd/popd directory stack. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical dirs usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ dirs -v
carol@prod-api-01:~$ pushd /lpj/k8s/base/ && pushd /lpj/ops/logs/ && dirs
# Key locations where dirs is used daily:
#  /lpj/k8s/base/       — Frequently pushed dir
#  /lpj/ops/logs/        — Log inspection location

Examples

Example 1: View the Stack with Numbers

Scenario: Carol has pushed 4 directories during an incident investigation and needs to see the full trail.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 ingress/
        ├── 📄 ingress.yaml             # Cilium Ingress
        └── 📄 gateway.yaml             # Gateway API

Command:

cd /lpj && pushd /lpj/jobpost && pushd /lpj/jobpost/templates && pushd /lpj/k8s/ingress && dirs -v

Output:

0 /lpj/k8s/ingress 1 /lpj/jobpost/templates 2 /lpj/jobpost 3 /lpj

📝 What happened: Four entries in the stack, numbered 0-3. Index 0 is the current directory (/lpj/k8s/ingress). Index 3 is the project root — the first directory pushed. The stack grows leftward; popping will return to index 1.

Example 2: Print One Per Line (Script-Friendly)

Scenario: A deployment script uses dirs -p to iterate over the stack.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
    ├── 📄 models.py                    # Job, Company, Application models

    ├── 📄 urls.py                      # App URL routing

Command:

dirs -p

Output:

/lpj/k8s/ingress /lpj/jobpost/templates /lpj/jobpost /lpj

📝 What happened: One entry per line (-p) — ideal for shell scripts that need to iterate over the stack with while read dir; do ...; done. No index numbers, just clean paths.

Example 3: Clear the Stack

Scenario: Eve finishes her audit and wants a clean directory stack.

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root

Example 4: Show Stack with Full Paths

Scenario: Carol has pushed into directories using ~ shortcuts and wants to see the real paths.

Output:

/lpj/k8s /home/carol/scripts /lpj

Example 5: Iterate the Stack in a Script

Scenario: A backup script iterates over all directories in the stack to verify they exist.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
    ├── 📄 models.py                    # Job, Company, Application models
    ├── 📄 views.py                     # View logic (web + API)
    ├── 📄 urls.py                      # App URL routing
    ├── 📄 serializers.py               # DRF serializers for API
    ├── 📄 admin.py                     # Django admin registration
    ├── 📄 tests.py                     # Unit and integration tests
    ├── 📁 templates/jobpost/
    │   ├── 📄 base.html
    │   ├── 📄 job_list.html
    │   ├── 📄 job_detail.html
    │   └── 📄 apply.html
    ├── 📁 static/jobpost/
    │   ├── 📄 style.css
    │   └── 📄 main.js
    └── 📁 migrations/
        └── 📄 0001_initial.py

Command:

dirs -p | while read dir; do echo "Checking: $dir"; ls -d "$dir" >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "  OK" || echo "  MISSING!"; done

Output:

Checking: /lpj/k8s/ingress OK Checking: /lpj/jobpost/templates OK Checking: /lpj/jobpost OK

📝 What happened: dirs -p printed one path per line, which while read consumed. Each directory was verified with ls -d. This pattern is used in deployment scripts to validate the directory stack before performing operations.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: dirs is a bash builtin — no man page, use help dirs. Know dirs -v for the numbered view (index 0 = current directory) and dirs -c to clear. The stack is LIFO: leftmost entry is the current directory (top of stack).

pushd

NAVIGATE Shell Builtin Directory Stack LFCS Domain 1

Push directory onto the stack and change to it — navigate without losing your place

pushd is a shell builtin that saves your current directory onto a LIFO stack, then changes to the target directory. It's the single most useful navigation command for incident response — push into logs, push into configs, and pop your way back.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, Carol uses pushd to bounce between /lpj/k8s/, /lpj/ops/logs/, and /lpj/anihpj/ during incident triage.

Syntax

pushd [DIRECTORY | +N | -N]

# Common patterns:
pushd /lpj/k8s           # Save current dir, cd to /lpj/k8s
pushd /lpj/ops/logs      # Stack: /lpj/ops/logs, /lpj/k8s, /lpj
pushd                     # Swap top two (like cd -, but stack-aware)
pushd +2                  # Rotate stack to bring 3rd entry to top
pushd -n /lpj/api         # Add to stack without changing directory

Parameters

ArgDescription
DIRECTORYPush current dir onto stack, then cd to DIRECTORY
+NRotate stack: bring Nth entry (0-indexed from left) to the top
-NRotate stack: bring Nth entry (0-indexed from right) to the top
-nAdd to stack without changing directory (push only)
(no arg)Swap top two stack entries (same effect as cd -)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — directory pushed and changed
1Error — directory not found or invalid argument

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Incident Response Navigation

# Carol investigating a 502 error — pushd builds her trail:
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj$ dirs -v
 0  /lpj

# Step 1: Check ingress logs
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj$ pushd /lpj/k8s/ingress
/lpj/k8s/ingress /lpj

carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/k8s/ingress$ tail -3 ingress.yaml
# upstream connect error (111: Connection refused) at 15:42

# Step 2: Check Django settings
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/k8s/ingress$ pushd /lpj/anihpj
/lpj/anihpj /lpj/k8s/ingress /lpj

carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/anihpj$ grep -n "ALLOWED_HOSTS" settings.py
23: ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['anihpj.com', '*.anihpj.com']

# Her trail: anihpj → ingress → root

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Push Directory

Daily Workflow: Carol uses pushd to navigate while maintaining a directory stack. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical pushd usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ pushd /lpj/k8s/base/
carol@prod-api-01:~$ pushd /lpj/ops/logs/
# Key locations where pushd is used daily:
#  /lpj/k8s/base/       — K8s manifest editing
#  /lpj/ops/logs/        — Log inspection

Examples

Example 1: Push Into Logs, Then Config

Scenario: Carol starts at root, pushes into logs, then into the API to investigate.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    └── 📁 logs/                        # grep / sed / awk / tail -f practice
        ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
        ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL only
        └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log

Command:

cd /lpj && pushd /lpj/ops/logs && pushd /lpj/api && dirs -v

Output:

0 /lpj/api 1 /lpj/ops/logs 2 /lpj

📝 What happened: The stack shows the push order: api was pushed last (index 0), logs before that (index 1), and root was the starting point (index 2). Pop will return to logs, then root.

Example 2: Rotate Stack with Numeric Index

Scenario: Bob needs to jump directly to the 3rd directory (index 2) without popping the top ones.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
    ├── 📄 models.py                    # Job, Company, Application models
    ├── 📄 views.py                     # View logic (web + API)
    ├── 📄 urls.py                      # App URL routing
    ├── 📄 serializers.py               # DRF serializers for API
    ├── 📄 admin.py                     # Django admin registration
    ├── 📄 tests.py                     # Unit and integration tests
    ├── 📁 templates/jobpost/

    │   └── 📄 main.js
    └── 📁 migrations/
        └── 📄 0001_initial.py

Command:

pushd +2

Output:

/lpj/jobpost /lpj /lpj/k8s/ingress /lpj/jobpost/templates

📝 What happened: pushd +2 rotated the stack — the entry at index 2 (/lpj/k8s/ingress) moved to the top. The other entries shifted right. This lets you jump to any directory in the stack without losing the trail.

    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh              # Cilium installation + verification
    ├── 📄 connectivity-test.sh         # End-to-end connectivity checks
    └── 📄 deploy.sh                    # Full deployment script

📄 Context — Robust Script Pattern:

# /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh uses pushd/popd:
# pushd /lpj/k8s/base >/dev/null
# kubectl apply -f .
# popd >/dev/null
# # Script safely returns to original directory

cd /lpj && pushd /lpj/k8s/base >/dev/null && kubectl apply -f . && popd >/dev/null && echo "Deployed, back in $(pwd)"

Output:

Deployed, back in /lpj

📝 What happened: The script changed to /lpj/k8s/base, deployed, then popped back. The final pwd confirms the return. Using pushd/popd in scripts prevents accidental directory drift — you always return to where you started.

Example 4: Push Without Changing Directory

Scenario: Alice wants to bookmark her current directory for later without navigating away.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
    ├── 📄 models.py                    # Job, Company, Application models
    ├── 📄 views.py                     # View logic (web + API)
    ├── 📄 urls.py                      # App URL routing
    ├── 📄 serializers.py               # DRF serializers for API

    │   ├── 📄 style.css
    │   └── 📄 main.js
    └── 📁 migrations/
        └── 📄 0001_initial.py

Command:

cd /lpj/jobpost && pushd -n /lpj/api && pwd && dirs -v

Output:

/lpj/jobpost 0 /lpj/jobpost 1 /lpj/api

📝 What happened: pushd -n added /lpj/api to the stack WITHOUT changing to it. Alice stayed in /lpj/jobpost but bookmarked the API directory. This is useful for building a navigation plan before executing it.

Example 5: Swap Top Two Directories

Scenario: Carol uses pushd without arguments to toggle between two directories — similar to cd - but stack-aware.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
    ├── 📁 base/                        # Core deployments & services
    ├── 📁 cilium/                      # Network policies (CNP, CCNP)
    ├── 📁 ingress/                     # Cilium Ingress & Gateway
    └── 📁 monitoring/                  # ServiceMonitor & dashboards

Command:

cd /lpj && pushd /lpj/k8s >/dev/null && pushd >/dev/null && pwd && pushd >/dev/null && pwd

Output:

/lpj /lpj/k8s

📝 What happened: pushd with no arguments swapped the top two stack entries. First swap returned to /lpj, second swap returned to /lpj/k8s. Unlike cd - which only remembers one directory, pushd can toggle through the entire stack.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: pushd is a bash builtin — use help pushd. Know: pushd DIR = push + cd, pushd (no args) swaps top two, pushd +N rotates. The stack is LIFO — the LAST directory you pushed is the FIRST you'll pop back to.

popd

NAVIGATE Shell Builtin Directory Stack LFCS Domain 1

Pop the top directory off the stack and return to it — retrace your steps

popd is a shell builtin that removes the top entry from the directory stack and changes to that directory. It's the return-trip companion to pushd — every push should eventually be paired with a pop.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, Carol pops back through her incident trail: from /lpj/anihpj/ back to /lpj/k8s/ingress/, then back to root.

Syntax

popd [-n] [+N | -N]

# Common patterns:
popd            # Pop top, cd to it
popd +2         # Remove 3rd entry (index 2) from stack
popd -n         # Pop without changing directory

Parameters

ArgDescription
(no arg)Pop the top directory off the stack and cd to it
+NRemove the Nth entry (0-indexed from left) from the stack
-NRemove the Nth entry (0-indexed from right) from the stack
-nPop from stack without changing directory

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — popped and directory changed
1Error — stack empty or invalid argument

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Retracing the Incident Trail

# Carol pops back through her investigation:
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/anihpj$ dirs -v
 0  /lpj/anihpj
 1  /lpj/k8s/ingress
 2  /lpj

# Pop back to ingress logs:
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/anihpj$ popd
/lpj/k8s/ingress /lpj

# Verify the fix in logs:
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/k8s/ingress$ tail -1 ingress.yaml
# Connection restored at 16:05

# Pop back to root:
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/k8s/ingress$ popd
/lpj

carol@prod-api-01:/lpj$ # Back where she started — stack is clean

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Pop Directory

Daily Workflow: Carol uses popd to return to previous directories after deep navigation. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical popd usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ popd
/lpj/ops/logs ~/lpj/k8s/base
carol@prod-api-01:~$ popd
# Key locations where popd is used daily:
#  Stack navigation     — Returning from deep dives
#  /lpj/ops/logs/        — Back from log inspection

Examples

Example 1: Pop Back Through Two Levels

Scenario: Carol pushes into two directories, then pops back step by step.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 ingress/
        ├── 📄 ingress.yaml             # Cilium Ingress
        └── 📄 gateway.yaml             # Gateway API

Command:

cd /lpj && pushd /lpj/k8s/ingress && pushd /lpj/anihpj && popd && pwd && popd && pwd

Output:

/lpj/k8s/ingress /lpj

📝 What happened: Two pops returned Carol from /lpj/anihpj through /lpj/k8s/ingress back to root. pwd after each pop confirmed the trail. The stack is now empty — all pushed directories have been visited.

Example 2: Pop Without Changing Directory

Scenario: Dave wants to remove entries from the stack but stay where he is.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
    ├── 📄 __init__.py
    ├── 📄 settings.py                  # Django settings (DB, apps, middleware)
    ├── 📄 urls.py                      # Root URL routing
    ├── 📄 wsgi.py                      # WSGI entry for Gunicorn
    ├── 📄 asgi.py                      # ASGI entry
    └── 📄 celery.py                    # Celery config (background tasks)

Command:

popd -n && pwd && dirs -v

Output:

/lpj/anihpj 0 /lpj/anihpj 1 /lpj

📝 What happened: popd -n removed the top entry from the stack without changing directories. Dave stayed in /lpj/anihpj but the stack shrank from 3 to 2 entries. Useful for cleaning the stack while staying put.

Example 3: Handle Empty Stack Gracefully

Scenario: A script checks if the stack has entries before popping.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml
├── 📄 requirements.txt
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

popd 2>/dev/null || echo "Stack is empty — already at root"

Output:

Stack is empty — already at root

📝 What happened: Trying to popd an empty stack produces an error (exit code 1). The || operator caught it and printed a friendly message. Always handle empty stacks in scripts to avoid unexpected failures.

Example 4: Remove a Specific Entry from the Stack

Scenario: Carol wants to remove only the 2nd entry without popping the top one.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    └── 📁 logs/                        # grep / sed / awk / tail -f practice
        ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
        ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL only
        └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log

Command:

dirs -v && popd -n +1 && echo "---" && dirs -v

Output:

0 /lpj/k8s/ingress 1 /lpj/ops/logs 2 /lpj --- 0 /lpj/k8s/ingress 1 /lpj

📝 What happened: popd -n +1 removed the entry at index 1 (/lpj/ops/logs) without changing directories. The -n flag suppressed the cd. This lets you surgically clean the stack — useful when you realize a pushed directory is no longer relevant.

Example 5: Pop All the Way Back to Root

Scenario: After a deep investigation, Alice wants to pop back to root in one command chain.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 ingress/
        ├── 📄 ingress.yaml             # Cilium Ingress
        └── 📄 gateway.yaml             # Gateway API

Command:

cd /lpj && pushd /lpj/k8s/cilium >/dev/null && pushd /lpj/k8s/ingress >/dev/null && while dirs -p | grep -q .; do popd 2>/dev/null || break; done && pwd

Output:

/lpj

📝 What happened: A while loop called popd until the stack was empty (exit code 1 breaks the loop). The final pwd confirmed Alice is back at root. This pattern is useful for cleanup functions that reset navigation state.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: popd is a bash builtin — use help popd. Know: popd (no args) removes the top and cd's to it, popd -n pops without changing directory, popd +N removes a specific entry. Stack empty? popd errors with exit code 1. Every pushd should have a matching popd.

📁 File Operations

Commands for creating, copying, moving, deleting, and linking files and directories — the core file manipulation toolkit used throughout every workflow in the anihpj/jobpost environment.

touch

CREATE File Operations Timestamp LFCS Domain 1

Create empty files or update file timestamps — the fastest way to make a new file

touch creates an empty file if it doesn't exist, or updates the access and modification timestamps of an existing file. It's the go-to for creating placeholder files, triggering file watchers, and setting specific timestamps for testing.

For anihpj/jobpost, touch is used for:

  • Creating empty __init__.py files in new Python packages
  • Triggering Django's auto-reload by touching settings.py
  • Creating log files before services start: touch /lpj/ops/logs/app.log
  • Setting consistent timestamps on deployment artifacts

Syntax

touch [OPTIONS] FILE...

# Common patterns:
touch newfile.txt               # Create empty file (or update timestamp)
touch -t 202606010800 deploy     # Set specific timestamp: Jun 1, 2026, 08:00
touch -a file.log               # Update access time only
touch -m file.log               # Update modification time only
touch -r reference.txt new.txt  # Copy timestamp from reference file

Parameters

FlagDescription
-aChange only the access time (atime)
-mChange only the modification time (mtime)
-c, --no-createDo not create the file if it doesn't exist
-d, --date=STRINGParse STRING as a date (e.g., "2026-01-01 12:00")
-t STAMPUse [[CC]YY]MMDDhhmm[.ss] timestamp format
-r, --reference=FILECopy timestamps from the reference FILE

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — file created or timestamp updated

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Create/Update Files

Daily Workflow: Carol uses touch to create placeholder files, trigger file watchers, and set consistent timestamps on deployment artifacts. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical touch usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ touch /lpj/ops/logs/app.log && ls -la /lpj/ops/logs/app.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 0 Jun 5 08:00 /lpj/ops/logs/app.log

carol@prod-api-01:~$ touch /lpj/jobpost/__init__.py
carol@prod-api-01:~$ touch /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml
# Key locations where touch is used daily:
#  /lpj/ops/logs/       — Log files created before services start
#  /lpj/jobpost/        — Python __init__.py for new packages
#  /lpj/k8s/base/       — Timestamp updates on manifests

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — File Creation Patterns

# Alice creates new files for a Django app:
alice@dev-01:/lpj$ cd /lpj/jobpost
alice@dev-01:/lpj/jobpost$ touch __init__.py
alice@dev-01:/lpj/jobpost$ touch new_views.py

# Carol touches a log file to ensure it exists before the service starts:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo -u anihpj touch /lpj/ops/logs/app.log
carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls -l /lpj/ops/logs/app.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj anihpj 0 Jun  3 16:00 /lpj/ops/logs/app.log

Examples

Example 1: Create an Empty Log File

Scenario: Carol needs to create a new log file before deploying a service that expects it to exist.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log
        ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
        └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log

Command:

touch /lpj/ops/logs/app.log && ls -l /lpj/ops/logs/app.log

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 0 Jun 3 16:00 /lpj/ops/logs/app.log

📝 What happened: An empty file (0 bytes) was created with the current timestamp. The service can now write to this file. Using touch is safer than echo "">file — it doesn't truncate an existing file.

Example 2: Create Multiple Files at Once

Scenario: Alice is scaffolding a new Django app and needs several empty files.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
    ├── 📄 __init__.py
    ├── 📄 views.py                     # APIView classes
    ├── 📄 urls.py                      # /api/v1/ routes
    └── 📄 serializers.py

Command:

cd /lpj/api && touch __init__.py views.py urls.py serializers.py && ls -l

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 0 Jun 3 16:05 __init__.py -rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 0 Jun 3 16:05 serializers.py -rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 0 Jun 3 16:05 urls.py -rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 0 Jun 3 16:05 views.py

📝 What happened: Four empty files created in one command. All share the same timestamp (16:05). touch accepts multiple arguments — far faster than creating files one by one.

Example 3: Update Modification Time Without Changing Content

Scenario: Carol wants Django's auto-reloader to detect a change in settings.py without actually editing it.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
    ├── 📄 __init__.py
    ├── 📄 settings.py                  # Django settings
    ├── 📄 urls.py                      # Root URL routing
    ├── 📄 wsgi.py                      # WSGI entry for Gunicorn
    ├── 📄 asgi.py                      # ASGI entry
    └── 📄 celery.py                    # Celery config

Command:

stat -c "%y" /lpj/anihpj/settings.py && touch -m /lpj/anihpj/settings.py && stat -c "%y" /lpj/anihpj/settings.py

Output:

2026-06-03 08:00:00.000000000 +0000 2026-06-03 16:10:23.000000000 +0000

📝 What happened: touch -m updated only the modification time — the file content is unchanged. The timestamp jumped from 08:00 to 16:10. Django's file watcher sees the mtime change and triggers a reload. This is a classic dev trick for forcing app restarts.

Example 4: Set a Specific Timestamp

Scenario: Eve needs to backdate a deployment artifact to match the release date for audit compliance.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh
    ├── 📄 connectivity-test.sh
    └── 📄 deploy.sh

Command:

touch -t 202606010800 /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh && ls -l /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh

Output:

-rwxr-xr-x 1 carol developers 2147 Jun 1 08:00 /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh

📝 What happened: The timestamp was set to June 1, 2026, 08:00 (-t YYYYMMDDhhmm). The file content is unchanged — only the metadata changed. This is useful for making deployment artifacts match their actual release date when they were extracted from a tarball.

Example 5: Copy Timestamp from Reference File

Scenario: Alice cloned a config file and wants the copy to have the same timestamp as the original.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
    ├── 📄 __init__.py
    ├── 📄 settings.py                  # Django settings
    ├── 📄 urls.py                      # Root URL routing
    ├── 📄 wsgi.py                      # WSGI entry for Gunicorn
    ├── 📄 asgi.py                      # ASGI entry
    └── 📄 celery.py                    # Celery config

Command:

touch -r /lpj/anihpj/settings.py /lpj/anihpj/settings_copy.py && ls -l /lpj/anihpj/settings*.py

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 3241 Jun 3 08:00 /lpj/anihpj/settings_copy.py -rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 3241 Jun 3 08:00 /lpj/anihpj/settings.py

📝 What happened: Both files now have identical timestamps. touch -r copies the mtime and atime from the reference file — no need to manually type the timestamp. This also preserves the original date for audit trails.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: Know the difference between atime (access) and mtime (modification). touch updates both by default. Use -a for access only, -m for modification only. touch -t takes the format [[CC]YY]MMDDhhmm[.ss] — memorize this. touch -r REF copies timestamps from a reference file.

mkdir

CREATE File Operations Directory LFCS Domain 1

Make directories — create one or more new folders in the filesystem

mkdir creates new directories. With -p, it creates parent directories as needed — no error if they already exist. Essential for project scaffolding, temporary workspaces, and deployment setup.

For anihpj/jobpost, mkdir is used for:

  • Scaffolding new Django app structures with nested directories
  • Creating backup directories: mkdir -p /lpj/ops/backups/daily
  • Setting up deployment directories with specific permissions
  • Creating temp workspaces for build artifacts

Syntax

mkdir [OPTIONS] DIRECTORY...

# Common patterns:
mkdir new_dir                   # Create a single directory
mkdir -p a/b/c/d                # Create nested path (all parents)
mkdir -m 755 public_dir         # Create with specific permissions
mkdir -v logs backups config    # Verbose + multiple directories
mkdir -p /lpj/ops/{logs,backups,systemd,cron}  # Brace expansion

Parameters

FlagDescription
-p, --parentsMake parent directories as needed; no error if directory exists
-m, --mode=MODESet file mode (permissions) at creation time, e.g., -m 755
-v, --verbosePrint a message for each created directory

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — all directories created
1Error — permission denied or path exists as a file

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Create Directories

/lpj/ops/backups/202606/

carol@prod-api-01:~$ mkdir -p /lpj/k8s/{base,cilium,ingress,monitoring}

Examples

Example 1: Create Nested Directories with -p

Scenario: Alice needs to create the full path for a new Django app's templates directory.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
    ├── 📄 models.py                    # Job, Company, Application
    ├── 📄 views.py                     # View logic (web + API)
    ├── 📄 urls.py                      # App URL routing
    ├── 📄 serializers.py               # DRF serializers
    ├── 📁 templates/jobpost/           # HTML templates
    ├── 📁 static/jobpost/              # CSS & JS
    └── 📁 migrations/                  # DB migrations

Command:

mkdir -p /lpj/jobpost/templates/jobpost && tree -d /lpj/jobpost/templates/

Output:

/lpj/jobpost/templates/ └── jobpost

📝 What happened: mkdir -p created both templates/ and templates/jobpost/ in one command. Without -p, creating templates/jobpost would fail if templates/ didn't already exist.

Example 2: Create Multiple Directories with Brace Expansion

Scenario: Carol scaffolds the k8s subdirectories in one line.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
    ├── 📁 base/                        # Core deployments & services
    ├── 📁 cilium/                      # Network policies
    ├── 📁 ingress/                     # Ingress & Gateway
    └── 📁 monitoring/                  # ServiceMonitor & dashboards

Command:

mkdir -pv /lpj/k8s/{base,cilium,ingress,monitoring}

Output:

mkdir: created directory '/lpj/k8s/base' mkdir: created directory '/lpj/k8s/cilium' mkdir: created directory '/lpj/k8s/ingress' mkdir: created directory '/lpj/k8s/monitoring'

📝 What happened: Brace expansion {a,b,c} expands to four separate arguments. Combined with -v, each created directory is confirmed. This is the idiomatic way to scaffold a project structure in one line.

Example 3: Create Directory with Specific Permissions

Scenario: Eve creates a directory that only the owner should access for storing audit findings.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

mkdir -m 700 /lpj/ops/audit && ls -ld /lpj/ops/audit

Output:

drwx------ 2 eve auditors 4096 Jun 3 16:15 /lpj/ops/audit

📝 What happened: -m 700 created the directory with rwx------ — only eve (the owner) can read, write, or enter. No group or world access. This is more secure than creating with default permissions and then running chmod.

Example 4: Idempotent Directory Creation

Scenario: Carol's deployment script ensures required directories exist without erroring if they already do.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/

📄 Context — Script Safety:

# /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh uses mkdir -p for idempotent setup:
# mkdir -p /lpj/ops/logs /lpj/ops/backups/daily
# # No error if directories already exist — safe for repeated runs

Command:

mkdir -p /lpj/ops/logs /lpj/ops/backups && echo "Directories ready" && ls -d /lpj/ops/*/

Output:

Directories ready /lpj/ops/backups/ /lpj/ops/cron/ /lpj/ops/logs/ /lpj/ops/systemd/

📝 What happened: mkdir -p silently succeeds even if directories already exist. No error, no warning — perfect for scripts that need to run repeatedly. The echo confirms the command completed.

Example 5: Combine -p and -m for Secure Nested Paths

Scenario: Dave needs a secure nested backup path where only the postgres user can access the leaf directory.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

mkdir -p -m 700 /lpj/ops/backups/postgres/daily && ls -lR /lpj/ops/backups/postgres/

Output:

/lpj/ops/backups/postgres/: total 4 drwx------ 2 dave dba 4096 Jun 3 16:20 daily

📝 What happened: Both postgres/ and daily/ were created with rwx------ (700). When -m is used with -p, the permission applies only to the LEAF directory — parents get default permissions. For full control, set permissions on each level separately.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: mkdir -p is one of the most-used flags on the exam. It creates parent directories AND doesn't error if the path already exists — making it idempotent and script-safe. Know -m MODE for setting permissions at creation time, and brace expansion {a,b,c} for creating multiple directories at once.

cp

COPY File Operations Core LFCS Domain 1

Copy files and directories — the fundamental duplication operation

cp creates copies of files and directories, preserving or modifying attributes like permissions, ownership, and timestamps. It's used constantly for backups, deployments, and configuration management.

For anihpj/jobpost, cp is used for:

  • Backing up K8s manifests before editing: cp deployment.yaml deployment.yaml.bak
  • Copying deployment artifacts between environments
  • Duplicating Django settings files for staging/production variants
  • Archiving logs with cp -a to preserve timestamps

Syntax

cp [OPTIONS] SOURCE... DEST

# Common patterns:
cp file.txt backup.txt                   # Copy a single file
cp -r /lpj/k8s/ /lpj/ops/backups/        # Recursive directory copy
cp -a source_dir/ dest_dir/              # Archive mode (preserve all)
cp -u src/*.py dest/                     # Update: copy only if newer
cp -i important.txt backup/              # Interactive (prompt before overwrite)
cp -v file1 file2 file3 /target/         # Verbose multi-file copy

Parameters

FlagDescription
-a, --archiveArchive mode: preserve permissions, ownership, timestamps, recurse. Same as -dR --preserve=all
-r, -RCopy directories recursively (use -a instead to preserve attributes)
-u, --updateCopy only when SOURCE is newer than destination or destination is missing
-v, --verbosePrint each file as it is copied
-i, --interactivePrompt before overwriting an existing file
-f, --forceIf destination cannot be opened, remove it and try again
-pPreserve mode, ownership, timestamps (subset of -a)
-l, --linkHard link files instead of copying (save disk space)
-s, --symbolic-linkMake symbolic links instead of copying
--parentsUse full source path under destination (recreate tree)
-n, --no-clobberDo not overwrite an existing file (safer than -i in scripts)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — all files copied

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Copy Files & Directories

Daily Workflow: Carol uses cp to back up configurations, duplicate manifest templates, and archive logs before rotation. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical cp usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ cp /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml /lpj/ops/backups/secrets.yaml.bak
carol@prod-api-01:~$ cp /lpj/ops/logs/app.log /lpj/ops/backups/app_$(date +%d).log
carol@prod-api-01:~$ cp -r /lpj/k8s/base/ /lpj/k8s/base-backup/
# Key locations where cp is used daily:
#  /lpj/k8s/base/       — Manifest backups before changes
#  /lpj/ops/logs/        — Log archiving
#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Target for copies

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Safe Copy Patterns

# Carol always backs up K8s manifests before editing:
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/k8s/base$ cp web-deployment.yaml web-deployment.yaml.bak
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/k8s/base$ ls -l web-deployment*
-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 1892 Jun  3 16:30 web-deployment.yaml
-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 1892 Jun  3 16:30 web-deployment.yaml.bak

# Alice copies the production settings as a base for staging:
alice@dev-01:/lpj/anihpj$ cp settings.py settings_staging.py
alice@dev-01:/lpj/anihpj$ ls -l settings*
-rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 3241 Jun  3 08:00 settings.py
-rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 3241 Jun  3 16:32 settings_staging.py

Examples

Example 1: Backup a File Before Editing

Scenario: Carol always creates a .bak copy of any config file before making changes — cheap insurance.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

cd /lpj/k8s/base && cp secrets.yaml secrets.yaml.bak && ls -l secrets*

Output:

-rw------- 1 carol developers 234 Jun 2 10:20 secrets.yaml -rw------- 1 carol developers 234 Jun 3 16:35 secrets.yaml.bak

📝 What happened: An exact copy was created with a .bak extension. The content is identical (234 bytes each). Note: cp does NOT preserve the original timestamp — the backup has a new mtime. Use cp -p or cp -a to preserve timestamps.

Example 2: Recursive Directory Copy for K8s Backup

Scenario: Carol backs up the entire k8s directory before a major cluster upgrade.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

cp -a /lpj/k8s/ /lpj/ops/backups/k8s-$(date +%Y%m%d)/ && ls -d /lpj/ops/backups/k8s-*/

Output:

/lpj/ops/backups/k8s-20260603/

📝 What happened: cp -a (archive mode) recursively copied the entire k8s directory tree, preserving ALL attributes — permissions, ownership, timestamps, and symlinks. The backup directory name includes today's date via command substitution. This is a production-grade backup pattern.

Example 3: Copy Only Newer Files

Scenario: Alice updates only the Python files that have changed since the last sync to the staging environment.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

cp -uv /lpj/jobpost/*.py /lpj/ops/backups/code-sync/

Output:

'/lpj/jobpost/views.py' -> '/lpj/ops/backups/code-sync/views.py' '/lpj/jobpost/models.py' -> '/lpj/ops/backups/code-sync/models.py'

📝 What happened: -u (update) only copied files where the source was newer. Two files were updated; unchanged files were skipped. -v confirmed each copy. This is much faster than copying everything — critical for large codebases.

Example 4: Safe Copy Without Overwriting

Scenario: Dave copies a database config but wants to avoid accidentally overwriting an existing file.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

cp -n /lpj/k8s/base/configmap.yaml /lpj/ops/backups/configmap.yaml 2>&1; echo "Exit: $?"

Output:

Exit: 0

📝 What happened: -n (no-clobber) silently skipped the copy because the destination already exists. Exit code 0 (success) — no error, just skipped. This is safer than -i in scripts because it never prompts and never overwrites.

Example 5: Verbose Multi-File Copy to Backup

Scenario: Carol copies all Cilium network policies to a backup directory before testing new rules.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

cp -v /lpj/k8s/cilium/*.yaml /lpj/ops/backups/cilium-policies/

Output:

'/lpj/k8s/cilium/cnp-baseline.yaml' -> '/lpj/ops/backups/cilium-policies/cnp-baseline.yaml' '/lpj/k8s/cilium/cnp-l7.yaml' -> '/lpj/ops/backups/cilium-policies/cnp-l7.yaml' '/lpj/k8s/cilium/cnp-dns.yaml' -> '/lpj/ops/backups/cilium-policies/cnp-dns.yaml' '/lpj/k8s/cilium/ccnp-host-firewall.yaml' -> '/lpj/ops/backups/cilium-policies/ccnp-host-firewall.yaml' '/lpj/k8s/cilium/cidrgroup-vpn.yaml' -> '/lpj/ops/backups/cilium-policies/cidrgroup-vpn.yaml'

📝 What happened: Five YAML policy files were copied. -v confirmed each source → destination pair. The wildcard *.yaml expanded to all matching files. Always use -v when bulk-copying — it creates an audit trail of what was copied.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: cp -a is the recommended way to copy directories — it preserves permissions, ownership, and timestamps. cp -r copies recursively but may change ownership to the current user. Use cp -n for safe scripts, cp -u for incremental syncs. The LFCS exam may test overwrite behavior: -i prompts, -n skips, -f forces.

mv

MOVE File Operations Core LFCS Domain 1

Move or rename files and directories — the single command for both operations

mv serves double duty: it renames files within the same directory, and moves them between directories. Unlike cp, it does not create a duplicate — it relocates the original. On the same filesystem, this is near-instant (just updating directory entries).

For anihpj/jobpost, mv is used for:

  • Renaming deployment artifacts: mv deploy-v1.yaml deploy-v2.yaml
  • Archiving old logs: mv app.log /lpj/ops/backups/app.log.old
  • Reorganizing project structure during refactors
  • Moving build outputs to deployment directories

Syntax

mv [OPTIONS] SOURCE... DEST

# Common patterns:
mv oldname.txt newname.txt              # Rename a file
mv file.txt /target/directory/          # Move to another directory
mv *.log /lpj/ops/backups/              # Move all .log files
mv -i draft.txt final.txt               # Interactive (prompt before overwrite)
mv -v *.yaml /archive/                  # Verbose multi-file move

Parameters

FlagDescription
-f, --forceDo not prompt before overwriting
-i, --interactivePrompt before overwriting an existing file
-n, --no-clobberDo not overwrite an existing file
-u, --updateMove only when SOURCE is newer or destination is missing
-v, --verbosePrint each file as it is moved
-t, --target-directory=DIRMove all SOURCEs into DIRECTORY (alternative syntax)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — all files moved/renamed
1Error — source not found or permission denied

Examples

Example 1: Rename a Configuration File

Scenario: Carol renames the current deployment manifest to version it before creating a new one.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

cd /lpj/k8s/base && mv web-deployment.yaml web-deployment-v2.yaml && ls web-deployment*

Output:

web-deployment-v2.yaml

📝 What happened: The file was renamed in-place — no copy was created. The inode number stays the same if on the same filesystem. This is much faster than cp + rm and preserves all file attributes.

Example 2: Move Logs to Archive

Scenario: Alice moves old log files to the backup directory for long-term storage.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

mv /lpj/ops/logs/app.log /lpj/ops/backups/app.log.$(date +%Y%m%d) && ls -l /lpj/ops/backups/

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj anihpj 196542 Jun 3 14:23 app.log.20260603

📝 What happened: The log file was moved AND renamed in one operation — the destination path includes a date suffix via command substitution. The original location (/lpj/ops/logs/app.log) is now empty. This is the standard log rotation pattern.

Example 3: Move Multiple Files with Wildcard

Scenario: Carol moves all Cilium policy YAML files to a versioned archive directory.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

mkdir -p /lpj/ops/backups/cilium-v1 && mv -v /lpj/k8s/cilium/*.yaml /lpj/ops/backups/cilium-v1/

Output:

renamed '/lpj/k8s/cilium/cnp-baseline.yaml' -> '/lpj/ops/backups/cilium-v1/cnp-baseline.yaml' renamed '/lpj/k8s/cilium/cnp-l7.yaml' -> '/lpj/ops/backups/cilium-v1/cnp-l7.yaml' renamed '/lpj/k8s/cilium/cnp-dns.yaml' -> '/lpj/ops/backups/cilium-v1/cnp-dns.yaml'

📝 What happened: Three files were moved in one command. -v confirmed each move. The wildcard *.yaml expanded to all matching files. Note the verb "renamed" — on the same filesystem, mv is just a rename operation.

Example 4: Safe Move Without Overwriting

Scenario: Bob moves a config file but wants to avoid accidentally overwriting an existing destination.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

mv -n /lpj/anihpj/settings_staging.py /lpj/ops/backups/settings_staging.py && echo "Moved" || echo "Skipped (file exists)"

Output:

Skipped (file exists)

📝 What happened: mv -n refused to overwrite the existing destination. The || operator caught the non-zero exit and printed a friendly message. Use -n in scripts to prevent accidental data loss from overwrites.

Example 5: Move Only Newer Files

Scenario: Alice syncs updated Python files to a shared code directory, only moving files that are newer than what's already there.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

mv -uv /lpj/api/*.py /lpj/ops/backups/api-sync/

Output:

renamed '/lpj/api/views.py' -> '/lpj/ops/backups/api-sync/views.py'

📝 What happened: Only views.py was moved — it was newer than the destination copy. The other files (urls.py, serializers.py) were skipped because they hadn't changed. -u prevents unnecessary moves and preserves the older destination files.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: mv is both "rename" and "move" — same filesystem = instant rename (inode unchanged), different filesystem = copy+delete. Know the overwrite flags: -i prompts, -n skips, -f forces. mv preserves permissions and ownership when moving within the same filesystem.

rm

DELETE File Operations Core LFCS Domain 1

Remove files or directories — permanent deletion with no trash bin

rm permanently deletes files and directories. There is no undo, no recycle bin — once removed, recovery requires filesystem forensics. Use with caution and always verify before running with -rf.

For anihpj/jobpost, rm is used for:

  • Cleaning up temporary build artifacts: rm -rf /tmp/build-*
  • Removing old backup files: rm /lpj/ops/backups/daily/*.old
  • Deleting compiled Python cache: find /lpj -name "*.pyc" -delete
  • Clearing log files before a fresh deployment

Syntax

rm [OPTIONS] FILE...

# Common patterns:
rm file.txt                     # Remove a single file
rm -rf old_directory/           # Force-recursive delete (DANGEROUS)
rm -i *.log                     # Interactive — confirm each file
rm -v *.tmp                     # Verbose — print each deletion
find . -name "*.pyc" -delete    # Find + delete pattern (safer than rm -rf)

Parameters

FlagDescription
-f, --forceIgnore nonexistent files, never prompt
-iPrompt before every removal
-IPrompt once before removing more than 3 files or recursively
-r, -RRemove directories and their contents recursively
-d, --dirRemove empty directories
--one-file-systemWhen recursive, stay on the same filesystem (safety net)
-v, --verbosePrint each file as it is removed

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — all files removed

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Remove Files & Directories

Daily Workflow: Carol uses rm carefully to clean up temporary files, old backups, and stale deployment artifacts. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical rm usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ rm /lpj/ops/logs/app.log.3
carol@prod-api-01:~$ rm -r /lpj/k8s/base-backup/
carol@prod-api-01:~$ rm -f /lpj/ops/backups/temp/*.tmp
# Key locations where rm is used daily:
#  /lpj/ops/logs/        — Removing old rotated logs
#  /lpj/k8s/              — Cleaning temporary manifests
#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Purging expired backups

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Safe Deletion Patterns

# Carol always verifies before deleting — "measure twice, rm once":

-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 0 Jun  1 08:00 secrets.yaml.old
carol@prod-api-01:/lpj/ops/backups$ rm -v *.old
removed 'configmap.yaml.old'
removed 'secrets.yaml.old'

alice@dev-01:/lpj$ find /lpj -name "*.pyc"  # Verify: should return nothing

Examples

Example 1: Remove Old Backup Files Verbosely

Scenario: Carol cleans up backup files older than 7 days to free disk space.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

ls /lpj/ops/backups/daily/ && rm -v /lpj/ops/backups/daily/app.log.20260520

Output:

app.log.20260520 app.log.20260601 app.log.20260603 removed '/lpj/ops/backups/daily/app.log.20260520'

📝 What happened: Carol listed the directory FIRST to verify which file to delete, then used rm -v for confirmation. The old log from May 20 was removed while newer backups were kept. Always ls before rm when deleting by name.

Example 2: Interactive Removal for Safety

Scenario: Alice wants to remove old YAML files but wants to confirm each one to avoid mistakes.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

rm -i /lpj/ops/backups/cilium-v1/*.yaml

Output:

rm: remove regular file '/lpj/ops/backups/cilium-v1/cnp-baseline.yaml'? y rm: remove regular file '/lpj/ops/backups/cilium-v1/cnp-l7.yaml'? y rm: remove regular file '/lpj/ops/backups/cilium-v1/cnp-dns.yaml'? n

📝 What happened: -i prompted for each file. Alice answered y for baseline and L7 policies, but n for DNS policy — she realized she still needs it. Interactive mode prevents catastrophic bulk deletions. Type y or n and press Enter for each.

Example 3: Force-Recursive Directory Removal

Scenario: Carol removes an entire old deployment directory that's no longer needed.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

rm -rf /lpj/ops/backups/cilium-v1/ && ls /lpj/ops/backups/cilium-v1/ 2>&1

Output:

ls: cannot access '/lpj/ops/backups/cilium-v1/': No such file or directory

📝 What happened: rm -rf removed the entire directory tree — all files and subdirectories — without any prompts. The ls afterwards confirms the directory is gone. Warning: rm -rf is the most dangerous command in Linux. Always double-check the path before pressing Enter.

Example 4: Use find Instead of rm -rf for Safety

Scenario: Alice wants to delete all .pyc files safely — find first, then delete.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
    ├── 📄 models.py                    # Job, Company, Application
    ├── 📄 views.py                     # View logic (web + API)
    ├── 📄 urls.py                      # App URL routing
    ├── 📄 serializers.py               # DRF serializers
    ├── 📁 templates/jobpost/           # HTML templates
    ├── 📁 static/jobpost/              # CSS & JS
    └── 📁 migrations/                  # DB migrations

Command:

find /lpj -name "*.pyc" -type f -print -delete

Output:

/lpj/jobpost/migrations/__pycache__/0001_initial.cpython-312.pyc /lpj/anihpj/__pycache__/settings.cpython-312.pyc

📝 What happened: find -delete deleted each .pyc file AND printed its path (-print). This is much safer than rm -rf *.pyc because find targets specific files by pattern and type. The output serves as an audit trail of what was deleted.

Example 5: Dry-Run Deletion Pattern

Scenario: Carol wants to see what would be deleted before actually removing anything.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log
        ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
        └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log

Command:

find /lpj/ops/logs -name "*.log" -type f && echo "--- Above files would be deleted ---"

Output:

/lpj/ops/logs/app.log /lpj/ops/logs/error.log /lpj/ops/logs/access.log --- Above files would be deleted ---

📝 What happened: find listed all .log files without deleting them — a dry run. To actually delete, replace -print with -delete or pipe to xargs rm. Always dry-run before bulk deletions. This is the SRE golden rule for destructive operations.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: rm -rf is the single most dangerous command. The exam may test safe alternatives: rm -i (interactive), find ... -delete (targeted), and the "dry-run first" pattern (ls or find before rm). Know that rm -rf / will destroy your system — no confirmation, no undo.

rmdir

DELETE File Operations LFCS Domain 1

Remove empty directories — the safe alternative to rm -rf for directories

rmdir removes empty directories only — it will refuse to delete a directory that contains files. This makes it inherently safer than rm -rf for directory cleanup. Use -p to remove nested empty directories in one pass.

Syntax

rmdir [OPTIONS] DIRECTORY...

# Common patterns:
rmdir empty_dir                 # Remove a single empty directory
rmdir -p a/b/c                  # Remove c, then b (if empty), then a (if empty)
rmdir -v old_logs/              # Verbose — confirm each removal

Parameters

FlagDescription
-p, --parentsRemove DIRECTORY and its ancestors (each must be empty)
--ignore-fail-on-non-emptyDo not report failure if directory is not empty
-v, --verbosePrint a message for each removed directory

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — directory removed
1Error — not empty, not found, or permission denied

carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls /lpj/ops/temp
/ carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls /lpj/ops/backups/temp/daily/weekly//

#  /lpj/ops/temp
#  /lpj/ops/temp
# /lpj/ops/backups/temp/daily/weekly/

📄 Context — Directory Cleanup:

# Carol removes empty directories after a deployment cleanup:
# Empty directories in /lpj/ are safe to remove
# rmdir only works on EMPTY directories — safety feature

Examples

Example 1: Remove an Empty Directory

Scenario: Alice created a test directory that's no longer needed.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

mkdir /lpj/ops/temp && rmdir -v /lpj/ops/temp

Output:

rmdir: removing directory, '/lpj/ops/temp'

📝 What happened: The empty directory was removed with confirmation. If the directory had contained files, rmdir would have failed with "Directory not empty" — preventing accidental data loss.

Example 2: Remove Nested Empty Directories

Scenario: Carol cleans up an empty nested backup path.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

rmdir -pv /lpj/ops/backups/temp/daily/weekly/

Output:

rmdir: removing directory, '/lpj/ops/backups/temp/daily/weekly/' rmdir: removing directory, '/lpj/ops/backups/temp/daily/' rmdir: removing directory, '/lpj/ops/backups/temp/'

📝 What happened: rmdir -p removed weekly/, then checked if daily/ was now empty (it was), removed it, then checked temp/ (also empty) and removed it too. Each level must be empty for the cascade to continue.

Example 3: Clean Up All Empty Directories

Scenario: After a refactor, Carol wants to find and remove all empty directories in the ops folder.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

find /lpj/ops -type d -empty -print -delete

Output:

/lpj/ops/backups/weekly /lpj/ops/backups/temp

📝 What happened: find -type d -empty found empty directories, -print showed what was found, -delete removed them. Two orphaned directories were cleaned up. This is safer than manually hunting with rmdir — find does the work and only targets empty ones.

Example 4: Verbose Batch Removal with Brace Expansion

Scenario: Carol cleans up temp directories with confirmation of each removal.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

mkdir -p /lpj/ops/temp/{a,b,c} && rmdir -v /lpj/ops/temp/{a,b,c} && rmdir -v /lpj/ops/temp

Output:

rmdir: removing directory, '/lpj/ops/temp/a' rmdir: removing directory, '/lpj/ops/temp/b' rmdir: removing directory, '/lpj/ops/temp/c' rmdir: removing directory, '/lpj/ops/temp'

What happened: -v confirmed each directory removal. Brace expansion {a,b,c} created then removed three subdirectories. The final rmdir removed the now-empty parent. Use -v for audit trails.

Example 5: Ignore Non-Empty in Cleanup Scripts

Scenario: A cleanup script tries to remove directories but should not fail if they contain files.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

rmdir --ignore-fail-on-non-empty /lpj/ops/temp 2>&1; echo "Exit: $?"

Output:

Exit: 0

What happened: Even though the directory was not empty, the flag suppressed the error. Exit code 0 means the script continues without interruption. Use in cleanup scripts where partial success is acceptable.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: rmdir only removes EMPTY directories — it's the safe alternative to rm -rf. Combine with find . -type d -empty -delete to find and remove all empty directories. rmdir -p cascades upward through empty parents. --ignore-fail-on-non-empty is useful in scripts where partial success is acceptable.

ln

LINK File Operations Symlink LFCS Domain 1

Create hard and symbolic links — connect files and directories without duplication

ln creates links between files. Symbolic links (-s) are pointers to another path — like shortcuts. Hard links share the same inode — they are the same file under different names. Symlinks are more common and work across filesystems.

For anihpj/jobpost, ln is used for:

  • Creating shortcuts to frequently accessed directories: ln -s /lpj/k8s/base ~/k8s
  • Linking shared config files between environments
  • Creating version-independent paths: ln -s deploy-v2.yaml deploy.yaml

Syntax

ln [OPTIONS] TARGET [LINK_NAME]

# Common patterns:
ln -s /lpj/k8s/base ~/k8s-base        # Symbolic link (shortcut)
ln file.txt file-hardlink.txt          # Hard link (same inode)
ln -sf /lpj/k8s/base/deploy-v2.yaml /lpj/deploy.yaml  # Force symlink update

Parameters

FlagDescription
-s, --symbolicCreate a symbolic link instead of a hard link
-f, --forceRemove existing destination files before linking
-r, --relativeCreate symbolic links relative to the link location (portable)
-n, --no-dereferenceTreat symlink destination as a normal file (with -f)
-v, --verbosePrint the name of each linked file

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — link created
1Error — target exists, permission denied, or invalid paths

Examples

Example 1: Create a Convenience Symlink

Scenario: Carol creates a shortcut from her home directory to the K8s base manifests.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

ln -sv /lpj/k8s/base ~/k8s-base && ls -l ~/k8s-base

Output:

'/home/carol/k8s-base' -> '/lpj/k8s/base' lrwxrwxrwx 1 carol developers 15 Jun 3 16:45 /home/carol/k8s-base -> /lpj/k8s/base

📝 What happened: A symlink was created — the l at the start of permissions confirms it's a link. The arrow -> shows the target. Carol can now cd ~/k8s-base instead of typing the full path. Symlinks always show rwxrwxrwx (777) permissions — the actual permissions are on the target.

Example 2: Version-Independent Deploy Link

Scenario: Alice creates a deploy.yaml symlink that always points to the latest deployment version.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

cd /lpj/k8s/base && ln -sf web-deployment-v2.yaml web-deployment.yaml && ls -l web-deployment*

Output:

lrwxrwxrwx 1 alice developers 22 Jun 3 16:50 web-deployment.yaml -> web-deployment-v2.yaml -rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 1892 Jun 3 16:30 web-deployment-v2.yaml

📝 What happened: ln -sf created a symlink that points to the versioned file. When v3 is ready, just run ln -sf web-deployment-v3.yaml web-deployment.yaml — scripts referencing web-deployment.yaml automatically use the latest version without changes.

Example 3: Create a Relative Symlink for Portability

Scenario: Carol creates a relative symlink so the project works regardless of where it's cloned.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

cd /lpj && ln -sr k8s/base/secrets.yaml ops/secrets-link.yaml && ls -l /lpj/ops/secrets-link.yaml

Output:

lrwxrwxrwx 1 carol developers 25 Jun 3 17:00 /lpj/ops/secrets-link.yaml -> ../k8s/base/secrets.yaml

📝 What happened: -r created a RELATIVE symlink (../k8s/base/...) instead of absolute (/lpj/k8s/base/...). Relative symlinks survive when the project is moved or cloned to a different path — essential for portable project structures.

Example 4: Force-Update a Symlink

Scenario: Alice updates an existing symlink to point to a new settings file for staging.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
    ├── 📄 __init__.py
    ├── 📄 settings.py                  # Django settings
    ├── 📄 urls.py                      # Root URL routing
    ├── 📄 wsgi.py                      # WSGI entry for Gunicorn
    ├── 📄 asgi.py                      # ASGI entry
    └── 📄 celery.py                    # Celery config

Command:

ln -sf /lpj/anihpj/settings_staging.py /lpj/anihpj/settings_active.py && ls -l /lpj/anihpj/settings_active.py

Output:

lrwxrwxrwx 1 alice developers 32 Jun 3 17:05 /lpj/anihpj/settings_active.py -> /lpj/anihpj/settings_staging.py

📝 What happened: -sf removed the old symlink and created a new one in one atomic operation. The active settings now point to the staging variant. This pattern is used in deployment scripts to atomically switch configurations without editing files.

Example 5: Hard Link for Zero-Space Backup

Scenario: Dave creates a hard link — same data, zero extra disk space consumed.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

ln /lpj/ops/backups/db_dump.sql /lpj/ops/backups/db_latest.sql && stat -c "%i %h %n" /lpj/ops/backups/db_*.sql

Output:

524291 2 /lpj/ops/backups/db_dump.sql 524291 2 /lpj/ops/backups/db_latest.sql

What happened: Both files share inode 524291 with link count 2. Zero additional disk space. Deleting one file does not free the data until ALL hard links are removed. Hard links cannot span filesystems.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: Know the difference: hard links share the same inode (cannot span filesystems, cannot link directories), symlinks are path pointers (can span filesystems, can link directories). ls -l shows symlinks with l and ->. readlink displays a symlink's target. Use -r for relative symlinks (portable), -sf for atomic symlink updates. A broken symlink (dangling) shows in red in ls --color.

stat

INFO File Operations Metadata LFCS Domain 1

Display detailed file and filesystem metadata — more than ls -l shows

stat reveals everything about a file: inode number, block count, all three timestamps (access, modify, change), permissions in octal, SELinux context, and birth time. It's the go-to for debugging timestamp issues and verifying file identity.

Syntax

stat [OPTIONS] FILE...

# Common patterns:
stat file.txt                           # Full metadata dump
stat -c "%a %n" file.txt                # Octal permissions + name
stat -c "%y" file.txt                   # Human-readable mtime
stat -f /lpj/                           # Filesystem stats (not file)

Parameters

FlagDescription
-c FORMAT, --format=FORMATUse specified FORMAT instead of default (see man stat for format codes)
-f, --filesystemDisplay filesystem status instead of file status
-L, --dereferenceFollow symlinks and stat the target file

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — file info displayed
1Error — file not found or permission denied

Examples

Example 1: Full File Metadata

Scenario: Carol needs the complete metadata for a K8s secret to verify it hasn't been tampered with.

lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml

        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

stat /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

Output:

File: /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml Size: 234 Blocks: 8 IO Block: 4096 regular file Device: 801h/2049d Inode: 524289 Links: 1 Access: (0600/-rw-------) Uid: (1000/anihpj) Gid: (1001/developers) Access: 2026-06-03 08:00:00.000000000 +0000 Modify: 2026-06-02 10:20:00.000000000 +0000 Change: 2026-06-02 10:20:00.000000000 +0000

📝 What happened: stat revealed the inode (524289), block count (8), exact permissions in octal (0600) and symbolic (-rw-------), all three timestamps (access, modify, change), and ownership. When Modify ≠ Change times differ, only content changed — when they match, metadata also changed.

Example 2: Extract Specific Fields

Scenario: Eve audits file permissions across the project using custom stat format.

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/

        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

stat -c "%a %U:%G %n" /lpj/k8s/base/*.yaml

Output:

644 anihpj:developers /lpj/k8s/base/configmap.yaml 600 anihpj:developers /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml 644 anihpj:developers /lpj/k8s/base/web-deployment.yaml

📝 What happened: -c "%a %U:%G %n" formats output as: octal-permissions owner:group filename. secrets.yaml stands out with 600 — exactly what Eve expects. This format is script-friendly and easy to pipe to grep for finding files with unexpected permissions.

Scenario: Eve audits all deployment files to verify no unauthorized modifications.

/lpj/k8s/base/api-deployment.yaml | Owner: carol | Modified: 2026-06-02 | Perms: 644 /lpj/k8s/base/configmap.yaml | Owner: carol | Modified: 2026-06-02 | Perms: 644 /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml | Owner: carol | Modified: 2026-06-02 | Perms: 600 /lpj/k8s/base/web-deployment.yaml | Owner: carol | Modified: 2026-06-02 | Perms: 644

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: stat shows three timestamps: atime (last read), mtime (last content change), ctime (last metadata change). Key format codes: %a (octal permissions), %n (name), %y (human mtime), %s (size), %U (owner). Use stat -f for filesystem stats like free inodes. stat -c with custom format is script-friendly.

Determine file type by examining magic bytes — what kind of file is this?

PARSE File Operations Path Manipulation LFCS Domain 1

Extract the filename or directory portion from a full path — essential for shell scripts

basename strips the directory and optional suffix from a path, returning just the filename. dirname strips the last component, returning the directory portion. Both are fundamental for script path manipulation.

basename /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml .yaml # "secrets"

Parameters

FlagDescription
-aSupport multiple arguments
-s SUFFIXStrip trailing SUFFIX from filename
-zSeparate output with NULL instead of newline

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Invalid arguments

realpath / readlink

RESOLVE File Operations Path Resolution LFCS Domain 1

Resolve symlinks and canonicalize paths — get the real location of any file

realpath resolves all symlinks and returns the absolute canonical path. readlink displays the target of a symbolic link. Together they answer "where does this actually point?" — critical for debugging symlink chains.

Syntax

realpath [OPTIONS] PATH
readlink [OPTIONS] PATH

# Common patterns:
realpath ~/k8s-base                     # Resolve to /lpj/k8s/base
readlink ~/k8s-base                     # Show link target: /lpj/k8s/base
readlink -f /lpj/deploy.yaml            # Follow chain to final target

Parameters

FlagDescription
-eFile must exist (error if not)
-mFile doesn't need to exist
-sStrip . and .. but don't resolve links
-LFollow symlinks (default)
-PDon't follow symlinks to final component

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error

Example 2: Get Absolute Path of a Relative File
