└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

cd /lpj/k8s/base && realpath secrets.yaml

Output:

/lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

📝 What happened: realpath converted a relative path to an absolute one, resolving any symlinks in the process. This is essential for systemd unit files and scripts that require absolute paths — just use realpath instead of manually constructing them.

Example 3: Compute Relative Path Between Directories

Scenario: Carol needs a portable relative path for a Docker volume mount.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log
        ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
        └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log

Command:

realpath --relative-to=/lpj/k8s/base /lpj/ops/logs

Output:

../../ops/logs

What happened: --relative-to computed the shortest relative path. Going up twice reaches /lpj, then ops/logs descends. Essential for portable configs.

Example 4: Verify a Symlink Chain

Scenario: Carol traces a chain of symlinks to find where a file actually lives.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

ln -sf /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml /tmp/secret-link && realpath /tmp/secret-link

Output:

/lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

What happened: realpath resolved the symlink through all intermediate links to the final canonical path. Unlike readlink which shows one hop, realpath follows the entire chain. Essential for debugging complex symlink structures.

Example 5: Canonicalize Paths in Scripts

Scenario: Alice normalizes user-supplied paths to avoid ../../../ traversal attacks.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
    ├── 📁 base/                        # Core deployments & services
    ├── 📁 cilium/                      # Network policies
    ├── 📁 ingress/                     # Ingress & Gateway
    └── 📁 monitoring/                  # ServiceMonitor & dashboards

Command:

realpath /lpj/k8s/../k8s/./base/secrets.yaml

Output:

/lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

What happened: realpath normalized the messy path — /lpj/k8s/../k8s/. collapsed to /lpj/k8s. This is critical for security: always canonicalize user-supplied paths to prevent directory traversal attacks.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: realpath resolves ALL symlinks to the final canonical path. readlink -f does the same. readlink (no flags) shows the direct link target — useful for seeing intermediate symlink steps. realpath --relative-to=/lpj /lpj/k8s/base outputs k8s/base.

shred

SECURE File Operations Security LFCS Domain 1

Overwrite a file repeatedly to hide its contents — secure deletion beyond rm

shred overwrites a file's contents multiple times with random data before optionally deleting it. rm only removes the directory entry — the data remains on disk until overwritten. shred makes forensic recovery infeasible.

For anihpj/jobpost, shred is used by Eve to securely erase sensitive files like secrets backups and database dumps before disposal.

Syntax

shred [OPTIONS] FILE...

# Common patterns:
shred -u secrets.txt            # Overwrite and remove
shred -z -u sensitive.yaml      # Overwrite, zero final pass, remove
shred -n 5 -u file.txt          # 5 overwrite passes, then remove

Parameters

FlagDescription
-uTruncate and remove the file after overwriting
-z, --zeroAdd a final overwrite with zeros to hide shredding
-n N, --iterations=NOverwrite N times (default is 3)
-f, --forceChange permissions to allow writing if necessary

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — file overwritten and removed
1Error — permission denied or file not found

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — shred

Daily Workflow: Carol uses shred throughout the anihpj deployment workflow. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical shred usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls /lpj/ops/backups/secrets.yaml.bak
/ carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls /lpj/ops/backups/secrets.yaml.bak:/ carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls /lpj/ops/logs/access.log/ 
# Key locations where shred is used daily:
#  /lpj/ops/backups/secrets.yaml.bak
# /lpj/ops/backups/secrets.yaml.bak: # /lpj/ops/logs/access.log

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

Examples

Example 1: Securely Delete a Secrets Backup

Scenario: Eve securely erases a secrets backup file — rm is not enough for sensitive data.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

shred -z -u -v /lpj/ops/backups/secrets.yaml.bak

Output:

shred: /lpj/ops/backups/secrets.yaml.bak: pass 1/4 (random)... shred: /lpj/ops/backups/secrets.yaml.bak: pass 2/4 (random)... shred: /lpj/ops/backups/secrets.yaml.bak: pass 3/4 (random)... shred: /lpj/ops/backups/secrets.yaml.bak: pass 4/4 (000000)... shred: /lpj/ops/backups/secrets.yaml.bak: removing shred: /lpj/ops/backups/secrets.yaml.bak: renamed to 00000000 shred: /lpj/ops/backups/secrets.yaml.bak: removed

📝 What happened: Four passes: three with random data, one final pass with zeros (-z), then the file was removed (-u). The -v flag confirmed each pass. After this, forensic recovery of the original content is effectively impossible. Compare with rm which only unlinks the filename.

Example 2: Overwrite Without Deleting

Scenario: Carol wipes a log file's contents but keeps the file for the running app.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log
        ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
        └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log

Command:

shred -z -n 1 -v /lpj/ops/logs/access.log && wc -c /lpj/ops/logs/access.log

Output:

shred: /lpj/ops/logs/access.log: pass 1/2 (random)... shred: /lpj/ops/logs/access.log: pass 2/2 (000000)... 89432 /lpj/ops/logs/access.log

What happened: The file was overwritten but NOT deleted (no -u flag). It still exists with the same byte count but original content is gone. Useful when the app needs the file to exist.

Example 3: Shred Old Backups via find

Scenario: Eve securely erases backup files older than 30 days before disk disposal.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

find /lpj/ops/backups -type f -mtime +30 -exec shred -z -u -v {} \;

Output:

shred: /lpj/ops/backups/daily/app.log.20260501: pass 1/4 (random)... shred: /lpj/ops/backups/daily/app.log.20260501: removed

What happened: find -exec shred combined targeted file selection with secure deletion. Enterprise-grade data disposal — far beyond what rm provides.

Example 4: Shred with Custom Pass Count

Scenario: Eve uses 7 overwrite passes for highly sensitive encryption key material.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

shred -n 7 -z -u -v /lpj/ops/backups/encryption_key.bak

Output:

shred: /lpj/ops/backups/encryption_key.bak: pass 1/8 (random)... shred: /lpj/ops/backups/encryption_key.bak: pass 2/8 (random)... shred: /lpj/ops/backups/encryption_key.bak: pass 7/8 (random)... shred: /lpj/ops/backups/encryption_key.bak: pass 8/8 (000000)... shred: /lpj/ops/backups/encryption_key.bak: removed

What happened: -n 7 performed 7 random passes (instead of default 3), plus 1 zero pass from -z = 8 total. More passes = more secure but slower. 3 passes is sufficient for most use cases; 7+ is for cryptographic material.

Example 5: Shred Only Specific Bytes

Scenario: Carol only needs to destroy the header of a file while keeping the rest intact.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 backups/                     # tar / gzip / rsync targets

Command:

dd if=/dev/urandom of=/lpj/ops/backups/partial.bin bs=64 count=1 conv=notrunc 2>/dev/null && echo "First 64 bytes overwritten with random data"

Output:

First 64 bytes overwritten with random data

What happened: dd overwrote only the first 64 bytes with random data from /dev/urandom. conv=notrunc prevented truncation. shred always overwrites the entire file — use dd when you need partial overwrites.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: shred overwrites file content — but does NOT work on SSDs with wear-leveling or on journaling filesystems with data journaling. For SSDs, use full-disk encryption from the start. shred -u overwrites then deletes; shred -z adds a zero pass to hide that shredding occurred.

👁️ File Viewing & Editing

Commands for reading, searching, and displaying file contents without opening a full editor. Used constantly for configuration inspection, log analysis, and debugging in the anihpj/jobpost environment.

cat

VIEW File Viewing Core LFCS Domain 1

Concatenate and display file contents — the simplest way to view a whole file

cat reads files sequentially and writes their contents to stdout. It's the fastest way to dump a file's contents to the terminal, combine multiple files, or pipe data into another command.

For anihpj/jobpost, cat is used for:

  • Quickly inspecting K8s manifests: cat /lpj/k8s/base/web-deployment.yaml
  • Combining configuration snippets: cat header.yaml body.yaml > combined.yaml
  • Piping file contents to grep: cat app.log | grep ERROR

Syntax

cat [OPTIONS] [FILE...]

# Common patterns:
cat file.txt                    # Display entire file
cat -n settings.py              # Number all lines
cat header body footer > all    # Concatenate files into one
cat >> file.txt                 # Type input and append (Ctrl+D to finish)

Parameters

FlagDescription
-n, --numberNumber all output lines
-b, --number-nonblankNumber only non-empty lines
-s, --squeeze-blankSuppress repeated empty output lines
-A, --show-allShow all non-printing characters (same as -vET)
-E, --show-endsDisplay $ at end of each line
-T, --show-tabsDisplay TAB characters as ^I

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — file(s) displayed

Example 2: Number Lines While Viewing Code

Scenario: Alice needs line numbers to discuss a bug with Bob at a specific line.

    ├── 📄 __init__.py
    ├── 📄 views.py
    ├── 📄 urls.py

1 from rest_framework.views import APIView 2 from rest_framework.response import Response 3 from jobpost.models import Job 4 5 class JobListView(APIView): 6 def get(self, request): 7 jobs = Job.objects.filter(is_active=True)

Scenario: Carol combines multiple Cilium policy files into one for bulk review.

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/

Output:

157 /tmp/all-policies.yaml

📝 What happened: Two YAML files were concatenated into one. The > redirector wrote the combined output to a new file. 157 total lines. Use >> to append instead of overwrite.

Example 4: Reveal Hidden Characters

Scenario: Carol debugs a YAML that looks correct but fails to parse.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml

Command:

cat -A /lpj/k8s/base/configmap.yaml | head -3

Output:

apiVersion: v1^M$ kind: ConfigMap^M$ metadata:^M$

📝 What happened: cat -A revealed ^M$ (Windows \r\n line endings). ^M = carriage return, $ = end of line. Fix with dos2unix or sed -i 's/\r$//' file.

Example 5: Number Only Non-Empty Lines

Scenario: Alice numbers code for review but wants a cleaner look by skipping blank lines.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
    ├── 📄 __init__.py
    ├── 📄 views.py
    ├── 📄 urls.py
    └── 📄 serializers.py

Command:

cat -b /lpj/api/views.py

Output:

1 from rest_framework.views import APIView 2 from rest_framework.response import Response 3 from jobpost.models import Job 4 class JobListView(APIView): 5 def get(self, request): 6 jobs = Job.objects.filter(is_active=True)

What happened: cat -b numbered only non-blank lines, skipping the empty line 4. Compare with cat -n which numbers everything. Use -b for cleaner code review output where blank lines are just spacing.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: cat concatenates files in order. cat -n numbers all lines; cat -b numbers non-blank only. Never use cat file | grep pattern — grep pattern file is more efficient (useless use of cat). Use cat -A to reveal hidden characters (tabs, trailing spaces, carriage returns).

less

VIEW File Viewing Pager LFCS Domain 1

View file contents one page at a time with backward navigation — more than 'more'

less is a paginator — it displays files one screen at a time with full navigation (forward, backward, search). Unlike cat, it doesn't flood your terminal. The mantra: "less is more" — it has all of more's features and many more.

Syntax

less [OPTIONS] FILE

# Common patterns:
less /lpj/ops/logs/app.log         # Paginate a log file
less -N /lpj/api/views.py          # With line numbers
less +F /lpj/ops/logs/app.log      # Start in follow mode (like tail -f)
less +/ERROR app.log               # Jump to first "ERROR" match

Navigation Keys

KeyAction
Space / fForward one page
bBackward one page
gGo to beginning of file
GGo to end of file
/patternSearch forward for pattern
?patternSearch backward for pattern
nNext search match
NPrevious search match
FFollow mode (like tail -f; Ctrl+C to exit)
qQuit

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — pager exited normally

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: less is the standard pager on modern Linux. It replaces more — "less is more." Key flags: -N (line numbers), -S (chop long lines), +F (follow mode), +/pattern (start at match). Use less for any file too large for cat.

head

VIEW File Viewing LFCS Domain 1

Output the first part of files — default 10 lines. Quick peek at the top of any file.

FlagDescription
-n NUMPrint first NUM lines (default 10). Use -n -5 for all but last 5 lines
-c NUMPrint first NUM bytes
-qNever print file name headers (when multiple files)
-vAlways print file name headers

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — lines displayed

Example 5: Preview Binary File Headers

Scenario: Eve checks the first 64 bytes of a suspicious file in hex format.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

head -c 64 /lpj/ops/backups/unknown_file | xxd

Output:

00000000: 1f8b 0800 0000 0000 0003 6dd0 4d6e 8330 ..........m.Mn.0 00000010: 1006 6034 8ea2 282b 56e2 02dc 802a ea31 ..`4..(+V....*.1 00000020: 5aa7 ead2 fbe9 082d 9e0b f6fb 46f2 0000 Z......-....F... 00000030: 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 ................

What happened: head -c 64 read the first 64 bytes of a binary file, then piped to xxd for hex display. The bytes 1f 8b at the start are the gzip magic number — confirming this is a compressed archive. head -c is essential for inspecting binary file headers.

Example 5: Negative Line Count (All But Last N)

📄 Context — Trim Trailing Lines:

# head -n -N prints all lines EXCEPT the last N
# head -n -1 file = all lines except the last
# Useful for: removing footers, trailing blank lines, summary rows
# tail -n +N does the opposite (skip first N-1 lines)

Scenario: Carol removes the trailing summary line from a report.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/

├── 📄 Dockerfile

├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

seq 10 | head -n -2

Output:

1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8

📝 What happened: All lines printed except the last 2. head -n -1 removes just the last line. head -n -0 prints all lines (equivalent to cat). The negative count is a GNU extension — not available on all Unix systems.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: head shows the TOP of files. Use -n N for line count, -c N for byte count. Combine with tail: head -n 50 file | tail -n 10 shows lines 41-50. Negative line counts (head -n -5) show all EXCEPT the last 5 lines.

tail

VIEW File Viewing Log Monitoring LFCS Domain 1

Output the last part of files — indispensable for real-time log monitoring with -f

tail is the SRE's best friend. The -f (follow) flag streams new lines as they're written — the standard tool for watching logs during deployments, incident response, and debugging. tail -F even reconnects if the file is rotated.

For anihpj/jobpost, Carol uses tail -f constantly during deployments to watch for errors in real-time.

Syntax

tail [OPTIONS] [FILE...]

# Common patterns:
tail app.log                        # Last 10 lines (default)
tail -n 100 app.log                 # Last 100 lines
tail -f /lpj/ops/logs/app.log       # Follow: watch in real time (Ctrl+C to stop)
tail -F /lpj/ops/logs/app.log       # Follow by name (survive log rotation)
tail -n +50 file.txt                # Lines starting from line 50

Parameters

FlagDescription
-n NUMPrint last NUM lines (default 10). -n +50 starts from line 50
-c NUMPrint last NUM bytes
-f, --followOutput appended data as the file grows (real-time monitoring)
-FSame as --follow=name --retry — survives log rotation
-qNever print file name headers

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — output displayed
1Error — file not found or permission denied

        ├── 📄 app.log

📝 What happened: head -60 | tail -10 = lines 51-60. Only the first 60 lines are read — efficient on multi-gigabyte logs. Use sed -n '51,60p' as an alternative for explicit line ranges.

Example 5: Follow by Name for Log Rotation

Scenario: Carol monitors a log that gets rotated nightly — tail -F survives the rotation.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log

Command:

tail -F /lpj/ops/logs/app.log

Output:

# Watching app.log in real time... tail: '/lpj/ops/logs/app.log' has been replaced; following end of new file # tail automatically reopens the new file and continues following

What happened: When logrotate moved app.log to app.log.1 and created a new app.log, tail -F detected the replacement and reopened the new file. tail -f (lowercase) would have silently stopped producing output because it follows the inode, not the name.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: tail -f is the most-used flag for real-time monitoring. tail -F survives log rotation (follows by name, not inode). Use -n +50 to show lines starting from line 50, or -c for byte-based tailing. Ctrl+C stops following.

tac

VIEW File Viewing Reverse

Concatenate and print files in reverse — "cat" spelled backward, and that's what it does

tac outputs a file with lines in reverse order — last line first, first line last. Surprisingly useful for log analysis (newest entries at top) and processing timestamp-ordered data.

Syntax

tac FILE

# Common patterns:
tac app.log                     # Reverse file: last line first
tac app.log | head -5           # 5 oldest lines in reverse order

Parameters

FlagDescription
-bAttach separator before records
-s SEPRecord separator (default: newline)
-rInterpret separator as regex

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Output:

2026-06-03 16:50:05 INFO Processing job listing request 2026-06-03 16:50:10 INFO Request completed in 45ms — 200 OK 2026-06-03 16:50:12 INFO Health check passed 2026-06-03 16:50:15 INFO Scheduled task: cleanup_expired_jobs 2026-06-03 16:50:20 INFO Cache invalidated for key: home:jobs

What happened: Double tac — reverse, take top 5, reverse back — gives the last 5 lines in their original order. This is equivalent to tail -5 but demonstrates how tac can be used as a processing step in pipelines.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: rev reverses characters per line; tac reverses line order. They are complementary: tac file | rev reverses both. Use rev with cut to extract the last field when delimiters are inconsistent: rev file | cut -d' ' -f1 | rev = last space-delimited field.

xxd

VIEW File Viewing Hex Dump

Make a hex dump or do the reverse — view binary files as hexadecimal

xxd displays file contents in hexadecimal format — essential for inspecting binary files, checking file signatures (magic bytes), and debugging encoding issues. It can also convert hex back to binary.

Syntax

xxd [OPTIONS] [FILE]

# Common patterns:
xxd file.bin                        # Hex dump with offsets
xxd -l 64 file.bin                  # First 64 bytes only
xxd -p file.bin                     # Plain hex dump (no offsets or ASCII)
echo "48656c6c6f" | xxd -r -p       # Convert hex back to text ("Hello")

Parameters

FlagDescription
-rReverse — convert hex dump back to binary
-pPlain hex dump (no offsets or ASCII)
-c NFormat N bytes per line (default 16)
-g NGroup N bytes together
-s NSkip N bytes before starting
-l NStop after N bytes
-iC include file output style

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error reading input

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: xxd is the standard hex dump tool. xxd -l N limits output to N bytes. xxd -p gives plain hex (no offsets). xxd -r -p converts hex back to binary. Use xxd to check file signatures, debug encoding, and inspect binary data. hexdump -C is an alternative with different formatting.

hexdump

VIEW File Viewing Hex Dump

Display file contents in hexadecimal, decimal, octal, or ASCII — alternative to xxd

hexdump is a flexible binary file viewer. The -C (canonical) format is the most readable — it shows hex + ASCII side by side, similar to xxd's default output. Available on most systems as part of bsdmainutils.

Syntax

hexdump [OPTIONS] FILE

# Common patterns:
hexdump -C file.bin                 # Canonical hex+ASCII display
hexdump -C -n 64 file.bin           # First 64 bytes
hexdump -C /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml | head

Parameters

FlagDescription
-CCanonical hex+ASCII display
-n NFirst N bytes only
-s NSkip N bytes before displaying

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

🔐 File Permissions

Commands for managing file and directory permissions, ownership, and access control. Essential for security hardening, multi-user environments, and ensuring the anihpj/jobpost deployment follows the principle of least privilege.

chmod

PERMISSIONS File Permissions Security LFCS Domain 3

Change file mode bits — set read, write, and execute permissions for owner, group, and others

chmod is the fundamental permission command. It sets who can read (r), write (w), and execute (x) a file or directory. Permissions can be specified in octal (e.g., 644) or symbolic notation (e.g., u+x).

For anihpj/jobpost, chmod is used for:

  • Restricting K8s secrets: chmod 600 /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml
  • Making scripts executable: chmod +x /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh
  • Securing sensitive directories: chmod 700 /lpj/ops/audit/
  • Setting deployment files read-only: chmod 444 /lpj/k8s/base/configmap.yaml

Syntax

chmod [OPTIONS] MODE FILE...

# Octal (numeric) notation:
chmod 644 file.txt          # rw-r--r--  (owner rw, group r, others r)
chmod 755 script.sh         # rwxr-xr-x  (owner rwx, group rx, others rx)
chmod 600 secrets.yaml      # rw-------  (owner rw only)

# Symbolic notation:
chmod u+x deploy.sh         # Add execute for user (owner)
chmod g-w file.txt          # Remove write for group
chmod o= file.txt           # Remove all permissions for others
chmod a+r *.yaml            # Add read for all (user+group+others)

Parameters

Flag / ModeDescription
-R, --recursiveChange files and directories recursively
-v, --verboseOutput a diagnostic for every file processed
-c, --changesLike verbose but report only when a change is made
uUser (owner) — symbolic target
gGroup — symbolic target
oOthers — symbolic target
aAll (u+g+o) — symbolic target
+Add permission — symbolic operator
-Remove permission — symbolic operator
=Set exact permission — symbolic operator

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — permissions changed

Examples

Example 1: Restrict K8s Secrets to Owner-Only

Scenario: Eve found secrets.yaml with world-readable permissions — a critical security risk.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

ls -l /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml && chmod 600 /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml && ls -l /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 234 Jun 2 10:20 /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml -rw------- 1 carol developers 234 Jun 2 10:20 /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

What happened: Permissions changed from 644 (world-readable) to 600 (owner-only). Octal 600 = rw-------: owner can read+write, group and others have NO access. K8s secrets, SSH keys, and .env files should always be 600 or 400.

Example 2: Make Scripts Executable

Scenario: Carol created a new deployment script but it won't run because it lacks execute permission.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh
    ├── 📄 connectivity-test.sh
    └── 📄 deploy.sh

Command:

ls -l /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh && chmod +x /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh && ls -l /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 1892 Jun 4 09:00 /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh -rwxr-xr-x 1 carol developers 1892 Jun 4 09:00 /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh

What happened: chmod +x added execute permission for all three levels (user, group, others). The permissions went from rw-r--r-- (644) to rwxr-xr-x (755). Now ./deploy.sh will run directly.

Example 3: Recursive Permission Change

Scenario: Carol ensures all files in the scripts directory are executable after a mass copy.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh
    ├── 📄 connectivity-test.sh
    └── 📄 deploy.sh

Command:

chmod -R +x /lpj/scripts/ && ls -l /lpj/scripts/

Output:

-rwxr-xr-x 1 carol developers 2147 Jun 4 09:00 cilium-setup.sh -rwxr-xr-x 1 carol developers 1234 Jun 4 09:00 connectivity-test.sh -rwxr-xr-x 1 carol developers 1892 Jun 4 09:00 deploy.sh

What happened: -R recursively applied +x to all files in /lpj/scripts/. All three scripts are now executable. Use -R carefully — it affects every file in the tree including non-scripts.

Example 4: Symbolic Notation — Remove Group Write

Scenario: Alice removes group write access from a config file to prevent accidental edits by other developers.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
    ├── 📄 __init__.py
    ├── 📄 settings.py
    ├── 📄 urls.py
    ├── 📄 wsgi.py
    ├── 📄 asgi.py
    └── 📄 celery.py

Command:

chmod g-w /lpj/anihpj/settings.py && ls -l /lpj/anihpj/settings.py

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 3241 Jun 4 09:00 /lpj/anihpj/settings.py

What happened: g-w removed write permission from the group. The group can still read but cannot modify. Symbolic notation is more readable than octal when you only want to change one permission level.

Example 5: Set Exact Permissions with =

Scenario: Eve locks down a directory so only the owner can access it — no group, no others.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

chmod go= /lpj/ops/audit && ls -ld /lpj/ops/audit

Output:

drwx------ 2 eve auditors 4096 Jun 4 09:00 /lpj/ops/audit

What happened: go= set group and others permissions to nothing — effectively chmod 700. The directory is now only accessible by eve. Use = when you want to set an exact permission mask regardless of what was there before.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: Octal permissions: read=4, write=2, execute=1. Sum them: rwx=7, rw-=6, r-x=5, r--=4. chmod 644 = owner rw, group r, others r. Symbolic: u/g/o/a + +/-/= + r/w/x. chmod -R is recursive. The LFCS exam WILL test permission interpretation — know the ls -l output cold.

chown

OWNERSHIP File Permissions Security LFCS Domain 3

Change file owner and group — transfer ownership of files and directories

chown changes who owns a file. Only root can change ownership (for security, users cannot give away their files). The colon syntax (user:group) changes both owner and group in one command.

For anihpj/jobpost, Carol uses chown to ensure the anihpj runtime user owns all project files after a deployment.

Syntax

chown [OPTIONS] OWNER[:GROUP] FILE...

# Common patterns:
chown anihpj file.txt                   # Change owner only
chown anihpj:developers file.txt        # Change owner AND group
chown :developers file.txt              # Change group only (same as chgrp)
chown -R anihpj:anihpj /lpj/jobpost/    # Recursive ownership change

Parameters

FlagDescription
-R, --recursiveChange files and directories recursively
-v, --verboseOutput a diagnostic for every file processed
-c, --changesReport only when a change is made
--reference=RFILEUse RFILE's owner and group rather than specifying values

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — ownership changed
1Error — invalid user, permission denied, or file not found

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Change Ownership

Daily Workflow: Carol uses chown to transfer file ownership between users and ensure correct service account permissions on deployment files. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo chown anihpj:developers /lpj/k8s/base/*.yaml
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /lpj/jobpost/static/
# Key locations where chown is used daily:

#  /lpj/ops/logs/         — Application logs
#  /lpj/scripts/          — Deployment scripts

Examples

Example 1: Transfer K8s Manifests to Runtime User

Scenario: Carol changes ownership of all K8s manifests from root to the anihpj runtime user.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

sudo chown -R anihpj:developers /lpj/k8s/ && ls -l /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

Output:

-rw------- 1 anihpj developers 234 Jun 2 10:20 /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

What happened: chown -R recursively changed both owner (to anihpj) and group (to developers) for every file under /lpj/k8s/. The runtime user now owns the manifests — required for kubectl apply.

Example 2: Copy Ownership from Reference File

Scenario: Alice created a new config and wants it to match the ownership of the existing one.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
    ├── 📄 __init__.py
    ├── 📄 settings.py
    ├── 📄 urls.py
    ├── 📄 wsgi.py
    ├── 📄 asgi.py
    └── 📄 celery.py

Command:

sudo chown --reference=/lpj/anihpj/settings.py /lpj/anihpj/settings_staging.py && ls -l /lpj/anihpj/settings*

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 3241 Jun 4 09:00 /lpj/anihpj/settings.py -rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 2980 Jun 4 09:00 /lpj/anihpj/settings_staging.py

What happened: --reference copied the owner and group from settings.py to settings_staging.py. Both are now alice:developers. This avoids typos when setting ownership manually.

Example 3: Change Group-Only with chown

Scenario: Carol changes only the group on a file using the chown colon syntax.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh
    ├── 📄 connectivity-test.sh
    └── 📄 deploy.sh

Command:

sudo chown :ops /lpj/scripts/cilium-setup.sh && ls -l /lpj/scripts/cilium-setup.sh

Output:

-rwxr-xr-x 1 carol ops 2147 Jun 4 09:00 /lpj/scripts/cilium-setup.sh

What happened: chown :ops changed only the group (to ops), leaving the owner (carol) untouched. The colon-before-group syntax makes chown also function as chgrp — useful in scripts where one command handles both cases.

Example 4: Recursive Ownership Fix After Git Clone

Scenario: Alice cloned the project as root and needs to fix ownership for the runtime user.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
    ├── 📄 models.py
    ├── 📄 views.py
    ├── 📄 urls.py
    ├── 📄 serializers.py
    ├── 📄 admin.py
    ├── 📄 tests.py
    ├── 📁 templates/jobpost/
    ├── 📁 static/jobpost/
    └── 📁 migrations/

Command:

sudo chown -Rv anihpj:developers /lpj/jobpost/ | tail -5

Output:

changed ownership of '/lpj/jobpost/views.py' from root:root to anihpj:developers changed ownership of '/lpj/jobpost/models.py' from root:root to anihpj:developers changed ownership of '/lpj/jobpost/admin.py' from root:root to anihpj:developers

What happened: chown -Rv recursively changed ownership and reported every change. Files that were root:root are now anihpj:developers. The -v flag creates an audit trail — essential for verifying the fix was applied.

Example 5: Verify Ownership Before and After

Scenario: Carol audits file ownership before and after a deployment to ensure no drift.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

stat -c "%U:%G %n" /lpj/k8s/base/*.yaml && sudo chown -R anihpj:developers /lpj/k8s/base/ && echo "---" && stat -c "%U:%G %n" /lpj/k8s/base/*.yaml

Output:

root:root /lpj/k8s/base/api-deployment.yaml root:root /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml --- anihpj:developers /lpj/k8s/base/api-deployment.yaml anihpj:developers /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

What happened: Before: root:root (wrong — files cloned as root). After: anihpj:developers (correct). Using stat -c before and after creates an audit trail proving the ownership fix. This pattern is essential for compliance and post-deployment verification.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: Only root can use chown. The colon syntax user:group changes both at once. chown :group file changes only the group. chown -R is recursive. --reference=RFILE copies ownership from another file — great for consistency.

chgrp

GROUP File Permissions LFCS Domain 3

Change group ownership — assign files to a different group

chgrp changes only the group ownership of a file. Unlike chown, regular users can use chgrp to change a file to any group they are a member of.

Syntax

chgrp [OPTIONS] GROUP FILE...

# Common patterns:
chgrp developers file.txt               # Change group to developers
chgrp -R ops /lpj/scripts/              # Recursive group change
chgrp --reference=model.txt new.txt     # Copy group from reference

Parameters

FlagDescription
-RRecursive — change group on all files under directory
-vVerbose — show each file changed
-cReport only when a change is made
--reference=RFILEUse RFILE's group instead of specifying

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — ownership changed
1Error — invalid user, permission denied, or file not found

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Permission denied or invalid group

Example 1: Share Files with Operations Team

Example 5: Reference-Based Group Change

📄 Context — Match Existing Permissions:

# --reference=RFILE copies group from reference file

Scenario: Alice matches a new file's group to an existing file.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
    ├── 📄 models.py
    ├── 📄 views.py

-rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 1024 Jun 4 10:30 /lpj/jobpost/new_models.py

📝 What happened: new_models.py now has the same group as models.py. --reference copies just the group. Use when you know a correct file exists but don't remember the group name. Works for chown and chmod too.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: chgrp changes only the group. Regular users can use it for groups they belong to. chgrp -R is recursive. chown user:group does both in one command — use whichever is clearer for your use case.

umask

DEFAULT File Permissions Shell Builtin LFCS Domain 3

Set default file creation permissions — control what permissions new files get

umask is a shell builtin that defines the permission bits to REMOVE from newly created files and directories. It's a mask: a bit set in umask means that permission will NOT be granted. Default umask is 022 (files get 644, dirs get 755).

Syntax

umask [MASK]                    # Set umask (no dash)
umask -S                        # Show in symbolic notation
umask                           # Show current umask (no args)

# Common values:
umask 022   # Files: 644 (rw-r--r--), Dirs: 755 (rwxr-xr-x)  [DEFAULT]
umask 002   # Files: 664 (rw-rw-r--), Dirs: 775 (rwxrwxr-x)  [group-writable]
umask 077   # Files: 600 (rw-------), Dirs: 700 (rwx------)  [fully private]

Parameters

FlagDescription
-SSymbolic notation (u=rwx,g=rx,o=rx)
-pOutput reusable for shell (umask 0022)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
022Default — owner rwx, group/other rx
002Shared — group also gets write
077Private — only owner can access

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Default Permissions

Daily Workflow: Carol uses umask to set default permission masks for new files and directories. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical umask usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ umask 027
carol@prod-api-01:~$ touch /lpj/ops/logs/new.log && ls -la /lpj/ops/logs/new.log
# Key locations where umask is used daily:
#  /lpj/ops/logs/        — Restricted log creation
#  /lpj/k8s/base/         — Group-readable manifests

Examples

Example 1: Check Current umask

Scenario: Carol verifies the default permissions that new files will receive.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/
├── 📁 jobpost/
├── 📁 api/
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml
├── 📄 requirements.txt
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/
├── 📁 ops/
└── 📁 scripts/

Command:

umask && umask -S

Output:

0022 u=rwx,g=rx,o=rx

What happened: The umask is 022 — meaning group and others will NOT have write permission. New files get 666 - 022 = 644 (rw-r--r--). New directories get 777 - 022 = 755 (rwxr-xr-x). The symbolic form confirms: user=rwx, group=rx, others=rx.

Example 2: Set Strict umask for Sensitive Work

Scenario: Eve sets a strict umask before creating sensitive audit files.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

umask 077 && touch /lpj/ops/audit/sensitive.txt && ls -l /lpj/ops/audit/sensitive.txt

Output:

-rw------- 1 eve auditors 0 Jun 4 09:00 /lpj/ops/audit/sensitive.txt

What happened: With umask 077, ALL group and other permissions are stripped. The new file has 600 (owner-only). This is the most secure default — use it when handling secrets, keys, or PII data.

Example 3: Group-Collaborative umask

Scenario: Alice sets a permissive umask so the developers group can edit shared files.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
    ├── 📄 models.py
    ├── 📄 views.py
    ├── 📄 urls.py
    ├── 📄 serializers.py
    ├── 📄 admin.py
    ├── 📄 tests.py
    ├── 📁 templates/jobpost/
    ├── 📁 static/jobpost/
    └── 📁 migrations/

Command:

umask 002 && touch /lpj/jobpost/shared_config.py && ls -l /lpj/jobpost/shared_config.py

Output:

-rw-rw-r-- 1 alice developers 0 Jun 4 09:00 /lpj/jobpost/shared_config.py

What happened: umask 002 leaves group-write enabled. New files get 664 (rw-rw-r--). Group members can now edit this file. This is ideal for shared project directories where multiple developers collaborate.

Example 4: Persist umask in Shell Config

Scenario: Carol sets a permanent umask for all users by adding it to /etc/profile.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/
├── 📁 jobpost/
├── 📁 api/
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml
├── 📄 requirements.txt
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/
├── 📁 ops/
└── 📁 scripts/

Command:

echo "umask 027" | sudo tee -a /etc/profile.d/anihpj-umask.sh && source /etc/profile.d/anihpj-umask.sh && umask

Output:

0027

What happened: umask 027 is now set: files get 640 (owner rw, group r), dirs get 750 (owner rwx, group rx, others nothing). This is more secure than the default 022 — group cannot read by default, others get nothing. Persisted in a profile.d script for all users.

Example 5: Test umask with New File Creation

Scenario: Eve demonstrates the effect of different umask values on newly created files.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/
├── 📁 jobpost/
├── 📁 api/
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 Dockerfile.dev
├── 📄 docker-compose.yml
├── 📄 requirements.txt
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/
├── 📁 ops/
└── 📁 scripts/

Command:

umask 077 && touch /tmp/test_077 && umask 002 && touch /tmp/test_002 && umask 022 && touch /tmp/test_022 && ls -l /tmp/test_*

Output:

-rw-rw-r-- 1 eve eve 0 Jun 4 09:00 /tmp/test_002 -rw-r--r-- 1 eve eve 0 Jun 4 09:00 /tmp/test_022 -rw------- 1 eve eve 0 Jun 4 09:00 /tmp/test_077

What happened: Three files created under different umasks: 077 gave 600 (private), 002 gave 664 (group-writable), 022 gave 644 (default). This side-by-side comparison clearly shows how umask subtracts from 666. The more restrictive the umask, the fewer permissions new files get.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: umask is the complement: permissions = base - umask. Files start at 666, directories at 777. umask 022 → files 644, dirs 755. umask 077 → files 600, dirs 700. umask is a shell builtin — no man page, use help umask. Set it in ~/.bashrc for persistence.

getfacl

ACL File Permissions Access Control Lists LFCS Domain 3

Get file access control lists — view extended permissions beyond the standard rwx model

getfacl displays Access Control Lists (ACLs) — a finer-grained permission system that allows multiple users and groups to have different permissions on the same file, beyond the traditional owner-group-others model.

Syntax

getfacl [OPTIONS] FILE...

# Common patterns:
getfacl file.txt                # Show ACL for a file
getfacl -R /lpj/k8s/            # Recursive ACL listing

Parameters

FlagDescription
-RRecursive — show ACLs for all files under directory
-tTabular output format
-dSkip header line (script-friendly)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — View ACLs

Daily Workflow: Carol uses getfacl to audit fine-grained ACL permissions for compliance. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical getfacl usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ getfacl /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml
carol@prod-api-01:~$ getfacl -R /lpj/jobpost/ | grep user:
# Key locations where getfacl is used daily:
#  /lpj/k8s/base/        — ACL audit on secrets
#  /lpj/jobpost/           — Per-user ACL verification

Examples

Example 1: Check ACL on K8s Secrets

Scenario: Eve checks if any extended ACLs have been set on the secrets file.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

getfacl /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

Output:

# file: /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml # owner: anihpj # group: developers user::rw- group::--- other::---

What happened: No extended ACL entries — only the standard POSIX permissions are shown. The user::rw- means the owner has read+write. If extended ACLs existed, you would see additional user:name:rwx or group:name:rwx entries.

Example 2: Recursive ACL Audit

Scenario: Eve audits all files in k8s/ for unexpected extended ACLs.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml

        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

getfacl -R /lpj/k8s/base/ 2>/dev/null | grep -E "^# file:|user:(?!:)"

Output:

# file: /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

What happened: Only the standard file header was found — no named user or group entries. This confirms no extended ACLs exist on any k8s base files. Regular ls -l would not reveal this; getfacl -R is necessary for a thorough ACL audit.

ACL snapshot saved

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: ACLs are shown by a + at the end of ls -l permissions (e.g., -rw-rwxr--+). getfacl reads them; setfacl writes them. ACLs allow per-user permissions beyond owner/group/others — essential for complex multi-team environments.

setfacl

ACL File Permissions Access Control Lists LFCS Domain 3

Set file access control lists — grant fine-grained permissions to specific users and groups

setfacl modifies ACLs, allowing you to grant read, write, or execute to specific users or groups beyond the standard owner-group-others model. Requires filesystem ACL support (enabled by default on ext4, xfs).

Syntax

setfacl [OPTIONS] ACL FILE...

# Common patterns:
setfacl -m u:eve:r secrets.yaml     # Grant eve read access
setfacl -m g:auditors:rx /lpj/ops/  # Grant auditors group read+execute
setfacl -x u:eve file.txt           # Remove eve's ACL entry
setfacl -b file.txt                 # Remove all extended ACLs

Parameters

FlagDescription
-m ACLModify ACL (add/change entry)
-x ACLRemove specific ACL entry
-bRemove all extended ACL entries
-RRecursive — apply to directory tree
-dSet default ACL for new files in directory
-kRemove default ACL

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Invalid syntax or permission denied

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Set ACLs

Daily Workflow: Carol uses setfacl to grant specific user access beyond standard groups. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical setfacl usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ setfacl -m u:eve:r /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml
carol@prod-api-01:~$ setfacl -m g:auditors:rx /lpj/ops/logs/
# Key locations where setfacl is used daily:
#  /lpj/k8s/base/        — Auditor read access
#  /lpj/ops/logs/          — Audit team log access

Examples

Example 1: Grant Specific User Access to Secrets

Scenario: Carol grants Eve (auditor) read-only access to secrets.yaml without changing group ownership.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

setfacl -m u:eve:r /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml && getfacl /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

Output:

# file: /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml # owner: anihpj # group: developers user::rw- user:eve:r-- group::--- mask::r-- other::---

What happened: Eve now has read access to secrets.yaml WITHOUT being the owner or in the group. The ACL shows user:eve:r--. The mask::r-- limits the maximum permission any named user/group can have.

Example 2: Grant Group Access to Directory

Scenario: Alice gives the auditors group read and execute on the k8s directory for inspection.

📁 Directory Snippet:

    ├── 📁 base/
    ├── 📁 cilium/
    ├── 📁 ingress/
    └── 📁 monitoring/

Command:

setfacl -m g:auditors:rx /lpj/k8s/ && getfacl /lpj/k8s/

Output:

# file: /lpj/k8s/ # owner: carol # group: developers user::rwx group::r-x group:auditors:r-x mask::r-x other::---

What happened: The auditors group now has read+execute on /lpj/k8s/. They can list its contents and traverse into subdirectories. This is more precise than adding them to the developers group — least privilege principle.

Output:

# file: /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml # owner: anihpj # group: developers user::rw- group::--- mask::--- other::---

What happened: Eve's ACL entry was removed. The file is back to standard POSIX permissions. The mask adjusted automatically. Always clean up ACLs after temporary access grants — stale ACLs are a security risk.

Example 4: Set Default ACL for New Files

Scenario: Alice sets a default ACL so new files in the shared directory automatically inherit group-write.

What happened: The default: entries mean new files and directories created inside /lpj/jobpost/ will automatically inherit these ACLs. The developers group will get rwx on all new items. This is the standard pattern for shared project directories.

Scenario: Eve audits all ACLs in the jobpost directory.

Scenario: Alice verifies bob's effective permissions on a file.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: setfacl -m modifies ACLs, -x removes entries, -b removes all. The mask limits maximum permissions for named users/groups. ACLs require filesystem support (mount with acl option). A + in ls -l output indicates ACLs are present.

lsattr

ATTR File Permissions Extended Attributes

List file attributes on ext filesystems — immutable, append-only, and more

lsattr displays extended filesystem attributes that go beyond standard permissions — like making a file immutable (cannot be modified even by root) or append-only.

Syntax

lsattr [OPTIONS] [FILE...]

# Common patterns:
lsattr file.txt                 # Show attributes
lsattr -R /lpj/k8s/             # Recursive
lsattr -d /lpj/k8s/             # Show directory attributes (not contents)

Parameters

FlagDescription
-RRecursive — show attributes for directory tree
-aInclude hidden files (names starting with .)
-dShow directory attributes, not contents
-vShow file version/generation number

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error

Common Attributes

FlagDescription
iImmutable — file cannot be modified, deleted, or renamed (even by root)
aAppend-only — file can only be appended to, not overwritten
eExtent format — file uses extents for mapping (default on ext4)

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — File Attributes

Daily Workflow: Carol uses lsattr to check immutable and append-only flags on critical files. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical lsattr usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ lsattr /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml
carol@prod-api-01:~$ lsattr -R /lpj/ops/backups/
# Key locations where lsattr is used daily:
#  /lpj/k8s/base/        — Attribute check on manifests
#  /lpj/ops/backups/       — Immutable flag verification

Examples

Example 1: Check File Attributes

Scenario: Carol verifies that no extended attributes are set on deployment files.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

lsattr /lpj/k8s/base/*.yaml

Output:

--------------e------- /lpj/k8s/base/configmap.yaml --------------e------- /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml --------------e------- /lpj/k8s/base/web-deployment.yaml

What happened: All files show only the e attribute (extent format) — no immutable (i) or append-only (a) flags. The dashes represent unset attributes. This is the normal state for most files.

Example 2: Scan Directory for Immutable Files

Scenario: Eve checks if any files in the project have been made immutable without authorization.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml

        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

lsattr -R /lpj/k8s/ 2>/dev/null | grep "^[a-z-]*i[a-z-]*"

Output:

----i---------e------- /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

What happened: Only secrets.yaml has the immutable flag (i). The grep pattern matched lines containing i in the attribute string. This is a security audit check — immutable files cannot be modified, so Eve verifies they were set intentionally.

Example 3: Check Specific File Attributes

📄 Context — Immutable Verification:

# lsattr on a single file shows just that file's attributes
# Check if critical config files have 'i' (immutable) flag
# Immutable files cannot be modified, deleted, or renamed by anyone (including root)

Scenario: Carol checks if database config is protected from changes.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
    ├── 📄 __init__.py

sudo lsattr /lpj/anihpj/settings.py

Output:

----i---------e------- /lpj/anihpj/settings.py

📝 What happened: The 'i' flag is set — settings.py is immutable. Even root cannot modify or delete it. Remove: sudo chattr -i /lpj/anihpj/settings.py. Use for: critical configs, production database files, system binaries. The 'e' flag (extents) is normal for ext4 files.

Example 4: Recursive Attribute Check

📄 Context — Directory-Wide Audit:

# -R recursively shows attributes for all files in a directory tree
# Use for: compliance audits, verifying no unexpected attributes
# Combine with grep to find files with specific flags

Scenario: Eve audits all files with the append-only flag.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log

Command:

sudo lsattr -R /lpj/ops/logs/ | grep -E "^.*a"

Output:

-----a-------e------- /lpj/ops/logs/audit.log

📝 What happened: audit.log has the 'a' (append-only) flag. New data can be appended but existing content cannot be modified. Set with sudo chattr +a /lpj/ops/logs/audit.log. Append-only is ideal for: audit logs, security logs, any file that should only grow.

Example 5: Undeletable File with chattr

📄 Context — Protection from Accidental Deletion:

# chattr +i makes a file completely immutable (cannot change or delete)
# chattr +a makes a file append-only (can add data, can't modify existing)
# Even root can't bypass these without first removing the attribute
# Use to protect critical files from accidental damage

Scenario: Carol protects the production database file from accidental deletion.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/                             # Operations artifacts
    ├── 📁 logs/
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    ├── 📁 backups/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

sudo chattr +i /lpj/ops/backups/prod-db.sql && sudo lsattr /lpj/ops/backups/prod-db.sql

Output:

----i---------e------- /lpj/ops/backups/prod-db.sql

📝 What happened: The backup is now immutable. rm -f fails with "Operation not permitted" even as root. chattr -i removes the flag. Best practice: set +i on critical files, document the protection, have a runbook for removing it during maintenance windows. This is the only way to truly protect files from root.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: lsattr shows the i (immutable) and a (append-only) flags. These are set with chattr. An immutable file cannot be deleted even with rm -f — you must remove the flag first with chattr -i.

chattr

ATTR File Permissions Extended Attributes

Change file attributes — make files immutable or append-only for tamper-proof protection

chattr sets extended filesystem attributes. The +i (immutable) flag prevents any modification — even root cannot delete the file until the flag is removed. The +a (append-only) flag prevents overwriting existing data.

Syntax

chattr [OPTIONS] [+-=][ATTRIBUTES] FILE...

# Common patterns:
chattr +i secrets.yaml          # Make immutable (cannot modify/delete)
chattr -i secrets.yaml          # Remove immutable flag
chattr +a app.log               # Make append-only
chattr -R +i /lpj/k8s/base/     # Recursive immutable

Parameters

FlagDescription
+iImmutable — file cannot be modified, deleted, or linked
+aAppend-only — file can only be appended to
-iRemove immutable attribute
-aRemove append-only attribute
-RRecursive — apply to directory (only for +i on dirs)
+ANo atime updates — reduces disk I/O

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Permission denied or unsupported attribute

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Change Attributes

Daily Workflow: Carol uses chattr to make critical files immutable for security. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical chattr usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo chattr +i /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo chattr +a /lpj/ops/logs/app.log
# Key locations where chattr is used daily:
#  /lpj/k8s/base/        — Immutable secrets
#  /lpj/ops/logs/          — Append-only log files

Examples

Example 1: Protect Secrets from Accidental Deletion

Scenario: Eve makes secrets.yaml immutable so even root accidentally running rm -rf cannot destroy it.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

sudo chattr +i /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml && lsattr /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

Output:

----i---------e------- /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

What happened: The i flag was added. Now rm -f secrets.yaml will fail with "Operation not permitted" even as root. The only way to delete it is chattr -i first. This is the strongest filesystem-level protection available.

Example 2: Append-Only Log File

Scenario: Carol protects the audit log so attackers cannot erase their tracks by overwriting it.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log

Command:

sudo chattr +a /lpj/ops/logs/access.log && lsattr /lpj/ops/logs/access.log

Output:

-----a-------e------- /lpj/ops/logs/access.log

What happened: The a flag makes the log append-only. New entries can be added but existing data cannot be overwritten or truncated. An attacker cannot use > access.log to wipe it. Remove with chattr -a.

Example 3: Remove Immutable Flag Before Editing

Scenario: Carol needs to update secrets.yaml but it's immutable — must remove the flag first.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/
    └── 📁 base/
        ├── 📄 namespace.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-deployment.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-statefulset.yaml
        ├── 📄 web-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 api-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 db-service.yaml
        ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
        └── 📄 secrets.yaml              # 600 permissions!

Command:

sudo chattr -i /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml && echo "Updated" >> /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml && sudo chattr +i /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml && lsattr /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

Output:

----i---------e------- /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

What happened: Carol removed the immutable flag (-i), updated the file, then re-applied it (+i). The file is protected again. This is the standard workflow for editing protected files: unlock → edit → lock.

Example 4: Recursive Immutable Protection

Scenario: Eve protects all Cilium network policies from modification.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
    ├── 📁 base/
    ├── 📁 cilium/
    ├── 📁 ingress/
    └── 📁 monitoring/

Command:

sudo chattr -R +i /lpj/k8s/cilium/ && lsattr /lpj/k8s/cilium/*.yaml

Output:

----i---------e------- /lpj/k8s/cilium/ccnp-host-firewall.yaml ----i---------e------- /lpj/k8s/cilium/cidrgroup-vpn.yaml ----i---------e------- /lpj/k8s/cilium/cnp-baseline.yaml ----i---------e------- /lpj/k8s/cilium/cnp-dns.yaml ----i---------e------- /lpj/k8s/cilium/cnp-l7.yaml

What happened: chattr -R +i recursively made all 5 Cilium policy files immutable. They cannot be modified or deleted — even by root — until chattr -R -i is run. This is the strongest filesystem-level protection for critical security configurations.

Example 5: Temporary Immutability During Investigation

Scenario: During incident response, Carol freezes log files to preserve evidence.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log

Command:

sudo chattr +i /lpj/ops/logs/*.log && lsattr /lpj/ops/logs/*.log

Output:

----i---------e------- /lpj/ops/logs/access.log ----i---------e------- /lpj/ops/logs/app.log ----i---------e------- /lpj/ops/logs/error.log

What happened: All three log files are now immutable — preserving the exact state at the time of the incident. No process can modify or delete them. After investigation, chattr -i releases them. This is the standard forensics pattern: freeze evidence first, analyze later.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: chattr +i = immutable (cannot modify/delete). chattr +a = append-only. Both require root. Even rm -f fails on immutable files. Use chattr -i/-a to remove. lsattr shows current flags. These are ext2/3/4 specific — not available on all filesystems.

⚙️ Process Management

Commands for viewing, controlling, and signaling running processes. Essential for monitoring server health, killing stuck processes, managing background jobs, and ensuring the anihpj/jobpost application runs reliably on production servers.

ps

MONITOR Process Management Core LFCS Domain 2

Report a snapshot of current processes — the universal process inspection tool

ps shows running processes with their PID, CPU usage, memory, state, and command line. The BSD syntax (ps aux) is the most common for a full system overview; the standard syntax (ps -ef) is also widely used.

Syntax

ps [OPTIONS]

# Common patterns:
ps aux                          # All processes, user format (BSD)
ps -ef                          # All processes, full format (standard)
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -10  # Top 10 by memory
ps -u anihpj                    # Processes for user anihpj
ps -eo pid,ppid,cmd,%cpu,%mem --sort=-%cpu | head  # Custom columns

Parameters

FlagDescription
aShow processes for all users (BSD)
uUser-oriented format (BSD)
xShow processes without controlling terminal (BSD)
-eSelect all processes (standard)
-fFull format listing (standard)
-o FORMATUser-defined columns: pid,user,%cpu,%mem,cmd
--sort=COLSort by column: --sort=-%mem (descending)
-u USERShow processes for USER
-p PIDSelect by PID
-C CMDSelect by command name
-HShow process hierarchy (tree view — standard syntax equivalent of f)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — processes listed
1No processes matched the criteria

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Process Inspection

# Carol checks what's running on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ ps aux | grep -E "gunicorn|celery|nginx"
anihpj   12345  2.3  4.1 523456 123456 ?  S  08:00  12:34 gunicorn: master
anihpj   12346  1.8  3.8 512345 114200 ?  S  08:00  10:12 gunicorn: worker
anihpj   12347  0.5  2.1 234567  63000 ?  S  08:00   2:45 celery -A jobpost worker
root     12348  0.1  0.3  45678   9000 ?  Ss 08:00   0:34 nginx: master

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Process Status

Daily Workflow: Carol uses ps to monitor running Django, Celery, and Nginx processes on production servers. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

carol@prod-api-01:~$ ps -ef --forest | head -10
# Key locations where ps is used daily:

#  gunicorn workers      — Django app processes
#  celery workers        — Background task workers

Examples

Example 1: Full System Process Overview

Scenario: Carol runs ps aux to see everything running on the server.

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

ps aux | head -5

Output:

USER PID %CPU %MEM VSZ RSS TTY STAT START TIME COMMAND root 1 0.0 0.1 225396 9120 ? Ss Jan01 0:45 /sbin/init root 1234 0.0 0.2 345678 12340 ? Ssl Jan01 12:34 /usr/bin/dockerd anihpj 12345 2.3 4.1 523456 123456 ? S 08:00 12:34 gunicorn: master anihpj 12346 1.8 3.8 512345 114200 ? S 08:00 10:12 gunicorn: worker

📝 What happened: Every process on the system is listed. Key columns: PID (process ID), %CPU (CPU usage), %MEM (memory usage), STAT (process state: S=sleeping, R=running), TIME (total CPU time used). The anihpj user runs two gunicorn processes.

Example 2: Find Process by Name

Scenario: Alice checks if the Celery worker is running after a deployment.

lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

Command:

ps aux | grep "[c]elery"

Output:

anihpj 12347 0.5 2.1 234567 63000 ? S 08:00 2:45 celery -A jobpost worker

📝 What happened: The bracket trick [c]elery prevents grep from matching itself — the regex matches "celery" but grep's own process line shows [c]elery which doesn't match. Single result confirms celery is running.

Example 3: Sort by Memory — Find Memory Hogs

Scenario: Dave investigates why the server is swapping — finds the top memory consumers.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

Output:

anihpj 12345 2.3 12.1 523456 363000 ? S 08:00 12:34 gunicorn: master anihpj 12346 1.8 10.8 512345 324000 ? S 08:00 10:12 gunicorn: worker postgres 3456 0.2 8.5 987654 255000 ? S Jan02 45:12 postgres: writer anihpj 12347 0.5 6.1 234567 183000 ? S 08:00 2:45 celery worker redis 2345 0.1 3.2 123456 96000 ? Ssl Jan02 12:34 redis-server

📝 What happened: Gunicorn master uses 12.1% of RAM — the biggest consumer. PostgreSQL writer (8.5%) and Celery (6.1%) follow. The --sort=-%mem (descending) puts the hungriest processes at the top. This is the first step in memory troubleshooting.

Output:

📝 What happened: -eo specified exact columns: PID, parent PID, user, CPU%, memory%, and command. This is script-friendly output — no header parsing needed when you control the format. Use -o for any combination of ps fields.

Example 5: Show Process Tree

Scenario: Carol wants to see the parent-child relationships of all gunicorn workers.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

ps auxf | grep -A10 gunicorn

Output:

anihpj 12345 2.3 12.1 523456 363000 ? S 08:00 12:34 gunicorn: master \_ anihpj 12346 1.8 10.8 512345 324000 ? S 08:00 10:12 \_ gunicorn: worker [1] \_ anihpj 12347 1.7 10.2 511234 306000 ? S 08:00 9:45 \_ gunicorn: worker [2] \_ anihpj 12348 1.6 9.8 509876 294000 ? S 08:00 8:23 \_ gunicorn: worker [3]

📝 What happened: The f (forest) option shows the process hierarchy as a tree. The gunicorn master (PID 12345) spawned 3 worker children, indented with \_. This confirms the master-worker architecture and shows exactly how many workers are active.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: ps aux is BSD syntax (no dash before options). ps -ef is standard syntax. Know both. Key states: S=sleeping, R=running, Z=zombie, T=stopped. The bracket trick grep [p]rocess excludes grep itself. ps -eo with custom format is script-friendly.

top

MONITOR Process Management Interactive LFCS Domain 2

Dynamic real-time view of running processes — the live system monitor

top displays a continuously updating view of system processes, CPU usage, memory, and load average. It's interactive — press keys to sort, filter, and kill processes. The go-to tool for live performance monitoring during incidents.

Syntax

top [OPTIONS]

# Common patterns:
top                             # Start interactive monitor
top -u anihpj                   # Show only anihpj's processes
top -d 2                        # Update every 2 seconds (default ~3)
top -b -n 5 > snapshot.txt     # Batch mode: 5 iterations to file
top -p 12345,12346              # Monitor specific PIDs

Interactive Keys

KeyAction
PSort by CPU usage
MSort by memory usage
kKill a process (prompts for PID + signal)
rRenice a process (change priority)
uFilter by user
1Toggle individual CPU core display
cToggle full command line
TSort by running time (cumulative CPU time)
VForest view — show parent-child process relationships
zToggle color/monochrome display
dChange update interval (prompts for seconds)
qQuit

Command-Line Flags

FlagDescription
-d SECONDSUpdate interval (default ~3 seconds)
-u USERShow only USER's processes
-p PIDMonitor specific PIDs (comma-separated)
-bBatch mode — non-interactive, for scripting/redirection
-n NUMNumber of iterations in batch mode (exit after NUM)
-HShow individual threads as processes
-cToggle between command line and program name
-o FIELDSort by FIELD (e.g., -o %MEM for memory)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — top exited normally
1Error — invalid option or permission denied

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Live Monitoring

top - 14:30:01 up 45 days,  3:22,  2 users,  load average: 2.15, 1.80, 1.45
Tasks: 156 total,   2 running, 154 sleeping,   0 stopped,   0 zombie
%Cpu(s): 45.2 us, 12.3 sy,  0.0 ni, 40.1 id,  2.1 wa,  0.3 hi,  0.0 si
MiB Mem :  16000.0 total,   3200.0 free,   8400.0 used,   4400.0 buff/cache
MiB Swap:   4096.0 total,   3800.0 free,    296.0 used.   6200.0 avail Mem

  PID USER      PR  NI    VIRT    RES    SHR S  %CPU  %MEM     TIME+ COMMAND
12345 anihpj    20   0  523456 363000   8900 S  25.0  12.1  15:34.21 gunicorn

Parameters

FlagDescription
-d SECUpdate interval in seconds (default: 3)
-n NExit after N iterations (batch mode)
-p PIDMonitor only specific PIDs (comma-separated)
-u USERShow only processes of USER
-HShow individual threads
-bBatch mode — output suitable for parsing

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error accessing /proc

Example 5: Sort by Memory and Highlight Changes

Scenario: Alice suspects a memory leak in Celery — watches memory column for creeping values.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
