Output:

# top opens with processes sorted by memory usage (highest first) # Alice presses 'c' to toggle full command line # She watches celery's %MEM column over 5 minutes: 6.1% → 6.4% → 6.8% → 7.2% # Confirmed: slow memory leak in celery worker

📝 What happened: -o %MEM starts top sorted by memory (alternative to pressing M). Alice pressed c to see full command lines, then watched celery's %MEM creep up over 5 minutes — confirming a memory leak that would eventually OOM the worker.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: top is interactive. Key keys: M (sort memory), P (sort CPU), k (kill), r (renice), 1 (per-core CPU). Load average: numbers < CPU cores = OK, numbers > CPU cores = overload. top -b -n 1 for scripting. htop is a nicer alternative with color and mouse support.

kill

SIGNAL Process Management Core LFCS Domain 2

Send a signal to a process — graceful termination or force kill

kill sends signals to processes by PID. Despite the name, it sends ANY signal — SIGTERM (15) for graceful shutdown, SIGKILL (9) for force-kill, SIGHUP (1) to reload config. Use kill -l to list all signals.

Syntax

kill [OPTIONS] PID...

# Common patterns:
kill 1234                       # SIGTERM — graceful shutdown
kill -9 1234                    # SIGKILL — force kill
kill -HUP 1234                  # SIGHUP — reload config
kill -l                         # List all signal names

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — signal sent to all specified PIDs
1Error — invalid PID, insufficient permissions, or process doesn't exist

Signal Cheat Sheet

SignalNumberAction
SIGHUP1Hangup — reload configuration (daemons)
SIGINT2Interrupt — same as Ctrl+C
SIGKILL9Force kill — cannot be caught or ignored
SIGTERM15Graceful termination (default)
SIGSTOP19Pause process — cannot be caught
SIGCONT18Resume paused process
SIGUSR110User-defined signal 1 — application-specific behavior
SIGUSR212User-defined signal 2 — application-specific behavior

Flags

FlagDescription
-l, --listList all available signal names
-s, --signal SIGNALSpecify signal by name (e.g., -s HUP) or number (e.g., -s 9)
-L, --tableList signal names and numbers in a formatted table

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

Parameters

FlagDescription
-lList all available signal names
-s SIGNALSend SIGNAL by name (e.g. -s TERM)
-SIGNUMSend signal by number (e.g. -9 for SIGKILL)
-LList signal names in a table

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — signal delivered
1Invalid PID or permission denied

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Send Signals

Daily Workflow: Carol uses kill to gracefully restart gunicorn workers and stop stuck processes. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical kill usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ kill -HUP $(pgrep -f gunicorn)
carol@prod-api-01:~$ kill -TERM 12345
# Key locations where kill is used daily:
#  gunicorn master       — Graceful reload with HUP
#  celery workers         — Safe shutdown with TERM
#  Stuck processes        — Force kill with KILL (last resort)

Examples

Example 1: Graceful Shutdown

Scenario: Carol gracefully stops the gunicorn master during a rolling update.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

kill 12345 && sleep 2 && ps -p 12345 >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "Still running" || echo "Stopped"

Output:

Stopped

📝 What happened: SIGTERM (default) told gunicorn to shut down gracefully — finish current requests, close connections, then exit. After 2 seconds, ps -p confirmed the process is gone. Always try SIGTERM first before SIGKILL.

Example 2: Force Kill a Stuck Process

Scenario: The Celery worker is hung and won't respond to SIGTERM — SIGKILL is the last resort.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

kill -9 12347 && ps -p 12347 >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "Still alive!" || echo "Force-killed"

Output:

Force-killed

📝 What happened: SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught or ignored — the kernel immediately terminates the process. No cleanup, no closing files, no saving state. Only use -9 when SIGTERM fails. It's the equivalent of pulling the power cord.

Example 3: Reload Nginx Configuration

Scenario: Carol applies new nginx config without dropping connections.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

kill -HUP $(pgrep nginx) && echo "Nginx reloaded"

Output:

Nginx reloaded

📝 What happened: SIGHUP (1) tells nginx to re-read its configuration WITHOUT stopping. pgrep nginx found the nginx PID. Connections are not dropped — users won't notice. This is the standard zero-downtime config reload pattern.

Example 4: Send SIGINT (Ctrl+C Equivalent)

Scenario: Alice starts a Django dev server and needs to stop it from another SSH session.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

kill -INT $(pgrep -f "manage.py runserver") && echo "Dev server interrupted"

Output:

Dev server interrupted

📝 What happened: SIGINT (2) is the same signal sent by Ctrl+C. The Django dev server caught it, ran its cleanup handlers (closing DB connections, saving state), and exited cleanly. This is more polite than SIGTERM for interactive programs that expect keyboard interrupts.

Example 5: Pause and Resume a Process

Scenario: Dave temporarily pauses a CPU-heavy batch job to run an urgent query, then resumes it.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

# Pause the batch job:
kill -STOP $(pgrep -f "batch_process") && echo "Batch paused"
# Run the urgent query...
# Resume the batch job:
kill -CONT $(pgrep -f "batch_process") && echo "Batch resumed"

Output:

Batch paused # ... urgent query runs with full CPU ... Batch resumed

📝 What happened: SIGSTOP (19) freezes a process instantly — it stops consuming CPU entirely but stays in memory. SIGCONT (18) unfreezes it. Unlike kill, SIGSTOP doesn't terminate — it's like pausing a video. The batch job resumed right where it was, with no data loss.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: Signal hierarchy: SIGTERM (15) first → SIGKILL (9) as last resort. SIGKILL cannot be caught — no cleanup. SIGHUP (1) reloads configs for daemons. SIGSTOP (19) pauses, SIGCONT (18) resumes. kill -l lists all signals. kill -9 -1 kills ALL processes you own — never use this.

pkill / killall

SIGNAL Process Management LFCS Domain 2

Signal processes by name — kill without looking up PIDs

pkill and killall send signals to processes by NAME instead of PID. pkill matches patterns (regex); killall matches exact names. Both are faster than ps | grep | kill.

Syntax

pkill [OPTIONS] PATTERN
killall [OPTIONS] NAME

# Common patterns:
pkill -f "celery -A jobpost"       # Match full command line
pkill -u anihpj nginx              # Kill nginx processes owned by anihpj
killall -HUP nginx                 # Reload all nginx processes

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — at least one process matched and was signaled
1No processes matched the pattern
2Syntax error in command

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

Parameters

FlagDescription
-SIGNALSignal to send (e.g. -TERM, -9)
-u USERMatch only processes owned by USER
-t TTYMatch only processes on terminal TTY
-fMatch against full command line, not just name
-nKill only the newest matching process
-oKill only the oldest matching process
-xExact name match required

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0At least one process matched
1No matching processes
2Syntax error

All anihpj redis connections force-killed

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: pkill matches patterns (partial/regex), killall matches exact names. pkill -f matches full command line. pkill -u USER restricts to a user. Both accept signal flags: -HUP, -9, etc. Use pgrep first to preview which processes would be matched.

nice / renice

PRIORITY Process Management LFCS Domain 2

Set or change process scheduling priority — control CPU allocation

nice launches a process with modified priority. renice changes priority of a running process. Priority ranges from -20 (highest) to 19 (lowest). Only root can set negative (higher) priorities. The niceness value is visible in top and ps in the NI column.

Syntax

nice -n PRIORITY COMMAND
renice PRIORITY -p PID

# Common patterns:
nice -n 10 tar -czf backup.tar.gz /lpj/    # Low-priority backup
renice 5 -p 12345                           # Reduce gunicorn priority
sudo renice -5 -p 12345                     # Boost gunicorn priority (root only)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — command launched or reniced
1Error — invalid priority value or permission denied (for negative nice)

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

Parameters

FlagDescription
-n NSet niceness to N (-20 highest priority to 19 lowest)
--adjustment=NSame as -n N

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
125nice itself failed
126Command found but not executable
127Command not found

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Process Priority

carol@prod-api-01:~$ nice -n -10 /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh
# Key locations where nice is used daily:
#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Low-priority backup jobs
#  /lpj/scripts/          — Deployment scripts at normal priority
#  CPU-intensive tasks    — Tar, gzip, database dumps

Examples

Example 1: Run Backup at Low Priority

Scenario: Dave runs a database backup but doesn't want it to compete with production traffic.

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

nice -n 19 pg_dump anihpj > /lpj/ops/backups/db_$(date +%Y%m%d).sql && echo "Backup complete"

Output:

Backup complete

📝 What happened: The backup ran at the lowest possible priority (nice 19). It yields CPU to any other process — production gunicorn workers get priority. The backup takes longer but doesn't affect response times.

Example 2: Lower Priority of a CPU-Hungry Process

Scenario: Alice's data migration is consuming too much CPU — renice it to minimize impact.

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

renice 15 -p $(pgrep -f "manage.py migrate") && ps -o pid,ni,cmd -p $(pgrep -f "manage.py migrate")

12350 (process ID) old priority 0, new priority 15 PID NI CMD 12350 15 python manage.py migrate

📝 What happened: The migration's priority was lowered from 0 (default) to 15. It now yields CPU to more important processes. The NI column in ps confirms the new value. Regular users can only increase niceness (lower priority).

Example 3: Boost Priority of Critical Service (Root Only)

Scenario: Carol temporarily boosts gunicorn's CPU priority during a Black Friday sale to handle extra traffic.

📁 Directory Snippet:

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

12345 (process ID) old priority 0, new priority -10 PID NI CMD 12345 -10 gunicorn: master [anihpj]

Example 4: Check Current Nice Value

Scenario: Alice wants to verify the niceness of all gunicorn and celery processes at a glance.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

Example 5: Run a Maintenance Script with Low I/O Priority Too

Scenario: Dave runs a filesystem scan that should yield both CPU AND I/O to production workloads.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log

ionice -c 2 -n 7 nice -n 19 find /lpj/ -type f -mtime +30 -ls > /lpj/ops/logs/old_files.txt && echo "Scan done"

Output:

Scan done

📝 What happened: ionice -c 2 -n 7 (best-effort, lowest I/O priority) combined with nice -n 19 (lowest CPU priority) ensures the find command yields both CPU and disk I/O to production services. This is the polite way to run maintenance — gunicorn responses are unaffected even during heavy disk scanning.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: Nice values: -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest). Default is 0. Only root can go negative (higher priority). Regular users can only increase niceness (lower priority). renice changes a running process; nice launches a new one. The NI column in top/ps shows current niceness.

bg / fg / jobs

JOB CONTROL Process Management Shell Builtin LFCS Domain 2

Manage background and foreground jobs — multitask in a single terminal

Shell job control lets you pause (Ctrl+Z), background (bg), foreground (fg), and list (jobs) processes running in your terminal session. Essential for long-running tasks like database dumps and file transfers.

Syntax

Ctrl+Z          # Suspend current foreground job
bg %1           # Resume job 1 in the background
fg %1           # Bring job 1 to the foreground
jobs            # List all background/stopped jobs
kill %1         # Kill job 1

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — job started/foregrounded, or jobs listed
1Error — no such job or job control not available

FlagDescription

%STRINGJob whose command starts with STRING
%+Current job (default)
%-Previous job

Exit CodeDescription

Example 3: Run Multiple Background Jobs and Track Them

Scenario: Carol runs three long tasks simultaneously — backup, log rotation, and a DB vacuum — tracking each.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

Output:

[1] 12501 Running pg_dump anihpj > /lpj/ops/backups/db.sql & [2] 12502 Running gzip /lpj/ops/logs/*.log & [3] 12503 Running vacuumdb -U anihpj anihpj & # jobs -l shows all three with PIDs

📝 What happened: Each & launched a new background job. jobs -l (long format) lists all three with their PIDs. Carol can now fg %2 to check on the gzip, or kill %3 to cancel the vacuum. Parallel task management without multiple terminals.

Example 4: Foreground a Background Job to Interact With It

Scenario: Alice started a Django management command in the background but it prompts for confirmation — she brings it to foreground.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

python manage.py flush --no-input &
# ... some time later ...
jobs
fg %1

Output:

[1]+ Stopped(SIGTTIN) python manage.py flush --no-input # fg %1 brings it back, Alice sees the prompt: You have requested a flush of the database. This will IRREVERSIBLY DESTROY all data. Are you sure you want to do this? [y/N]

📝 What happened: Background processes can't read from the terminal — when flush tried to prompt, it received SIGTTIN and stopped. fg %1 brought it to the foreground where Alice can answer the prompt. Always check jobs first to see which jobs are stopped vs. running.

Example 5: Use jobs for Shell Script Job Tracking

Scenario: Carol writes a deployment script that runs pre-deployment checks in parallel, waits for all to finish.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

# In deploy.sh:
python manage.py check --deploy &
pg_isready -h localhost &
curl -sf http://localhost:8080/health &
wait  # Wait for ALL background jobs to finish
echo "All checks passed — proceeding with deployment"

Output:

All checks passed — proceeding with deployment

📝 What happened: wait (without arguments) blocks until ALL background jobs complete. If any job fails, wait returns its exit code. This is a simple parallelism pattern — run 3 independent checks at once instead of sequentially, saving ~66% time.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: Ctrl+Z = suspend, bg = background, fg = foreground, jobs = list. %1 refers to job number 1. Command & runs in background immediately. All are shell builtins — use help bg, help fg, help jobs.

nohup / disown

PERSIST Process Management LFCS Domain 2

Protect processes from SIGHUP — keep them running after you log out

When you close a terminal, the shell sends SIGHUP to all child processes, killing them. nohup immunizes a command against SIGHUP at launch time. disown removes an already-running job from the shell's job table so it survives logout.

Syntax

nohup COMMAND &                  # Launch immune to hangup
disown %1                        # Remove job 1 from shell's job table
disown -h %1                     # Don't send SIGHUP but keep in job table

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — command launched (nohup) or job disowned
126Command found but not executable
127Command not found

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

Parameters

FlagDescription
(none)nohup takes no flags — just the command to run

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — command launched
125nohup itself failed
126Command not executable
127Command not found

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — No Hangup

Daily Workflow: Carol uses nohup to run long deployment scripts that survive SSH disconnection. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical nohup usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ nohup /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh > /lpj/ops/logs/deploy_nohup.log 2>&1 &
carol@prod-api-01:~$ tail -f /lpj/ops/logs/deploy_nohup.log
# Key locations where nohup is used daily:
#  /lpj/scripts/          — Deployment scripts with nohup
#  /lpj/ops/logs/          — nohup output logged here
#  Long-running tasks      — Migrations, backups, imports

Examples

Example 1: Run a Long Migration That Survives Logout

Scenario: Alice needs to run a 2-hour database migration but might lose her SSH connection.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log

Command:

nohup python manage.py migrate > /lpj/ops/logs/migration.log 2>&1 &

Output:

[1] 12500 nohup: ignoring input and appending output to 'nohup.out'

📝 What happened: nohup launched the migration immune to SIGHUP. Even if Alice's SSH disconnects, the migration continues. Output is redirected to migration.log for later review. & runs it in the background.

Example 2: Disown an Already-Running Job

Scenario: Carol started a long backup in the foreground, backgrounded it, but forgot nohup. She disown's it.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

# Started: pg_dump anihpj > backup.sql
# Ctrl+Z to suspend, then: bg
# Now disown it:
disown %1 && jobs

Output:

# jobs returns nothing — the backup is detached from the shell # It will continue running even if Carol logs out

📝 What happened: disown removed the backup from the shell's job table. It's still running — just no longer tied to Carol's terminal session. Use this when you forget nohup before starting a long task.

Example 3: Start a Background Server That Survives Everything

Scenario: Alice starts a development Celery worker that must keep running even if her terminal crashes.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log

Command:

nohup celery -A jobpost worker --loglevel=info > /lpj/ops/logs/celery_dev.log 2>&1 & disown

Output:

[1] 12510

📝 What happened: nohup + disown double-protection: nohup makes it immune to SIGHUP, disown removes it from the shell's job table entirely. Even if Alice's terminal window crashes or she force-closes it, the celery worker continues. Output goes to celery_dev.log.

Example 4: Check nohup Output in Real Time

Scenario: Dave started a long-running migration with nohup and wants to check progress without disturbing it.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    └── 📁 logs/
        ├── 📄 app.log
        ├── 📄 error.log
        └── 📄 access.log

Command:

nohup python manage.py migrate > /lpj/ops/logs/migration.log 2>&1 &
# Later, check progress:
tail -f /lpj/ops/logs/migration.log

Output:

Applying contenttypes.0001_initial... OK Applying auth.0001_initial... OK Applying jobpost.0001_initial... OK Applying jobpost.0002_add_indexes... OK # tail -f shows live progress, Ctrl+C to stop watching (migration continues)

📝 What happened: tail -f follows the log file in real time, showing migration progress. Pressing Ctrl+C stops tail but NOT the migration — it's protected by nohup and continues. This is the standard pattern for monitoring long-running headless processes.

Example 5: nohup vs screen/tmux — When to Use Each

Scenario: Carol decides whether to use nohup or tmux for a critical 4-hour database repair.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

# Option A: nohup — fire and forget, check logs later
nohup pg_restore -d anihpj /lpj/ops/backups/db_full.dump > /lpj/ops/logs/restore.log 2>&1 &

# Option B: tmux — reattach later to interact
tmux new -s db_repair
pg_restore -d anihpj /lpj/ops/backups/db_full.dump  # Can interact if prompts appear
# Ctrl+B, D to detach; tmux attach -t db_repair to return

Output:

# nohup: Output goes to restore.log — check with tail -f # tmux: Can reattach and see full scrollback, answer prompts, Ctrl+C if needed

📝 What happened: nohup is simpler: one command, no sessions to manage, check logs later. tmux/screen is better for interactive tasks where you might need to answer prompts or monitor visually. Use nohup for fully automated scripts; use tmux for anything that might need human intervention.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: nohup protects a NEW process; disown protects an EXISTING job. nohup output goes to nohup.out unless redirected. disown -h removes SIGHUP but keeps the job visible. Both are shell builtins.

pgrep / pidof / watch

FIND Process Management LFCS Domain 2

Find processes by name and run commands periodically — essential monitoring tools

pgrep finds PIDs by name pattern. pidof finds the PID of an exact program name. watch runs a command repeatedly at intervals — like a mini-monitoring dashboard in your terminal.

Syntax

pgrep [OPTIONS] PATTERN
pidof PROGRAM
watch [OPTIONS] COMMAND

# Common patterns:
pgrep -f "gunicorn"                 # Find PIDs matching gunicorn in full command
pidof nginx                         # Find PID of nginx
watch -n 2 "ps aux | grep celery"   # Monitor celery every 2 seconds
watch -d df -h                      # Watch disk usage, highlight changes

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — at least one process matched (pgrep/pidof) or watch ran to completion
1No processes matched (pgrep/pidof), or error in watch command

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

Parameters

FlagDescription
-u USERMatch processes owned by USER
-lList process names along with PIDs
-fMatch against full command line
-xExact name match required
-aShow full command line in output
-nShow only the newest process
-vInvert — show processes NOT matching

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0At least one match
1No match
2Syntax error

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Find PID by Name

Daily Workflow: Carol uses pgrep to find process IDs for service management and monitoring scripts. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

12845
carol@prod-api-01:~$ pgrep -u anihpj -a
# Key locations where pgrep is used daily:

Example 4: Count Processes Per User

Scenario: Carol audits which users have the most processes on the production server.

Every 2.0s: ps -eo pid,%mem,comm --sort=-%mem | head -8 PID %MEM COMMAND 12345 12.3 gunicorn ← highlights flash when %MEM changes 12346 10.8 gunicorn 3456 8.5 postgres 12347 7.2 celery ← climbed from 6.8% — highlighted by -d 12348 6.9 gunicorn 2345 3.2 redis-server 12349 1.5 celery 1 0.1 systemd

📝 What happened: watch -d highlights values that change between refreshes. Dave spots celery climbing from 6.8% to 7.2% memory — the highlight draws attention. Combine watch with any pipeline for a live dashboard. Ctrl+C exits when done.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: pgrep -f matches full command line; pgrep without -f matches only process name (15 chars). pidof requires exact program name. watch -d highlights differences between refreshes. watch -n SECS sets interval. Ctrl+C exits watch.

🖥️ System Information

Commands for inspecting system state: OS version, uptime, memory, disk space, hardware info, kernel modules, and system messages. Essential for troubleshooting, capacity planning, and verifying the anihpj/jobpost production environment across all 11 servers.

uname

SYSTEM System Information Core LFCS Domain 4

Print system information — kernel, hostname, architecture, and OS

uname displays key system identifiers: kernel name, hostname, kernel release, kernel version, machine hardware name, and operating system. It is the first command to run on an unfamiliar server to understand the environment.

For the anihpj/jobpost project, uname is essential for:

  • Verifying kernel version compatibility before installing Kubernetes components
  • Confirming architecture (x86_64 vs ARM) before pulling Docker images
  • Auditing all 11 servers for consistent kernel versions
  • Documenting the OS baseline in deployment runbooks
  • Troubleshooting kernel-module-dependent features like Cilium eBPF

Syntax

uname [OPTIONS]

# Common patterns:
uname                   # Kernel name (Linux)
uname -a                # All system information
uname -r                # Kernel release
uname -m                # Machine hardware name (x86_64, aarch64)
uname -o                # Operating system

Parameters

FlagDescription
-a, --allPrint all info: kernel-name nodename kernel-release kernel-version machine processor hardware-platform OS
-s, --kernel-namePrint kernel name (default: Linux)
-n, --nodenamePrint network node hostname
-r, --kernel-releasePrint kernel release (e.g., 5.15.0-91-generic)
-v, --kernel-versionPrint kernel version (build date string)
-m, --machinePrint machine hardware name (e.g., x86_64, aarch64)
-p, --processorPrint processor type or "unknown"
-i, --hardware-platformPrint hardware platform or "unknown"
-o, --operating-systemPrint operating system (e.g., GNU/Linux)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — system information printed
1Error — invalid option

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Server Baseline Audit

Daily Workflow: Carol runs uname -a on every server to verify consistent kernel versions across the anihpj fleet before deploying kernel-dependent features like Cilium eBPF.

carol@prod-api-01:~$ uname -a

hostname / hostnamectl

IDENTITY System Information Core LFCS Domain 4

Show or set the system hostname — identify which server you are on

hostname displays or temporarily sets the system hostname. hostnamectl (systemd) provides a richer interface for viewing and persistently changing the hostname. In a multi-server anihpj environment with 11 servers, checking the hostname is a critical safety habit before running destructive commands.

Syntax

hostname [OPTIONS]
hostnamectl [COMMAND]

# Common patterns:
hostname                        # Show hostname
hostname -f                     # Show FQDN (fully qualified domain name)
hostname -I                     # Show all IP addresses
hostnamectl set-hostname NAME   # Permanently change hostname (systemd)

Parameters

FlagDescription
-a, --aliasAlias name (if set)
-d, --domainDNS domain name
-f, --fqdn, --longFully qualified domain name (FQDN)
-i, --ip-addressIP address(es) of the host
-I, --all-ip-addressesAll network addresses (excluding loopback)
-s, --shortShort hostname (before first dot)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — hostname displayed or set
1Error — permission denied or invalid hostname

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: hostname shows/changes hostname temporarily (lost on reboot). hostnamectl set-hostname changes it permanently (writes /etc/hostname). hostname -f for FQDN. hostname -I (capital i) prints all IPs — useful in scripts. Know hostnamectl for systemd-based systems.

uptime

STATUS System Information LFCS Domain 4

Show how long the system has been running — plus load average and user count

uptime displays the current time, how long the system has been up, how many users are logged in, and the load average for the past 1, 5, and 15 minutes. It is the quickest health check — if uptime is low, something recently rebooted; if load is high, something is overloaded.

Syntax

uptime [OPTIONS]

# Common patterns:
uptime              # Standard output
uptime -p           # Pretty format (human-readable uptime)
uptime -s           # Since when the system has been up

Parameters

FlagDescription
-p, --prettyShow uptime in pretty format: "up 2 weeks, 3 days, 5 hours"
-s, --sinceShow system up since: "2024-06-01 08:00:00"
-h, --helpDisplay help and exit

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — uptime displayed
1Error — cannot read /proc/uptime

 14:30:05 up 3 min,  1 user,  load average: 0.85, 0.45, 0.20
# ⚠️ prod-db-01 rebooted 3 minutes ago — investigate immediately!

Example 2: Interpret High Load Average

Scenario: Alice checks the API server during a traffic spike and sees elevated load numbers.

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:

📄 Context — Load Average Interpretation:

# Load average rules of thumb:
#   Load < CPU cores = normal (no queuing)
#   Load = CPU cores = fully utilized (optimal)
#   Load > CPU cores = queue forming (processes waiting)
#   Load > 2× CPU cores = significant overload
#
# This server has 4 CPU cores.
# Expected baseline for prod-api-01: 0.5-1.5 (moderate traffic)

Command:

uptime

Output:

14:35:00 up 45 days, 3:27, 4 users, load average: 5.20, 3.80, 2.10

📝 What happened: Load 5.20 on a 4-core server = processes are queuing. The rising trend (5.20 > 3.80 > 2.10) shows the spike is recent. 4 users suggests multiple team members are investigating. Alice should run top next to identify the CPU-hungry process.

Example 5: Script Server Reboot Detection Across Fleet

📁 Directory Snippet:

lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root

📄 Context — Uptime Monitoring Script:

# Script: /lpj/scripts/uptime-check.sh
# Runs every hour via cron. Alerts if any server has < 24h uptime.
#   for host in $(cat /lpj/scripts/hosts.txt); do
#     up=$(ssh "$host" "uptime -p")
#     if echo "$up" | grep -qE "minute|hour" && ! echo "$up" | grep -q "day"; then
#       echo "ALERT: $host recently rebooted: $up"
#     fi
#   done

Command:

for host in prod-web-01 prod-api-01 prod-db-01; do echo -n "$host: "; ssh $host "uptime -p"; done

Output:

prod-web-01: up 45 days, 3 hours, 30 minutes prod-api-01: up 45 days, 3 hours, 28 minutes prod-db-01: up 3 minutes

📝 What happened: prod-web-01 and prod-api-01 show 45 days — normal. prod-db-01 shows only 3 minutes — it just rebooted! This triggers an immediate alert: check why the database restarted, verify replication is catching up, ensure no data corruption occurred.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: Load average < CPU cores = normal; Load > CPU cores = overload. Three numbers: 1-min, 5-min, 15-min. Rising 1-min with low 15-min = recent spike. All three high = sustained overload. uptime -s shows boot time; uptime -p for reports. /proc/loadavg contains the raw load data.

who

USERS System Information LFCS Domain 2

Show who is logged in — current user sessions

who displays who is currently logged into the system — username, terminal, login time, and originating IP address. It reads from /var/run/utmp. Essential for checking if it's safe to perform maintenance.

Syntax

who [OPTIONS]

# Common patterns:

who -H                      # With column headings
who -b                      # Last boot time

who -a                      # All available info

Parameters

FlagDescription
-a, --allSame as -b -d --login -p -r -t -T -u
-b, --bootTime of last system boot
-H, --headingPrint column headings
-q, --countShow login names and count only
-uShow idle time for each user

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: who reads /var/run/utmp. who -b = boot time. who -q = user count. who -u = idle times. who -a = everything. Use who to check active sessions before maintenance; use w for what users are running; use last for historical logins.

w

USERS System Information LFCS Domain 2

Show who is logged in and what they are doing — the active user monitor

w displays who is logged in AND what command each user is currently running. It also shows the system uptime, load average, and per-user CPU time. The WHAT column is the key differentiator from who — it reveals exactly what each user is executing.

Syntax

w [OPTIONS] [USER]

# Common patterns:
w                           # All users + what they're doing
w carol                     # Show only carol's sessions
w -h                        # No header (script-friendly)

Parameters

FlagDescription
-h, --no-headerDon't print the header line
-s, --shortShort format — omit login time, JCPU, PCPU
-fToggle FROM field (on/off)
USERShow information for specific user only

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

15:30:01 up 45 days, 4:22, 3 users, load average: 0.15, 0.10, 0.08 USER TTY FROM WHAT carol pts/0 192.168.1.50 w -s alice pts/1 192.168.1.100 -bash bob pts/2 192.168.1.101 vim /lpj/api/views.py

📝 What happened: -s removed LOGIN@, IDLE, JCPU, and PCPU columns — only USER, TTY, FROM, and WHAT remain. This compact format is ideal for quick "who's doing what" checks without the performance metrics clutter.

Example 5: Before/After Service Restart

Scenario: Carol runs w before and after restarting gunicorn to confirm no users were disrupted.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

echo "=== BEFORE ===" && w -s && sudo systemctl restart gunicorn && sleep 3 && echo "=== AFTER ===" && w -s

Output:

=== BEFORE === USER TTY FROM WHAT carol pts/0 192.168.1.50 -bash alice pts/1 192.168.1.100 -bash === AFTER === USER TTY FROM WHAT carol pts/0 192.168.1.50 -bash alice pts/1 192.168.1.100 -bash

📝 What happened: Both users survived the gunicorn restart — their SSH sessions and bash prompts were unaffected. The session count stayed at 2. This confirms gunicorn restarts don't disrupt user sessions. Combine with w to document pre/post maintenance state.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: w = who + what. The WHAT column shows the running command. w USER filters to one user. w -s = short format. w -h = no header (script-friendly). Always run w before restarting services to see who might be affected.

last

AUDIT System Information LFCS Domain 2

Show login and reboot history — the system's session audit trail

last reads from /var/log/wtmp to display the history of all logins, logouts, and system reboots. It is the primary tool for security auditing — when did each user log in, from where, and for how long? last reboot shows reboot history.

Syntax

last [OPTIONS] [USER...] [TTY...]

# Common patterns:
last                        # Full login history
last -5                     # Last 5 logins
last reboot                 # Reboot history only
last alice                  # Alice's login history
last -f /var/log/wtmp.1     # Read rotated wtmp file

Parameters

FlagDescription
-NUMShow only NUM most recent entries (e.g., -10)
-f FILERead from FILE instead of /var/log/wtmp
-RDon't display hostname field
-xShow system shutdown entries and runlevel changes
rebootShow only reboot entries (pseudo-user)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

📝 What happened: A suspicious root login from 10.0.0.99 at 3:15 AM — this IP is NOT in the anihpj network. Combined with the reboot at 3:10, this suggests unauthorized access. Eve must investigate 10.0.0.99 immediately.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: last reads /var/log/wtmp. last reboot = reboot history. last USER = user's login history. last -x includes shutdowns and runlevel changes. last -f wtmp.1 reads rotated logs. Use last for security audits — it reveals when, from where, and for how long each user accessed the system.

dmesg

KERNEL System Information LFCS Domain 2

Print kernel ring buffer messages — hardware detection, driver loading, and boot diagnostics

dmesg displays messages from the kernel ring buffer — the kernel's internal log. This is where hardware detection, driver initialization, and kernel errors appear. Essential for troubleshooting boot issues, hardware problems, and kernel panics.

Syntax

dmesg [OPTIONS]

# Common patterns:
dmesg                           # Full kernel log
dmesg | tail -20                # Most recent kernel messages
dmesg -H                        # Human-readable timestamps
dmesg -T                        # Human-readable timestamps (legacy)
dmesg -l err                    # Error messages only
dmesg | grep -i usb             # USB-related messages

Parameters

FlagDescription
-H, --humanHuman-readable output with relative timestamps
-T, --ctimeHuman-readable timestamps (absolute time)
-l, --level LEVELSFilter by log level: emerg, alert, crit, err, warn, notice, info, debug
-f, --facility FACILITYFilter by facility: kern, user, mail, daemon, etc.
-w, --followWait for new messages (like tail -f for kernel)
--clearClear the ring buffer (requires root)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — messages displayed

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Boot Diagnostics

# Carol checks kernel messages after a suspicious reboot on prod-db-01:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ dmesg -T | tail -20
[Wed Jun  4 03:10:15 2026] EXT4-fs (sda1): mounted filesystem with ordered data mode
[Wed Jun  4 03:10:16 2026] e1000e: eth0 NIC Link is Up 1000 Mbps Full Duplex
[Wed Jun  4 03:10:18 2026] PostgreSQL: starting database server

📝 What happened: The kernel booted at 03:10 AM — confirming the unauthorized reboot time. It's a QEMU virtual machine (not bare metal). dmesg -T adds human-readable timestamps; without -T, times are in seconds since boot.

Output:

# dmesg -w waits for new messages... [ +0.000000] usb 1-1: new high-speed USB device number 3 using ehci-pci [ +0.234567] usb 1-1: New USB device found, idVendor=0781, idProduct=5583 [ +0.345678] usb-storage 1-1:1.0: USB Mass Storage device detected [ +0.456789] scsi host6: usb-storage 1-1:1.0 [ +0.567890] sd 6:0:0:0: [sdb] 31277232 512-byte logical blocks: (16.0 GB)

📝 What happened: dmesg -w followed the kernel log in real time. The USB device was detected, identified as mass storage, and assigned /dev/sdb (16GB). This confirms the kernel recognized the drive. Without -w, you would need to re-run dmesg manually to see new messages.

Example 5: Check for Cilium eBPF Compatibility

Scenario: Carol verifies the kernel supports eBPF features required by Cilium.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

dmesg | grep -i "bpf\|ebpf\|cilium" && echo "eBPF detected" || echo "No eBPF — Cilium may not work"

Output:

[ 0.123456] bpf: BPF memory model registered [ 5.678901] cilium: eBPF datapath initialized — 256 preallocated maps eBPF detected

📝 What happened: Two confirming messages: the kernel registered BPF memory model at boot, and Cilium initialized its eBPF datapath. If these messages are absent, Cilium falls back to non-eBPF mode (reduced functionality). This is the first check when Cilium network policies fail to apply.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: dmesg reads from /dev/kmsg (kernel ring buffer). dmesg -T shows human-readable timestamps. dmesg -l err filters errors. dmesg -w follows in real time. The buffer is circular — very old messages may be overwritten. Use journalctl -k as an alternative on systemd systems.

free

MEMORY System Information LFCS Domain 2

Display memory usage — total, used, free, swap, buffers, and cache

free shows the system's memory status: total RAM, used, free, shared, buffer/cache, and available. It also shows swap usage. The available column is the most important — it estimates how much memory is available for new processes without swapping.

Syntax

free [OPTIONS]

# Common patterns:
free -h                     # Human-readable output
free -m                     # Show in megabytes
free -h -s 2                # Refresh every 2 seconds
free -h -c 5                # Show 5 snapshots then exit
free -t                     # Show a totals line

Parameters

FlagDescription
-h, --humanHuman-readable output (Ki, Mi, Gi)
-mShow output in megabytes
-gShow output in gigabytes
-s, --seconds SECRepeat every SEC seconds (continuous monitoring)
-c, --count COUNTRepeat COUNT times only
-w, --wideWide output mode — separate buffers and cache columns
-t, --totalShow a line with totals (for RAM + swap)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — memory stats displayed

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Memory Monitoring

# Dave checks memory after noticing swap usage on prod-api-01:
dave@prod-api-01:~$ free -h
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:            15Gi       8.2Gi       2.1Gi       456Mi       5.1Gi       6.3Gi
Swap:          4.0Gi       296Mi       3.7Gi

# Concern: 296MB of swap is in use — some memory pressure exists
# But 6.3Gi available means no immediate risk of OOM

Example 1: Quick Memory Check

Scenario: Carol checks memory on prod-api-01 before a high-traffic deployment.

total used free shared buff/cache available Mem: 15Gi 8.2Gi 2.1Gi 456Mi 5.1Gi 6.3Gi Swap: 4.0Gi 296Mi 3.7Gi

📝 What happened: 15Gi total RAM, 8.2Gi used, 6.3Gi available. The key insight: free (2.1Gi) is just unused memory — available (6.3Gi) includes reclaimable buffer/cache. 6.3Gi available is healthy. 296MB swap used indicates minor memory pressure but not critical.

Example 2: Continuous Memory Monitoring

Scenario: Alice watches memory usage in real time during a Django migration to spot leaks.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

Output:

total used free shared buff/cache available Mem: 15Gi 7.8Gi 2.5Gi 450Mi 5.1Gi 6.7Gi Mem: 15Gi 8.1Gi 2.2Gi 452Mi 5.1Gi 6.4Gi Mem: 15Gi 8.5Gi 1.8Gi 455Mi 5.1Gi 6.0Gi Mem: 15Gi 9.0Gi 1.3Gi 458Mi 5.1Gi 5.5Gi Mem: 15Gi 9.4Gi 0.9Gi 460Mi 5.1Gi 5.1Gi

📝 What happened: Over 10 seconds (5 snapshots at 2-second intervals), used memory grew from 7.8Gi to 9.4Gi while available dropped from 6.7Gi to 5.1Gi. This steady creep during a migration suggests the migration process is consuming memory — not yet critical but worth investigating if it continues.

Example 3: Show in Megabytes for Script Parsing

Scenario: Dave's monitoring script parses free output numerically for a Grafana dashboard.

📁 Directory Snippet:

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

Output:

Used: 8400MB, Available: 6451MB, Used%: 54%

📝 What happened: free -m outputs in megabytes (integers, no Gi/Mi suffixes) making it easy to parse with awk. 54% memory usage with 6.4GB available is healthy. This pattern feeds into monitoring dashboards for trend analysis.

Example 4: Wide Output with Buffers/Cache Separated

Scenario: Alice needs to distinguish between actual used memory and cached memory.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

free -hw

Output:

total used free shared buffers cache available Mem: 15Gi 8.2Gi 2.1Gi 456Mi 1.2Gi 3.9Gi 6.3Gi Swap: 4.0Gi 296Mi 3.7Gi

📝 What happened: -w (wide) separates buffers (1.2Gi) and cache (3.9Gi) into distinct columns. Buffers hold raw disk blocks; cache stores file data. Combined they're 5.1Gi of reclaimable memory — explaining why available (6.3Gi) is much higher than free (2.1Gi).

Example 5: Show Totals with Swap

Scenario: Dave needs combined RAM + swap totals for a capacity planning report.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app

├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

free -ht

Output:

total used free shared buff/cache available Mem: 15Gi 8.2Gi 2.1Gi 456Mi 5.1Gi 6.3Gi Swap: 4.0Gi 296Mi 3.7Gi Total: 19Gi 8.5Gi 10Gi

📝 What happened: -t added a totals line: 19Gi combined memory (15Gi RAM + 4Gi swap). 8.5Gi used, 10Gi free+available. This is the number for capacity planning — the server has about 10Gi headroom before memory becomes constrained.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: Don't fixate on the free column — available is what matters for new processes. Linux uses free RAM for buffers/cache (good!). Low available + high swap used = real memory pressure. free -h -s 2 for live monitoring. /proc/meminfo has the raw data.

df

DISK System Information LFCS Domain 2

Report filesystem disk space usage — see how full your disks are

df shows the total, used, and available space for all mounted filesystems. It's the first command to run when a deployment fails with "No space left on device." Also shows inode usage with -i — critical when you have space but can't create files.

Syntax

df [OPTIONS] [FILE...]

# Common patterns:
df -h                       # Human-readable, all filesystems
df -h /var/log              # Check space on a specific mount
df -i                       # Inode usage instead of blocks
df -T                       # Show filesystem type
df -h -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs  # Exclude temporary filesystems

Parameters

FlagDescription
-h, --human-readablePrint sizes in human-readable format (1K, 234M, 2G)
-i, --inodesList inode information instead of block usage
-l, --localLimit listing to local filesystems only
-T, --print-typePrint filesystem type (ext4, xfs, tmpfs, etc.)
-t, --type=TYPELimit to filesystems of given TYPE (e.g., -t ext4)
-x, --exclude-type=TYPEExclude filesystems of given TYPE
--totalProduce a grand total line

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — disk usage displayed

Example 1: Basic Disk Space Check

Scenario: Carol checks overall disk health after a "No space left" deployment error.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

df -h

Output:

Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/sda1 50G 42G 5.5G 89% / tmpfs 7.8G 1.2M 7.8G 1% /dev/shm /dev/sdb1 200G 145G 45G 77% /mnt/data tmpfs 1.6G 8.0K 1.6G 1% /run/user/1000

📝 What happened: Root filesystem is 89% full with only 5.5GB remaining — the likely cause of the deployment failure. /mnt/data has 45GB free (77%). tmpfs entries are RAM-based and not a concern. Focus cleanup on /: check /var/log and /tmp first.

Example 2: Check Specific Mount Point

Scenario: Alice checks if /lpj (on /mnt/data) has enough space for a large database backup.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

├── 📄 manage.py

└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

df -h /lpj/ops/backups/

Output:

Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/sdb1 200G 145G 45G 77% /mnt/data

📝 What happened: /lpj/ops/backups is on /dev/sdb1 (mounted at /mnt/data). 45GB free — more than enough for a database dump (~500MB). The backup can proceed. Always check the specific mount point before large write operations.

Example 3: Check Inode Usage

Scenario: Dave's PostgreSQL reports "No space left on device" but df shows 45GB free. The problem: out of inodes.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

df -i /mnt/data

Output:

Filesystem Inodes IUsed IFree IUse% Mounted on /dev/sdb1 13107200 13095000 12200 99% /mnt/data

📝 What happened: 99% inode usage! Only 12,200 inodes remain. Each file/directory consumes one inode — you can have free space but no inodes. This is common with millions of small files (log rotations, cache files). Solution: delete or archive old small files.

Example 4: Show Filesystem Types

Scenario: Carol needs to know which filesystems are ext4 vs xfs for a backup script.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

df -hT

Output:

Filesystem Type Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/sda1 ext4 50G 42G 5.5G 89% / tmpfs tmpfs 7.8G 1.2M 7.8G 1% /dev/shm /dev/sdb1 xfs 200G 145G 45G 77% /mnt/data

📝 What happened: -T added a Type column: root is ext4, /mnt/data is xfs, tmpfs is RAM-based. This matters because ext4 and xfs have different tools — fsck.ext4 vs xfs_repair for recovery. Knowing filesystem types is essential for maintenance scripts.

Example 5: Exclude Noise with -x

Scenario: Carol wants a clean view of real disk usage, filtering out temporary filesystems.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

df -h -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs -x squashfs

Output:

Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/sda1 50G 42G 5.5G 89% / /dev/sdb1 200G 145G 45G 77% /mnt/data

📝 What happened: -x excluded tmpfs, devtmpfs, and squashfs — showing only real disk filesystems. Two devices: root (50GB, 89% — needs attention) and data (200GB, 77% — healthy). This filtered view is ideal for capacity planning reports.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: df -h for human-readable disk space. df -i for inode usage — critical when "disk full" but space exists. df -T shows filesystem types. df -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs filters noise. Know that df shows filesystem-level usage; du shows directory-level usage.

du

DISK System Information LFCS Domain 2

Estimate file space usage — find what's consuming your disk space

du recursively calculates disk usage of files and directories. While df tells you a filesystem is full, du tells you WHAT is filling it up. Essential for disk cleanup and capacity analysis.

Syntax

du [OPTIONS] [FILE...]

# Common patterns:
du -sh *                    # Size of each item in current directory
du -sh /lpj/ops/logs/       # Total size of logs directory
du -h --max-depth=2 /lpj/   # Two levels deep
du -sh * | sort -rh | head -10  # Top 10 largest items

Parameters

FlagDescription
-h, --human-readableHuman-readable sizes (K, M, G)
-s, --summarizeDisplay only a total for each argument
-d, --max-depth=NPrint total for directories only N levels deep
-c, --totalProduce a grand total
--timeShow time of last modification
-a, --allWrite counts for all files, not just directories

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — usage displayed

  45M   /var/tmp

Example 5: Compare du vs df

Scenario: Carol demonstrates why df and du can show different numbers on the same filesystem.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

echo "df -h:" && df -h /mnt/data | tail -1 && echo "du -sh /mnt/data:" && du -sh /mnt/data 2>/dev/null

Output:

df -h: /dev/sdb1 200G 145G 45G 77% /mnt/data du -sh /mnt/data: 143G /mnt/data

📝 What happened: df shows 145G used; du shows 143G — a 2GB difference. This is normal: df counts filesystem metadata and deleted-but-open files, while du only counts files visible in the directory tree. A large gap suggests processes holding deleted files open — use lsof | grep deleted to find them.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: du -sh * is the go-to for finding directory sizes. du -h --max-depth=N limits depth. du -sh * | sort -rh | head finds the largest items. du counts actual file sizes; df counts filesystem blocks. They can differ — investigate large gaps with lsof | grep deleted.

lscpu                           # Full CPU info

lscpu -p                        # CPU list in CSV format

FlagDescription
-a, --allPrint both online and offline CPUs
-e, --extendedExtended parseable format (human-readable table)
-p, --parseParseable format (CSV, no human formatting)
-J, --jsonJSON output format

0Success

lspci

HARDWARE System Information LFCS Domain 4

List all PCI devices — network cards, storage controllers, GPUs, and more

lspci -v                    # Verbose output

Parameters

FlagDescription
-kShow kernel drivers handling each device
-v, -vv, -vvvIncreasing verbosity levels
-s [[BUS:]DEVICE]Show only devices at specified PCI address
-nnShow numeric vendor and device IDs
-tShow bus tree structure

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Command:

lspci -nn | grep -i net

Output:

00:03.0 Ethernet controller [0200]: Intel Corporation 82540EM Gigabit Ethernet Controller [8086:100e] (rev 03)

📝 What happened: Vendor ID 8086 (Intel), Device ID 100e (82540EM). The [8086:100e] format is the standard PCI ID — searchable in driver databases and kernel bug trackers. Use this to find the exact driver and known issues.

-[0000:00]-+-00.0 +-01.0 +-01.1 +-02.0 \-03.0

📝 What happened: All 5 devices are on bus 0000:00 — a flat topology with no PCI bridges. This is typical for virtual machines. Physical servers would show multiple buses connected via PCI bridges. The tree view helps identify NUMA node affinities.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: lsblk shows block devices in a tree. lsblk -f adds filesystem info (UUID, type). lsblk -d shows disks only. lsblk -J for JSON. Use before fdisk, mkfs, or mount to understand the current layout. LVM devices appear as lvm type.

Example 2: Check for Cilium eBPF Modules

Scenario: Alice verifies eBPF kernel modules are loaded for Cilium network policies.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

lsmod | grep -E "bpf|bpfilter|xt_bpf"

Output:

bpf 348160 3 xt_bpf 16384 2 bpfilter 24576 0

📝 What happened: Three eBPF-related modules loaded: bpf (core eBPF infrastructure, 3 dependents), xt_bpf (iptables eBPF match, 2 dependents), and bpfilter (packet filtering). All required for Cilium eBPF datapath. If any were missing, Cilium would fall back to non-eBPF mode.

└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

echo "Loaded modules: $(lsmod | wc -l)"

Output:

Loaded modules: 97

📝 What happened: 97 modules loaded. The first line is a header, so 96 actual modules. A significant deviation from this count on another server suggests missing or extra drivers. Use lsmod | wc -l as a quick fleet consistency check.

Example 4: Check Overlay/Storage Modules

Scenario: Carol verifies Docker's overlay filesystem modules are loaded.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

lsmod | grep -E "overlay|ext4|xfs"

Output:

overlay 151552 1 ext4 1048576 1 xfs 1568768 1

📝 What happened: Overlay (Docker's filesystem), ext4 (root), and xfs (data disk) are all loaded. The Used by=1 for overlay means Docker is using it. If overlay was missing, Docker would fail to start. Always check these three after a kernel update.

Example 5: Size Analysis — Largest Modules

Scenario: Carol identifies the largest kernel modules consuming kernel memory.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API app
├── 📄 Dockerfile
├── 📄 manage.py
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

lsmod | sort -k2 -rn | head -5

Output:

xfs 1568768 1 ext4 1048576 1 overlay 151552 1 bpf 348160 3 e1000e 282624 0

📝 What happened: xfs (1.5MB) and ext4 (1MB) are the largest modules — filesystem drivers are inherently large. bpf at 348KB is the eBPF subsystem. Module size affects kernel memory footprint but is not typically a concern unless total kernel memory usage is excessive (>500MB).

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: lsmod reads /proc/modules. Columns: Module (name), Size (bytes), Used by (dependency count). If Used by > 0, the module is in use and cannot be removed with rmmod. Use lsmod | grep PATTERN to check if a specific driver loaded.

modinfo

KERNEL System Information LFCS Domain 4

Display detailed information about a kernel module — version, dependencies, parameters

modinfo extracts metadata from a kernel module (.ko file): its version, author, description, license, file path, dependencies, and configurable parameters. Essential for checking driver versions and available tuning knobs.

Syntax

modinfo [OPTIONS] MODULE

# Common patterns:
modinfo e1000e                  # All info about e1000e driver
modinfo -F version e1000e       # Just the version field
modinfo -F parm e1000e          # Just the parameters
modinfo -n e1000e               # Just the filename

Parameters

FlagDescription
-F, --field FIELDPrint only the specified field (e.g., version, author, description)
-n, --filenamePrint the module filename only
-0, --nullNull-delimited output (for scripts)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Module not found

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: modinfo MODULE shows all module metadata. modinfo -F version MODULE = version only. modinfo -F parm MODULE = tunable parameters. modinfo -n MODULE = file path. Use before loading modules to verify compatibility.

sysctl

KERNEL System Information LFCS Domain 4

Configure kernel parameters at runtime — tune the kernel without rebooting

sysctl reads and writes kernel parameters from /proc/sys/. It can change network settings, memory management, and security parameters during runtime. Persistent changes go in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/.

Syntax

sysctl [OPTIONS] [PARAMETER[=VALUE]]

# Common patterns:
sysctl -a                               # List all parameters
sysctl vm.swappiness                    # Read a parameter
sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10              # Write a parameter
sysctl -p                               # Load settings from /etc/sysctl.conf
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward              # Check if IP forwarding is on

Parameters

FlagDescription
-a, --allDisplay all current kernel parameters
-w, --writeWrite a value to a kernel parameter (requires root for most)
-p, --load[=FILE]Load settings from FILE (default: /etc/sysctl.conf)
-n, --valuesShow only values, no parameter names

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Example 1: Check Memory Swappiness

Scenario: Carol checks the swappiness value before deciding to tune it for PostgreSQL.

📁 Directory Snippet:

lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root

Example 2: Verify Kubernetes Networking Prerequisites

Scenario: Alice checks kernel parameters required for Kubernetes pod networking.

└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding

Output:

net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1 net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1 net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding = 1

📝 What happened: All three must be 1 for Kubernetes networking. ip_forward enables packet routing between pods. bridge-nf-call-iptables ensures iptables rules apply to bridged traffic (required by kube-proxy). If any is 0, pod networking breaks.

Example 4: Persist a Parameter

Scenario: Carol permanently sets vm.swappiness to 10 for the database server.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

echo "vm.swappiness=10" | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-anihpj-db.conf && sudo sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-anihpj-db.conf

Output:

vm.swappiness = 10

📝 What happened: The parameter was written to a .conf file and immediately applied. The 99- prefix ensures it loads last (applied alphabetically). This survives reboots — systemd-sysctl applies all /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf files at boot.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root

Command:

sysctl -n vm.swappiness

Output:

10

📝 What happened: -n printed only the value (10) without "vm.swappiness =". This is ideal for scripts that need numeric comparison: if [ "$(sysctl -n vm.swappiness)" -gt 50 ]; then echo "Too high"; fi.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: sysctl PARAM reads, sysctl -w PARAM=VALUE writes. sysctl -p loads from /etc/sysctl.conf. Persist in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf. Key params: vm.swappiness, net.ipv4.ip_forward, kernel.hostname. Changes are immediate but non-persistent unless saved to a .conf file.

🌐 Networking

Commands for network diagnostics, data transfer, remote access, and service connectivity testing. Used daily by the anihpj team for debugging connectivity, downloading dependencies, managing remote servers, and monitoring network health across all 11 servers.

ping

TEST Networking Core LFCS Domain 4

Send ICMP ECHO_REQUEST to network hosts — test reachability, latency, and packet loss

ping is the universal network connectivity test. It sends ICMP echo requests and measures response time and packet loss. Essential for verifying that a server is reachable and that the network path is healthy.

For anihpj/jobpost, ping is used for:

  • Verifying connectivity between app servers and the database server
  • Testing DNS resolution: ping prod-db-01 confirms DNS works
  • Monitoring latency between microservices during incident response
  • Validating firewall rules allow ICMP between security zones

Syntax

ping [OPTIONS] DESTINATION

# Common patterns:
ping google.com                 # Continuous ping (Ctrl+C to stop)
ping -c 5 anihpj.com            # Exactly 5 pings
ping -i 0.5 192.168.1.1         # Fast ping (0.5s interval)
ping -s 1000 10.0.0.1           # Large packet size test
ping -w 10 10.0.0.1             # Timeout after 10 seconds

Parameters

FlagDescription
-c COUNTStop after sending COUNT packets
-i INTERVALWait INTERVAL seconds between pings (default 1, root can set < 0.2)
-s PACKETSIZESend PACKETSIZE bytes of data (default 56, plus 8 ICMP header = 64)
-t TTLSet Time To Live (max hops)
-w DEADLINETimeout after DEADLINE seconds regardless of -c
-W TIMEOUTTime to wait for each response in seconds
-fFlood ping — send 100+/sec (root only, for stress testing)
-DPrint timestamp before each line
-qQuiet output — only summary at end

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success — at least one response received
1No responses (host unreachable or packet loss 100%)
2Error — invalid option or DNS resolution failed

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Connectivity Test

Daily Workflow: Carol pings all production servers to verify network reachability before deployment. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical ping usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ ping -c 2 prod-web-01
64 bytes from prod-web-01 (192.168.10.10): icmp_seq=1 ttl=64
carol@prod-api-01:~$ ping -c 2 prod-db-01

Examples

#  prod-web-01:80       — Nginx HTTP
#  prod-api-01:8000     — Django REST API
#  prod-db-01:5432      — PostgreSQL
#  prod-redis-01:6379   — Redis cache
Example 1: Quick Connectivity Test

Scenario: Carol checks if prod-db-01 is reachable after a network change.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

ping -c 3 prod-db-01

Output:

PING prod-db-01 (192.168.10.30) 56(84) bytes of data. 64 bytes from prod-db-01 (192.168.10.30): icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=1.23 ms 64 bytes from prod-db-01 (192.168.10.30): icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=1.15 ms 64 bytes from prod-db-01 (192.168.10.30): icmp_seq=3 ttl=64 time=1.18 ms --- prod-db-01 ping statistics --- 3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss, time 2003ms rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 1.15/1.18/1.23/0.03 ms

📝 What happened: 3/3 packets received, 0% loss, ~1.2ms average latency. The database server is reachable with excellent latency — the network change was successful. ttl=64 confirms the server is on the same network (no router hops).

Example 2: DNS Resolution Verification

Scenario: Alice verifies DNS is resolving correctly after a DNS server migration.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests

└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:

# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

ping -c 1 prod-api-01 && echo "DNS OK" || echo "DNS FAILED"

Output:

PING prod-api-01.anihpj.internal (192.168.10.20) 56(84) bytes of data. 64 bytes from prod-api-01 (192.168.10.20): icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.98 ms DNS OK

📝 What happened: The hostname resolved to 192.168.10.20 and the ping succeeded. If DNS had failed, ping would exit with code 2 ("unknown host") and the script would catch it. This one-liner is the standard DNS health check.

Example 3: Test Packet Size / MTU

Scenario: Bob tests the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) between servers.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

ping -c 2 -s 1472 -M do prod-web-01

Output:

PING prod-web-01 (192.168.10.10) 1472(1500) bytes of data. 1480 bytes from prod-web-01 (192.168.10.10): icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=1.50 ms 1480 bytes from prod-web-01 (192.168.10.10): icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=1.45 ms

📝 What happened: 1472 bytes payload + 28 bytes headers = 1500 byte MTU. The ping succeeded with -M do (Don't Fragment). If the path MTU was lower, the ping would fail with "message too long". This confirms the network path supports standard 1500-byte frames.

Example 4: Flood Ping for Stress Testing

Scenario: Carol stress-tests the network link between prod-web-01 and prod-api-01.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

sudo ping -f -c 1000 prod-api-01

Output:

PING prod-api-01 (192.168.10.20) 56(84) bytes of data. --- prod-api-01 ping statistics --- 1000 packets transmitted, 998 received, 0.2% packet loss, time 8999ms rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.89/1.12/2.34/0.18 ms, ipg/ewma 9.01/1.15 ms

📝 What happened: 1000 packets at flood rate (~111/sec), only 0.2% loss. The network link handles high throughput with minimal jitter (stddev 0.18ms). 2 packets were lost — likely buffer overflow on the receiving NIC. This is excellent performance for a production workload.

Example 5: Audible Ping for Cable Testing

Scenario: Dave is physically at the server rack testing a new network cable.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

ping -a 192.168.10.30

Output:

# Terminal beeps on each response — no need to watch the screen # Dave plugs in the cable, hears a beep, and knows it's connected # Press Ctrl+C to stop

📝 What happened: ping -a emits an audible beep for each response. When you're physically at a server rack or patch panel, you don't need to watch the screen — the beep tells you the cable is connected. A classic sysadmin trick.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: ping -c N limits count. Exit 0 = success, 1 = no reply, 2 = error. ping -i sets interval (root for < 0.2s). ping -s tests MTU. ping -f floods (root only). ICMP may be blocked by firewalls — a failed ping doesn't always mean the host is down.

curl

HTTP Networking Core LFCS Domain 4

Transfer data from/to servers — the swiss army knife for API testing, downloads, and web debugging

curl supports HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SFTP, and dozens of other protocols. It is the go-to tool for testing REST APIs, downloading files, checking HTTP headers, and debugging web services. Every API developer and SRE uses curl daily.

For anihpj/jobpost, curl is used for:

  • Testing the jobpost REST API endpoints during development
  • Verifying health check endpoints: curl -f http://localhost:8000/health
  • Debugging ingress/load balancer routing with header inspection
  • Downloading dependencies from internal artifact repositories

Syntax

curl [OPTIONS] URL

# Common patterns:
curl https://api.anihpj.com/health           # GET request
curl -X POST -d '{"key":"val"}' URL          # POST JSON
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" URL    # With auth header
curl -o file.tar.gz URL                      # Download to file
curl -I https://anihpj.com                   # Headers only

Parameters

FlagDescription
-X, --request METHODHTTP method: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH
-H, --header LINECustom header (repeatable)
-d, --data DATASend data in request body
-o, --output FILEWrite output to FILE
-O, --remote-nameSave with remote filename
-L, --locationFollow redirects
-s, --silentSilent mode (no progress/errors)
-v, --verboseVerbose output (show request + response)
-i, --includeInclude response headers in output
-I, --headFetch headers only (HEAD request)
-k, --insecureAllow insecure TLS (self-signed certs)
-u, --user USER:PASSBasic authentication
-w, --write-out FORMATOutput after completion (e.g., timing info)
--connect-timeout SECMax time for connection attempt

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
6Couldn't resolve host (DNS)
7Failed to connect
28Operation timeout

Example 3: Verbose Debugging

Scenario: Bob debugs why the API returns 502 — uses verbose curl to see the full exchange.
