curl -v http://prod-api-01:8000/api/v1/jobs/ 2>&1 | head -20

Output:

* Trying 192.168.10.20:8000... * Connected to prod-api-01 (192.168.10.20) port 8000 > GET /api/v1/jobs/ HTTP/1.1 > Host: prod-api-01:8000 > User-Agent: curl/7.81.0 > Accept: */* * Empty reply from server * Closing connection 0 curl: (52) Empty reply from server

📝 What happened: -v reveals the full HTTP exchange: connection succeeded but the server returned an empty reply — the backend (gunicorn) is not responding. This is the critical clue: the problem is at the application layer, not the network. Without -v, you would only see the cryptic error code 52.

Example 5: Measure API Response Time

Scenario: Alice measures detailed timing for the jobpost API to monitor performance.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

curl -w "\nDNS: %{time_namelookup}s | Connect: %{time_connect}s | TTFB: %{time_starttransfer}s | Total: %{time_total}s\n" -o /dev/null -s http://prod-api-01:8000/api/v1/jobs/

Output:

DNS: 0.001s | Connect: 0.003s | TTFB: 0.089s | Total: 0.092s

📝 What happened: DNS took 1ms (local cache), TCP connect 3ms (same subnet), Time-To-First-Byte 89ms (application processing), total 92ms. TTFB dominates — most of the time is spent in the application, not the network. This breakdown helps identify whether latency is network or application.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" for status-only checks. curl -v for debugging. curl -L follows redirects. curl -k ignores TLS errors (only for testing!). curl -w with timing variables is essential for performance monitoring.

wget

DOWNLOAD Networking LFCS Domain 4

Non-interactive network downloader — reliable large-file downloads with retry and resume

wget is built for reliability: it retries on failure, resumes interrupted downloads, and can mirror entire websites. Unlike curl (which streams to stdout), wget saves to files by default. Ideal for automated downloads in scripts and CI/CD pipelines.

Syntax

wget [OPTIONS] URL

# Common patterns:
wget https://example.com/file.tar.gz        # Download file
wget -O output.tar.gz URL                   # Custom output name
wget -c URL                                 # Resume partial download
wget -b URL                                 # Background download
wget -i urls.txt                            # Download from URL list

Parameters

FlagDescription
-O FILEWrite to FILE instead of remote name
-c, --continueResume a partial download
-b, --backgroundGo to background after startup
-i FILERead URLs from FILE
--limit-rate=NLimit download speed (e.g., 500k, 2m)
-t, --tries=NSet number of retries (0 = unlimited)
-q, --quietNo output

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Generic error
4Network failure

Resuming download for jobpost-worker.tar (60% complete) HTTP request sent, awaiting response... 206 Partial Content Length: 250M (262144000), 100M remaining Saving to: 'jobpost-worker.tar' 100%[++++++++++++] 250M 45.2M/s in 2.2s

📝 What happened: -c sent a Range header requesting only the remaining 40% (100MB). The server responded with HTTP 206 (Partial Content). Downloaded the remaining 100MB at 45.2MB/s. Saved ~3 minutes vs starting from scratch.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

wget --tries=10 --waitretry=30 https://ci.anihpj.internal/artifacts/test-report.html

Output:

--2026-06-04 16:20:00-- https://ci.anihpj.internal/artifacts/test-report.html Connecting... failed: Connection refused. Retrying (1/10)... failed: Connection refused. Retrying (2/10)... connected. HTTP request sent, awaiting response... 200 OK Length: 45678 (45K) [text/html] Saving to: 'test-report.html' 2026-06-04 16:20:32 (45.6 KB/s) - 'test-report.html' saved [45678/45678]

📝 What happened: First 2 attempts failed (CI server restarting). 3rd attempt succeeded. --waitretry=30 waited 30 seconds between retries. This resilience pattern is essential in CI/CD pipelines where artifact servers may be temporarily unavailable.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: wget -c resumes downloads. wget --limit-rate controls bandwidth. wget -b backgrounds. wget --mirror clones sites. wget -i urls.txt batch downloads. Unlike curl, wget saves to files by default and handles retries natively.

ssh

REMOTE Networking Core LFCS Domain 4

OpenSSH remote login — securely connect to servers, execute commands, and create tunnels

ssh is the backbone of remote Linux administration. It provides encrypted shell access, remote command execution, port forwarding (tunnels), and file transfer (scp/sftp). Every server in the anihpj fleet is managed exclusively via SSH.

Syntax

ssh [OPTIONS] [USER@]HOST [COMMAND]

# Common patterns:
ssh prod-web-01                                 # Login
ssh -p 2222 staging-01                          # Custom port
ssh -i ~/.ssh/anihpj_key carol@prod-api-01      # With private key
ssh prod-api-01 "systemctl status gunicorn"     # Remote command
ssh -L 5432:localhost:5432 prod-db-01           # Port tunnel

Parameters

FlagDescription
-p PORTPort to connect to (default: 22)
-i KEYFILEPrivate key for public key authentication
-v, -vv, -vvvVerbose (debugging — more v = more detail)
-L PORT:HOST:PORTLocal port forwarding (tunnel)
-NNo remote command (for tunnels only)
-fBackground after authentication
-AEnable agent forwarding
-CCompress all data

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
255Connection failed

ssh-copy-id jenkins@staging-01 && ssh jenkins@staging-01 "echo 'Key-based auth works'"

Output:

/usr/bin/ssh-copy-id: INFO: Source of key(s): /home/alice/.ssh/id_rsa.pub /usr/bin/ssh-copy-id: INFO: 1 key(s) remain to be installed Number of key(s) added: 1 Key-based auth works

📝 What happened: ssh-copy-id appended alice's public key to ~jenkins/.ssh/authorized_keys on staging-01. The second ssh command confirmed it works — no password prompt. This is the standard method for setting up CI/CD SSH access.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: ssh USER@HOST COMMAND runs a remote command. ssh -L creates local tunnels. ssh -v debugs. Key files must have 600 permissions. ~/.ssh/authorized_keys must be 600. ssh-copy-id sets up key-based auth. Use -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no only in trusted environments.

scp

TRANSFER Networking LFCS Domain 4

Secure copy — transfer files between hosts over SSH

scp copies files between local and remote hosts using the SSH protocol. It's the simplest way to move files between servers — same authentication as SSH, same encryption. Use -r for directories and -P for custom ports.

Syntax

scp [OPTIONS] SOURCE... DESTINATION

# Common patterns:
scp file.txt prod-web-01:/lpj/              # Local → Remote
scp prod-web-01:/lpj/app.log ./             # Remote → Local
scp -r /lpj/k8s/ prod-api-01:/backup/       # Recursive directory

Parameters

FlagDescription
-rRecursively copy directories
-P PORTSSH port (note: capital P, unlike ssh)
-pPreserve timestamps, permissions
-CCompress during transfer
-i KEYFILEIdentity file (private key)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error

📝 What happened: 234MB transferred directly from prod-db-01 to backup-nas — the data never touched Carol's laptop. scp routes through the initiating host by default; add -3 for a direct server-to-server transfer that avoids the local machine entirely.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: scp uses SSH. -r for directories. -P for port (capital P!). -p preserves attributes. -C compresses. -3 for direct server-to-server copy. Always test SSH connectivity first: ssh HOST "echo ok" before scp.

rsync

SYNC Networking LFCS Domain 4

Fast, versatile file copying — delta transfers, mirroring, and backups over SSH

rsync only transfers the DIFFERENCES between source and destination — making it vastly more efficient than scp for repeated syncs. Supports local and remote sync, compression, bandwidth limiting, and partial transfers. The gold standard for backups and deployments.

Syntax

rsync [OPTIONS] SOURCE... DEST

# Common patterns:
rsync -avz /lpj/ backup-nas:/backup/         # Archive sync with compression
rsync -avz --delete /source/ /dest/           # Mirror (delete extras on dest)
rsync -avzn /source/ /dest/                   # Dry run
rsync -avz --exclude="*.pyc" /src/ /dest/     # Exclude patterns

Parameters

FlagDescription
-a, --archiveArchive mode: preserve permissions, timestamps, symlinks, recurse
-v, --verboseVerbose output
-z, --compressCompress during transfer
-n, --dry-runShow what would be transferred without doing it
--deleteDelete files on dest not present on source (true mirror)
--progressShow per-file progress
--exclude=PATTERNExclude files matching pattern
--bwlimit=RATELimit bandwidth (KBps)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
23Partial transfer (some files failed)
24Source files vanished during transfer

sending incremental file list ./ ops/logs/app.log ops/backups/daily/db_dump_20260604.sql sent 245M bytes received 1.2K bytes 49.0M bytes/sec total size is 2.3G speedup is 9.41 Backup synced

Example 3: Bandwidth-Limited Sync

Scenario: Carol syncs logs during business hours with a 500KB/s limit.

📁 Environment Snippet:

lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API

# anihpj Servers:

# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

rsync -avz --bwlimit=500 /lpj/ops/logs/ monitoring-01:/logs/prod-api/

Output:

app.log 524,288 100% 500.00kB/s 0:00:01 (xfr#1) error.log 196,542 100% 500.00kB/s 0:00:00 (xfr#2) sent 721K bytes received 48 bytes 480.67K bytes/sec total size is 720K speedup is 1.00

📝 What happened: Transfer capped at exactly 500KB/s — production traffic unaffected. The speedup of 1.00 means these files were new (no delta optimization possible). For existing files, rsync would transfer only the changed bytes.

Example 5: Show Progress for Large File

Scenario: Carol transfers a 2GB database dump with a progress bar.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

db_full.dump 2,147,483,648 100% 45.23MB/s 0:00:45 (xfr#1, to-chk=0/1) sent 2.15G bytes received 35 bytes 47.73M bytes/sec total size is 2.15G speedup is 1.00

📝 What happened: 2.15GB transferred in 45 seconds at 45MB/s. --progress shows real-time percentage and speed, -h makes sizes human-readable. Speedup 1.00 means the file is new — rsync couldn't delta-optimize (the whole file was transferred).

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: rsync -avz is the go-to for syncs. -n for dry-run previews. --delete for true mirroring. --bwlimit controls bandwidth. Trailing / on source means "contents of". --exclude for filtering. rsync over SSH is encrypted; rsync daemon (: :) is not.

netstat

CONNECTIONS Networking LFCS Domain 4

Print network connections, routing tables, and interface statistics — the classic network inspection tool

netstat displays active connections, listening ports, routing tables, and per-protocol statistics. While ss is its modern replacement, netstat is still universally available and widely used. Key flags: -tulnp (TCP/UDP listeners with process info).

Syntax

netstat [OPTIONS]

# Common patterns:
netstat -tulnp                  # All listening TCP/UDP ports with PIDs
netstat -an                     # All connections (numeric)
netstat -r                      # Routing table
netstat -i                      # Interface statistics

Parameters

FlagDescription
-t, --tcpTCP connections
-u, --udpUDP connections
-l, --listeningListening sockets only
-n, --numericShow numeric addresses (no DNS lookup — faster)
-p, --programShow PID/program name (requires root)
-a, --allShow both listening and non-listening
-r, --routeKernel routing table
-i, --interfacesInterface statistics

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Example 1: Check What's Listening

Scenario: Carol verifies that gunicorn, nginx, and postgres are listening on prod-api-01.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests

# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

sudo netstat -tulnp | head -10

Output:

Proto Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address Foreign Address State PID/Program tcp 0 0 0.0.0.0:8000 0.0.0.0:* LISTEN 12345/gunicorn tcp 0 0 0.0.0.0:80 0.0.0.0:* LISTEN 1234/nginx tcp 0 0 127.0.0.1:5432 0.0.0.0:* LISTEN 3456/postgres tcp 0 0 0.0.0.0:22 0.0.0.0:* LISTEN 789/sshd

📝 What happened: Four services listening: gunicorn (8000), nginx (80), postgres (5432, localhost-only), and sshd (22). -tulnp = TCP, UDP, Listening, Numeric, Program. The localhost-only binding for postgres (127.0.0.1) is correct — no external access allowed.

Example 2: All Active Connections

Scenario: Carol checks all active connections to identify which servers are communicating.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API

# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

netstat -ant | grep ESTABLISHED | head -5

Output:

tcp 0 0 192.168.10.20:8000 192.168.10.10:45678 ESTABLISHED tcp 0 0 192.168.10.20:5432 192.168.10.20:54320 ESTABLISHED tcp 0 0 192.168.10.20:8000 192.168.10.11:45680 ESTABLISHED

📝 What happened: Three established connections: prod-web-01/02 connecting to the API (port 8000), and a local postgres connection. -ant = All, Numeric, TCP — the numeric flag prevents DNS resolution delays. Use this during incident response to map the service dependency graph.

Example 3: Interface Statistics

Scenario: Carol checks network interface stats after a suspected packet loss incident.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests

# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

netstat -i

Output:

Iface MTU RX-OK RX-ERR RX-DRP TX-OK TX-ERR TX-DRP eth0 1500 1234567 0 0 987654 0 0 lo 65536 45678 0 0 45678 0 0

📝 What happened: eth0: 1.2M packets received, 987K transmitted, zero errors or drops. The network interface is clean — the packet loss must be happening upstream (router/switch). If RX-DRP was non-zero, the kernel ring buffer might be full (increase with sysctl).

Example 4: Check SSH Connections

Scenario: Eve audits all active SSH connections for unauthorized access.

lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

tcp 0 0 192.168.10.20:22 192.168.1.50:54321 ESTABLISHED 789/sshd: carol tcp 0 0 192.168.10.20:22 192.168.1.100:54322 ESTABLISHED 1234/sshd: alice

📝 What happened: Two SSH connections: carol (from 192.168.1.50) and alice (from 192.168.1.100). Both are authorized IPs. If an unknown IP appeared here, Eve would investigate immediately. The PID/program column shows which SSH session belongs to which user.

# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

netstat -ant | awk '{print $6}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Output:

45 ESTABLISHED 12 TIME_WAIT 5 LISTEN 2 CLOSE_WAIT 1 SYN_RECV

📝 What happened: 45 established (active), 12 TIME_WAIT (just closed, normal), 5 listening. 2 CLOSE_WAIT is the concern — these are connections where the remote end closed but the local application hasn't called close(). CLOSE_WAIT connections indicate a potential application bug or resource leak.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: netstat -tulnp is the most-used form. -n avoids DNS delays. -p needs root for all processes. ss is the modern replacement (faster, more features). Know the TCP states: LISTEN, ESTABLISHED, TIME_WAIT, CLOSE_WAIT, SYN_SENT.

ss

CONNECTIONS Networking LFCS Domain 4

Socket statistics — the modern, faster replacement for netstat

ss is the modern replacement for netstat. It's faster (reads directly from kernel), shows more detailed socket info (timers, memory), and supports filtering. Prefer ss over netstat on modern systems.

Syntax

ss [OPTIONS] [FILTER]

# Common patterns:
ss -tlnp                        # TCP listeners with PIDs (netstat equivalent)
ss -s                           # Summary statistics
ss dst 192.168.10.30            # Filter by destination
ss sport = :8000                # Filter by source port

Parameters

FlagDescription
-t, --tcpTCP sockets
-u, --udpUDP sockets
-l, --listeningListening sockets
-n, --numericNumeric (no DNS resolution)
-p, --processesShow process info
-s, --summarySummary statistics
-a, --allAll sockets

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Example 1: Modern netstat -tulnp

Scenario: Carol checks listening services on prod-api-01 using ss instead of netstat.

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

Command:

sudo ss -tlnp

Output:

State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:Port Process LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:8000 0.0.0.0:* users:(("gunicorn",pid=12345,fd=4)) LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:80 0.0.0.0:* users:(("nginx",pid=1234,fd=6)) LISTEN 0 128 127.0.0.1:5432 0.0.0.0:* users:(("postgres",pid=3456,fd=3))

📝 What happened: Same result as netstat but ss is faster (reads from /proc/net/tcp directly). The Recv-Q/Send-Q columns show socket buffer backlogs — non-zero values indicate the application is slow to process data.

ss -s

Output:

Total: 156 TCP: 89 (estab 45, closed 32, timewait 12) Transport Total IP IPv6 RAW 1 0 1 UDP 12 8 4 TCP 89 72 17

📝 What happened: 156 total sockets: 89 TCP, 12 UDP, 1 RAW. 45 established TCP connections, 32 closed, 12 in TIME_WAIT. This summary is perfect for a quick health assessment — high TIME_WAIT is normal for web servers; high CLOSE_WAIT indicates application issues.

Scenario: Carol checks all connections to the database server prod-db-01.

📝 What happened: Two connections to prod-db-01:5432 from the API server. ss filtering is more powerful than grep — dst matches the destination address directly. Also supports src, sport, dport, and state filters like state established.

Example 4: Show Process Memory for Sockets

Scenario: Dave checks socket memory usage to diagnose a potential buffer bloat.

📁 Environment Snippet:

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

ss -tm state established '( sport = :8000 )'

Output:

State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:Port ESTAB 0 0 192.168.10.20:8000 192.168.10.10:45678 skmem:(r0,rb212992,t0,tb87040,f0,w0,o0,bl0,d0)

📝 What happened: -m shows socket memory: receive buffer 212KB, transmit buffer 87KB. The r0/t0 means buffers are not full. High rb/tb values with non-zero r/t suggest the application is consuming/producing data slower than the network — a performance bottleneck.

Example 5: Count TIME_WAIT Connections

Scenario: Carol checks for excessive TIME_WAIT sockets after a load test.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API

# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l

Output:

1247

📝 What happened: 1,247 sockets in TIME_WAIT. This is expected after a load test — each connection stays in TIME_WAIT for 60 seconds before being recycled. If this persists after the test, tune net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse. Modern ss makes state filtering trivial compared to netstat + grep.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: ss -tlnp = netstat replacement. ss -s for summary. ss dst IP or ss sport = :PORT for filtering. ss -m for memory info. Always prefer ss over netstat on modern Linux — faster, more features, actively maintained.

ip

NETWORK Networking LFCS Domain 4

Show/manipulate routing, devices, and tunnels — the modern replacement for ifconfig, route, arp

ip from the iproute2 suite replaces ifconfig, route, and arp. It provides a unified interface for addresses, links, routes, and neighbors. Essential for modern Linux networking management.

Syntax

ip [OPTIONS] OBJECT {COMMAND | help}

# Common patterns:
ip addr show                        # Show all IP addresses
ip link show                        # Show network interfaces
ip route show                       # Show routing table
ip neigh show                       # Show ARP table (neighbors)

Parameters

Object/FlagDescription
addr, aIP addresses (IPv4/IPv6)
link, lNetwork interfaces (up/down, MTU, MAC)
route, rRouting table entries
neigh, nARP/NDP neighbors
-s, -statsShow statistics
-4, -6IPv4 or IPv6 only

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Scenario: Carol checks the ARP cache to verify MAC address resolution.

Output:

192.168.10.1 dev eth0 lladdr 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e REACHABLE 192.168.10.30 dev eth0 lladdr 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:6f STALE 192.168.10.10 dev eth0 lladdr 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:7a REACHABLE

📝 What happened: Three ARP entries: gateway (REACHABLE), prod-db-01 (STALE — not recently used but valid), prod-web-01 (REACHABLE). STALE entries are normal — they transition to REACHABLE on next use. If an expected IP is missing, the host may be down or on a different subnet.

Example 5: Bring Interface Down/Up

Scenario: Carol bounces eth0 to apply a new MTU setting.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API

# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

sudo ip link set eth0 down && sleep 1 && sudo ip link set eth0 up && ip link show eth0 | grep state

Output:

2: eth0: mtu 1500 qdisc fq_codel state UP

📝 What happened: Interface brought down then back up. The state is UP with LOWER_UP (physical link detected). WARNING: This drops all connections! Only do this during maintenance windows. For production, use ip link set dev eth0 mtu 9000 without bouncing — many NICs support online MTU changes.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: ip addr replaces ifconfig. ip route replaces route. ip neigh replaces arp. ip -s link for stats. ip link set up/down for interface control. The iproute2 suite is standard on all modern Linux distributions.

Configure network interfaces — the classic (deprecated) tool replaced by ip

ifconfig is the traditional interface configurator. It's deprecated in favor of ip but still appears on the LFCS exam and many legacy systems. Know it for the exam; use ip in practice.

# Common patterns:
ifconfig                        # All active interfaces
ifconfig eth0                   # Specific interface
ifconfig -a                     # All interfaces (including down)

Parameters

FlagDescription
-aShow all interfaces, including down
-sShort list (like netstat -i)
upActivate interface
downDeactivate interface

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: ifconfig is deprecated but still tested. Know: ifconfig -a (all), ifconfig eth0 (specific), output format (flags, inet, netmask, RX/TX). Prefer ip addr in practice. ifconfig -s for compact output. No package required on most systems (part of net-tools).

dig

DNS Networking LFCS Domain 4

DNS lookup utility — the most flexible DNS diagnostic tool

dig (Domain Information Groper) queries DNS servers and displays detailed responses. It's the standard tool for DNS troubleshooting — shows the full query/response chain, supports all record types, and has clean output. Replaces nslookup.

Syntax

dig [@SERVER] NAME [TYPE] [OPTIONS]

# Common patterns:
dig anihpj.com                          # A record (default)
dig anihpj.com MX                       # Mail exchange records
dig @8.8.8.8 anihpj.com                 # Query specific DNS server
dig -x 192.168.10.20                    # Reverse lookup (PTR)
dig anihpj.com +short                   # Just the answer

Parameters

FlagDescription
@SERVERQuery specified DNS server
+shortConcise answer only
+noall +answerShow only the answer section
ANYAll record types
-x IPReverse DNS lookup (PTR)
+traceTrace delegation path from root

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success (got answer)
9No reply from server

Example 1: Basic A Record Lookup

Scenario: Carol checks the DNS resolution for the anihpj domain.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

Output:

93.184.216.34

📝 What happened: +short returned just the IP — clean for scripts. Without +short, dig shows the full DNS response including query time, server, flags, and authority section. Use +short for automation, full output for debugging.

Example 2: Query Specific DNS Server

Scenario: Alice verifies DNS propagation by querying Google's public DNS.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

dig @8.8.8.8 prod-api-01.anihpj.internal +short

Output:

192.168.10.20

📝 What happened: Google DNS (8.8.8.8) resolved the internal hostname. This confirms the internal DNS zone is accessible from external resolvers (probably shouldn't be for security!). Internal zones should only resolve from internal DNS servers.

Example 3: Trace DNS Delegation

Scenario: Carol traces the full DNS resolution path to debug a misconfigured delegation.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

dig anihpj.com +trace | head -20

Output:

. 518400 IN NS a.root-servers.net. . 518400 IN NS b.root-servers.net. com. 172800 IN NS a.gtld-servers.net. anihpj.com. 172800 IN NS ns1.anihpj.com. anihpj.com. 300 IN A 93.184.216.34

📝 What happened: Full delegation path: root servers → .com TLD → ns1.anihpj.com → A record. Each step shows which nameserver is authoritative. If any step fails, DNS resolution breaks. +trace is essential for diagnosing delegation issues.

prod-api-01.anihpj.internal.

📝 What happened: Reverse DNS resolved 192.168.10.20 to prod-api-01. This is the PTR record lookup — 20.10.168.192.in-addr.arpa. If this returns nothing, the reverse zone isn't configured (common for internal networks).

Example 5: Check MX Records

Scenario: Carol verifies mail server configuration for the anihpj domain.

📁 Environment Snippet:

lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

dig anihpj.com MX +short

Output:

10 mail.anihpj.com. 20 mail2.anihpj.com.

📝 What happened: Two MX records: primary (priority 10) and backup (priority 20). Lower priority = preferred. The trailing dots indicate fully qualified domain names. This confirms the mail infrastructure is properly configured.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: dig +short for scripts. dig @SERVER to query specific DNS. dig -x IP for reverse DNS. dig +trace traces delegation. Know record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, PTR, TXT, SOA. dig ANY queries all records.

nslookup

DNS Networking LFCS Domain 4

Query DNS servers interactively — the older DNS tool still found on many systems

nslookup is the traditional DNS query tool. It has both interactive and non-interactive modes. While dig is preferred for scripts, nslookup is still commonly available and may appear on the exam. Know both.

Syntax

nslookup [OPTIONS] [HOST] [SERVER]

# Common patterns:
nslookup anihpj.com                     # Query default DNS
nslookup anihpj.com 8.8.8.8             # Query specific server
nslookup -type=MX anihpj.com            # Specific record type

Parameters

FlagDescription
-type=TYPERecord type: A, MX, NS, PTR, CNAME, SOA
-debugShow full debugging output
-timeout=NQuery timeout in seconds
SERVERQuery specified DNS server instead of default

Parameters

FlagDescription
-type=TYPERecord type: A, MX, NS, PTR, CNAME, etc.
-debugShow debugging information
SERVERQuery specified DNS server

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Query failed

host

DNS Networking LFCS Domain 4

Simple DNS lookup utility — the most straightforward DNS query tool

host is the simplest DNS tool — cleaner output than nslookup, less verbose than dig. Great for quick lookups and scripts. Supports A, AAAA, MX, NS, PTR, and TXT records.

Syntax

host [OPTIONS] NAME [SERVER]

# Common patterns:
host anihpj.com                 # A/AAAA records
host -t MX anihpj.com           # Specific type
host 192.168.10.20              # Reverse lookup
host anihpj.com 8.8.8.8         # Query specific server

Parameters

FlagDescription
-aQuery all record types (ANY)
-t TYPEQuery specific record type: A, MX, NS, TXT, etc.
-vVerbose output with full DNS response details
-W SECSWait SECS seconds for a reply
SERVERQuery specified DNS server

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Query failed

📝 What happened: -v adds dig-like detail: header flags, question section, answer section, and query time. This bridges the gap between host's simplicity and dig's thoroughness.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: host NAME for quick A/AAAA. host -t TYPE NAME for specific records. host IP for reverse DNS. host -a for all records. The simplest DNS tool — preferred for quick checks and scripts over dig/nslookup.

traceroute

DIAGNOSTIC Networking LFCS Domain 4

Print the route packets take to a network host — find where the path breaks

traceroute maps the network path between your server and a destination by sending packets with increasing TTL values. Each hop reveals a router along the path. Essential for identifying WHERE a network failure occurs.

Syntax

traceroute [OPTIONS] HOST

# Common patterns:
traceroute anihpj.com                   # Default UDP
traceroute -I anihpj.com                # ICMP (like Windows tracert)
traceroute -n anihpj.com                # No DNS (faster)
traceroute -m 15 anihpj.com             # Max 15 hops

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success (reached destination)

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

Parameters

FlagDescription
-nNo DNS resolution — show IPs only
-m MAX_TTLMaximum TTL / hop count (default: 30)
-p PORTDestination port (default: 33434)
-q NNumber of probes per hop (default: 3)
-w SECTimeout per probe in seconds
-IUse ICMP Echo instead of UDP
-TUse TCP SYN probes

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Target reached
1Socket error or interrupted

Output:

traceroute to backup-nas (192.168.50.10), 30 hops max 1 192.168.10.1 0.452 ms 0.389 ms 0.401 ms 2 192.168.1.1 1.234 ms 1.156 ms 1.198 ms 3 192.168.50.10 2.345 ms 2.289 ms 2.312 ms

📝 What happened: Three hops: API server → local gateway (.10.1) → core router (.1.1) → backup NAS (.50.10). Each hop shows 3 RTT samples. If any hop shows * * *, that router is not responding (firewall blocking or down).

Example 2: ICMP Traceroute

Scenario: Alice uses ICMP mode (like Windows tracert) because UDP is blocked.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

traceroute -I -n anihpj.com

Output:

1 192.168.10.1 0.452 ms 2 10.0.0.1 2.134 ms 3 93.184.216.34 15.456 ms (reached)

📝 What happened: ICMP probes reached the destination. ICMP mode is more likely to get through firewalls than UDP (default). Use -I when default traceroute shows only stars — the UDP probes may be blocked by intermediate firewalls.

Example 3: Limit Hops

Scenario: Carol only wants to see the first 5 hops to identify the local network path.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests

# anihpj Servers:

# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

traceroute -n -m 5 anihpj.com

Output:

1 192.168.10.1 0.452 ms 2 10.0.0.1 1.234 ms 3 * * * 4 * * * 5 * * * (max hops reached)

📝 What happened: Only the first 2 hops responded — the rest are beyond 5 hops. -m 5 limits to 5 hops maximum. Use this to focus on the local network segment when troubleshooting internal connectivity.

Example 4: TCP Traceroute to Specific Port

Scenario: Carol traces the path to port 5432 (PostgreSQL) on prod-db-01.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

sudo traceroute -T -p 5432 prod-db-01

Output:

traceroute to prod-db-01 (192.168.10.30), 30 hops max, 60 byte packets 1 prod-db-01 (192.168.10.30) 0.856 ms 0.812 ms 0.845 ms

📝 What happened: Direct connection — only 1 hop. TCP mode (-T) sends SYN packets to port 5432. This tests actual application connectivity — if the port is closed, the traceroute shows where the connection is refused. More reliable than ICMP for firewalled targets.

Example 5: Identify Network Bottleneck

Scenario: Carol finds which hop is causing latency in the anihpj CDN path.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

traceroute -n cdn.anihpj.com

Output:

1 192.168.10.1 0.452 ms 2 10.0.0.1 1.234 ms 3 203.0.113.1 45.678 ms ← LATENCY SPIKE! 4 93.184.216.34 46.123 ms

📝 What happened: Hop 3 introduces 44ms of latency — the bottleneck is between the ISP edge (hop 2) and the CDN edge (hop 3). This hop might be a congested peering point or a long-distance inter-city link. traceroute pinpointed exactly where the delay occurs.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: traceroute -n avoids DNS delays. traceroute -I uses ICMP. traceroute -T -p PORT uses TCP. Stars (* * *) mean no response — firewall or timeout. -m N limits hops. Requires root for ICMP/TCP modes on some systems.

nc (netcat)

SWISS ARMY Networking LFCS Domain 4

TCP/IP swiss army knife — read/write to network connections, port scanning, file transfer

nc (netcat) is the most versatile networking tool. It can connect to any TCP/UDP port, listen for connections, transfer files, and perform port scans. The "swiss army knife" of TCP/IP — if you need to test if a port is open, nc is the answer.

Syntax

nc [OPTIONS] HOST PORT      # Connect mode
nc -l -p PORT                # Listen mode
nc -zv HOST PORT             # Port scan (verbose, no data)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Connection refused

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

Parameters

FlagDescription
-lListen mode — wait for incoming connections
-p PORTLocal port to bind to
-vVerbose output
-zZero-I/O mode — scan without sending data
-w SECTimeout for connections
-uUDP mode instead of TCP
-kKeep listening after client disconnects
-e CMDExecute CMD after connection (dangerous — often disabled)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Connection refused or error

Example 1: Test Port Connectivity

Scenario: Carol checks if PostgreSQL is accepting connections on prod-db-01.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API

# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

nc -zv prod-db-01 5432 && echo "Port open" || echo "Port closed"

Output:

Connection to prod-db-01 (192.168.10.30) 5432 port [tcp/postgresql] succeeded! Port open

📝 What happened: -z (zero-I/O mode — don't send data), -v (verbose). PostgreSQL is accepting connections. This is the fastest way to verify a service is listening — faster than telnet and more reliable than ping.

Example 4: Quick File Transfer

Scenario: Carol transfers a log file from one server to another using nc.

📁 Environment Snippet:

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

# Receiver (prod-web-01):
nc -l -p 9999 > received_log.txt &
# Sender (prod-api-01):
nc prod-web-01 9999 < /lpj/ops/logs/error.log && echo "Sent"

Output:

Sent

📝 What happened: Raw TCP file transfer — no encryption, no authentication. Only use in trusted networks! The receiver listens on port 9999; the sender connects and pipes the file. For production, use scp or rsync instead.

Example 5: Check UDP Service

Scenario: Carol tests if the DNS server (UDP port 53) is responding.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

echo "test" | nc -u -w1 192.168.10.1 53 && echo "UDP responding" || echo "No UDP response"

Output:

No UDP response

📝 What happened: -u for UDP, -w1 for 1-second timeout. UDP is connectionless — nc can't tell if the packet was received. "No response" is expected for DNS unless you send a valid DNS query. Use dig for actual DNS testing.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: nc -zv HOST PORT for port testing. nc -l -p PORT for listening. -u for UDP. -w SECS for timeout. nc is not encrypted — don't use for production file transfers. Use ncat (nmap version) for SSL support.

nmap

SCAN Networking Security

Network discovery and security auditing — the definitive port scanner

nmap scans hosts and networks to discover open ports, running services, and OS fingerprints. Essential for security audits and network inventory. Always get authorization before scanning — unauthorized scanning may be illegal.

Syntax

nmap [OPTIONS] TARGET

# Common patterns:
nmap prod-api-01                    # Basic TCP scan of 1000 common ports
nmap -p 22,80,443 prod-api-01       # Scan specific ports
nmap -sV prod-api-01                # Version detection
nmap -sn 192.168.10.0/24            # Ping sweep (host discovery)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

Parameters

FlagDescription
-sSTCP SYN scan (stealth, default for root)
-sTTCP connect scan (no raw socket needed)
-sUUDP port scan
-p PORTPort range (e.g. -p 22,80,443 or -p 1-1000)
-sVService/version detection
-OOS detection
-AAggressive — OS, version, script scanning
-T0..5Timing template (0=paranoid, 3=normal, 5=insane)
-oN FILENormal output to FILE
-oX FILEXML output to FILE

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0All hosts scanned successfully
1Some hosts down or errors

Starting Nmap scan at 16:30 Nmap scan report for prod-api-01 (192.168.10.20) PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 8.9p1 (Ubuntu) 80/tcp open http nginx 1.18.0 |_http-title: anihpj — jobpost API 8000/tcp open http gunicorn 21.2.0 |_http-server-header: gunicorn/21.2.0 Service Info: OS: Linux; CPE: cpe:/o:linux:linux_kernel

📝 What happened: -A combines OS detection, version detection, script scanning, and traceroute. The HTTP title "anihpj — jobpost API" confirms the application identity. Always use -A with caution — it generates significant traffic and may trigger IDS alerts.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: nmap -p PORT HOST for port scanning. nmap -sn NETWORK for ping sweep. nmap -sV for version detection. nmap -A for aggressive (comprehensive). Always get authorization. Know the port states: open, closed, filtered, unfiltered.

arp

L2 Networking LFCS Domain 4

Manipulate the ARP cache — map IP addresses to MAC addresses

arp displays and modifies the kernel's ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) table. ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on the local network. Use ip neigh for modern systems; know arp for the exam.

Syntax

arp [OPTIONS]

# Common patterns:
arp -a                          # Show all ARP entries
arp -n                          # Numeric (no hostname resolution)
arp -d 192.168.10.30            # Delete an entry

Parameters

FlagDescription
-aDisplay all ARP entries (alternate BSD style)
-nNumeric display — no hostname resolution
-d HOSTDelete an ARP entry
-s HOST MACAdd a static (permanent) ARP entry
-i IFACESelect interface

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

sudo arp -d 192.168.10.99 && arp -n | grep 192.168.10.99 || echo "Entry removed"

Output:

Entry removed

📝 What happened: The ARP entry for 192.168.10.99 was deleted. The next communication with that IP will trigger a new ARP request. If an attacker was ARP spoofing, deleting and letting it re-resolve may reveal the real MAC.

Example 3: Modern Alternative

Scenario: Carol uses ip neigh instead of arp (preferred on modern systems).

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

ip neigh show

Output:

192.168.10.1 dev eth0 lladdr 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e REACHABLE 192.168.10.10 dev eth0 lladdr 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:7a STALE

📝 What happened: Same data as arp but with state information: REACHABLE (recently confirmed) vs STALE (not recently used). ip neigh is the modern replacement — prefer it over arp for new scripts.

Example 4: Check for Duplicate IPs

Scenario: Carol checks if an IP conflict exists by looking for duplicate entries.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

arp -n | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -d

Output:

# No output = no duplicates

📝 What happened: No duplicate IPs found. If duplicates appeared, two different MACs would claim the same IP — an IP address conflict that causes intermittent connectivity and ARP table flapping.

Example 5: Static ARP Entry

Scenario: Carol adds a permanent ARP entry for the gateway to prevent ARP spoofing.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

sudo arp -s 192.168.10.1 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e && arp -n 192.168.10.1

Output:

Address HWtype HWaddress Flags Mask Iface 192.168.10.1 ether 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e CM eth0

📝 What happened: Flag M = Permanent (manually added). This static entry won't expire and won't be overwritten by ARP replies — protecting against ARP spoofing attacks on the gateway. Remove with arp -d.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: arp -n for ARP table. arp -d IP to delete. arp -s IP MAC for static. Prefer ip neigh on modern systems. Know the Flags: C (Complete), M (Permanent), P (Published). ARP is L2 — only works on the local subnet.

tcpdump

CAPTURE Networking Security

Capture and analyze network packets — the definitive packet sniffer

tcpdump captures network packets and displays them in real-time or saves them to a file for later analysis. Essential for debugging network protocols, investigating security incidents, and understanding application traffic patterns.

Syntax

tcpdump [OPTIONS] [FILTER]

# Common patterns:
sudo tcpdump -i eth0                        # Capture on eth0
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 80                # HTTP traffic only
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 192.168.10.30     # To/from specific host
sudo tcpdump -w capture.pcap                # Write to file
sudo tcpdump -r capture.pcap                # Read from file

Parameters

FlagDescription
-i IFACEInterface to capture on (default: lowest-numbered)
-nNo DNS resolution (faster)
-nnNo DNS or port name resolution
-c COUNTCapture only COUNT packets
-w FILEWrite raw packets to FILE (for Wireshark)
-r FILERead packets from FILE
-APrint packets in ASCII (human-readable)
-XPrint packets in hex AND ASCII

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Packet Capture

Daily Workflow: Carol uses tcpdump to capture and analyze network traffic for debugging API issues. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical tcpdump usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 8000 -c 10
listening on eth0, link-type EN10MB

Examples

#  prod-api-01:8000     — Django REST API
#  prod-db-01:5432      — PostgreSQL

Example 1: Capture HTTP Traffic

Scenario: Alice captures web traffic to debug a 500 error on the jobpost API.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 8000 -c 5 2>/dev/null | head -15

Output:

16:30:01.123456 IP 192.168.10.10.45678 > prod-api-01.8000: Flags [P.] GET /api/v1/jobs/ HTTP/1.1 Host: prod-api-01:8000 User-Agent: curl/7.81.0

📝 What happened: -A printed the HTTP request in ASCII. The source is 192.168.10.10 (prod-web-01), destination is the API on port 8000. Flag [P.] = PUSH + ACK. -c 5 stopped after 5 packets.

Example 2: Capture to File for Wireshark

Scenario: Carol captures traffic for offline analysis in Wireshark.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API

# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/capture.pcap host prod-db-01 and port 5432 &

Output:

tcpdump: listening on eth0, link-type EN10MB (Ethernet), capture size 262144 bytes # Backgrounded — capturing PostgreSQL traffic to prod-db-01 # Kill with: sudo pkill tcpdump

📝 What happened: tcpdump runs in the background, capturing all traffic between the API server and prod-db-01 on port 5432. The .pcap file can be opened in Wireshark for deep protocol analysis. Use -c COUNT to auto-stop after N packets.

Example 3: Filter by Host and Port

Scenario: Carol captures only traffic between prod-api-01 and the Redis server.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API

# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn host prod-redis-01 and port 6379 -c 3

Output:

16:30:05.123 IP 192.168.10.20.45678 > 192.168.10.35.6379: Flags [P.], seq 1:45 16:30:05.125 IP 192.168.10.35.6379 > 192.168.10.20.45678: Flags [P.], seq 1:89 16:30:05.126 IP 192.168.10.20.45678 > 192.168.10.35.6379: Flags [.], ack 90

📝 What happened: Three packets: API → Redis (PUSH, 45 bytes), Redis → API (PUSH, 89 bytes reply), API → Redis (ACK). -nn shows numeric IPs and ports. The Redis conversation is fast (~1ms round trip) — confirming low latency between API and cache.

Example 4: Read Saved Capture

Scenario: Alice analyzes a previously captured pcap file for a post-incident review.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API

# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

tcpdump -r /tmp/capture.pcap -nn | head -5

Output:

16:30:01.123456 IP 192.168.10.10.45678 > 192.168.10.20.8000: Flags [S] 16:30:01.123789 IP 192.168.10.20.8000 > 192.168.10.10.45678: Flags [S.] 16:30:01.124012 IP 192.168.10.10.45678 > 192.168.10.20.8000: Flags [.] 16:30:01.124345 IP 192.168.10.10.45678 > 192.168.10.20.8000: Flags [P.]

📝 What happened: The TCP 3-way handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK, followed by data (PUSH). This is the standard TCP connection establishment. -r reads from a file — no root required for reading saved captures.

Example 5: Debug TLS Handshake

Scenario: Carol captures the TLS handshake to verify the correct certificate is presented.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure & server layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Servers:
# prod-web-01/02    — Nginx web servers (port 80/443)
# prod-api-01       — Django API server (port 8000)
# prod-db-01        — PostgreSQL (port 5432)
# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn port 443 -c 10

Output:

16:30:10.123 IP 192.168.1.100.54321 > 192.168.10.10.443: Flags [S] 16:30:10.124 IP 192.168.10.10.443 > 192.168.1.100.54321: Flags [S.] 16:30:10.125 IP 192.168.1.100.54321 > 192.168.10.10.443: Flags [.] 16:30:10.126 IP 192.168.1.100.54321 > 192.168.10.10.443: Flags [P.] (Client Hello) 16:30:10.130 IP 192.168.10.10.443 > 192.168.1.100.54321: Flags [P.] (Server Hello + Certificate)

📝 What happened: TCP handshake followed by TLS Client Hello and Server Hello. The certificates are encrypted after the handshake — you can see the handshake structure but not the certificate content without the session key. For full TLS decryption, use Wireshark with the private key.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: tcpdump -i eth0 -nn port N for targeted capture. -w file.pcap saves for Wireshark. -r file.pcap reads captures. -A for ASCII, -X for hex+ASCII. Filter syntax: host, port, src, dst, and/or. Requires root.

iwconfig

WIRELESS Networking WiFi

Configure wireless network interfaces — the ifconfig equivalent for WiFi

iwconfig displays and configures wireless network interface parameters: SSID, frequency, signal strength, encryption key, and bit rate. The wireless equivalent of ifconfig. Use iw (nl80211) on modern systems.

Syntax

iwconfig [INTERFACE] [OPTIONS]

# Common patterns:
iwconfig                        # All wireless interfaces
iwconfig wlan0                  # Specific interface
iwconfig wlan0 essid "anihpj"   # Connect to SSID

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

iptraf-ng

MONITOR Networking Traffic

Interactive IP LAN monitor — real-time network traffic statistics

iptraf-ng is an interactive ncurses-based network monitoring tool. Shows real-time per-connection traffic, interface statistics, and LAN station monitoring. Ideal for identifying bandwidth hogs during incidents.

Syntax

sudo iptraf-ng                    # Interactive menu
sudo iptraf-ng -i eth0            # Interface stats
sudo iptraf-ng -g                 # General interface stats

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success (user exited normally)

# prod-redis-01     — Redis cache (port 6379)
# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

sudo iptraf-ng -g

Output:

# Shows all interface statistics in a table: # eth0: In: 89.2 Mbps Out: 45.1 Mbps Total: 1.2TB since boot # lo: In: 12.3 Mbps Out: 12.3 Mbps Total: 45GB since boot

📝 What happened: eth0 has transferred 1.2TB since boot — expected for a production server. lo shows equal in/out (loopback). If a secondary interface shows unexpected traffic, investigate for misrouted packets or unauthorized connections.

📄 Context — Per-Host Traffic:

# -e shows traffic statistics by MAC address on the LAN

# monitoring-01     — Prometheus+Grafana (port 9090/3000)

Command:

sudo iptraf-ng -e eth0

Output:

# Real-time display of all MAC addresses seen on eth0 # Columns: MAC Address, PktsIn, BytesIn, PktsOut, BytesOut # Sort by total bytes to find top talkers

📝 What happened: All LAN hosts are listed with traffic counters. This is like a real-time network traffic map. Each MAC address shows bidirectional stats. The host with the most bytes is likely the bandwidth hog. Press S to cycle through sort modes.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: iptraf-ng is the modern version (replaces iptraf). -i IFACE for interface stats. -g for general. Interactive — use Q to quit. Alternative: iftop for bandwidth-per-host. For non-interactive monitoring, use sar -n DEV.

👥 User & Group Management

Commands for creating, modifying, and managing Linux users and groups. The anihpj/jobpost team uses dedicated service accounts (anihpj, jenkins, www-data) with group-based permissions (developers, sudo) — proper user management is the foundation of Linux security.

useradd

ACCOUNTUser ManagementCoreLFCS Domain 3

Create a new user account — the foundation of multi-user Linux security

useradd creates new Linux user accounts with default settings from /etc/default/useradd and /etc/login.defs. It creates the home directory, sets the default shell, and assigns UID/GID.

For anihpj/jobpost, useradd is used for:

  • Creating developer accounts (alice, bob) with /home directories
  • Setting up service accounts (jenkins) with nologin shell
  • Onboarding new team members with proper group assignments

Syntax

useradd [OPTIONS] USERNAME
# Common: sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash alice | sudo useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin jenkins

Parameters

FlagDescription
-m, --create-homeCreate the user's home directory
-s SHELLSet login shell (e.g., /bin/bash, /usr/sbin/nologin)
-g GROUPSpecify primary group
-G GROUPSAdd to supplementary groups (comma-separated)
-r, --systemCreate a system account (no aging, UID < 1000)
-u UIDSpecify numeric user ID
-d DIRSpecify home directory path

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error (cannot update password file)
9Username already exists

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Developer Onboarding

# Carol onboards a new developer, eve, to the anihpj team:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G developers,docker -c "Eve Auditor" eve
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo passwd eve
New password: ********
Retype new password: ********
passwd: password updated successfully
carol@prod-api-01:~$ id eve
uid=1005(eve) gid=1005(eve) groups=1005(eve),1000(developers),998(docker)

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Create User

Daily Workflow: Carol uses useradd to create accounts for new developers joining the anihpj team. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical useradd usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo useradd -m -G developers -s /bin/bash bob
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin anihpj

Examples

# anihpj users managed daily:
#  alice, bob        — Developer accounts
#  carol             — DevOps admin (sudo)
#  dave, eve, jenkins — DBA, auditor, CI/CD
#  www-data, anihpj  — Service accounts
Example 1: Create a Developer Account

Scenario: Carol adds a new backend developer to the team.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G developers,sudo -c "Bob API Developer" bob

Output:

# No output on success — verify with: id bob uid=1003(bob) gid=1003(bob) groups=1003(bob),1000(developers),27(sudo)

📝 What happened: Bob's account created with home directory, bash shell, and membership in developers and sudo groups. -c adds a comment (full name). The home directory is populated from /etc/skel with default .bashrc, .profile.

Example 2: System Account for Services

Scenario: Carol creates a system account for Jenkins CI with no login shell.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin -d /var/lib/jenkins jenkins

Output:

# Verify: grep jenkins /etc/passwd jenkins:x:998:998::/var/lib/jenkins:/usr/sbin/nologin

📝 What happened: Jenkins service account created with UID < 1000 (system), nologin shell (no interactive login), and custom home at /var/lib/jenkins. System accounts cannot log in interactively — they only run services.

Example 3: Create Account with Specific UID

Scenario: Carol ensures consistent UIDs across servers for NFS file sharing.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo useradd -u 1500 -m -s /bin/bash anihpj

Output:

id anihpj uid=1500(anihpj) gid=1500(anihpj) groups=1500(anihpj)

📝 What happened: anihpj account created with UID 1500 (matching across all servers). Consistent UIDs are critical for NFS — if UID 1500 owns files on the NFS server, the same UID must exist on all clients.

Example 4: Create User Without Home Directory

Scenario: Carol creates a temporary auditor account that doesn't need persistence.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo useradd -M -s /bin/bash auditor

Output:

ls /home/auditor ls: cannot access '/home/auditor': No such file or directory

📝 What happened: -M (--no-create-home) skips home directory creation. The account exists in /etc/passwd but has no persistent storage. Useful for one-time audit access where no permanent footprint is desired.

Example 5: Dry-Run User Creation

Scenario: Carol previews what useradd will do before creating the account.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo useradd -D && sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash dave --dry-run 2>&1 || echo "(No dry-run; check /etc/default/useradd)"

Output:

GROUP=100 HOME=/home INACTIVE=-1 SHELL=/bin/sh SKEL=/etc/skel CREATE_MAIL_SPOOL=no

📝 What happened: -D shows defaults that useradd will use: GROUP=100 (users), home at /home, shell=/bin/sh. Note: DEFAULT shell is /bin/sh — always specify -s /bin/bash explicitly for interactive users.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G group1,group2 user is the standard creation pattern. -r for system accounts. -M skips home. Check /etc/default/useradd for defaults. useradd -D shows them. UIDs < 1000 are system; >= 1000 are regular.

usermod

ACCOUNTUser ManagementLFCS Domain 3

Modify an existing user account — change groups, shell, home, or lock accounts

usermod modifies existing user accounts. Use it to add users to groups, change their shell, lock or unlock accounts, rename users, and move home directories. Always use the -a (append) flag with -G to avoid removing existing group memberships.

Syntax

usermod [OPTIONS] USERNAME
# Common: sudo usermod -aG docker alice | sudo usermod -s /bin/zsh bob | sudo usermod -L eve

Parameters

FlagDescription
-a, --appendAppend to supplementary groups (use with -G)
-G GROUPSSet supplementary groups (use -aG to append)
-s SHELLChange login shell
-L, --lockLock account (disable password)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Team Role Changes

# Alice transitions from API dev to DevOps — Carol adds her to docker and sudo groups:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo usermod -aG docker,sudo alice
carol@prod-api-01:~$ groups alice
alice : alice developers docker sudo

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Modify User

Daily Workflow: Carol uses usermod to update group memberships when team roles change. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical usermod usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo usermod -aG docker alice
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo usermod -s /bin/bash anihpj

Examples

# anihpj users managed daily:
#  alice, bob        — Developer accounts
#  carol             — DevOps admin (sudo)
#  dave, eve, jenkins — DBA, auditor, CI/CD
#  www-data, anihpj  — Service accounts
Example 1: Add User to Groups (Safely)

Scenario: Carol adds Bob to the docker group for container access.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo usermod -aG docker bob && groups bob

Output:

bob : bob developers docker

📝 What happened: Bob now belongs to bob, developers, and docker groups. -aG APPENDS — never use -G alone as it replaces all groups. If you forget -a, Bob would lose the developers group. ALWAYS use -aG.

Example 2: Change User Shell

Scenario: Alice prefers zsh over bash for her development workflow.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo usermod -s /bin/zsh alice && grep alice /etc/passwd

Output:

alice:x:1001:1001:Alice Django Dev:/home/alice:/bin/zsh

📝 What happened: Alice's shell changed from /bin/bash to /bin/zsh. Last field in /etc/passwd confirms the change. Ensure the shell exists in /etc/shells before changing. Use chsh -s /bin/zsh as non-root alternative.

Example 3: Lock/Unlock an Account

Scenario: Carol locks Eve's account during a security investigation.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo usermod -L eve && sudo passwd -S eve

Output:

eve L 01/15/2025 0 99999 7 -1

📝 What happened: The L in passwd -S output means "Locked". The password is disabled — eve cannot log in with password but can still use SSH keys. Use usermod -U eve to unlock. Locking adds ! before the password hash in /etc/shadow.

Example 4: Rename a User

Scenario: A developer's username changed from "david" to "dave" for consistency.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo usermod -l dave -d /home/dave -m david

Output:

# No output on success — verify: grep dave /etc/passwd dave:x:1004:1004:Dave DBA:/home/dave:/bin/bash

📝 What happened: -l changed the login name from david to dave, -d set new home, -m moved contents. All three flags are needed for a clean rename. Files owned by the old UID remain unchanged — only the name mapping changes.

Example 5: Set Account Expiry

Scenario: Carol sets a contractor's account to expire on March 31.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo usermod -e 2025-03-31 contractor && sudo chage -l contractor | grep "Account expires"

Output:

Account expires : Mar 31, 2025

📝 What happened: -e YYYY-MM-DD sets an expiration date. After March 31, the contractor account will be disabled automatically. Combine with chage for more granular password aging policies.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: usermod -aG appends groups (never use -G alone). -L locks, -U unlocks. -s changes shell. -l NEW OLD renames. -e DATE sets expiry. -d DIR -m moves home. Changes apply on next login, not current session.

userdel

ACCOUNTUser ManagementLFCS Domain 3

Delete a user account — clean removal with optional home directory deletion

userdel removes user accounts from the system. By default it only removes the /etc/passwd entry — use -r to also remove the home directory and mail spool. Always audit running processes before deleting a service account.

Syntax

userdel [OPTIONS] USERNAME
# Common: sudo userdel -r contractor | sudo userdel auditor

Parameters

FlagDescription
-r, --removeRemove home directory and mail spool
-f, --forceForce removal even if user is logged in
-ZRemove SELinux user mapping

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Offboarding a Team Member

# Carol offboards a departing contractor from prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo pkill -u contractor  # Kill running processes
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo userdel -r contractor
carol@prod-api-01:~$ grep contractor /etc/passwd || echo "Account removed"
Account removed

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Delete User

Daily Workflow: Carol uses userdel to remove accounts when team members leave the project. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical userdel usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo userdel -r old_contractor
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo userdel jenkins  # Remove CI user

Examples
