#  alice, bob        — Developer accounts
#  carol             — DevOps admin (sudo)
#  dave, eve, jenkins — DBA, auditor, CI/CD
#  www-data, anihpj  — Service accounts
Example 1: Full Removal with Home Directory

Scenario: Carol permanently removes a departed contractor's account.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo userdel -r contractor && ls /home/contractor 2>&1

Output:

ls: cannot access '/home/contractor': No such file or directory

📝 What happened: -r removed both the account AND the home directory. No trace remains. Without -r, /home/contractor would be orphaned — taking disk space with no owner. Always use -r for permanent offboarding.

Example 2: Remove Without Deleting Files

Scenario: Carol removes an account but preserves the home directory for audit.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo userdel auditor && ls -ld /home/auditor

Output:

drwxr-xr-x 2 1007 1007 4096 Jan 15 10:00 /home/auditor

📝 What happened: The account is gone from /etc/passwd but the home directory remains — now owned by UID 1007 (the old auditor UID). Files are preserved for forensic review but no user owns them. Archive to /lpj/ops/archives/ before deletion.

Example 3: Check Before Deleting

Scenario: Carol verifies no processes are running as the user before deletion.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

ps -u jenkins && echo "Processes found!" || sudo userdel jenkins

Output:

PID TTY TIME CMD 2841 ? 00:00:05 java jenkins has running processes — aborting deletion.

📝 What happened: Jenkins has an active java process. Deleting the account could crash the CI service. Always run ps -u USERNAME first. Stop the service (systemctl stop jenkins) before deleting service accounts.

Example 4: Force Delete Logged-In User

Scenario: An attacker is logged in — Carol force-deletes the compromised account.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests

└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo userdel -f compromised_user && echo "Account forcefully removed"

Output:

userdel: user compromised_user is currently used by process 12543 Account forcefully removed

📝 What happened: -f forced deletion even though the user had active processes. The account entry was removed but the processes may continue running under the old UID. Use pkill -9 -u USER first, then userdel for clean removal.

Example 5: Audit Orphaned Files

Scenario: Carol finds files owned by deleted users using their old UIDs.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root

sudo find / -nouser -type f 2>/dev/null | head -5

Output:

/home/auditor/.bash_history /tmp/auditor-session.log /var/spool/mail/auditor

📝 What happened: Three files owned by UID 1007 (the old auditor) — no matching username exists. -nouser finds files where the UID doesn't map to any /etc/passwd entry. Clean up with find / -nouser -delete after confirming they're not needed.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: userdel -r removes account + home. userdel (without -r) keeps home. -f forces even if logged in. Check ps -u USER before deleting. find / -nouser finds orphaned files. find / -nogroup finds files with deleted groups.

passwd

AUTHUser ManagementSecurityLFCS Domain 3

Change user passwords and manage password aging policies

passwd changes passwords for user accounts. As root, you can change any user's password. Regular users can only change their own. Also provides password status information (-S) and account lock/unlock (-l, -u).

Syntax

passwd [OPTIONS] [USERNAME]
# Common: passwd | sudo passwd alice | passwd -S alice | sudo passwd -l eve

Parameters

FlagDescription
-S USERShow password status (locked, set, etc.)
-l, --lockLock account (disable password)
-u, --unlockUnlock account
-e, --expireForce password change at next login

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Password Policy Enforcement

carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo passwd -e alice
passwd: password expiry information changed.
# Alice logs in and is prompted:
alice@prod-api-01:~$ ssh prod-api-01
You are required to change your password immediately (administrator enforced)
Current password: ********
New password: ************

New password: ********
Retype new password: ********

Example 1: Check Password Status

Scenario: Carol audits the password status of all anihpj team accounts.

sudo passwd -S alice && sudo passwd -S bob && sudo passwd -S jenkins

alice P 01/15/2025 0 99999 7 -1 bob P 12/01/2024 0 99999 7 -1 jenkins L 11/20/2024 0 99999 7 -1

📝 What happened: Fields: User Status(P=password/L=locked/NP=no password) LastChange MinAge MaxAge WarnDays InactiveDays. Alice and Bob have passwords; jenkins is locked (service account). All have 99999 day max (no forced change).

Example 5: Set Minimum Password Age

Scenario: Carol prevents users from cycling through passwords to bypass history.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API

# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo passwd -n 7 alice && sudo passwd -S alice | awk '{print $3}'

Output:

7

📝 What happened: -n 7 sets minimum password age to 7 days. Alice cannot change her password more than once every 7 days. This prevents users from cycling through 5 passwords quickly to reuse their favorite one. The 3rd field of passwd -S shows min days.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: passwd -S shows status (P/L/NP). -l/-u lock/unlock. -e forces change on next login. -d deletes password (dangerous). -n DAYS sets min age, -x DAYS max age. -w DAYS warning period. /etc/shadow stores the hash.

chage

AUTHUser ManagementSecurityLFCS Domain 3

Change user password expiry information — enforce password aging policies

chage (change aging) manages password and account expiration. More granular than passwd — set max password age, warning days, inactivity period, and account expiration. Critical for compliance (PCI-DSS, SOC2 require password rotation).

Syntax

chage [OPTIONS] USERNAME
# Common: chage -l alice | sudo chage -M 90 alice | sudo chage -E 2025-12-31 contractor

Parameters

FlagDescription
-l, --listShow account aging information
-M DAYSMax days before password must be changed
-m DAYSMin days between password changes
-W DAYSWarning days before password expires

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Last password change                                    : Jan 15, 2025
Password expires                                        : Apr 15, 2025
Password inactive                                       : never
Account expires                                         : never
Minimum number of days between password change          : 7
Maximum number of days between password change          : 90
Number of days of warning before password expires       : 14

Example 1: Set 90-Day Password Rotation

Scenario: Carol enforces PCI-DSS compliance with 90-day max password age.

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root

# Verify: sudo chage -l alice | grep -E "Maximum|warning" Maximum number of days between password change : 90 Number of days of warning before password expires : 14

groupadd

GROUPUser ManagementLFCS Domain 3

Create a new group — organize users for permission management

groupadd creates new groups in /etc/group. Groups are the foundation of Linux permission management — instead of assigning permissions to individual users, assign them to groups. The anihpj project uses groups extensively: developers, docker, sudo, www-data.

Syntax

groupadd [OPTIONS] GROUPNAME
# Common: sudo groupadd developers | sudo groupadd -g 1500 projectx

Parameters

FlagDescription
-g GIDSpecify numeric group ID
-r, --systemCreate a system group (GID < 1000)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo groupadd -g 1500 anihpj

developers:x:1000:
anihpj:x:1500:

📝 What happened: getent group queries the name service switch (NSS) — works for both local (/etc/group) and LDAP/AD groups. Shows GID 1000 with members alice, bob, dave. Prefer getent over grep /etc/group for accuracy in networked environments.

Example 5: Prevent Duplicate Groups

Scenario: Carol's automation script checks before creating a group to avoid errors.

📁 Environment Snippet:

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root

# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

getent group developers >/dev/null && echo "Group exists" || sudo groupadd developers

Output:

Group exists

📝 What happened: The script checked first — group already exists, so no creation attempted. This pattern is essential for idempotent provisioning scripts. Without the check, groupadd returns error code 9 (group already exists).

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: groupadd GROUP creates with next GID. -g GID sets specific GID. -r for system groups (< 1000). getent group checks existence. /etc/group stores groups. groupdel GROUP removes. Members added via usermod -aG.

Example 5: Proper Group Deletion Workflow

Scenario: Carol follows a safe workflow to remove a group completely.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj project & user layout:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project root
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

# anihpj Users & Groups:
# alice    — Senior Django developer (groups: developers, docker)
# bob      — API developer (groups: developers)
# carol    — DevOps lead (groups: developers, ops, docker, sudo)
# dave     — Database admin (groups: dba)
# eve      — Security auditor (groups: auditors)
# jenkins  — CI/CD pipeline (groups: docker)
# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

# Step 1: Check if anyone uses this as primary group
grep :$(getent group oldproject | cut -d: -f3): /etc/passwd && echo "Users found!" || echo "No primary users"
# Step 2: Find and reassign files
sudo find / -group oldproject -exec chgrp developers {} \; 2>/dev/null
# Step 3: Delete the group
sudo groupdel oldproject

Output:

No primary users # Files reassigned to developers group # Group deleted

📝 What happened: Three-step safe deletion: check primary users, reassign files, then delete. This prevents orphaned GIDs and ensures no user is left without a primary group. Always follow this workflow for production groups.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: groupdel GROUP removes groups. Cannot delete primary group of any user. find / -group NAME finds owned files. find / -nogroup finds orphaned GIDs. Always reassign files before deleting. /etc/group stores groups; /etc/gshadow stores group passwords.

0Always succeeds

📝 What happened: The group membership is in /etc/group (confirmed by getent) but Alice's CURRENT session doesn't see it. Group changes require re-login. Alice must run newgrp docker or log out and back in. This is the #1 FAQ of Linux group management.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: groups shows current user's groups. groups USER shows any user. First group is primary. Changes via usermod -aG require re-login. newgrp GROUP starts a new shell with that primary group. /etc/group stores supplementary members.

su

AUTHUser ManagementCoreLFCS Domain 3

Switch User — change to another user account with their environment

su (substitute user) switches to another user. Without arguments, switches to root. Use su - (with hyphen) for a full login shell with the target user's environment. Critical difference: su keeps current env; su - loads the target user's full profile.

Syntax

su [OPTIONS] [USERNAME]
# Common: su - alice | su - | su -c "command" alice

Parameters

FlagDescription
-, -l, --loginFull login shell (load profile, set env, cd to home)
-c CMDRun a single command as the target user
-s SHELLUse specified shell instead of target's default

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Example 3: su vs su - (Critical Difference)

Scenario: Alice demonstrates why su - matters for environment variables.

# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo su anihpj -c "echo PATH=\$PATH" && sudo su - anihpj -c "echo PATH=\$PATH"

Output:

PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/home/anihpj/.local/bin:/lpj/venv/bin

📝 What happened: Without -, PATH is generic (system defaults). With -, PATH includes anihpj's custom paths (virtualenv, local bin). The Django virtualenv is only in the login PATH — using su without - would miss it and run the system Python instead.

Scenario: Carol checks if a system account with nologin can be accessed via su.

# www-data — Nginx service user
# anihpj   — App runtime (no login shell)

Command:

sudo su -s /bin/bash jenkins

Output:

jenkins@prod-api-01:/var/lib/jenkins$ whoami jenkins

📝 What happened: -s /bin/bash overrode jenkins' nologin shell. This is a security concern — it bypasses the nologin restriction. Only root can do this. If you see this in logs and didn't authorize it, investigate immediately. Use sudo -u jenkins CMD for safer service account access.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: su - USER gives full login shell (always use -). su without - keeps current env. su - defaults to root. -c CMD runs single command. -s SHELL overrides shell. Prefer sudo -u USER for better audit. sudo su - is the common pattern on Ubuntu.

sudo

AUTHUser ManagementCoreLFCS Domain 3

Execute commands as another user — the secure alternative to su

sudo (superuser do) runs commands with elevated privileges. Unlike su, sudo logs every command, supports fine-grained permissions via /etc/sudoers, and uses the user's own password (not root's). This is the primary privilege escalation tool in modern Linux.

Syntax

sudo [OPTIONS] COMMAND
# Common: sudo apt update | sudo -u anihpj python manage.py | sudo -i

Parameters

FlagDescription
-u USERRun as specified user (default: root)
-iLogin shell (like su -)
-sRun shell (keeps current env)
-l, --listList allowed commands

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📝 What happened: -u anihpj ran the command as anihpj, not root. This is the CORRECT way to run service-specific commands. The file permissions, virtualenv, and database connections all work correctly because the process runs as the service owner.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: sudo -u USER CMD runs as another user. sudo -l lists permissions. visudo edits sudoers safely. NOPASSWD: for passwordless scripts. Rules go in /etc/sudoers.d/. Sudo logs to /var/log/auth.log. Always prefer sudo over su for audit trails.

lastlog

AUDITUser ManagementSecurityLFCS Domain 3

Display last login information for all users — security audit tool

lastlog reads /var/log/lastlog and shows the last login time for every user on the system. Essential for security audits — identifies stale accounts, unexpected logins, and users who have never logged in.

Syntax

lastlog [OPTIONS]
# Common: lastlog | lastlog -u alice | lastlog -b 30

Parameters

FlagDescription
-u USERShow only specified user
-b DAYSShow only users who logged in before DAYS ago
-t DAYSShow users who logged in more recently than DAYS

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

newgrp

GROUPUser ManagementLFCS Domain 3

Start a new shell with a different primary group — apply group changes immediately

newgrp starts a new shell with the specified group as the primary GID. This is the solution to "I was added to a group but can't access files yet" — no logout required. New files created in this shell will be owned by the new primary group.

Syntax

newgrp [GROUP]
# Common: newgrp docker | newgrp developers

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Immediate Group Access

# Alice was just added to the docker group but can't use docker yet:

Got permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket

alice@prod-api-01:~$ docker ps
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE     COMMAND   CREATED   STATUS   PORTS   NAMES
123abc456def   nginx     "nginx"   2h ago    Up 2h    80/tcp  web-01

Parameters

FlagDescription
-Simulate login shell — reset environment
GROUPGroup name to switch to (must be member)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0New shell started
1Not a member of the group

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — New Group

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: newgrp GROUP starts a shell with new primary group. exit returns to original. newgrp (no args) resets to default. Primary group determines new file ownership. This avoids logout/login for group changes. sg GROUP -c "CMD" runs one command with different primary group.

🗜️ Archive & Compression

Commands for creating, extracting, and compressing archives. The anihpj/jobpost team uses tar for deployments, gzip for log rotation, and zip for cross-platform sharing. Compression saves bandwidth and storage — critical for database backups and log archives.

tar

ARCHIVECompressionCoreLFCS Domain 4

Tape ARchiver — create, extract, and manipulate archive files

tar bundles files and directories into a single archive file, often combined with compression (gzip, bzip2, xz). The universal tool for software distribution, backups, and deployments.

For anihpj/jobpost, tar is used for:

  • Creating database backup archives before maintenance
  • Packaging Django static files for deployment
  • Archiving rotated logs to save space
  • Distributing code snapshots between servers

Syntax

tar [OPTIONS] [ARCHIVE] [FILE...]
# Common: tar -czf backup.tar.gz /lpj/ | tar -xzf backup.tar.gz | tar -tzf backup.tar.gz

Parameters

FlagDescription
-c, --createCreate new archive
-x, --extractExtract from archive
-t, --listList archive contents
-f ARCHIVEUse archive file (required)
-zFilter through gzip (.tar.gz)
-jFilter through bzip2 (.tar.bz2)
-JFilter through xz (.tar.xz)
-v, --verboseList files processed
-C DIRChange to DIR before operation
--exclude=PATTERNExclude files matching pattern
--strip-components=NStrip N leading path components

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Some files differ (--diff) or error
2Fatal error

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Database Backup

# Carol creates a compressed backup of the jobpost database dump:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ pg_dump -U anihpj jobpost > /tmp/jobpost_dump.sql
carol@prod-db-01:~$ tar -czf /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_db_$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz /tmp/jobpost_dump.sql
carol@prod-db-01:~$ ls -lh /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_db_20250604.tar.gz
-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 2.4M Jun  4 02:00 jobpost_db_20250604.tar.gz

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Tape Archive

carol@prod-api-01:~$ tar -czf /lpj/ops/backups/k8s_backup.tar.gz /lpj/k8s/

Examples

#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Primary backup directory
#  /lpj/ops/logs/         — Log archives before rotation
#  backup-nas:/backups/   — Network-attached storage
Example 1: Create a Compressed Archive

Scenario: Carol creates a gzip-compressed backup of the entire jobpost project.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

tar -czf /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_backup.tar.gz /lpj/jobpost/

Output:

# No output (quiet mode) — verify: ls -lh /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_backup.tar.gz -rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 8.5M Jun 4 10:00 jobpost_backup.tar.gz

📝 What happened: -c created the archive, -z compressed with gzip, -f specified the output file. The original 45MB Django project compressed to 8.5MB. The -f flag MUST come last because the filename follows immediately after.

Example 2: Extract to Specific Directory

Scenario: Alice restores the database backup to a staging server for testing.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

tar -xzf /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_db_20250604.tar.gz -C /tmp/restore/

Output:

ls /tmp/restore/tmp/ jobpost_dump.sql

📝 What happened: -x extracted, -C /tmp/restore/ changed to that directory first. The file was extracted as /tmp/restore/tmp/jobpost_dump.sql. The archive preserved the original absolute path (/tmp/jobpost_dump.sql). Use --strip-components=1 to remove the leading /tmp/.

Example 3: List Archive Contents

Scenario: Carol checks what's inside an archive before extracting it.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

tar -tzf /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_backup.tar.gz | head -10

Output:

lpj/jobpost/ lpj/jobpost/manage.py lpj/jobpost/requirements.txt lpj/jobpost/jobpost/ lpj/jobpost/jobpost/__init__.py lpj/jobpost/jobpost/settings.py lpj/jobpost/jobpost/urls.py lpj/jobpost/jobpost/wsgi.py

📝 What happened: -t listed contents without extracting. Shows the full directory structure. Always use -t before extracting unknown archives — it reveals if the archive creates files in unexpected locations. Tarbombs (archives that extract to ./) are a security risk.

Example 4: Exclude Files During Creation

Scenario: Alice creates a clean source archive excluding cache and virtualenv.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

tar -czf jobpost_source.tar.gz --exclude="*.pyc" --exclude="__pycache__" --exclude="venv" /lpj/jobpost/

Output:

ls -lh jobpost_source.tar.gz -rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 1.2M Jun 4 10:15 jobpost_source.tar.gz

📝 What happened: Archive created WITHOUT .pyc files, __pycache__ dirs, or the venv folder. Size went from 8.5MB (full) to 1.2MB (source only). Always exclude generated files from source archives — they bloat the archive and cause merge conflicts.

Example 5: Extract Single File

Scenario: Carol extracts only the settings.py file from the archive.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

tar -xzf jobpost_backup.tar.gz --wildcards "*/settings.py" && ls lpj/jobpost/jobpost/settings.py

Output:

lpj/jobpost/jobpost/settings.py

📝 What happened: Only settings.py was extracted from a multi-file archive. --wildcards enables glob patterns. Use tar -xzf archive.tar.gz path/to/file for exact paths. Much faster than extracting everything for one config file.

Example 6: Verbose Creation

Scenario: Carol creates a compressed log archive with verbose output to see every file.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

tar -czvf /lpj/ops/backups/logs_$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz /lpj/ops/logs/

Output:

lpj/ops/logs/ lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log lpj/ops/logs/nginx/access.log lpj/ops/logs/nginx/error.log lpj/ops/logs/celery.log lpj/ops/logs/redis.log

📝 What happened: -v printed every file as it was added to the archive. Useful for verifying which files are included and spotting unexpected paths. Without -v, tar is silent on success. Remove -v in scripts to reduce log noise.

Example 7: Extract a Single File

Scenario: Alice extracts only the settings.py file from a full project backup.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

tar -xzf /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_backup.tar.gz lpj/jobpost/jobpost/settings.py && ls lpj/jobpost/jobpost/settings.py

Output:

lpj/jobpost/jobpost/settings.py

📝 What happened: Only settings.py was extracted from the multi-GB archive. The path must match exactly what tar -tzf shows. Use tar -xzf archive.tar.gz --wildcards "*/settings.py" if you don't know the exact path. Much faster than extracting the entire archive for one file.

Example 8: Append Files to Archive

Scenario: Carol forgot to include the README — she appends it to the existing tar.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

tar -rf /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_backup.tar /lpj/README.md && tar -tf /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_backup.tar | grep README

Output:

lpj/README.md

📝 What happened: -r appended README.md to the archive. This only works on UNCOMPRESSED tar files — you cannot append to .tar.gz, .tar.bz2, or .tar.xz archives. If you need to modify a compressed archive, decompress first, append, then recompress.

Example 9: Compare Archive with Filesystem

Scenario: Carol checks if any files have changed since the last backup was created.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

tar -df /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_backup.tar /lpj/jobpost/ 2>&1 | head -5

Output:

lpj/jobpost/jobpost/settings.py: Mod time differs lpj/jobpost/jobpost/settings.py: Size differs lpj/jobpost/jobpost/views.py: Mod time differs

📝 What happened: -d (diff) compared the archive against the live filesystem. settings.py changed in both modification time and size (someone edited config), views.py's timestamp changed (touched or re-deployed). Run before backups to see what will be captured, or after to verify integrity.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: tar -czf (create gzip), tar -xzf (extract), tar -tzf (list). -v shows files processed. -r appends (uncompressed only). -d compares archive vs filesystem. -C DIR extracts elsewhere. --exclude skips files. --strip-components=N removes path depth. -j for bzip2, -J for xz.

gzip

COMPRESSCompressionLFCS Domain 4

Compress files using Lempel-Ziv coding — reduce file sizes for storage and transfer

gzip compresses individual files using LZ77. Each file is replaced by a compressed .gz version. The most common compression tool on Linux — used by logrotate for log compression and tar for .tar.gz archives.

Syntax

gzip [OPTIONS] [FILE...]
# Common: gzip large_file.log | gzip -k data.csv | gzip -9 backup.sql

Parameters

FlagDescription
-k, --keepKeep original file (don't delete)
-1 ... -9Compression level: 1 fastest, 9 best
-v, --verboseShow compression ratio
-r, --recursiveCompress files in directories recursively
-t, --testTest compressed file integrity

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Log Compression

# Carol compresses yesterday's Django log to save disk space:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls -lh /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj developers 125M Jun 3 23:59 jobpost.log
carol@prod-api-01:~$ gzip -k /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log
carol@prod-api-01:~$ ls -lh /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log*
-rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj developers 125M Jun 3 23:59 jobpost.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj developers  12M Jun 3 23:59 jobpost.log.gz

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — GNU Zip

Daily Workflow: Carol uses gzip to compress log files before archiving to save disk space. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

carol@prod-api-01:~$ gzip -k /lpj/ops/backups/db_dump.sql

Examples

Example 1: Basic Compression

Scenario: Carol compresses a large SQL dump before transfer.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

gzip jobpost_dump.sql && ls -lh jobpost_dump.sql.gz

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 2.4M Jun 4 02:00 jobpost_dump.sql.gz

📝 What happened: Original .sql file (45MB) was replaced by .sql.gz (2.4MB) — 94.7% compression. gzip removes the original file by default. Use -k to keep it. SQL/text files compress extremely well; binary files (images, videos) compress poorly.

Example 2: Keep Original File

Scenario: Alice compresses logs but keeps the original for active debugging.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

gzip -k /lpj/ops/logs/access.log && ls -lh /lpj/ops/logs/access.log*

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj developers 50M Jun 4 08:00 access.log -rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj developers 5.2M Jun 4 08:00 access.log.gz

📝 What happened: -k kept the original 50MB log AND created a 5.2MB compressed copy. Useful when processes still need the original file (nginx writes to access.log). Logrotate uses gzip without -k — it moves the file first, then compresses.

Example 3: Best Compression Level

Scenario: Carol uses maximum compression for a long-term archive.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

gzip -9v jobpost_dump.sql

Output:

jobpost_dump.sql: 94.8% -- replaced with jobpost_dump.sql.gz

📝 What happened: -9 used maximum compression (best ratio, slowest). -v showed the ratio: 94.8%. Compare: level 1 gives ~85% quickly, level 6 (default) ~92%, level 9 gives ~95% slowly. For backups, level 9 is worth the wait.

Example 4: Fastest Compression

Scenario: Alice needs quick compression during a real-time pipeline.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

gzip -1v /tmp/streaming_data.json

Output:

streaming_data.json: 78.2% -- replaced with streaming_data.json.gz

📝 What happened: -1 used fastest compression — 78.2% ratio in milliseconds. Lower compression ratio but much faster. Use -1 in real-time pipelines where throughput matters more than disk space. Default -6 balances speed and ratio.

Example 5: Test Integrity

Scenario: Carol verifies compressed backup files haven't been corrupted.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

gzip -t /lpj/ops/backups/*.gz && echo "All OK" || echo "Corruption found!"

Output:

All OK

📝 What happened: -t tested all .gz files for CRC checksum errors — all passed. Run integrity checks before deleting originals or before restoring from backups. A corrupted .gz file will produce "unexpected end of file" errors during decompression.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: gzip FILE replaces with .gz. -k keeps original. -1..-9 sets compression level. -v shows ratio. -t tests integrity. gunzip decompresses. zcat FILE.gz views without decompressing. gzip works on individual files — use tar for directories.

gunzip

DECOMPRESSCompressionLFCS Domain 4

Decompress .gz files — restore compressed files to their original form

gunzip decompresses files compressed with gzip (.gz). Equivalent to gzip -d. Can also decompress files created by compress (.Z), zip, and pack. The most common decompression tool in daily Linux use.

Syntax

gunzip [OPTIONS] [FILE...]
# Common: gunzip file.gz | gunzip -k file.gz | gunzip -c file.gz > output

Parameters

FlagDescription
-k, --keepKeep compressed file after decompression
-c, --stdoutWrite to stdout, keep original unchanged
-v, --verboseShow name and percentage reduction
-t, --testTest integrity without decompressing

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

alice@dev-01:~$ ls -lh /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_latest.sql.gz

alice@dev-01:~$ gunzip -k /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_latest.sql.gz
alice@dev-01:~$ ls -lh /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_latest.sql*
-rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj developers 45M Jun 4 02:00 jobpost_latest.sql
-rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj developers 2.4M Jun 4 02:00 jobpost_latest.sql.gz

carol@prod-api-01:~$ gunzip /lpj/ops/backups/db_dump.sql.gz

Example 1: Basic Decompression

Scenario: Alice decompresses a gzipped log file for analysis.

-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data 50M Jun 4 08:00 access.log

📝 What happened: access.log.gz (5.2MB) decompressed to access.log (50MB). The .gz file was deleted. gunzip replaces the .gz with the decompressed version by default. Use -k to keep the .gz file after decompression.

Example 2: Decompress to stdout

Scenario: Carol pipes decompressed content directly to grep without writing to disk.

📝 What happened: -c decompressed to stdout without modifying the .gz file. The content was piped to grep — no temporary file needed. This is faster than decompressing to disk first, especially for large archives.

Scenario: Eve the auditor decompresses a log while preserving the original for evidence.

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/

📝 What happened: -k kept the compressed original alongside the decompressed version. Essential for chain-of-custody in audits — the original .gz file preserves exact timestamps and sizes for evidence integrity.

Example 4: Verbose Decompression

Scenario: Carol checks compression statistics when restoring multiple backups.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)

jobpost_db.gz: 94.7% -- replaced with jobpost_db.sql static_files.gz: 72.3% -- replaced with static_files.tar configs.gz: 88.1% -- replaced with configs.json

📝 What happened: -v showed compression ratios for each file. Text files (SQL, JSON) compressed best (88-95%), binary files (tar with images) compressed less (72%). Use verbose mode to audit compression efficiency across file types.

Example 5: Recursive Decompression

Scenario: Alice decompresses all .gz files under the logs directory at once.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz

    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

gunzip -r /lpj/ops/logs/archive/

Output:

# All .gz files under archive/ and subdirectories are decompressed. # Original .gz files are replaced by decompressed versions.

📝 What happened: -r recursed into subdirectories, decompressing every .gz file found. Equivalent to find /lpj/ops/logs/archive/ -name "*.gz" -exec gunzip {} \; but more efficient. Beware: this replaces all .gz files — use -k with -r if you want to keep originals.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: gunzip FILE.gz decompresses and removes .gz. gunzip -k keeps original. gunzip -c outputs to stdout (pipe-friendly). gunzip -r recurses directories. Equivalent to gzip -d. zcat/zless/zgrep work on .gz without decompressing.

zip

ARCHIVECompressionCross-PlatformLFCS Domain 4

Create ZIP archives — the universal cross-platform compression format

zip creates compressed archives in the ZIP format, readable on Windows, macOS, and Linux without additional tools. Unlike tar+gzip which is Linux-native, ZIP is the format of choice when sharing with non-Linux users or uploading to web portals.

Syntax

zip [OPTIONS] ZIPFILE FILE...
# Common: zip -r archive.zip folder/ | zip -e secret.zip file.txt | zip -r backup.zip /lpj/

Parameters

FlagDescription
-rRecurse into directories (REQUIRED for folders)
-eEncrypt with password
-qQuiet mode
-9Best compression

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

# Alice packages Django templates for a frontend contractor on Windows:
alice@dev-01:~$ zip -r /tmp/jobpost_templates.zip /lpj/jobpost/templates/
adding: lpj/jobpost/templates/ (stored 0%)
adding: lpj/jobpost/templates/base.html (deflated 68%)
adding: lpj/jobpost/templates/jobpost/ (stored 0%)
alice@dev-01:~$ ls -lh /tmp/jobpost_templates.zip
-rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 125K Jun 4 10:30 jobpost_templates.zip

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Zip Archive

Daily Workflow: Carol uses zip to create cross-platform archives for sharing with Windows users. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical zip usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ zip -r /lpj/ops/backups/configs.zip /lpj/k8s/
carol@prod-api-01:~$ zip /lpj/ops/backups/reports.zip /lpj/ops/reports/*.txt

Examples

# Backup locations in anihpj infrastructure:
#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Primary backup directory
#  /lpj/ops/logs/         — Log archives before rotation
#  backup-nas:/backups/   — Network-attached storage
Example 1: Compress a Directory

Scenario: Carol creates a ZIP of the Kubernetes manifests for a vendor review.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

zip -r /tmp/k8s_manifests.zip /lpj/k8s/

Output:

adding: lpj/k8s/ (stored 0%) adding: lpj/k8s/base/web-deployment.yaml (deflated 78%) adding: lpj/k8s/base/api-deployment.yaml (deflated 76%) adding: lpj/k8s/ingress/ingress.yaml (deflated 82%)

📝 What happened: -r is REQUIRED for directories — without it, zip only stores the directory name (empty). Each file shows compression percentage. YAML files compress well (76-82%). The vendor can open this on Windows with built-in ZIP support.

Example 2: Password-Protected Archive

Scenario: Carol encrypts a sensitive database config before emailing it.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

zip -e /tmp/db_config.zip /lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml

Output:

Enter password: ******** Verify password: ******** adding: lpj/k8s/base/secrets.yaml (deflated 65%)

📝 What happened: -e encrypted the ZIP with a password. The file cannot be extracted without the password. This uses ZIP's legacy PKZIP encryption — adequate for casual use but not for highly sensitive data. For strong encryption, use gpg -c instead.

Example 3: Quiet Mode for Scripts

Scenario: Alice's CI script creates a ZIP silently for deployment.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

zip -rq /tmp/deploy.zip /lpj/jobpost/static/ && echo "Done"

Output:

Done

📝 What happened: -q suppressed all output — only "Done" printed. Perfect for CI/CD scripts where verbose output clutters logs. Use -rq in all automated ZIP creation. Check exit code for success/failure instead of parsing output.

Example 4: Best Compression

Scenario: Carol maximizes compression for an archive bound for slow upload.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

zip -9r /tmp/jobpost_full.zip /lpj/jobpost/

Output:

adding: lpj/jobpost/manage.py (deflated 72%) adding: lpj/jobpost/jobpost/settings.py (deflated 85%) # ... 847 files compressed

📝 What happened: -9 used maximum compression — took longer but produced the smallest possible ZIP. The difference vs default (-6) is typically 2-5% smaller for text files but significantly slower. Worth it for files being uploaded over slow connections.

Example 5: Add Files to Existing ZIP

Scenario: Alice forgot to include the Dockerfile — she adds it without recreating.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

zip -r /tmp/jobpost_full.zip /lpj/Dockerfile

Output:

updating: lpj/Dockerfile (deflated 64%)

📝 What happened: Dockerfile was added to the existing ZIP archive. Zip can update in-place — no need to recreate the entire archive. Use zip -d archive.zip file.txt to delete a file from the archive. Much faster than tar which requires full recreation.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: zip -r archive.zip folder/ — always use -r for directories. -e encrypts. -q silences output. -9 best compression. zip -u updates only changed files. unzip extracts. ZIP is universal (Windows/Mac/Linux) unlike tar.gz which is Linux-native.

unzip

DECOMPRESSCompressionCross-PlatformLFCS Domain 4

Extract ZIP archives — the universal decompression tool

unzip extracts files from ZIP archives. Supports listing contents, testing integrity, and selective extraction. Works with ZIP files created on any platform (Windows, macOS, Linux).

Syntax

unzip [OPTIONS] ZIPFILE [FILE...]
# Common: unzip archive.zip | unzip -l archive.zip | unzip archive.zip -d /target/

Parameters

FlagDescription
-lList contents without extracting
-d DIRExtract to specified directory
-oOverwrite files without prompting
-nNever overwrite existing files

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📝 What happened: -l listed archive contents with sizes and dates. Three YAML files, 5.7KB total. Always list before extracting — especially for archives from untrusted sources. A ZIP bomb (small archive that decompresses to GBs) will be obvious from the listing.

Example 3: Extract to Target Directory

Scenario: Carol extracts vendor dashboards to the monitoring directory.

Example 4: Selective Extraction

Scenario: Alice extracts only CSS files from the frontend assets ZIP.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/

Example 5: Test Archive Integrity

Scenario: Carol verifies a downloaded ZIP isn't corrupted before deploying.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

unzip -t /tmp/deploy_package.zip

Output:

Archive: /tmp/deploy_package.zip testing: jobpost/static/style.css OK testing: jobpost/static/app.js OK testing: jobpost/templates/base.html OK No errors detected in compressed data of /tmp/deploy_package.zip.

📝 What happened: -t tested CRC checksums for every file — all passed. Run integrity checks before deploying from ZIP archives. A corrupted ZIP will report "bad CRC" for affected files. Equivalent to gzip -t for .gz files.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: unzip archive.zip extracts to current dir. -d DIR extracts elsewhere. -l lists contents. -t tests integrity. -o overwrites without asking. Glob patterns filter files. unzip handles archives from any platform.

bzip2

COMPRESSCompressionLFCS Domain 4

Compress files using Burrows-Wheeler algorithm — better ratio than gzip, slower

bzip2 compresses files with better ratios than gzip (especially for text), at the cost of slower speed. Creates .bz2 files. Commonly used with tar (tar -cjf). Best for long-term archival where compression ratio matters more than speed.

Syntax

bzip2 [OPTIONS] [FILE...]
# Common: bzip2 large_file.log | bzip2 -k data.sql | bzip2 -9 backup.tar

Parameters

FlagDescription
-k, --keepKeep original file
-1 ... -9Compression level (1 fast, 9 best)
-v, --verboseShow compression ratio

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 180M Jan 1 2024 jobpost_2024.tar
carol@prod-db-01:~$ bzip2 -kv jobpost_2024.tar
jobpost_2024.tar: 5.471:1, 1.462 bits/byte, 81.72% saved, 180M in, 32M out.

Example 1: Compress a SQL Dump

Scenario: Carol uses bzip2 for better compression on database backups.

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/

-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 1.8M Jun 4 02:00 jobpost_dump.sql.bz2

📝 What happened: The SQL dump compressed to 1.8MB (vs ~2.4MB with gzip). bzip2 typically achieves 10-20% better compression than gzip on text files but takes 2-3x longer. Trade-off: use gzip for speed, bzip2 for size, xz for maximum compression.

Scenario: Carol verifies archived files before deleting originals.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: bzip2 FILE compresses to .bz2. -k keeps original. -1..-9 levels. -v shows stats. -t tests. bunzip2 or bzip2 -d decompresses. With tar: -cjf creates .tar.bz2. bzip2 beats gzip for text, but xz beats bzip2.

bunzip2

DECOMPRESSCompressionLFCS Domain 4

Decompress .bz2 files — restore bzip2-compressed data

bunzip2 decompresses .bz2 files. Functionally identical to bzip2 -d. Used to restore bzip2-compressed archives, logs, and database dumps to their original form.

Syntax

bunzip2 [OPTIONS] [FILE...]
# Common: bunzip2 file.bz2 | bunzip2 -k archive.tar.bz2 | bunzip2 -c log.bz2 | grep ERROR

Parameters

FlagDescription
-k, --keepKeep compressed file
-c, --stdoutOutput to stdout
-v, --verboseShow decompression stats

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Example 1: Basic Decompression

Scenario: Alice decompresses a bzip2 log file for debugging.

📁 Directory Snippet:

lpj/
└── 📁 ops/

-rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj developers 250M Jun 1 00:00 jobpost.log

📝 What happened: 18MB .bz2 expanded to 250MB log file. The .bz2 was deleted. bunzip2 is a symlink to bzip2 — running bunzip2 is identical to bzip2 -d. Use whichever is more intuitive for your workflow.

Example 2: Pipe to stdout

Scenario: Carol pipes decompressed data directly to grep for error analysis.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)

    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

bunzip2 -c /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log.bz2 | grep "CRITICAL" | wc -l

Output:

23

📝 What happened: -c decompressed to stdout — no temporary file needed. 23 CRITICAL-level log entries found. The .bz2 file remained unchanged. This pipe pattern works for any compressed format: gzip/gunzip, bzip2/bunzip2, xz/unxz all support -c.

Example 4: Decompress Multiple Files

Scenario: Carol decompresses all month-end backup archives at once.

Output:

# All .bz2 files in the directory are decompressed. # Original .bz2 files are replaced by the decompressed versions.

📝 What happened: Each .bz2 was decompressed and replaced. Equivalent to for f in *.bz2; do bunzip2 "$f"; done. Add -k to keep originals. Unlike unzip, bunzip2 doesn't support listing contents — use bzip2 -t to verify integrity first.

Example 5: Compare with gzip

Scenario: Alice compares the decompressed size and speed of bzip2 vs gzip.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

time bunzip2 large_file.bz2 && time gunzip large_file.gz && echo "bzip2 vs gzip comparison"

Output:

real 0m2.345s # bunzip2 real 0m0.856s # gunzip # gzip is ~3x faster at decompression. But bzip2 file was 30% smaller.

📝 What happened: gzip decompressed 3x faster but the bzip2 archive was 30% smaller. Trade-off: bzip2 for long-term storage (decompress once), gzip for frequent access (decompress often). Choose based on your access pattern, not just compression ratio.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: bunzip2 FILE.bz2 decompresses (same as bzip2 -d). -k keeps .bz2. -c pipes to stdout. bzip2 has better ratio but is slower than gzip. With tar: tar -xjf archive.tar.bz2. xz achieves even better ratios.

xz

COMPRESSCompressionLFCS Domain 4

Compress with LZMA2 — best compression ratio, modern standard for Linux packages

xz uses the LZMA2 algorithm which achieves the best compression ratios of the common tools. Creates .xz files. Used by systemd journal, kernel images, and modern package distributions. Default tool for tar -cJf.

Syntax

xz [OPTIONS] [FILE...]
# Common: xz large_file.log | xz -k data.sql | xz -9 backup.tar

Parameters

FlagDescription
-k, --keepKeep original file
-1 ... -9Compression level (0-9, default 6)
-v, --verboseShow compression ratio
-T NUse N threads (parallel compression)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Maximum Compression Archival

# Carol compresses the annual database backup with xz for cold storage:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ ls -lh jobpost_annual_dump.tar
-rw-r--r-- 1 carol developers 2.1G Dec 31 23:59 jobpost_annual_dump.tar
carol@prod-db-01:~$ xz -kv -T4 jobpost_annual_dump.tar
jobpost_annual_dump.tar (1/1)
  100%   2.1G / 195.3 MiB = 11.001  (4 threads)

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — XZ Compress

Daily Workflow: Carol uses xz for maximum compression on long-term archival backups sent to backup-nas. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

carol@prod-api-01:~$ xz -k /lpj/ops/logs/error.log

Examples

#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Primary backup directory
#  /lpj/ops/logs/         — Log archives before rotation
#  backup-nas:/backups/   — Network-attached storage
Example 1: Maximum Compression

Scenario: Carol compresses the year-end database backup for offsite storage.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

xz -9vk jobpost_annual_dump.tar

Output:

jobpost_annual_dump.tar (1/1) 100% 2.1G / 195.3 MiB = 11.001

📝 What happened: -9 max compression, -v verbose, -k keep original. 2.1GB compressed to 195MB — 91% reduction, 11:1 ratio. xz consistently beats gzip (typically ~85%) and bzip2 (~88%) for text/data files. The trade-off is speed — xz is the slowest of the three.

Example 2: Multi-Threaded Compression

Scenario: Carol uses all 4 CPU cores to compress faster on the database server.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

xz -T4 -k /lpj/ops/backups/large_backup.tar

Output:

# Compression completed at ~4x the speed of single-threaded xz. # Thread count should not exceed CPU cores — check with nproc.

📝 What happened: -T4 used 4 threads, dramatically speeding up compression. xz is the only common compressor with native multi-threading — gzip and bzip2 are single-threaded. Use -T0 to auto-detect CPU count. Multi-threading uses more memory.

Example 3: Decompress with unxz

Scenario: Alice restores the annual backup for compliance review.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)

    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

unxz -k jobpost_annual_dump.tar.xz && ls -lh jobpost_annual_dump.tar

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 2.1G Dec 31 23:59 jobpost_annual_dump.tar

📝 What happened: unxz (same as xz -d) restored the 2.1GB tar from 195MB .xz. -k kept the compressed version. xz decompression is fast — the LZMA2 algorithm is asymmetric: slow compression, fast decompression. Ideal for "compress once, read many" use cases.

Example 4: Fastest Compression

Scenario: Carol needs quick compression during a pipeline with some space savings.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:

└── 📁 ops/

Output:

streaming_output.log (1/1) 100% 45.0 MiB / 8.2 MiB = 5.488

📝 What happened: -1 fastest compression — 5.5:1 ratio (vs ~7:1 at default level 6). Level 1 xz is still better than gzip level 9 for text. Even at the fastest setting, xz compresses well — the speed penalty vs gzip is smaller at lower levels.

Example 5: Compare Compression Tools

Scenario: Carol benchmarks all three compressors on a production log file.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

cp jobpost.log test.log && time gzip -k test.log && time bzip2 -k test.log && mv test.log test2.log && time xz -k test2.log && ls -lh test*

Output:

# gzip: 100MB → 12MB (88%), 1.2s # bzip2: 100MB → 9.5MB (90.5%), 3.8s # xz: 100MB → 7.8MB (92.2%), 8.5s # Conclusion: gzip for speed, bzip2 for balance, xz for size.

📝 What happened: Clear trade-off: gzip=fastest/least compression, xz=slowest/best compression, bzip2=middle ground. Choice depends on: frequency of access (gzip for daily), storage cost (xz for archival), CPU availability (gzip on busy servers).

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: xz FILE compresses to .xz. -k keeps original. -1..-9 levels. -T N threads. unxz or xz -d decompresses. With tar: tar -cJf creates .tar.xz, tar -xJf extracts. xz = best ratio, slowest. Used for kernel images and packages.

unxz

DECOMPRESSCompressionLFCS Domain 4

Decompress .xz files — restore LZMA2-compressed data

unxz decompresses .xz files. Equivalent to xz -d. The LZMA2 algorithm used by xz is asymmetric: decompression is much faster than compression, making xz ideal for "compress once, read many" scenarios like package distribution and log archival.

Syntax

unxz [OPTIONS] [FILE...]
# Common: unxz file.xz | unxz -k archive.tar.xz | unxz -c log.xz | less

Parameters

FlagDescription
-k, --keepKeep compressed file
-c, --stdoutOutput to stdout
-v, --verboseShow decompression info

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

-rw-r--r-- 1 anihpj developers 195M Dec 31 23:59 jobpost_2024.tar.xz

Example 1: Basic Decompression

Scenario: Carol decompresses an xz-archived kernel log for analysis.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz

    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

unxz /var/log/kern.log.xz && ls -lh /var/log/kern.log

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 45M Jan 15 02:00 kern.log

📝 What happened: 4.5MB .xz decompressed to 45MB log. xz decompression is fast — typically 2-3x faster than compression. This asymmetry is intentional: packages are compressed once (by maintainers) and decompressed millions of times (by users).

Example 2: Pipe to Pager

Scenario: Alice reads a compressed log directly without creating a temporary file.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

unxz -c /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log.xz | less

Output:

# The decompressed log opens in less — scroll, search, and navigate # without ever writing the full 250MB file to disk.

📝 What happened: -c decompressed to stdout, piped directly to less. No disk I/O for the decompressed content — only the compressed .xz file was read. This is far more efficient than decompressing to disk first, especially on storage-constrained systems.

Example 3: Keep Originals During Batch Decompression

Scenario: Carol decompresses all month-end .xz files while archiving originals.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

unxz -k /lpj/ops/backups/*.tar.xz && echo "Decompressed, originals kept"

Output:

Decompressed, originals kept

📝 What happened: All .tar.xz files decompressed, but .xz originals preserved. This doubles disk usage temporarily — ensure sufficient space before batch operations. After verification, delete .xz files with rm *.xz to reclaim space.

Example 4: Test Integrity

Scenario: Carol checks .xz file integrity before offsite transfer.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

xz -t /lpj/ops/backups/*.tar.xz && echo "All valid"

Output:

All valid

📝 What happened: xz -t tested integrity (unxz itself has no -t flag — use xz -t). All files passed CRC checks. Always verify compressed archives before: transferring over network, writing to tape/offsite, or deleting originals.

Example 5: Measure Decompression Speed

Scenario: Carol benchmarks how long it takes to decompress the annual backup.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

time unxz -c /lpj/ops/backups/jobpost_annual.tar.xz > /dev/null

Output:

real 0m12.345s user 0m11.200s sys 0m1.100s # 2.1GB decompressed in 12 seconds — ~175 MB/s throughput.

📝 What happened: 2.1GB decompressed to /dev/null (no disk write) in 12 seconds. The bottleneck is CPU, not disk. xz decompression at default level 6 uses ~65MB RAM. Higher compression levels (-9) use more memory during decompression too — up to ~674MB.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: unxz FILE.xz decompresses (same as xz -d). -k keeps .xz. -c pipes to stdout. Use xz -t to test integrity (unxz has no -t). xz decompression is fast (2-3x faster than compression). tar -xJf extracts .tar.xz directly.

zcat

VIEWCompressionLFCS Domain 4

View compressed files without decompressing — cat for .gz files

zcat is identical to gunzip -c — it decompresses to stdout without modifying the original. Perfect for quick inspection of compressed logs, configs, and data files. Works on .gz and .Z files. The fastest way to peek inside compressed text.

Syntax

zcat [FILE...]
# Common: zcat file.gz | zcat log.gz | grep ERROR | zcat dump.sql.gz | head -20

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Quick Log Inspection

# Carol quickly checks yesterday's compressed Django error log:

2025-06-03 23:58:01 WARNING  Slow query detected (2.3s)
2025-06-03 23:58:15 ERROR    Celery task timeout
2025-06-03 23:59:01 WARNING  Rate limit exceeded for IP 10.0.0.99
# No decompressed file created — the .gz remains untouched on disk.

Parameters

FlagDescription
-fForce decompression even if file has no .gz suffix
-lList compression info (same as gzip -l)
(none)Decompress and write to stdout

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Not a gzip file or file not found

📝 What happened: zless decompresses on the fly and pipes to less. All less commands work: /pattern search, g top, G bottom, q quit. Much faster than decompressing to disk first. The original .gz stays compressed.

Example 2: Open at First Error

Scenario: Alice opens the compressed log directly at the first ERROR entry.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

zless +/ERROR /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log.gz

Output:

# Opens at the first line containing "ERROR" — jump straight to the problem.

📝 What happened: +/pattern passes the search command to less on startup. The file opens directly at the first ERROR match. This is a less feature, not zless-specific — works with regular less +/pattern file too.

Example 3: Compare zless with Manual Decompression

Scenario: Carol shows why zless is better than decompressing to disk first.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives (tar.gz, zip)
    │   ├── 📄 full_backup_20260605.tar.gz
    │   ├── 📄 db_dump_20260605.sql.gz
    │   └── 📄 configs_20260605.zip
    ├── 📁 systemd/
    └── 📁 cron/

Command:

# Slow way: 2 steps, 250MB disk used
gunzip -k jobpost.log.gz && less jobpost.log && rm jobpost.log
# Fast way: 1 step, 0 extra disk used
zless jobpost.log.gz

Output:

# zless saves time and disk space — no temporary file, immediate reading. # For a 250MB compressed log (2.5GB decompressed), the difference is huge.

📝 What happened: zless avoids: disk space for decompressed file (2.5GB), time to write 2.5GB to disk, I/O contention on busy systems, cleanup of temporary file. On production servers with tight storage, this matters enormously.

Example 5: No .gz Extension Required

Scenario: Carol views a gzip-compressed file that has no .gz extension.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/

Output:

# Even without a .gz extension, zless detects gzip format and decompresses. # zless checks the magic bytes (0x1F 0x8B) at the start of the file.

📝 What happened: zless (via gzip) detects compression by magic bytes, not file extension. Even if a file is named .bin, .tmp, or has no extension, zless will decompress it if it's valid gzip format. This is important for forensic analysis of unknown files.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: zless FILE.gz — pager for compressed files. Same as zcat FILE.gz | less. All less commands work (/search, n, g, G, q). +/pattern opens at first match. No disk space needed for decompression. zless for .gz, bzless for .bz2, xzless for .xz.

zgrep

SEARCHCompressionLFCS Domain 4

Search compressed files — grep for .gz files without decompressing

zgrep is a wrapper that decompresses .gz files and runs grep on the output. Supports all grep options. The essential tool for searching through compressed log archives without first decompressing them to disk.

Syntax

zgrep [GREP_OPTIONS] PATTERN [FILE...]
# Common: zgrep ERROR *.gz | zgrep -i "timeout" access.log.gz | zgrep -c "500" *.gz

Parameters

FlagDescription
-iCase-insensitive search
-cCount matching lines
-nShow line numbers
-vInvert match (non-matching lines)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Matches found
1No matches

jobpost.log.1.gz:2025-06-02 14:30:15 ERROR PostgreSQL too many clients
jobpost.log.2.gz:2025-06-01 09:15:00 WARNING Database pool exhausted

/lpj/ops/logs/nginx/access.log.1.gz:10.0.0.99 - - [03/Jun/2025:15:00:00] "GET /admin HTTP/1.1" 403 256 /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost/jobpost.log.2.gz:2025-06-01 16:00:00 WARN Rate limit exceeded for IP 10.0.0.99

📝 What happened: The suspicious IP 10.0.0.99 appeared in both nginx (403 forbidden) and Django logs (rate limit). zgrep doesn't support -r natively on .gz files — use find -exec zgrep for recursive search. This is a standard pattern in forensic analysis.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: zgrep PATTERN *.gz searches compressed files. All grep flags work (-i, -v, -c, -n, -A, -B). Equivalent to zcat file.gz | grep. No disk space needed. zgrep for .gz, bzgrep for .bz2, xzgrep for .xz. Use find -exec zgrep for recursive.

📝 Text Processing

Commands for searching, filtering, transforming, and analyzing text. These are the core tools for log analysis, data wrangling, and shell scripting — every SRE uses them daily. The anihpj/jobpost team relies on grep for log debugging, sed for config updates, and awk for metrics extraction.

grep

SEARCHText ProcessingCoreLFCS Domain 4

Global Regular Expression Print — the most-used text search tool in Linux

grep searches for patterns in text files and streams. It is arguably the most-used command in any SRE/Platform Engineer's toolkit. Used daily for parsing logs during incidents, filtering process lists, auditing configs, and building data pipelines.

For anihpj/jobpost, grep is used for:

  • Searching Django logs for ERROR/WARN patterns during incidents
  • Filtering ps aux to find specific processes (nginx, gunicorn, celery)
  • Auditing Kubernetes manifests for security misconfigurations
  • Extracting IPs and status codes from nginx access logs

Syntax

grep [OPTIONS] PATTERN [FILE...]
command | grep [OPTIONS] PATTERN
# Common: grep ERROR app.log | grep -r "TODO" /lpj/ | ps aux | grep "[n]ginx"

Parameters

FlagDescription
-iCase-insensitive matching
-vInvert match (show non-matching lines)
-r, -RRecursive directory search
-nPrint line numbers
-cPrint only count of matching lines
-A NUMPrint NUM lines of trailing context (After)
-B NUMPrint NUM lines of leading context (Before)
-C NUMPrint NUM lines of context (Center)
-lPrint only filenames with matches
-wMatch whole words only (not substrings)
-xMatch whole lines exactly
-qQuiet — no output, just exit status
-m NUMStop after NUM matches
-HPrint filename with each match
-hSuppress filename prefix in output
-LPrint only filenames WITHOUT matches
-aProcess binary files as text
--include=GLOBSearch only files matching GLOB
--exclude=GLOBSkip files matching GLOB

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Matches found
1No matches
2Error

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Incident Response

2025-06-04 14:22:05 Exception: django.db.utils.OperationalError
2025-06-04 14:22:05 Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/lpj/jobpost/views.py", line 142, in get_job_listings
    jobs = JobPost.objects.filter(status='active')
# Carol identifies the root cause: database timeout in views.py line 142.

# Matches only "error" as a standalone word. # Does NOT match: "errors", "terror", "errorcheck", "supererror".

📝 What happened: -w matched "error" only when surrounded by non-word characters (spaces, punctuation, line boundaries). Without -w, grep "error" matches "errors", "terror", "errorlog" etc. Always use -w when you want exact word matches, not substrings.

Example 10: Invert Match with Line Numbers

Scenario: Carol views a config file excluding all comment and blank lines for clarity.

Output:

1:apiVersion: apps/v1 2:kind: Deployment 3:metadata: 4: name: web 7:spec: 8: replicas: 3

📝 What happened: -v inverted the match — showing lines that do NOT match comments (^\s*#) or blank lines (^\s*$). -n showed the original line numbers. This is the standard SRE pattern for viewing active configuration: grep -v '^#\|^$' config.conf. The config is now 6 lines of actual content instead of 25 with comments.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: grep -i case-insensitive. grep -v invert. grep -rn recursive with line numbers. grep -A/B/C N context. grep -c count. grep -l filenames only. grep -w whole words. grep -q silent (scripts). grep -oP extract with Perl regex. [n]ginx trick avoids self-match. grep -E = egrep, grep -F = fgrep. --include/--exclude filter by filename.

egrep

SEARCHText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Extended grep — supports | (OR), +, ?, {} without backslash escaping

egrep is equivalent to grep -E. It interprets patterns as extended regular expressions (ERE), supporting alternation (|), one-or-more (+), zero-or-one (?), and brace repetition ({n,m}) without backslash escaping. Preferred for readable complex patterns.

Syntax

egrep [OPTIONS] PATTERN [FILE...]
# Same as: grep -E [OPTIONS] PATTERN [FILE...]

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Matches found
1No matches

Parameters

FlagDescription
-iCase-insensitive matching
-vInvert match — show non-matching lines
-cCount matching lines only
-nShow line numbers
-rRecursive — search directories
-lList matching filenames only
-oShow only matched part of line
-EExtended regex (always on for egrep)
-A NShow N lines after match
-B NShow N lines before match

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0At least one match
1No match
2Syntax error

fgrep

SEARCHText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Fixed-string grep — literal text search, no regex interpretation, much faster

fgrep is equivalent to grep -F. It treats the pattern as a literal string — no regex metacharacters are interpreted. This makes it faster (no regex engine) and safer (no accidental regex matches). Use when searching for exact strings containing special characters.

Syntax

fgrep [OPTIONS] PATTERN [FILE...]
# Same as: grep -F [OPTIONS] PATTERN [FILE...]

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Matches found
1No matches

sed

TRANSFORMText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Stream editor — find, replace, delete, and transform text in pipelines

sed performs text transformations on a stream or file. Used for find-and-replace, deletion, insertion, and extraction. Ideal for inline file editing in scripts and CI/CD pipelines. Unlike an interactive editor, sed processes the entire stream non-interactively.

Syntax

sed [OPTIONS] 'SCRIPT' [FILE...]
# Common: sed 's/old/new/' file | sed -i 's/localhost/prod/g' config | sed '/DEBUG/d' log

Parameters

FlagDescription
-i[SUFFIX]Edit files in-place (with optional backup suffix)
-nSuppress automatic printing (use with p command)
-e SCRIPTAdd script to commands (for multiple scripts)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

jenkins@ci-runner-01:~$ grep -E "DEBUG|HOST" /lpj/anihpj/settings.py
DEBUG = False
DATABASE_HOST = 'prod-db-01.anihpj.com'

sed -i.bak 's/DEBUG = True/DEBUG = False/' /lpj/anihpj/settings.py && ls /lpj/anihpj/settings.py*

Output:

settings.py # Modified: DEBUG = False settings.py.bak # Original: DEBUG = True

📝 What happened: -i.bak edited in-place AND created settings.py.bak as backup. The .bak suffix is the backup extension — use any suffix. This is safer than -i alone, which has no undo. Always use -i.bak in production scripts.

sed '/DEBUG/d' /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log | head -5

2025-06-04 08:00:00 INFO Server starting 2025-06-04 08:00:01 WARN Disk usage at 85% 2025-06-04 08:00:02 INFO Connecting to database

📝 What happened: /pattern/d deleted all lines matching "DEBUG". The output is cleaner — only INFO, WARN, ERROR remain. Combine with regex: sed '/DEBUG\|TRACE/d' deletes both. This is the sed equivalent of grep -v DEBUG.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: s/old/new/g replace all (g=global). s/old/new/ replaces first only. -i.bak in-place with backup. /pattern/d delete lines. -n 'N,Mp' print range. -e multiple scripts. ^ line start, $ line end. & = matched text in replacement.

awk

PROCESSText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Pattern scanning and processing language — column-based data extraction and reporting

awk processes text line by line, splitting each into fields. Powerful for column-based data extraction, calculations, and report generation. Think of it as "Excel for the command line" — sum columns, compute averages, filter rows by value.

Syntax

awk [OPTIONS] 'PROGRAM' [FILE...]
# Common: awk '{print $1, $3}' file | awk -F: '{print $1, $7}' /etc/passwd | awk '$3 > 1000' file

Parameters

Flag/VariableDescription
-F SEPSet field separator (default: whitespace)
$0Entire current line
$1, $2, ...$NFIndividual fields
NRCurrent line number
NFNumber of fields in current line

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Log Analytics

# Carol analyzes Django log response times to find slow endpoints:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ awk '{print $NF}' /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log | grep -oP '\d+ms' | sed 's/ms//' | awk '{sum+=$1; count++} END {print "Avg:", sum/count "ms", "Count:", count}'
Avg: 245.3ms Count: 15432

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Text Processor

carol@prod-api-01:~$ awk '/ERROR/{count++} END{print count}' /lpj/ops/logs/app.log

Examples

📝 What happened: $5 is the file size column from ls -l. {sum += $5; count++} runs on EVERY line. END {print ...} runs once after all lines. This is the classic awk accumulator pattern — sum in the body, output in END.

Example 5: Count Unique Values

Scenario: Alice counts how many times each HTTP status code appears in logs.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
│   ├── 📄 models.py
