Command:

awk '{count[$NF]++} END {for (code in count) print code, count[code]}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort -k2 -rn

Output:

200 15234 404 1423 500 312 502 89

📝 What happened: count[$NF]++ created an associative array keyed by status code. The END block iterated and printed. This is awk's superpower — associative arrays for grouping and counting. Equivalent to SELECT code, COUNT(*) GROUP BY code in SQL.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: -F: sets delimiter. $1..$N fields, $0 whole line, $NF last field. NR line number, NF field count. BEGIN {} runs before, {} every line, END {} after. awk is a full programming language — variables, arrays, loops, math.

sort

ORDERText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Sort lines of text — alphabetically, numerically, by column, or random

sort sorts text lines. Sorts alphabetically by default; supports numeric (-n), reverse (-r), column-based (-k), and human-readable (-h) sorting. Almost always paired with uniq for counting and deduplication.

Syntax

sort [OPTIONS] [FILE...]
# Common: sort file | sort -n numbers | sort -k2 -rn data | sort -u names

Parameters

FlagDescription
-nSort numerically (not alphabetically)
-rReverse order
-uUnique only (remove duplicates)
-k POSSort by key position (e.g., -k2 for column 2)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

carol@prod-web-01:~$ awk '{print $1}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
  15234 10.0.0.45
   8421 192.168.1.100
   3215 10.0.0.52

uniq

FILTERText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Report or omit repeated lines — deduplication and counting

uniq filters adjacent duplicate lines. Almost always used after sort for complete deduplication. Essential for counting occurrences (-c), showing only duplicates (-d), or only unique lines (-u).

Syntax

uniq [OPTIONS] [INPUT [OUTPUT]]
# Common: sort file | uniq | sort file | uniq -c | sort -rn | uniq -d file

Parameters

FlagDescription
-cPrefix lines with count of occurrences
-dPrint only duplicate (repeated) lines
-uPrint only unique (non-repeating) lines

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Output:

10.0.0.45 10.0.0.52 192.168.1.100

📝 What happened: -d showed only lines that appear MORE THAN ONCE. Single-occurrence IPs were filtered out. This is useful for finding repeat visitors, potential scrapers, or brute-force attempts. Opposite of -u (unique only).

Example 3: Find Only Uniques

Scenario: Carol finds IPs that only hit the server once (potential one-off scans).

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
│   ├── 📄 models.py
│   ├── 📄 views.py
│   └── 📄 tests.py
├── 📁 api/
│   ├── 📄 views.py
│   └── 📄 serializers.py
├── 📁 k8s/base/
│   ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
│   └── 📄 secrets.yaml

│   ├── 📄 app.log
│   ├── 📄 error.log
│   └── 📄 access.log
└── 📁 scripts/
    └── 📄 deploy.sh

Command:

awk '{print $1}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -u

Output:

10.0.0.99 203.0.113.45 198.51.100.22

📝 What happened: -u showed only lines appearing EXACTLY ONCE. These three IPs hit the server once — potential port scans or probes. Investigate unknown single-access IPs for security. The vast majority of traffic came from repeat IPs.

Example 4: Skip Fields When Comparing

Scenario: Alice compares log lines ignoring the timestamp (first field).

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
│   ├── 📄 models.py
│   ├── 📄 views.py
│   └── 📄 tests.py
├── 📁 api/
│   ├── 📄 views.py
│   └── 📄 serializers.py
├── 📁 k8s/base/
│   ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
│   └── 📄 secrets.yaml
├── 📁 ops/logs/
│   ├── 📄 app.log
│   ├── 📄 error.log
│   └── 📄 access.log
└── 📁 scripts/
    └── 📄 deploy.sh

Command:

awk '{$1=""; print}' /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log | sort | uniq -c -f 0 | sort -rn | head -3

Output:

5234 ERROR Database connection timeout 3210 WARN Disk usage at 85% 1543 INFO Health check passed

📝 What happened: -f 0 skipped 0 fields before comparing — but we already removed the timestamp with awk. The actual use is uniq -f 1 to skip the first field when comparing. This counts unique messages regardless of when they occurred, showing the most frequent non-timestamp patterns.

Example 5: Count Without sort (Only Adjacent)

Scenario: Carol demonstrates why sort is needed before uniq.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
│   ├── 📄 models.py
│   ├── 📄 views.py
│   └── 📄 tests.py
├── 📁 api/
│   ├── 📄 views.py
│   └── 📄 serializers.py
├── 📁 k8s/base/
│   ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
│   └── 📄 secrets.yaml
├── 📁 ops/logs/
│   ├── 📄 app.log
│   ├── 📄 error.log
│   └── 📄 access.log
└── 📁 scripts/
    └── 📄 deploy.sh

Command:

echo -e "alice\nbob\nalice\ncarol\nalice" | uniq -c && echo "---" && echo -e "alice\nbob\nalice\ncarol\nalice" | sort | uniq -c

Output:

1 alice 1 bob 1 alice 1 carol 1 alice --- 3 alice 1 bob 1 carol

📝 What happened: Without sort, uniq only merged ADJACENT duplicates — alice appeared 3 times non-adjacently so was counted 3 separate times. With sort, all alices were grouped and counted as 3. This is the #1 uniq mistake — ALWAYS sort before uniq for full deduplication.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: ALWAYS sort | uniq (uniq only merges adjacent). -c counts. -d duplicates only. -u uniques only. -f N skip fields. sort | uniq -c | sort -rn is the count-rank pipeline. sort -u is equivalent to sort | uniq but faster.

cut

EXTRACTText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Extract sections from lines — columns by delimiter or characters by position

cut extracts columns from delimited files (CSV, TSV, /etc/passwd) or characters by position. Simple and fast — the go-to tool for column extraction when you don't need awk's full power.

Syntax

cut OPTION [FILE...]
# Common: cut -d: -f1,7 /etc/passwd | cut -c1-10 file | cut -d',' -f2 data.csv

Parameters

FlagDescription
-d DELIMUse DELIM as field delimiter (default: TAB)
-f NSelect field N (comma-separated, ranges: 1-3)
-c NSelect character positions

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: cut -d: -f1,7 /etc/passwd extracts fields. -c1-10 characters. -f2- field 2 to end. --output-delimiter changes separator. cut is simpler than awk for basic column work. Does NOT handle quoting — use awk for complex CSV.

tr

TRANSLATEText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Translate or delete characters — character-level text transformation

tr translates, deletes, or squeezes characters from standard input. Operates at the character level (not lines or fields). Ideal for case conversion, whitespace normalization, and removing unwanted characters from streams.

Syntax

tr [OPTIONS] SET1 [SET2]
# Common: tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' | tr -d '\r' | tr -s ' '

Parameters

FlagDescription
-dDelete characters in SET1
-sSqueeze repeated characters to one
-cComplement SET1 (use opposite set)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Log Sanitization

# Carol normalizes mixed-case log output for consistent analysis:

2025-06-04 14:22:01 error database connection timeout
2025-06-04 14:22:05 error redis connection refused
2025-06-04 14:30:00 critical out of memory

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' case conversion. -d delete chars. -s squeeze repeats. -c complement set. tr reads stdin only (no filename args). Need redirection: tr ... < file. Uses POSIX classes: [:alnum:], [:space:], [:digit:].

paste

MERGEText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Merge lines of files — join files side-by-side as columns

paste merges corresponding lines from multiple files, separated by TAB (or custom delimiter). The horizontal equivalent of cat (which merges vertically). Perfect for combining data from separate sources into table format.

Syntax

paste [OPTIONS] [FILE...]
# Common: paste file1 file2 | paste -d',' names.csv ids.csv | paste -s file

Parameters

FlagDescription
-d DELIMUse DELIM as delimiter (default: TAB)
-sPaste sequentially (horizontal, one file at a time)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

│   ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
│   └── 📄 secrets.yaml
├── 📁 ops/logs/
│   ├── 📄 app.log
│   ├── 📄 error.log
│   └── 📄 access.log
└── 📁 scripts/
    └── 📄 deploy.sh

Command:

echo -e "prod-web-01\nprod-web-02\nprod-api-01\nprod-db-01" | paste -sd','

Output:

prod-web-01,prod-web-02,prod-api-01,prod-db-01

📝 What happened: -s pasted all lines from the input into a SINGLE line, using comma as delimiter. The column became a comma-separated row. This is the fastest way to convert a newline-separated list to a comma-separated string for configs or scripts.

alice Django Developer /bin/zsh bob API Developer /bin/bash carol DevOps Lead /bin/bash

📝 What happened: Three files merged side-by-side with TAB separators. Line 1 of each file became row 1, line 2 became row 2, etc. If files have different lengths, missing lines are empty. paste handles any number of input files.

Scenario: Carol formats a key-value list by pasting every two lines as columns.

📝 What happened: paste - - used stdin twice — the first - reads line 1,3,5; the second reads line 2,4,6. This transforms a single-column alternating list into two columns. Very useful for key-value data where keys and values alternate on separate lines.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: paste file1 file2 merges side-by-side. -d',' custom delimiter. -s serial (horizontal). paste - - converts alternating lines to columns. Use <(cmd) process substitution to paste command output. Opposite: cut extracts columns from merged data.

join

MERGEText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Join lines of two files on a common field — SQL JOIN for text files

join merges two sorted files by matching a common key field. Think of it as a SQL JOIN for delimited text files. Both files must be SORTED by the join field. More sophisticated than paste (which merges by line position, not key).

Syntax

join [OPTIONS] FILE1 FILE2
# Common: join -t: -1 3 -2 1 file1 file2 | join -j 2 sorted1 sorted2

Parameters

FlagDescription
-t CHARField delimiter
-1 NJoin field in FILE1 (default: 1)
-2 NJoin field in FILE2 (default: 1)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Scenario: Carol matches UIDs from /etc/passwd with detailed info from another file.

📝 What happened: -t: set colon delimiter, -1 3 joined on field 3 (UID) of passwd, -2 1 joined on field 1 of uid_info. Both files were sorted by UID first. This is a proper relational join — much more powerful than paste for data merging.

Scenario: Carol performs a clean inner join for a report with no header lines.

📁 Directory Snippet:

lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

Output:

alice,Django Developer bob,API Developer carol,DevOps Lead

📝 What happened: tail -n +2 stripped header lines before joining, then the CSVs were sorted and joined on the first comma-separated field. -t',' set delimiter. This is the standard pattern for joining CSV data — strip headers, sort, join.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: join FILE1 FILE2 joins on first field. -t: delimiter. -1 N/-2 N join fields. -j N same field in both. -a N include unmatched. BOTH files must be SORTED by join field. join does inner joins; -a adds outer joins.

wc

COUNTText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Word count — count lines, words, characters, and bytes in files

wc counts lines, words, characters, and bytes. One of the most frequently used tools for quick file statistics. Essential for: checking log volume, verifying file sizes, counting matches, and monitoring data pipelines.

Syntax

wc [OPTIONS] [FILE...]
# Common: wc -l file | wc -w file | wc -c file | grep ERROR log | wc -l

Parameters

FlagDescription
-lPrint line count (most used)
-wPrint word count
-cPrint byte count
-mPrint character count (multibyte aware)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Log Volume Monitoring

carol@prod-api-01:~$ wc -l /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log
15234 /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log
carol@prod-api-01:~$ grep -c "ERROR" /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log
47
carol@prod-api-01:~$ echo "Error rate: $(echo "scale=2; 47/15234*100" | bc)%"
Error rate: 0.31%

split

SPLITText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Split a file into pieces — break large files into manageable chunks

split divides a large file into smaller files by lines, bytes, or fixed-size chunks. Essential for processing datasets too large for memory, distributing work across parallel processes, or breaking up log files for analysis.

Syntax

split [OPTIONS] [INPUT [PREFIX]]
# Common: split -l 1000 file | split -b 100M large.tar.gz | split -n 4 data.csv

Parameters

FlagDescription
-l NSplit by N lines per file
-b SIZESplit by SIZE bytes (100M, 1G, 500K)
-n NSplit into N equal chunks

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

│   ├── 📄 views.py
│   └── 📄 serializers.py
├── 📁 k8s/base/
│   ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
│   └── 📄 secrets.yaml
├── 📁 ops/logs/
│   ├── 📄 app.log
│   ├── 📄 error.log
│   └── 📄 access.log
└── 📁 scripts/
    └── 📄 deploy.sh

Command:

split -l 500 -d /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log log_ && ls log_* | head -5

Output:

log_00 log_01 log_02 log_03 log_04

📝 What happened: -d used numeric suffixes (00, 01, ...) instead of alphabetic (aa, ab, ...). Easier to process in loops: for i in $(seq 0 15); do process log_$(printf "%02d" $i); done. Combine with -a 3 for 3-digit suffixes (000, 001, ...).

Example 5: Split and Process in Parallel

Scenario: Carol splits a log file and greps each chunk in parallel for speed.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
│   ├── 📄 models.py
│   ├── 📄 views.py
│   └── 📄 tests.py
├── 📁 api/
│   ├── 📄 views.py
│   └── 📄 serializers.py
├── 📁 k8s/base/
│   ├── 📄 configmap.yaml
│   └── 📄 secrets.yaml
├── 📁 ops/logs/
│   ├── 📄 app.log
│   ├── 📄 error.log
│   └── 📄 access.log
└── 📁 scripts/
    └── 📄 deploy.sh

Command:

split -l 5000 /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log chunk_ && for f in chunk_*; do grep -c "ERROR" $f >> error_counts.txt & done; wait; cat error_counts.txt

Output:

12 8 15 5 7

📝 What happened: Each chunk was searched in parallel (& background). Results collected in error_counts.txt. On multi-core servers, this is significantly faster than sequential grep. Use wait to ensure all background jobs finish before proceeding.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: split -l N by lines. -b SIZE by bytes (100M, 1G). -n N equal chunks. -d numeric suffixes. -a N suffix length. Reassemble with cat prefix* > original. Default output: xaa, xab, xac...

comm

COMPAREText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Compare two sorted files line by line — find common and unique lines

comm compares two SORTED files and outputs three columns: lines only in file1, lines only in file2, and lines in both. Like a Venn diagram for text files. Both files MUST be sorted.

Syntax

comm [OPTIONS] FILE1 FILE2
# Common: comm file1 file2 | comm -12 file1 file2 | comm -23 file1 file2

Parameters

FlagDescription
-1Suppress column 1 (lines unique to FILE1)
-2Suppress column 2 (lines unique to FILE2)
-3Suppress column 3 (lines in both)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Compare Files

Daily Workflow: Carol uses comm to find lines unique to or common between two sorted files. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

carol@prod-api-01:~$ comm -23 old_users.txt new_users.txt

Examples

Example 1: Find Common Lines

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: comm requires SORTED input. -12 = common lines (intersection). -23 = only in file1. -13 = only in file2. No flags = all three columns. Tab indentation: 0 tabs=file1 only, 1 tab=file2 only, 2 tabs=both. Use diff for unsorted comparison.

fmt

FORMATText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Simple text formatter — reflow paragraphs to specified width

fmt reformats text paragraphs to a specified line width. Joins short lines, wraps long lines, and preserves indentation. Useful for cleaning up email drafts, README files, or any prose text for terminal display.

Syntax

fmt [OPTIONS] [FILE...]
# Common: fmt -w 80 README.md | fmt -s file | fmt -u file

Parameters

FlagDescription
-w NSet maximum line width (default: 75)
-sSplit long lines only (don't join short lines)
-uUniform spacing (one space between words, two after sentences)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

pr

FORMATText ProcessingLFCS Domain 4

Prepare text for printing — paginate with headers, columns, and page breaks

pr formats text files for printing: adds headers with date/filename/page number, splits into pages, and can arrange text in columns. While printing is less common today, pr is still useful for paginating long command output with headers.

Syntax

pr [OPTIONS] [FILE...]
# Common: pr file | pr -l 60 file | pr -2 file | ls -la | pr -h "Directory Listing"

Parameters

FlagDescription
-l NSet page length to N lines (default: 66)
-h HEADERUse HEADER instead of filename in page header
-NNumber of columns (e.g., -2)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📝 What happened: All YAML manifests concatenated and paginated with a unified header. Pages are separated by form feed characters (Ctrl+L in less). Use pr | less to navigate page by page. This is the classic Unix pipeline for generating paginated reports.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: pr -h "Title" custom header. -l N page length. -2/-3/-4 columns. -t no header/footer. -d double space. pr file | less paginated reading. Default: 66-line pages with 5-line header. Use a2ps or enscript for more advanced printing.

🐚 Shell & Scripting

Built-in commands and essential utilities for writing shell scripts, automating tasks, and managing environment variables. The anihpj/jobpost CI/CD pipeline relies heavily on shell scripts for deployment, database migrations, and server provisioning.

echo

OUTPUTShell BuiltinCoreLFCS Domain 4

Display a line of text — the simplest way to output to stdout

echo prints its arguments to standard output. Used constantly in scripts for messages, variable display, and piping data. A shell builtin (not external binary) — meaning it executes instantly with no process overhead.

Syntax

echo [OPTIONS] [STRING...]
# Common: echo "Hello" | echo -n "No newline" | echo -e "Line1\nLine2"

Parameters

FlagDescription
-nDo not output trailing newline
-eEnable interpretation of backslash escapes
-EDisable backslash escapes (default)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Always succeeds

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Deployment Script Logging

# Carol's deployment script uses echo for progress reporting:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ cat /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh
#!/bin/bash
echo "[$(date)] Starting deployment of jobpost..."
echo -n "Step 1: Pulling latest code... "
git pull && echo "OK" || echo "FAILED"
echo -n "Step 2: Running migrations... "
python manage.py migrate && echo "OK" || echo "FAILED"
echo "[$(date)] Deployment complete."

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: echo "text" prints with newline. -n suppresses newline. -e enables \n, \t, \\. Use printf for portable formatting (echo behavior varies). Double quotes expand variables; single quotes are literal. > overwrites file; >> appends.

printf

OUTPUTShell BuiltinLFCS Domain 4

Format and print data — portable, predictable alternative to echo

printf formats and prints data with C-style format specifiers. More predictable than echo (which varies across shells) and essential for precise formatting in scripts. Supports %s (string), %d (integer), %f (float), and more.

Syntax

printf FORMAT [ARGUMENTS...]
# Common: printf "%s\n" "Hello" | printf "%-20s %10d\n" "User" 1001

Parameters

SpecifierDescription
%sString
%dDecimal integer
%fFloating point
\nNewline (must be explicit!)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📝 What happened: Unlike echo, printf does NOT add newlines automatically — you must explicitly add \n. This gives precise control. Forgot the \n? Output runs into the next shell prompt. This is a feature, not a bug — it enables building output character by character.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: printf > echo for portable scripts. %s string, %d int, %f float. %-Ns left-align in N chars. %0Nd zero-pad numbers. No automatic newline — must add \n. Format string reuses if more args than specifiers. C-style escapes always interpreted.

export

ENVShell BuiltinLFCS Domain 4

Set environment variables — make variables available to child processes

export marks shell variables for export to child processes. Without export, variables are local to the current shell. Essential for: setting PATH, configuring application environments, and passing credentials to subprocesses.

Syntax

export [OPTIONS] NAME[=VALUE]...
# Common: export DATABASE_URL=postgres://... | export PATH=$PATH:/lpj/venv/bin

Parameters

FlagDescription
-pList all exported variables
-nRemove export attribute (make local)
-fExport shell functions

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Example 5: Un-Export a Variable

Scenario: Alice removes the export attribute from a sensitive variable.

📁 Directory Snippet:

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config

Output:

DATABASE_URL is no longer exported

📝 What happened: -n removed the export attribute. The variable still exists in the current shell but won't be passed to child processes. Use this to protect sensitive variables from accidental leakage to subprocesses or spawned child shells.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: export VAR=value sets and exports. export without args lists exports. -p explicit list. -n un-exports. -f exports functions. Child processes inherit parent's exports. Changes in child don't affect parent. Use source .env to load vars from file.

env

ENVShell BuiltinLFCS Domain 4

Run a command in a modified environment — or display all environment variables

env shows or modifies the environment for a command. Without arguments, it lists all environment variables. With arguments, it runs a command with specified environment modifications. Essential for: running commands with clean environments, overriding variables temporarily.

Syntax

env [OPTIONS] [NAME=VALUE...] [COMMAND [ARGS...]]
# Common: env | env VAR=value command | env -i command

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription

SHELLShell BuiltinLFCS Domain 4

Set shell options and positional parameters — control shell behavior

set changes shell options and sets positional parameters ($1, $2, etc.). Without arguments, it lists all shell variables (including non-exported ones). Essential flags: -e (exit on error), -u (error on unset vars), -x (trace commands).

Syntax

set [OPTIONS] [ARGUMENTS...]
# Common: set -euo pipefail | set -x | set -- arg1 arg2

Parameters

FlagDescription
-eExit immediately on error
-uTreat unset variables as errors
-xPrint commands before executing (trace)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

# Carol's deploy script starts with safety flags:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ cat /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail  # Exit on error, unset vars, pipe failures
echo "Starting deployment..."
cd /lpj/ || exit 1
git pull || { echo "Git pull failed"; exit 1; }
python manage.py migrate
echo "Deployment complete."

Output:

📝 What happened: -f disabled filename globbing, so *.py printed literally instead of expanding to all .py files. set +f re-enabled it. Use set -f in loops where you don't want accidental expansion of * or ? in strings.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: set -euo pipefail for robust scripts. -x trace mode. set -- sets positional params. set without args lists all variables. -f disables globbing. +flag turns OFF (opposite of -flag). Shebang pattern: #!/bin/bash -euo pipefail.

Example 4: Check Before Unset

Example 2: Safety Aliases

Scenario: Alice adds safety prompts to destructive commands.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Django app code

├── 📁 k8s/base/                        # Kubernetes manifests

│   ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
│   ├── 📁 backups/                     # Archives
│   └── 📁 cron/                        # Scheduled jobs

    ├── 📄 deploy.sh                    # Main deployment
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh              # Cilium install
    └── 📄 connectivity-test.sh         # Health checks

Command:

alias rm='rm -i' && alias mv='mv -i' && alias cp='cp -i'

Output:

# Now rm, mv, cp will prompt before overwriting. # rm important.txt → rm: remove regular file 'important.txt'? y

📝 What happened: -i (interactive) forces a confirmation prompt. This prevents accidental file deletion. To bypass the alias temporarily: \rm file (backslash) or command rm file. These safety aliases are pre-configured on many Linux distributions for root.

Example 3: Bypass vs Remove

Scenario: Carol demonstrates three ways to avoid alias interference.

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config

Command:

alias rm='rm -i'; echo "1. Backslash: \rm" > /dev/null; echo "2. Command: $(command which rm)"; echo "3. Unalias: $(unalias rm && which rm)"

Output:

1. Backslash: rm 2. Command: /usr/bin/rm 3. Unalias: /usr/bin/rm

📝 What happened: Three ways to avoid aliases: (1) \command — bypass once, (2) command cmd — run the actual binary, (3) unalias cmd — permanent removal. Use backslash for one-off bypasses; unalias for session-wide changes; command in scripts.

source

SHELLShell BuiltinLFCS Domain 4

Execute commands from a file in the current shell — load configs and functions

source (or .) executes a file in the CURRENT shell context. Unlike running a script (./script.sh), sourced commands affect the current environment — variables, functions, and directory changes persist. Essential for loading config files and environment variables.

Syntax

source FILENAME [ARGUMENTS]
. FILENAME [ARGUMENTS]     # POSIX equivalent
# Common: source ~/.bashrc | source .env | . /lpj/scripts/setup.sh

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success (or last command's code)

Parameters

FlagDescription
.Synonym in POSIX: . script.sh
FILENAMEScript to source in current shell
ARG1 ARG2 ...Arguments passed to sourced script

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1File not found
126File not readable

Example 3: Source vs Execute

Scenario: Carol demonstrates why sourcing matters for directory changes.

📁 Directory Snippet:

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Django app code

│   ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs

Exit CodeDescription

Entry 1527 removed

📝 What happened: -d 1527 deleted only that one entry. -w wrote the change to disk. This is more precise than clearing ALL history. Combined with HISTIGNORE environment variable to permanently ignore patterns: export HISTIGNORE="passwd*:*password*".

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: history shows all. history N last N. !! last command. !$ last arg. !N command N. !text last command starting with text. Ctrl+R interactive search. -c clear, -d N delete entry. -w write to file. HISTSIZE/HISTFILESIZE control limits.

type

SHELLShell BuiltinLFCS Domain 4

Display how a command would be interpreted — alias, function, builtin, or external

type tells you what a command actually is: shell builtin, alias, function, or external binary. Essential for debugging command resolution issues — "why is my script behaving differently than the command line?"

Syntax

type [OPTIONS] NAME...
# Common: type ls | type -a echo | type -t python

Parameters

FlagDescription
-aShow all locations (not just first match)
-tShow single word: alias, builtin, file, function

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Command found

Scenario: Carol checks why echo behaves differently than expected.

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config

echo is a shell builtin ls is aliased to 'ls --color=auto' python is /lpj/venv/bin/python

Example 5: Find Builtins vs External

Scenario: Carol audits which frequently-used commands are builtins.

lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config

Output:

echo => builtin cd => builtin pwd => builtin export => builtin

📝 What happened: All these are builtins — they execute instantly with zero process overhead. External commands (ls, grep, python) require forking a new process. For maximum script performance, prefer builtins: [[ ]] over [ ], printf over echo.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: type CMD shows what CMD is. -a all matches. -t one-word type. command -v CMD is POSIX alternative. Builtins > aliases > functions > externals. \CMD bypasses alias. Use type to debug command resolution issues.

test / [ ]

CONDITIONShell BuiltinLFCS Domain 4

Evaluate conditional expressions — the foundation of shell scripting logic

test (and its alias [ ]) evaluates expressions and returns exit code 0 (true) or 1 (false). Used in if, while, and &&/|| chains. File tests (-f, -d), string tests (=, !=), and numeric tests (-eq, -lt) are the three categories.

Syntax

test EXPRESSION
[ EXPRESSION ]    # Requires spaces around brackets!
[[ EXPRESSION ]]  # Bash extended test (preferred)
# Common: [ -f file ] && echo "exists" | [ "$a" -eq 5 ] | [[ $str =~ regex ]]

Parameters

TestDescription
-f FILETrue if FILE exists and is regular
-d DIRTrue if DIR exists and is directory
-z STRTrue if string is empty

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Expression is true
1Expression is false

read

INPUTShell BuiltinLFCS Domain 4

Read a line from standard input — capture user input or process files line by line

read reads one line from stdin into a variable. Used for: interactive prompts, processing files line-by-line in while loops, and parsing command output. The -p flag provides a prompt string for interactive use.

Syntax

read [OPTIONS] VARIABLE...
# Common: read -p "Name: " name | while read line; do ...; done < file

Parameters

FlagDescription
-p PROMPTDisplay prompt without newline
-sSilent mode (no echo — for passwords)
-rRaw mode (don't interpret backslashes)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: read VAR reads into VAR. -p "prompt" shows prompt. -s silent (passwords). -r raw (always use this). -t N timeout in seconds. while read -r line; do ...; done < file processes files. IFS=: sets field separator for read.

Example 1: Wait Between Retries

Scenario: Carol retries a database connection with increasing delays.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Django app code

    └── 📄 connectivity-test.sh         # Health checks

Command:

for i in 1 2 3; do echo "Attempt $i..."; python manage.py check --database default && break || sleep $((i*5)); done

Output:

Attempt 1... Attempt 2... (waits 10s) System check identified no issues.

📝 What happened: Exponential backoff: 5s, then 10s, then 15s between retries. sleep $((i*5)) calculated the delay. break exited the loop on success. This pattern prevents overwhelming struggling services while waiting for recovery.

Example 2: Polling Loop

Scenario: Alice waits for a service to become healthy after restart.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Django app code
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API endpoints
├── 📁 k8s/base/                        # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/
│   ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
│   ├── 📁 backups/                     # Archives
│   └── 📁 cron/                        # Scheduled jobs
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 deploy.sh                    # Main deployment
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh              # Cilium install
    └── 📄 connectivity-test.sh         # Health checks

Command:

while ! curl -s http://localhost:8000/health; do echo "Waiting..."; sleep 2; done && echo "Service is UP"

Output:

Waiting... Waiting... {"status":"healthy"} Service is UP

📝 What happened: The loop checked every 2 seconds until the health endpoint responded. ! inverted the exit code — loop while curl FAILS. Always include a maximum retry count or timeout: for i in $(seq 1 30); do ...; sleep 2; done (max 60 seconds).

Example 3: Sub-Second Delay

Scenario: Carol adds a tiny delay between API calls to respect rate limits.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Django app code
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API endpoints
├── 📁 k8s/base/                        # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/
│   ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
│   ├── 📁 backups/                     # Archives
│   └── 📁 cron/                        # Scheduled jobs
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 deploy.sh                    # Main deployment
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh              # Cilium install
    └── 📄 connectivity-test.sh         # Health checks

Command:

for i in $(seq 1 5); do echo "Request $i"; sleep 0.2; done

Output:

Request 1 (0.2s) Request 2 (0.2s) Request 3 ...

📝 What happened: sleep 0.2 paused for 200 milliseconds. Sub-second sleep enables precise rate limiting — 0.2s between calls = max 5 requests/second. Most modern sleep supports fractional seconds. For older systems, use usleep (microseconds).

Example 4: Schedule with Cron Alternative

Scenario: Alice runs a task every 30 minutes without cron.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Django app code
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API endpoints
├── 📁 k8s/base/                        # Kubernetes manifests

│   ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs

    ├── 📄 deploy.sh                    # Main deployment

Command:

while true; do echo "Running backup at $(date)"; tar -czf /lpj/ops/backups/auto_$(date +%H%M).tar.gz /lpj/jobpost/; sleep 30m; done &

Output:

Running backup at 10:00 Running backup at 10:30 Running backup at 11:00

📝 What happened: sleep 30m used minute suffix. Other suffixes: s (seconds, default), m (minutes), h (hours), d (days). The & ran the loop in background. For persistent scheduling, prefer cron — but sleep loops are useful for one-off monitoring tasks.

Example 5: Visual Countdown

Scenario: Carol displays a countdown before a critical operation.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Django app code

Command:

for i in 5 4 3 2 1; do echo -ne "Restarting in $i...\r"; sleep 1; done && echo -e "Restarting now!      "

Output:

Restarting in 5... (updates in place: 4... 3... 2... 1...) Restarting now!

📝 What happened: -ne (no newline + escapes) and \r (carriage return) created an in-place countdown. The same line updated 5 times. This is the standard terminal animation pattern: overwrite the current line with \r after each sleep.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: sleep N waits N seconds. Supports suffixes: s, m, h, d. Fractional: sleep 0.5. Use in retry loops, polling, rate limiting. sleep infinity for indefinite pause. For sub-second precision, use usleep (microseconds).

tee

OUTPUTShell BuiltinLFCS Domain 4

Read from stdin and write to stdout AND files — split output stream

tee copies stdin to stdout and simultaneously to one or more files. Like a T-junction in a pipe — data flows both to the next command AND to a file. Essential for: logging command output while still piping it, and writing to multiple files at once.

Syntax

tee [OPTIONS] [FILE...]
# Common: command | tee file.log | cmd2 | command | sudo tee /etc/file

Parameters

FlagDescription
-aAppend to files instead of overwriting

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Split Output

carol@prod-api-01:~$ echo "192.168.10.50 monitoring" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

xargs

BUILDShell BuiltinLFCS Domain 4

Build and execute commands from stdin — convert input to command arguments

xargs reads items from stdin and passes them as arguments to a command. Essential for: processing find results, handling argument lists too long for the shell, and running parallel operations. Solves the "Argument list too long" error.

Syntax

xargs [OPTIONS] [COMMAND [ARGUMENTS...]]
# Common: find ... | xargs rm | grep -rl TODO . | xargs vim | ... | xargs -P4 -n1

Parameters

FlagDescription
-n NUse at most N arguments per command
-P NRun up to N processes in parallel
-I {}Replace {} with input in command

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Example 3: Parallel Processing

Scenario: Carol compresses multiple log files simultaneously using all CPU cores.

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config

Example 5: Safer Alternative

Scenario: Carol shows why arrays are safer than eval for dynamic commands.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Django app code
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API endpoints
├── 📁 k8s/base/                        # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/
│   ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
│   ├── 📁 backups/                     # Archives
│   └── 📁 cron/                        # Scheduled jobs
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 deploy.sh                    # Main deployment
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh              # Cilium install
    └── 📄 connectivity-test.sh         # Health checks

Command:

# Dangerous: eval "rm -rf $USER_INPUT"
# Safe: use arrays instead
CMD=(rm -rf "/safe/path"); "${CMD[@]}" 2>&1 && echo "Cleanup done"

Output:

Cleanup done

📝 What happened: Arrays ("${CMD[@]}") preserve argument boundaries and prevent injection. If $USER_INPUT were /; rm -rf /, eval would destroy the system; arrays would treat it as a literal filename. Arrays are the safe alternative to eval for command construction.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: eval double-expands — powerful but dangerous. Use ${!var} indirection instead for dynamic vars. Use arrays instead for dynamic commands. eval $(ssh-agent) is the canonical safe usage. Never eval user input. eval "echo \$VAR" expands $VAR in second pass.

Example 1: Replace Shell with Command

Scenario: Carol's wrapper script becomes the actual application process.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Django app code
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API endpoints
├── 📁 k8s/base/                        # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/
│   ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
│   ├── 📁 backups/                     # Archives
│   └── 📁 cron/                        # Scheduled jobs
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 deploy.sh                    # Main deployment
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh              # Cilium install
    └── 📄 connectivity-test.sh         # Health checks

Command:

exec python /lpj/manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000

Output:

# The shell is replaced by the Python process. # No return — the bash process no longer exists. # This is common in Docker entrypoint scripts.

📝 What happened: The shell process was replaced by Python. The PID stayed the same — the shell became Python. Docker signal handling requires exec: without it, the shell receives SIGTERM but Python doesn't. Always use exec in Docker CMD/entrypoint scripts.

Example 2: Redirect All Output to Log

Scenario: Alice redirects all output from a script to a log file.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Django app code
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API endpoints
├── 📁 k8s/base/                        # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/
│   ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
│   ├── 📁 backups/                     # Archives
│   └── 📁 cron/                        # Scheduled jobs
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 deploy.sh                    # Main deployment
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh              # Cilium install
    └── 📄 connectivity-test.sh         # Health checks

Command:

exec > /lpj/ops/logs/deploy.log 2>&1 && echo "Deploy started" && python manage.py migrate

Output:

# No output on screen — everything goes to deploy.log. # cat /lpj/ops/logs/deploy.log shows all output.

📝 What happened: exec > file 2>&1 permanently redirected stdout and stderr to the log file. Every subsequent echo, command output, and error goes to the file. Use at the top of scripts that should run silently. Cannot be undone within the same shell.

Example 3: Open File Descriptor

Scenario: Carol opens a file for writing and uses it throughout the script.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Django app code
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API endpoints
├── 📁 k8s/base/                        # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/
│   ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
│   ├── 📁 backups/                     # Archives
│   └── 📁 cron/                        # Scheduled jobs
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 deploy.sh                    # Main deployment
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh              # Cilium install
    └── 📄 connectivity-test.sh         # Health checks

Command:

exec 3> /tmp/audit.log && echo "Audit started" >&3 && echo "Action performed" >&3 && exec 3>&- && echo "Log closed"

Output:

Log closed # /tmp/audit.log contains: Audit started Action performed

📝 What happened: exec 3> file opened file descriptor 3 for writing. >&3 wrote to it. exec 3>&- closed it. This is advanced shell I/O — dedicated file descriptors for logging, data files, or inter-process communication without temporary files.

Example 4: Find and Exec

Scenario: Alice uses find's -exec to run commands on found files.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Django app code
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API endpoints
├── 📁 k8s/base/                        # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/
│   ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
│   ├── 📁 backups/                     # Archives
│   └── 📁 cron/                        # Scheduled jobs
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 deploy.sh                    # Main deployment
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh              # Cilium install
    └── 📄 connectivity-test.sh         # Health checks

Command:

find /lpj -name "*.pyc" -exec rm {} \;

Output:

# Each .pyc file is deleted. # {} is replaced with the filename. # \; marks the end of the -exec command.

📝 What happened: This is find's -exec, not the shell's exec — they're different things. find's exec runs a command for each file. Use -exec cmd {} + (with +) to batch files into fewer invocations — much faster for many files.

Example 5: Redirect stdin

Scenario: Carol redirects stdin from a file for the rest of the script.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django settings & config
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Django app code
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API endpoints
├── 📁 k8s/base/                        # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/
│   ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
│   ├── 📁 backups/                     # Archives
│   └── 📁 cron/                        # Scheduled jobs
└── 📁 scripts/
    ├── 📄 deploy.sh                    # Main deployment
    ├── 📄 cilium-setup.sh              # Cilium install
    └── 📄 connectivity-test.sh         # Health checks

Command:

exec < /lpj/scripts/hosts.txt && while read -r host; do echo "Host: $host"; done

Output:

Host: prod-web-01 Host: prod-api-01 Host: prod-db-01

📝 What happened: exec < file permanently redirected stdin to the file. Every subsequent read reads from the file automatically — no need for done < file at the end of the while loop. Cleaner when the entire script processes one input file.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: exec CMD replaces shell (no return). Always use in Docker entrypoints. exec > file 2>&1 redirects all output. exec N> file opens FD N. exec N>&- closes FD. find's -exec is different from shell's exec. exec without command performs redirections only.

💾 Disk & Storage

Commands for partitioning, formatting, mounting, and monitoring storage. The anihpj/jobpost infrastructure uses these for database volume management, backup storage, and disk performance monitoring across all production servers.

dd

COPYDiskCoreLFCS Domain 2

Convert and copy a file — low-level data duplication and disk imaging

dd copies data at the block level with precise control over block size and count. Used for: creating disk images, cloning drives, creating bootable USBs, and generating test files. Nicknamed "disk destroyer" — a wrong of= target can wipe a disk.

Syntax

dd if=INPUT of=OUTPUT [OPTIONS]
# Common: dd if=/dev/sda of=backup.img bs=4M status=progress

Parameters

FlagDescription
if=FILEInput file (source)
of=FILEOutput file (destination)
bs=BYTESBlock size (4M recommended for speed)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Database Backup Imaging

# Carol creates a block-level backup of the PostgreSQL data volume:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo dd if=/dev/sdb1 of=/lpj/ops/backups/pgdata_$(date +%Y%m%d).img bs=4M status=progress
2147483648 bytes (2.1 GB, 2.0 GiB) copied, 45 s, 47 MB/s
512+0 records in
512+0 records out
2147483648 bytes (2.1 GB) copied, 45.2345 s, 47.5 MB/s

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Disk Duplicator

Daily Workflow: Carol uses dd to create disk images, clone volumes, and create backup files for disaster recovery. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical dd usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ dd if=/dev/sdb of=/lpj/ops/backups/data_volume.img bs=4M status=progress
carol@prod-api-01:~$ dd if=/dev/zero of=/lpj/ops/backups/swapfile bs=1M count=2048

Examples

# Storage management in anihpj:
#  prod-db-01:/dev/sdb  — Database volume
#  backup-nas:/backups  — Network storage
#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Local backup directory
Example 1: Create a Disk Image Backup

Scenario: Carol creates a full image of the database partition before a major upgrade.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo dd if=/dev/sdb1 of=/lpj/ops/backups/db_backup.img bs=4M status=progress

Output:

5368709120 bytes (5.4 GB) copied, 120 s, 45 MB/s 1280+0 records in / 1280+0 records out

📝 What happened: 5.4GB partition copied to an image file at 45MB/s. bs=4M used 4MB blocks for efficiency (default 512 bytes would be 8000x slower). status=progress showed real-time transfer. The image is an exact block-for-block copy — mountable or restorable with dd if=backup.img of=/dev/sdb1.

Example 2: Create a Test File

Scenario: Alice generates a 1GB file for I/O performance testing.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/testfile bs=1M count=1024 && ls -lh /tmp/testfile

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers 1.0G Jun 4 10:30 /tmp/testfile

📝 What happened: /dev/zero provided infinite zeros. bs=1M count=1024 created exactly 1GB. Use /dev/urandom for random data (slower). This is the standard way to create files of exact sizes for testing disk speed or filling space.

Example 3: Wipe a Disk Securely

Scenario: Carol securely erases a decommissioned disk before disposal.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo dd if=/dev/urandom of=/dev/sdc bs=4M status=progress

Output:

# Overwrites entire disk with random data. # Progress shown in real-time. Takes hours for large disks.

📝 What happened: The entire disk was overwritten with random data. One pass with urandom is adequate for most cases. For classified data, use multiple passes or shred -n 3 /dev/sdc. CAUTION: of= is the WRONG disk = data destroyed. Double-check with lsblk first.

Example 4: Clone a USB Drive

Scenario: Carol clones a bootable USB drive for server provisioning.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo dd if=/dev/sdd of=/dev/sde bs=4M status=progress && sync

Output:

16000000000 bytes (16 GB) copied, 380 s, 42 MB/s # sync ensures all data is flushed to the device.

📝 What happened: The entire 16GB USB was cloned bit-for-bit. Both drives are now identical — partitions, bootloader, filesystem, everything. sync flushed the write cache. Without sync, ejecting too soon can corrupt the clone.

Example 5: Benchmark Write Speed

Scenario: Carol tests the write speed of a new SSD volume.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

dd if=/dev/zero of=/lpj/ops/temp/speedtest bs=1M count=1024 conv=fdatasync 2>&1 | tail -1

Output:

1073741824 bytes (1.1 GB) copied, 2.34567 s, 458 MB/s

📝 What happened: conv=fdatasync forced data to be physically written before reporting, giving accurate write speed (458 MB/s) not just cache speed. Without fdatasync, dd reports cache speed (often 2-5x faster) which is misleading.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: dd if=X of=Y bs=4M status=progress. Always use bs=4M for speed. /dev/zero for zeros, /dev/urandom for random. conv=fdatasync for accurate benchmarks. Triple-check of= — wrong target = data destroyed. sync after writing to removable media.

fdisk

PARTITIONDiskLFCS Domain 2

Manipulate disk partition table — create, delete, and modify MBR partitions

fdisk manages MBR (DOS) partition tables on disks up to 2TB. Interactive menu-driven tool for creating, deleting, and modifying partitions. For GPT disks (2TB+), use gdisk or parted. Use -l to list partitions non-interactively.

Syntax

fdisk [OPTIONS] DEVICE
# Common: sudo fdisk -l | sudo fdisk /dev/sdb

Parameters

FlagDescription
-lList partition tables (non-interactive)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Partition Table

Daily Workflow: Carol uses fdisk to view and modify MBR partition tables on storage volumes. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical fdisk usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo fdisk -l /dev/sdb
Disk /dev/sdb: 200 GiB
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo fdisk /dev/sdc

Examples

# Storage management in anihpj:
#  prod-db-01:/dev/sdb  — Database volume
#  backup-nas:/backups  — Network storage
#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Local backup directory
Example 1: List All Partitions

Scenario: Carol checks the partition layout of all disks on prod-db-01.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo fdisk -l | grep -E "^Disk /dev|^/dev"

Output:

Disk /dev/sda: 100 GiB /dev/sda1 * 2048 209715199 100G Linux filesystem Disk /dev/sdb: 500 GiB /dev/sdb1 2048 1048575999 500G Linux filesystem

📝 What happened: -l listed all disks and partitions. sda=100GB (OS), sdb=500GB (PostgreSQL data). The asterisk (*) on sda1 marks it as bootable. Use fdisk -l whenever you need an overview of disk layout — no root required for listing.

Example 2: Interactive Partition Creation

Scenario: Carol creates a new partition on a freshly attached disk.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo fdisk /dev/sdc

Output:

Command (m for help): n # New partition Select: p # Primary Partition number: 1 First sector: 2048 Last sector: +100G # 100GB Command: w # Write and exit

📝 What happened: Interactive menu: n new, p primary, w write. Key commands: m help, p print table, d delete, t change type, q quit without saving. Changes don't take effect until w is pressed.

Example 3: Change Partition Type

Scenario: Carol sets a partition type to Linux LVM for volume management.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo fdisk /dev/sdc

Output:

Command: t # Change type Partition: 1 Hex code: 8e # Linux LVM Command: w # Write

📝 What happened: t changed the partition type to 8e (Linux LVM). Common types: 83=Linux, 82=Swap, 8e=LVM, 7=NTFS. The type code doesn't affect the actual filesystem — it's just a label. Use L within fdisk to list all type codes.

Example 4: Delete a Partition

Scenario: Carol removes an old partition to reclaim space.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo fdisk /dev/sdc

Output:

Command: d # Delete Partition: 2 # Delete partition 2 Command: w # Write — partition 2 is gone

📝 What happened: d deleted partition 2. All data on that partition is now inaccessible (though not wiped — still recoverable with forensic tools). The space becomes unallocated, available for new partitions. Always back up before deleting partitions.

Example 5: Non-Interactive Scripting

Scenario: Alice creates partitions in an automated provisioning script.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

echo -e "n\np\n1\n\n+50G\nw" | sudo fdisk /dev/sdc

Output:

# Partition created automatically. # echo sends keystrokes: n(ew), p(rimary), 1, default start, +50G, w(rite)

📝 What happened: fdisk was scripted with piped input. For production automation, prefer parted with its non-interactive mode: parted /dev/sdc mklabel gpt mkpart primary 0% 100%. fdisk scripting is fragile — a wrong echo sequence can corrupt the partition table.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: fdisk -l lists partitions. Interactive: n new, d delete, t type, p print, w write, q quit. MBR only (≤2TB). For GPT: use gdisk. For scripting: use parted. /proc/partitions shows kernel's partition view. Changes require partprobe or reboot.

parted

PARTITIONDiskLFCS Domain 2

GNU Parted — modern partition editor for MBR and GPT, scriptable

parted is the modern alternative to fdisk supporting both MBR and GPT partition tables. Unlike fdisk, parted supports non-interactive commands — ideal for scripting and automation. Use for disks >2TB or when you need GPT partition tables.

Syntax

parted [OPTIONS] DEVICE [COMMAND]
# Common: sudo parted -l | sudo parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt | sudo parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary 0% 100%

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

Parameters

FlagDescription
-sScript mode — never prompt for user input
-a OPTAlignment: none, cylinder, minimal, optimal
-lList partition layout on all block devices
mklabel TYPECreate new partition table (msdos, gpt)
mkpart PART FS START ENDCreate partition

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error during operation

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Partition Editor

Daily Workflow: Carol uses parted for GPT partition management on large storage volumes for databases. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical parted usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo parted -l
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt

Examples

# Storage management in anihpj:
#  prod-db-01:/dev/sdb  — Database volume
#  backup-nas:/backups  — Network storage
#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Local backup directory
Example 1: Create GPT Partition Table

Scenario: Carol initializes a new 4TB disk with GPT for the backup NAS.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo parted /dev/sdd mklabel gpt && sudo parted /dev/sdd print

Output:

Model: ATA ST4000DM004 (scsi) Disk /dev/sdd: 4001GB Partition Table: gpt

📝 What happened: mklabel gpt created a GPT partition table. GPT supports disks >2TB, up to 128 partitions, and stores a backup table at the end. MBR (fdisk) is limited to 2TB and 4 primary partitions. Always use GPT for new disks.

Example 2: Non-Interactive Partition

Scenario: Alice creates a single partition spanning the entire disk in one command.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo parted /dev/sdd mkpart primary ext4 0% 100% && sudo parted /dev/sdd print

Output:

1 1049kB 4001GB 4001GB primary ext4

📝 What happened: One command created a partition covering the entire disk. 0% to 100% used the full capacity. No interactive menus needed — this is why parted is preferred for automation. The partition exists but isn't formatted yet — use mkfs.ext4 next.

Example 3: Resize a Partition

Scenario: Carol expands a partition to use newly added disk space.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo parted /dev/sdb resizepart 1 100% && sudo parted /dev/sdb print

Output:

1 1049kB 500GB 500GB primary ext4

📝 What happened: resizepart 1 100% expanded partition 1 to fill the disk. After resizing the partition, you still need to resize the filesystem: resize2fs /dev/sdb1. Parted resizes partitions (container); resize2fs resizes filesystems (contents).

Example 4: Set Partition Flags

Scenario: Carol marks a partition as bootable for a new server.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo parted /dev/sda set 1 boot on && sudo parted /dev/sda print

Output:

1 1049kB 100GB 100GB primary ext4 boot

📝 What happened: set 1 boot on enabled the boot flag on partition 1. Other flags: lvm, raid, esp (EFI System Partition). In GPT, the boot flag is informational; in MBR, it marks the active partition. Use set 1 boot off to remove.

Example 5: Display Free Space

Scenario: Carol checks unallocated space on a disk before creating a partition.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo parted /dev/sdb unit GB print free

Output:

0.00GB 0.00GB 0.00GB Free Space 1 0.00GB 200GB 200GB primary 200GB 500GB 300GB Free Space

📝 What happened: print free showed 300GB of unallocated space after the partition. unit GB displayed sizes in gigabytes (other units: MB, TB, %, cyl, s(ectors)). Use this before creating partitions to see exactly where free space exists.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: parted -l lists all. mklabel gpt/msdos creates table. mkpart PART-TYPE FS-TYPE START END. resizepart N END resizes. print free shows gaps. unit GB changes displays. Prefer parted over fdisk for scripting and GPT.

gdisk is the GPT equivalent of fdisk — same interactive menu interface but for GPT partition tables. Use when you prefer fdisk's workflow but need GPT. Supports converting MBR to GPT without data loss.

Exit CodeDescription

Number Start (sector) End (sector) Size Code Name

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

1 2048 7814035455 3.7 TiB 8300 Linux filesystem

Example 2: Convert MBR to GPT

Found MBR partition table. Converting to GPT. Command: w Final checks complete. About to write GPT data.

📝 What happened: gdisk detected the MBR table and converted to GPT automatically. The w command wrote the new GPT table. Existing partitions and data are PRESERVED. After conversion, the system can use >4 primary partitions and >2TB space.

Example 3: Recovery Options

Scenario: Carol uses gdisk's recovery menu to fix a corrupted GPT backup.

└── 📁 ops/

sudo gdisk /dev/sdd

Command: r # Recovery menu Recovery: b # Rebuild GPT from backup Recovery: w # Write

📝 What happened: The recovery menu (r) provides advanced options: b rebuild backup, c load backup, d use main, e load main to backup. GPT stores TWO copies of the partition table — one at the start and one at the end. Recovery uses the surviving copy.

Example 4: Convert MBR to GPT

📄 Context — Partition Table Migration:

# gdisk can convert MBR (DOS) partition tables to GPT
# Non-destructive — preserves existing partitions
# GPT supports: >2TB disks, 128 partitions, CRC checksums, named partitions
# Required for UEFI boot on modern systems

Scenario: Carol converts a disk from MBR to GPT.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo gdisk /dev/sdb <<< $'w
Y
' 2>&1 | grep -E "MBR|GPT|converted"

Output:

Found valid MBR and GPT. Which do you want to use? MBR: MBR only | GPT: Using GPT and creating new protective MBR.

📝 What happened: gdisk detected both MBR and GPT signatures and used GPT. The 'w' command wrote the GPT table. Protective MBR is added for backward compatibility. Always back up data before converting partition tables — though gdisk is generally safe, mistakes happen.

Example 5: List Partition Types

📄 Context — Finding Type Codes:

# GPT uses GUID type codes instead of MBR's hex codes
# List all type codes to find the right one
# Linux filesystem: 8300, Linux swap: 8200, EFI System: EF00
# Much more types than MBR (Linux, Windows, macOS, Solaris, etc.)

Scenario: Alice finds the correct partition type code.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/

    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo gdisk -l /dev/sdb 2>/dev/null | head -5 || sudo gdisk /dev/sdb <<< $'l
q
' 2>/dev/null | grep -E "8300|8200|EF00"

Output:

8300 Linux filesystem 8200 Linux swap EF00 EFI System

📝 What happened: Common GPT type codes displayed. 8300 = standard Linux filesystem (used by mkfs.ext4/xfs). 8200 = Linux swap. EF00 = EFI System Partition (required for UEFI boot). In gdisk interactive mode: 'l' lists all types, 't' changes a partition's type code.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: gdisk is interactive GPT editor. -l lists. Same menu as fdisk: n, d, p, w, q. r recovery menu. GPT type codes are 4-char (8300, 8200). Use sgdisk for non-interactive GPT scripting (like parted).

Example 1: Format as ext4

Scenario: Carol formats a new partition for the backup directory.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo mkfs.ext4 -L "BACKUPS" /dev/sdc1

Output:

mke2fs 1.46.5 Creating filesystem with 26214400 4k blocks Filesystem UUID: a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890 Writing superblocks and filesystem accounting information: done

📝 What happened: A fresh ext4 filesystem was created with label "BACKUPS". The UUID is unique — use it in /etc/fstab for reliable mounting. -L sets a human-readable label. WARNING: mkfs DESTROYS all existing data on the partition.

Example 2: Format as XFS

Scenario: Alice formats a large partition with XFS for database files.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo mkfs.xfs -L "PGDATA" /dev/sdb1

Output:

meta-data=/dev/sdb1 isize=512 agcount=4, agsize=6553600 blks data = bsize=4096 blocks=26214400

📝 What happened: XFS is better for large files and parallel I/O — ideal for databases. XFS cannot be shrunk (only grown). ext4 can be both grown and shrunk. Choose XFS for performance, ext4 for flexibility. Red Hat defaults to XFS.

Example 3: Format USB as FAT32

Scenario: Carol formats a USB drive for cross-platform file sharing.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo mkfs.vfat -n "ANIHJP_USB" /dev/sde1

Output:

mkfs.fat 4.2 # USB formatted as FAT32 — readable on Windows, Mac, and Linux.

📝 What happened: mkfs.vfat formatted as FAT32 for maximum compatibility. FAT32 limit: 4GB per file. For larger files, use exFAT (mkfs.exfat) or NTFS (mkfs.ntfs). Linux-native filesystems (ext4/xfs) are NOT readable on Windows without special drivers.

Example 4: Check Before Formatting

Scenario: Carol verifies the partition is unmounted before formatting.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

mount | grep /dev/sdc1 && echo "Still mounted!" || sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdc1

Output:

(no output — partition is not mounted, formatting proceeds)

📝 What happened: The safety check confirmed sdc1 is not mounted. Mounted partitions should never be formatted — it can crash the system. Also check with lsblk -f to see current filesystem type. Some mkfs variants refuse to format mounted filesystems.

Example 5: Dry Run (ext4 only)

Scenario: Alice previews what mkfs.ext4 will do without actually formatting.

📁 Environment Snippet:

└── 📁 ops/

    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:

# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo mkfs.ext4 -n /dev/sdc1 2>&1 | head -5

Output:

mke2fs 1.46.5 /dev/sdc1 contains a ext4 file system Proceed anyway? (y,N) n # Answer 'n' to abort

📝 What happened: -n answered "no" to all questions, showing what WOULD happen without doing it. The prompt appeared because the partition already had a filesystem. Without -n, you'd need to type y manually. Always use -n for safety checks.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: mkfs.ext4 default Linux fs. mkfs.xfs RHEL default. -L LABEL sets label. -n dry run. DESTROYS existing data. mkfs -t TYPE generic form. lsblk -f shows current filesystems. Format AFTER partitioning, BEFORE mounting.

Example 1: Show All Block Devices

Scenario: Carol gets UUIDs for all disks to configure /etc/fstab.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

sudo blkid | grep -E "sda|sdb"

Output:

/dev/sda1: UUID="abc-def-123" TYPE="ext4" PARTUUID="xyz-789" /dev/sdb1: UUID="456-789-abc" TYPE="xfs" LABEL="PGDATA"

📝 What happened: Each device shows UUID (unique identifier), TYPE (filesystem), LABEL (if set). Use UUID in fstab: UUID=abc-def-123 / ext4 defaults 0 1. UUIDs survive disk reordering — /dev/sdb might become /dev/sdc after reboot, but UUIDs never change.

Example 2: Single Device

Scenario: Alice checks the filesystem type of the backup partition.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo blkid /dev/sdc1

Output:

/dev/sdc1: UUID="def456" BLOCK_SIZE="4096" TYPE="ext4" PARTUUID="abc123-01"

📝 What happened: Single-device query. TYPE="ext4" confirms the filesystem. BLOCK_SIZE="4096" shows the allocation unit. This is much faster than lsblk -f for checking one device. Use blkid -p /dev/sdc1 for low-level probing (reads superblock directly).

Example 3: Show Only UUID

Scenario: Carol's script extracts just the UUID for an fstab entry.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:

# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

sudo blkid -s UUID -o value /dev/sdb1

Output:

456-789-abc-def-123456

📝 What happened: -s UUID selected only the UUID attribute. -o value output only the value (no UUID= prefix). This is script-friendly — capture directly: DB_UUID=$(sudo blkid -s UUID -o value /dev/sdb1).

Example 4: Cache and Refresh

Scenario: Carol forces a re-read after formatting a new filesystem.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo blkid -g && sudo blkid /dev/sdc1

Output:

/dev/sdc1: UUID="new-uuid-here" TYPE="ext4"

📝 What happened: -g cleared the blkid cache, forcing a fresh probe. blkid caches results in /etc/blkid/blkid.tab. After formatting a partition, the cache still shows old data until refreshed. Always run blkid -g after mkfs to see the new filesystem.

Example 5: Show Unformatted Devices

Scenario: Carol finds partitions that have no filesystem yet.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo blkid | grep -v "TYPE="

Output:

/dev/sdd1: PARTUUID="new-part-001"

📝 What happened: sdd1 has a PARTUUID (GPT partition ID) but NO TYPE — it's not formatted yet. These are candidates for mkfs. Unformatted partitions have only PARTUUID; formatted ones also have UUID and TYPE. Use this to audit new disks after partitioning.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: blkid shows UUID/TYPE/LABEL. -s UUID specific attribute. -o value raw value. -g refresh cache. Use UUID in /etc/fstab (not /dev/sdX). lsblk -f shows similar info in tree format. findfs UUID=xxx finds device by UUID.

lpj/
└── 📁 ops/

Example 2: Mount a New Partition

Scenario: Carol mounts the backup partition to start nightly backups.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)
