sudo mkdir -p /lpj/ops/backups && sudo mount /dev/sdc1 /lpj/ops/backups && df -h /lpj/ops/backups

Output:

Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/sdc1 200G 45G 155G 23% /lpj/ops/backups

📝 What happened: The mount point directory must exist before mounting. Now /lpj/ops/backups points to the sdc1 partition. The original contents of /lpj/ops/backups (if any) are hidden while the partition is mounted. Permanent mount: add to /etc/fstab.

Example 3: Mount with Options

Scenario: Carol mounts a partition read-only for a forensic audit.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo mount -o ro,noexec /dev/sdd1 /mnt/forensic && mount | grep forensic

Output:

/dev/sdd1 on /mnt/forensic type ext4 (ro,noexec)

📝 What happened: ro = read-only (no writes allowed). noexec = prevent execution of binaries. Combined, this creates a secure forensic mount — files can be read but not modified or executed. Common options: rw, noatime, nosuid, nodev.

Example 4: Remount Read-Write

Scenario: Alice temporarily remounts root as read-write for system recovery.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo mount -o remount,rw /

Output:

# Root is now writable. No output on success. # Verify: mount | grep " / "

📝 What happened: remount changes mount options without unmounting. rw made root writable. This is the standard recovery pattern: root is often mounted ro after filesystem errors. Remount rw to fix issues, then remount ro after repair.

Example 5: Mount ISO Image

Scenario: Alice mounts a downloaded ISO to access its contents without burning.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo mount -o loop /tmp/ubuntu-server.iso /mnt/iso && ls /mnt/iso | head -5

Output:

boot casper dists EFI install

📝 What happened: -o loop created a loop device, treating the ISO file as a block device. The ISO's contents are now browsable at /mnt/iso. This works for any disk image: .iso, .img, .vmdk. Unmount with umount /mnt/iso.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: mount DEV DIR mounts. mount lists all. -t TYPE specifies fs. -o OPTIONS sets options. -o remount,rw changes without unmounting. -o loop for ISO files. /etc/fstab for permanent mounts. findmnt is a modern alternative.

umount

UNMOUNTDiskLFCS Domain 2

Unmount filesystems — safely detach storage before removal

umount (no 'n'!) detaches a mounted filesystem. The filesystem must not be in use — no open files, no process working directories. Use -l (lazy unmount) to detach immediately and clean up when no longer busy. Always unmount before unplugging or formatting.

Syntax

umount [OPTIONS] DEVICE|MOUNTPOINT
# Common: sudo umount /mnt/data | sudo umount /dev/sdc1 | sudo umount -l /busy/mount

Parameters

FlagDescription
-lLazy unmount (detach now, clean later)
-fForce unmount (unreachable NFS)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Unmount Filesystem

Daily Workflow: Carol uses umount before storage maintenance and to safely detach backup volumes. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical umount usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo umount /data
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo umount -l /backup  # Lazy unmount

Examples

# Storage management in anihpj:
#  prod-db-01:/dev/sdb  — Database volume
#  backup-nas:/backups  — Network storage
#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Local backup directory
Example 1: Unmount by Mount Point

Scenario: Carol unmounts the backup drive before physically removing it.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo umount /lpj/ops/backups && echo "Safe to remove" || echo "Still in use!"

Output:

Safe to remove

📝 What happened: Unmount by mount point is the easiest method. You can also unmount by device: umount /dev/sdc1. If it fails with "target is busy", use lsof /lpj/ops/backups to find processes using it, then either kill them or use -l.

Example 2: Find and Kill Blocking Processes

Scenario: Carol figures out who's using the mount before forcing unmount.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo lsof /lpj/ops/backups 2>/dev/null | head -3

Output:

COMMAND PID USER FD TYPE DEVICE SIZE NODE NAME bash 2841 alice cwd DIR 8,33 4096 2 /lpj/ops/backups tar 12345 root 3w REG 8,33 45M 15 /lpj/ops/backups/db.tar

📝 What happened: Alice's bash session has /lpj/ops/backups as its working directory, and a tar process is writing to it. lsof shows which processes are blocking the unmount. Solution: cd /tmp in Alice's session, kill the tar, then unmount.

Example 3: Lazy Unmount

Scenario: Carol needs to unmount immediately even though processes are using it.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo umount -l /lpj/ops/backups && echo "Detached" && mount | grep backups || echo "No longer mounted"

Output:

Detached No longer mounted

📝 What happened: -l detached the mount point immediately from the directory tree. Existing processes can still read/write to their open files, but new accesses see the underlying directory. The filesystem fully unmounts when all references close. Safer than -f.

Example 4: Unmount All

Scenario: Carol unmounts everything from a specific disk before hot-swapping.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo umount /dev/sdc* && echo "All partitions of sdc unmounted"

Output:

All partitions of sdc unmounted

📝 What happened: The glob /dev/sdc* matched all partitions (sdc1, sdc2, etc.). Each was unmounted sequentially. Use umount -a -t ext4 to unmount all ext4 filesystems. umount -a unmounts everything in /etc/fstab (except /).

Example 5: Force Unmount for NFS

Scenario: An NFS server went down and the mount is unresponsive.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo umount -f -l /mnt/nfs_share && echo "NFS forcefully unmounted"

Output:

NFS forcefully unmounted

📝 What happened: -f forced the unmount (needed for unreachable NFS). -l made it lazy. Combined, this is the nuclear option for stuck NFS mounts. Without these flags, umount would hang indefinitely waiting for the dead NFS server.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: umount (no 'n'!). -l lazy (detach now). -f force (NFS). lsof MOUNTPOINT finds blocking processes. umount -a unmounts all. Always unmount before removing USB drives or formatting. "target is busy" = something is using it.

swapon

SWAPDiskLFCS Domain 2

Enable swap devices and files — activate virtual memory

swapon activates swap areas (partitions or files). Swap provides virtual memory when RAM is exhausted. Use -s to show current swap usage. Modern systems often use swap files instead of partitions for flexibility.

swapon [OPTIONS] [DEVICE|FILE]
# Common: sudo swapon /dev/sda2 | sudo swapon /swapfile | swapon --show

Parameters

FlagDescription
--showDisplay swap usage summary
-aActivate all swap in /etc/fstab

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

carol@prod-db-01:~$ swapon --show

Examples

# Storage management in anihpj:
#  prod-db-01:/dev/sdb  — Database volume
#  backup-nas:/backups  — Network storage
#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Local backup directory
Example 1: Show Swap Usage

Scenario: Carol checks if the server is using swap during high memory load.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

swapon --show

Output:

NAME TYPE SIZE USED PRIO /dev/sda2 partition 4G 512M -2

📝 What happened: 4GB swap partition, 512MB in use (12.5%). Using swap isn't necessarily bad — the kernel swaps out idle pages. PRIO determines which swap to use first (higher = preferred). If USED is near SIZE, add more swap or RAM.

Example 2: Activate Swap File

Scenario: Carol creates and activates a swap file on the database server.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile bs=1M count=2048 && sudo chmod 600 /swapfile && sudo mkswap /swapfile && sudo swapon /swapfile

Output:

Setting up swapspace version 1, size = 2 GiB # Swap file activated. Verify: swapon --show

📝 What happened: Created a 2GB file, set secure permissions, formatted as swap, and activated it. Swap files are more flexible than partitions — they can be resized or removed without repartitioning. Not recommended on Btrfs (use loop device).

Example 3: Activate All Fstab Swaps

Scenario: Carol enables all swap entries defined in /etc/fstab after boot.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo swapon -a && swapon --show

Output:

NAME TYPE SIZE USED PRIO /dev/sda2 partition 4G 0M -2 /swapfile file 2G 0M -3

📝 What happened: -a read /etc/fstab for all swap entries and activated them. Both swap partition and swap file are now active. This is run during boot by systemd. Use swapoff -a to deactivate all.

Example 4: Set Swap Priority

Scenario: Carol gives the SSD swap higher priority than the HDD swap.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo swapon -p 10 /dev/nvme0n1p2 && swapon --show

Output:

NAME TYPE SIZE USED PRIO /dev/nvme0n1p2 partition 8G 0M 10 /dev/sda2 partition 4G 0M -2

📝 What happened: -p 10 set priority to 10 (higher than default -2). The kernel uses higher-priority swap first. This ensures the faster NVMe swap is used before the slower SATA swap. Max priority is 32767.

Example 5: Monitor Swap Pressure

Scenario: Alice checks how aggressively the kernel is using swap.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness && free -h | grep Swap

Output:

60 Swap: 6.0Gi 512Mi 5.5Gi

📝 What happened: Swappiness=60 (default) means the kernel starts swapping when ~40% RAM is used. Lower values (10-20) keep more in RAM; higher values (80-100) swap more aggressively. For database servers, set vm.swappiness=10 in /etc/sysctl.conf to prefer RAM.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: swapon --show displays swap. swapon -a activates fstab swaps. swapon FILE activates file. -p N sets priority. swapoff deactivates. mkswap formats. vm.swappiness controls aggressiveness. free -h shows usage.

swapoff

SWAPDiskLFCS Domain 2

Disable swap devices — deactivate virtual memory

swapoff deactivates swap areas. The kernel moves swapped pages back to RAM first — if RAM is full, swapoff will fail. Use -a to deactivate all swap. Essential before: removing a swap partition, resizing swap files, or testing without swap.

Syntax

swapoff [OPTIONS] [DEVICE|FILE]
# Common: sudo swapoff /swapfile | sudo swapoff -a

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

FlagDescription
-aDisable all swap areas in /etc/fstab
-vVerbose — show each swap area being disabled
DEVICESpecific swap device to disable

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Example 1: Deactivate a Swap File

Scenario: Carol removes a swap file before deleting it.

📁 Environment Snippet:

lpj/
└── 📁 ops/

sudo swapoff /swapfile && sudo rm /swapfile && echo "Swap file removed"

Swap file removed

📝 What happened: swapoff moved contents back to RAM, then deactivated the file. The file was then safely deleted. If swapoff fails (not enough RAM), add temporary swap elsewhere first, then retry. Never delete an active swap file — it will crash the system.

Example 2: Deactivate All Swap

# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

sudo swapoff -a && echo "All swap deactivated" && free -h | grep Swap

Output:

All swap deactivated Swap: 0B 0B 0B

📝 What happened: -a deactivated everything in /proc/swaps. Total swap is now 0. Reactivate with swapon -a. This is useful for testing application behavior under memory pressure without swap interference. Don't do this on production unless you have plenty of RAM.

mkswap

SWAPDiskLFCS Domain 2

Set up a Linux swap area — format a partition or file as swap

mkswap initializes a device or file for use as swap space. Must be run BEFORE swapon. This writes the swap signature to the device. Like mkfs but for swap — all existing data is destroyed.

Syntax

mkswap [OPTIONS] DEVICE|FILE
# Common: sudo mkswap /dev/sda2 | sudo mkswap /swapfile

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Make Swap

Daily Workflow: Carol uses mkswap to initialize swap partitions and files on production servers. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical mkswap usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo mkswap /dev/sda2
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo mkswap /lpj/ops/backups/swapfile

#  backup-nas:/backups  — Network storage

Example 1: Format Partition as Swap

Scenario: Carol formats a partition for swap on a memory-constrained server.

📁 Environment Snippet:

lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs

    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:

# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo mkswap /dev/sda3 && sudo swapon /dev/sda3 && swapon --show | grep sda3

Output:

Setting up swapspace version 1, size = 4 GiB

Parameters

FlagDescription
-L LABELSet swap area label
-fForce — skip device size sanity checks
-p SIZESet page size in bytes
DEVICEBlock device or file to initialize (DESTRUCTIVE)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error
/dev/sda3 partition 4G 0M -2

📝 What happened: mkswap wrote the swap signature (UUID and version info). swapon activated it. The partition now appears in /proc/swaps. For permanent swap, add to /etc/fstab: /dev/sda3 none swap sw 0 0.

Example 2: Set UUID Explicitly

Scenario: Alice creates swap with a specific UUID for consistent fstab entries.

sudo mkswap -U abc123-def456 /dev/sdb2 && sudo blkid /dev/sdb2

Output:

/dev/sdb2: UUID="abc123-def456" TYPE="swap"

📝 What happened: -U set a specific UUID instead of generating a random one. Useful for cloning setups where you want identical UUIDs across servers. Without -U, a random UUID is generated — fine for most cases.

Scenario: Carol verifies a partition is NOT mounted or in use before mkswap.

Setting up swapspace version 1, size = 2 GiB

Example 4: Swap Usage Before Disabling

📄 Context — Safety Check:

# Before swapoff, check swap usage with swapon --show

Scenario: Alice checks swap before deciding to disable it.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

swapon --show && free -h | grep Swap

Output:

NAME TYPE SIZE USED PRIO /dev/sda3 part 8G 256M -2 Swap: 8.0Gi 256Mi 7.8Gi

📝 What happened: Only 256MB of 8GB swap is used — safe to swapoff. If Used were close to Total, swapoff could take several minutes. The PRIO column shows priority (-2 is default). Higher priority swap is used first.

Example 5: Swapoff with Label

📄 Context — Persistent References:

# swapoff can reference swap by device path, UUID, or LABEL
# Using labels/UUIDs is more reliable than device names
# Device names (/dev/sda3) can change between boots

Scenario: Carol disables swap by UUID for reliability.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo swapoff UUID=$(findmnt -no UUID /dev/sda3 2>/dev/null || blkid -s UUID -o value /dev/sda3) && echo "Swap disabled by UUID"

Output:

Swap disabled by UUID

📝 What happened: Swap was disabled using its UUID instead of device path. This is resilient to device renumbering. Use blkid to find UUIDs. In /etc/fstab, using UUID=... for swap entries ensures consistent mounting across reboots.

Example 4: Create Swap File

📄 Context — Adding Swap Without Partitioning:

# Swap files are more flexible than swap partitions
# Create, resize, remove without repartitioning
# Must be preallocated (dd fallocate) before mkswap
# Performance: slightly slower than partition, negligible for SSD

Scenario: Carol creates a 2GB swap file.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile bs=1M count=2048 && sudo chmod 600 /swapfile && sudo mkswap /swapfile && sudo swapon /swapfile && swapon --show | grep swapfile

Output:

Setting up swapspace version 1, size = 2 GiB /swapfile file 2G 0B -2

📝 What happened: 2GB swap file created and activated. chmod 600 is critical — world-readable swap exposes memory contents. Add to fstab: /swapfile none swap sw 0 0. Swap files can be resized: swapoff → dd → mkswap → swapon. Much more flexible than partitions.

Example 5: Check Swap Signature

📄 Context — Verify Swap Devices:

# blkid can identify swap signatures (UUID, label)
# Verify swap was correctly created with mkswap
# UUID is generated automatically — used in fstab
# Use blkid to find UUIDs for persistent configuration

Scenario: Alice verifies the swap signature on a new swap device.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo blkid /dev/sda3 | grep -o 'UUID="[^"]*"' && sudo blkid /swapfile | grep -o 'UUID="[^"]*"'

Output:

UUID="abc123-def456" UUID="ghi789-jkl012"

📝 What happened: Both swap partition and swap file have UUIDs — confirmed as valid swap. Use UUIDs in /etc/fstab for reliable identification: UUID=abc123 none swap sw 0 0. Without UUID, device names may change between boots.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: mkswap DEVICE formats for swap. -U UUID sets UUID. Run BEFORE swapon. Destroys existing data. mkswap /swapfile works on files too. Add to /etc/fstab for persistence. swapoff then mkswap to resize/recreate.

losetup

LOOPDiskLFCS Domain 2

Set up and control loop devices — treat files as block devices

losetup associates loop devices (/dev/loop0, etc.) with regular files, making the file accessible as a block device. This enables: mounting disk images, accessing encrypted volumes, and creating filesystems inside files without partitions.

Syntax

losetup [OPTIONS] LOOPDEVICE FILE
# Common: sudo losetup -f | sudo losetup /dev/loop0 disk.img | losetup -a

Parameters

FlagDescription
-fFind first unused loop device
-aList all loop devices
-dDetach loop device

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Loop Device

Daily Workflow: Carol uses losetup to mount disk images as loop devices for inspection and recovery. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical losetup usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo losetup -f /lpj/ops/backups/data_volume.img
carol@prod-api-01:~$ losetup -a

Examples

# Storage management in anihpj:
#  prod-db-01:/dev/sdb  — Database volume
#  backup-nas:/backups  — Network storage
#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Local backup directory
Example 1: List Loop Devices

Scenario: Carol checks what loop devices are currently in use.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

losetup -a

Output:

/dev/loop0: [2049]:12345 (/var/lib/snapd/snaps/core_12345.snap) /dev/loop1: [2049]:12346 (/var/lib/snapd/snaps/lxd_6789.snap)

📝 What happened: Two snap packages are mounted via loop devices. Snap uses loop devices extensively — each snap package is a squashfs image mounted on a loop device. This is a common sight on Ubuntu servers with snap packages installed.

Example 2: Attach Disk Image

Scenario: Alice mounts a downloaded disk image to inspect its contents.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo losetup -f /lpj/ops/backups/db_backup.img && losetup -a | grep db_backup

Output:

/dev/loop3: [2049]:23456 (/lpj/ops/backups/db_backup.img)

📝 What happened: -f found the first free loop device (loop3) and attached the image file. The file is now accessible as /dev/loop3 — it can be mounted, partitioned, or used as a block device. mount /dev/loop3 /mnt to access contents.

Example 3: Detach Loop Device

Scenario: Carol cleans up after finishing with the disk image.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo umount /mnt && sudo losetup -d /dev/loop3 && echo "Detached"

Output:

Detached

📝 What happened: Always unmount before detaching (-d). If detach fails with "device busy", something is still using it — check with lsof /dev/loop3. losetup -D detaches ALL loop devices (dangerous — may affect running snap packages).

Example 4: Mount ISO via Loop

📄 Context — Access Disk Images:

# Mount ISO/CD images without burning to physical media
# losetup creates a loop device, then mount normally
# Or use: mount -o loop image.iso /mnt (shortcut)
# Loop devices allow files to be treated as block devices

Scenario: Carol mounts an ISO image to access its contents.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo losetup -f /tmp/ubuntu.iso && sudo mount /dev/loop0 /mnt && ls /mnt | head -5

Output:

boot casper dists EFI isolinux

📝 What happened: ISO contents accessible at /mnt. -f finds the first free loop device. Cleanup: umount /mnt && losetup -d /dev/loop0. Shortcut: mount -o loop image.iso /mnt handles loop setup automatically. Loop devices are numbered 0-7 by default.

Example 5: List All Loop Devices

📄 Context — Device Inventory:

# losetup -a lists all active loop devices
# Shows: loop device, backing file, read-only status
# Useful for: finding what's mounted, freeing devices
# Each loop device consumes one /dev/loopN entry

Scenario: Alice checks which loop devices are in use.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

losetup -a

Output:

/dev/loop0: [2049]:12345 (/tmp/ubuntu.iso) /dev/loop1: [2049]:12346 (/tmp/data.img)

📝 What happened: Two loop devices active: loop0 (ISO) and loop1 (disk image). The numbers in brackets are device major:minor and inode. Free a device: losetup -d /dev/loop0. All loop devices share the same kernel module. Max loops controlled by max_loop parameter.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: losetup -a lists all loops. -f FILE attaches to next free. -d DEVICE detaches. -D detaches all. Loop devices treat files as block devices. Snap uses loops heavily. mount -o loop FILE DIR is shorthand (auto-creates loop).

iostat

MONITORDiskLFCS Domain 2

Report I/O statistics — monitor disk read/write performance

iostat reports CPU and I/O statistics for devices and partitions. Essential for: identifying disk bottlenecks, monitoring throughput, and capacity planning. Part of the sysstat package. Use -x for extended (detailed) statistics.

Syntax

iostat [OPTIONS] [INTERVAL [COUNT]]
# Common: iostat -x 2 5 | iostat -d sda | iostat -p sda 1

Parameters

FlagDescription
-xExtended statistics (detailed)
-d DEVICEShow only specified device
INTERVAL COUNTRefresh every INTERVAL seconds, COUNT times

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — I/O Statistics

Daily Workflow: Carol uses iostat to monitor disk performance on database and backup servers. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical iostat usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ iostat -x 1 3
Device   r/s   w/s   rkB/s   wkB/s  await
sdb    45.2  120.3  8500   24500   3.2

Examples

# Storage management in anihpj:
#  prod-db-01:/dev/sdb  — Database volume
#  backup-nas:/backups  — Network storage
#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Local backup directory
Example 1: Basic I/O Stats

Scenario: Carol checks disk throughput on the database server.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

iostat -x 2 3

Output:

Device r/s w/s rKB/s wKB/s await %util sda 15.2 45.3 234.5 1890.2 3.4 85.2 sdb 85.3 12.1 4523.1 234.5 1.2 45.3

📝 What happened: sda: 85% utilization (bottleneck!). sdb: 45% utilization (healthy). await = average I/O wait time in ms. r/wKB/s = read/write throughput. If %util hits 100%, the disk is saturated — add more disks or optimize queries.

Example 2: Monitor Specific Device

Scenario: Alice watches the PostgreSQL data disk during a heavy query.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

iostat -x -d sdb 1 10

Output:

Device r/s w/s rKB/s wKB/s await %util sdb 125.3 8.2 8543.2 123.4 5.2 92.1 # Peak during query sdb 45.2 3.1 1234.5 45.2 1.3 32.1 # After query completes

📝 What happened: Real-time monitoring every 1 second. During the query: 125 reads/sec, 92% utilization, 5.2ms await. After: dropped to 32% utilization. The disk was near saturation during the query — consider adding indexes or upgrading to SSD.

Example 3: One-Time Snapshot

Scenario: Carol captures a point-in-time I/O snapshot for a report.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

iostat -x 1 1 | grep -E "Device|sda|sdb"

Output:

Device r/s w/s rKB/s wKB/s await %util sda 5.2 10.1 123.4 456.7 2.1 25.3 sdb 45.3 5.2 2345.1 234.5 1.8 42.1

📝 What happened: 1 1 = one sample with 1-second interval. This is the standard pattern for scripts: capture current stats without continuous monitoring. For historical data, use sar -d which records I/O stats continuously.

Example 4: Monitor Specific Device

📄 Context — Focused I/O Monitoring:

# iostat DEVICE shows stats for just one disk
# Focus on the disk hosting your database or application
# Combine with interval: iostat -x sdb 2
# More efficient than monitoring all disks

Scenario: Carol monitors only the database disk for I/O saturation.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

iostat -x sdb 2 3

Output:

Device r/s w/s rkB/s wkB/s await svctm %util sdb 45.2 23.1 1234.5 567.8 12.34 2.34 85.23 sdb 52.3 18.9 1456.7 432.1 15.67 2.12 92.45

📝 What happened: %util at 85-92% — the database disk is nearly saturated. await (12-15ms) is high for SSD. Consider adding more disks or migrating to NVMe. 2 3 = 2-second interval, 3 reports. Use -p DEVICE for partition-level detail.

Example 5: JSON Output for Monitoring

📄 Context — Dashboard Integration:

# -o JSON provides structured machine-readable output
# Parse with jq or Python for monitoring pipelines
# Stable format across versions (unlike text output)
# Perfect for Prometheus/Grafana ingestion

Scenario: Alice exports I/O stats in JSON for the monitoring dashboard.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

iostat -o JSON -x 2 1 | python3 -m json.tool | head -8

Output:

{"sysstat":{"hosts":[{"nodename":"prod-db-01","statistics":[{"disk":[{"disk_device":"sda","r/s":12.34,"%util":45.23}]}]}]}}

📝 What happened: Structured JSON output — parse with jq '.sysstat.hosts[0].statistics[0].disk[] | {dev: .disk_device, util: ."%util"}'. Much more reliable than parsing text output which changes format between versions. Use -o JSON for all automated monitoring.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: iostat -x extended stats (use this). -d DEV specific device. N M N-second interval, M times. Key metrics: %util (saturation), await (latency), r/s w/s (IOPS). Part of sysstat package. sar -d for historical data.

iotop

MONITORDiskLFCS Domain 2

I/O top — interactive I/O monitor, like top for disk usage

iotop shows per-process I/O usage in real-time. Like top but for disk activity. Shows which processes are reading/writing, how much, and at what rate. Essential for identifying disk hogs. Requires root or NET_ADMIN capability.

Syntax

iotop [OPTIONS]
# Common: sudo iotop | sudo iotop -o | sudo iotop -b -n 1

Parameters

FlagDescription
-oOnly show processes with I/O activity
-bBatch mode (non-interactive, for logging)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — I/O Monitor

Daily Workflow: Carol uses iotop to identify processes causing high disk I/O on production servers. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical iotop usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo iotop -b -n 1 | head -10
Total DISK READ: 45.20 M/s | Total DISK WRITE: 120.50 M/s

Examples

# Storage management in anihpj:
#  prod-db-01:/dev/sdb  — Database volume
#  backup-nas:/backups  — Network storage
#  /lpj/ops/backups/     — Local backup directory
Example 1: Interactive Monitoring

Scenario: Carol runs iotop to find what's hammering the disk during a performance issue.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo iotop -o

Output:

TID PRIO USER DISK READ DISK WRITE COMMAND 2841 be/4 postgres 45.32 M/s 2.15 M/s postgres: writer 3124 be/4 root 12.45 M/s 0.05 M/s tar -czf backup.tar.gz /lpj/

📝 What happened: -o filtered to only processes with I/O. PostgreSQL is doing heavy reads (45MB/s), tar is doing backup reads (12MB/s). Interactive keys: r reverse sort, o toggle only-active, q quit. Like top, but for disk.

Example 2: Batch Snapshot

Scenario: Alice captures a one-time I/O snapshot for a cron job.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo iotop -bon 1 | head -5

Output:

Total DISK READ: 65.23 M/s | Total DISK WRITE: 12.45 M/s TID PRIO USER DISK READ DISK WRITE COMMAND 2841 be/4 postgres 45.32 M/s 2.15 M/s postgres 3124 be/4 root 12.45 M/s 0.05 M/s tar

📝 What happened: -bon 1 batch mode, only-active, one iteration. This is script-friendly — capture to file with iotop -bon 1 >> /lpj/ops/logs/io_snapshot.log. Useful for periodic monitoring in cron.

Example 3: Accumulated I/O

Scenario: Carol checks total I/O since boot to find the biggest disk user.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo iotop -a -o -b -n 1

Output:

TID PRIO USER DISK READ DISK WRITE COMMAND 2841 be/4 postgres 2.34 G 456.78 M postgres 1523 be/4 syslog 890.45 M 23.45 M rsyslogd

📝 What happened: -a showed accumulated I/O since process start (not current rate). PostgreSQL has read 2.34GB total — expected for a database. rsyslogd has written 23MB — normal logging. Use -a for "who consumed the most disk over time" vs rate for "who is consuming right now".

Example 4: Batch Mode for Scripts

📄 Context — Non-Interactive Capture:

# -b batch mode outputs to stdout (no ncurses)
# -n 1 single iteration for one-shot capture
# -o only processes with actual I/O activity
# Essential for cron jobs and monitoring scripts

Scenario: Alice captures an iotop snapshot for a nightly report.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo iotop -b -n 1 -o | head -8

Output:

Total DISK READ: 45.23 M/s | Total DISK WRITE: 23.45 M/s TID PRIO USER DISK READ DISK WRITE COMMAND 2841 be/4 postgres 35.12 M/s 15.23 M/s postgres: writer 2845 be/4 anihpj 8.45 M/s 5.67 M/s python manage.py

📝 What happened: PostgreSQL leads I/O at 35MB/s read. Without -b, iotop uses ncurses interactive mode which hangs in cron. -o filters out idle processes — cleaner output. Pipe to grep or awk for further processing.

Example 5: Monitor Specific Process

📄 Context — Targeted I/O Profiling:

# -p PID monitors only a specific process
# Multiple PIDs: -p 1234,5678
# Lower overhead than full system monitoring
# Useful for profiling application I/O behavior

Scenario: Carol profiles PostgreSQL I/O exclusively.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj storage & device layout:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application logs
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives & disk images
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

# Storage devices on prod-api-01:
# /dev/sda     — 50GB system disk
# /dev/sdb     — 200GB data volume (mounted at /data)
# /dev/sdc     — 500GB backup volume (mounted at /backup)

Command:

sudo iotop -b -n 1 -p $(pgrep -f postgres | head -1)

Output:

TID PRIO USER DISK READ DISK WRITE COMMAND 2841 be/4 postgres 35.12 M/s 15.23 M/s postgres: writer

📝 What happened: Only PostgreSQL I/O shown — cleaner and faster. pgrep -f postgres dynamically finds the PID. Use -a for accumulated I/O since process start. This targeted monitoring is essential for database performance tuning.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: sudo iotop -o shows active I/O processes. -a accumulated I/O. -b batch mode. -n N iterations. Interactive: r reverse sort, o filter active, a toggle accumulated. Requires root. Alternative: pidstat -d 1 for per-process I/O stats.

📊 Log & Monitoring

Commands for viewing logs, tracing processes, and monitoring system performance. The anihpj/jobpost team relies on journalctl for service logs, strace for debugging, and vmstat/sar for performance analysis during incidents.

journalctl

LOGMonitoringCoreLFCS Domain 5

Query the systemd journal — centralised log management for all services

journalctl queries and displays logs from the systemd journal. All systemd-managed services log here — no more hunting through /var/log for individual files. Supports filtering by service, time, priority, and boot.

Syntax

journalctl [OPTIONS] [MATCHES]
# Common: journalctl -u nginx | journalctl -f | journalctl --since "1 hour ago"

Parameters

FlagDescription
-u UNITShow logs for specific systemd unit
-fFollow mode (like tail -f)
--since TIMEShow logs since TIME ("1 hour ago", "yesterday")

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Example 3: Filter by Priority

Scenario: Carol checks only errors and warnings from the last boot.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/

Jun 04 08:00:01 kernel: ACPI Error: No handler for Region Jun 04 08:00:15 jobpost[2841]: WARNING: Database connection pool exhausted

📝 What happened: -p err..warning filtered to priority levels between err (3) and warning (4). Levels: emerg(0), alert(1), crit(2), err(3), warning(4), notice(5), info(6), debug(7). -b limited to current boot. Critical for incident triage — filter out noise.

2345

Scenario: Carol checks how much space the systemd journal is consuming.

        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

Output:

Archived and active journals take up 256.0M on disk.

📝 What happened: 256MB of journal data. Configure limits in /etc/systemd/journald.conf: SystemMaxUse=500M. Use journalctl --vacuum-size=100M to shrink. The journal automatically rotates — older entries are archived and eventually deleted.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: journalctl -u UNIT service logs. -f follow. -b current boot. -p PRIO filter by level. --since/--until time range. --disk-usage size. _PID= filter by PID. _UID= by user. Binary logs — no text files to grep.

lsof

DIAGNOSEMonitoringLFCS Domain 5

List open files — see every file, socket, and pipe in use by every process

lsof (LiSt Open Files) lists all open files — regular files, directories, sockets, pipes, and devices. In Linux, "everything is a file", so lsof reveals: which process is using a port, who has a file open, what deleted files still consume disk space.

Syntax

lsof [OPTIONS] [NAME]
# Common: lsof -i :80 | lsof /var/log/syslog | lsof -p 2841 | lsof -u alice

Parameters

FlagDescription
-i [:PORT]List network connections (optional port)
-p PIDFiles opened by process PID
-u USERFiles opened by user

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Example 1: Who's Using a Port

Scenario: Carol finds which process is blocking port 8000.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

sudo lsof -i :8000

Output:

COMMAND PID USER FD TYPE DEVICE NODE NAME python 2841 anihpj 3u IPv4 12345 TCP *:8000 (LISTEN)

📝 What happened: Python PID 2841 (anihpj user) is listening on port 8000. This is the standard way to diagnose "port already in use" errors. Also shows TCP state: LISTEN, ESTABLISHED, CLOSE_WAIT. lsof -i tcp shows ALL TCP connections.

Example 2: Find Open Files by Process

Scenario: Alice checks what files the jobpost Django process has open.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

sudo lsof -p $(pgrep -f "manage.py") | head -8

Output:

COMMAND PID USER FD TYPE DEVICE NODE NAME python 2841 anihpj cwd DIR 8,1 456 /lpj python 2841 anihpj rtd DIR 8,1 2 / python 2841 anihpj txt REG 8,1 789 /lpj/venv/bin/python3 python 2841 anihpj 3u IPv4 12345 TCP *:8000 (LISTEN)

📝 What happened: cwd=current working dir (/lpj), rtd=root dir, txt=executable binary, 3u=file descriptor 3 (the listening socket). This gives a complete picture of what a process is doing. Essential for debugging "too many open files" errors.

Example 3: Deleted But Still Open

Scenario: Carol finds why disk space isn't freed after deleting a large log file.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

sudo lsof | grep deleted | head -3

Output:

python 2841 anihpj 4w REG 8,1 524288000 12345 /lpj/ops/logs/jobpost.log (deleted)

📝 What happened: jobpost.log was deleted but the Python process still has it open (FD 4w). The 500MB file won't be freed until the process closes it or is restarted. This is the #1 cause of "df shows full but du shows less" — lsof finds the culprit.

Example 4: Files by User

Scenario: Eve audits all files opened by a specific user.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL

    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

sudo lsof -u www-data | wc -l && sudo lsof -u www-data | head -5

Output:

47 COMMAND PID USER FD TYPE DEVICE NODE NAME nginx 2841 www-data cwd DIR 8,1 456 /usr/share/nginx nginx 2841 www-data 5w REG 8,1 789 /var/log/nginx/access.log

📝 What happened: www-data has 47 open files. This is the nginx worker — it has the access log open for writing. Audit user file usage for security: unexpected open files may indicate compromise. Use lsof -u ^root to exclude root.

Example 5: Network Connections Summary

Scenario: Carol gets a quick overview of all network activity on the server.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

sudo lsof -i -P -n | grep ESTABLISHED | awk '{print $1, $9}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Output:

12 nginx 10.0.0.45:443->192.168.1.100:52341 5 postgres 10.0.0.30:5432->10.0.0.50:45231 3 python 0.0.0.0:8000 (LISTEN)

📝 What happened: -i network only, -P port numbers (not names), -n no DNS resolution (faster). 12 nginx connections, 5 PostgreSQL, 3 listening. The -P -n combo is essential for speed — DNS resolution can hang lsof for minutes.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: lsof -i :PORT who's using port. -p PID process files. -u USER user files. grep deleted freed space not reclaimed. -P -n no DNS (faster). +D DIR files under directory. -t terse (PIDs only). Requires root for full output.

strace

TRACEMonitoringLFCS Domain 5

Trace system calls and signals — see exactly what a process is doing

strace intercepts and records system calls made by a process. Shows every file open, network connect, memory allocation, and signal received. The ultimate debugging tool for "why is this process stuck?" — no code changes needed.

Syntax

strace [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]
strace [OPTIONS] -p PID
# Common: strace ls | strace -p 2841 | strace -c python app.py

Parameters

FlagDescription
-p PIDAttach to running process
-cCount and summarize system calls
-e EXPRFilter by expression (e.g., trace=open,read)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Examples

Example 1: Attach to Running Process

Scenario: Carol debugs a stuck jobpost worker that's not processing tasks.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

sudo strace -p $(pgrep -f "celery") -e trace=network 2>&1 | head -5

Output:

connect(5, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(6379)}, 16) = -1 ECONNREFUSED connect(5, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(6379)}, 16) = -1 ECONNREFUSED

📝 What happened: Celery is repeatedly trying to connect to Redis on port 6379 and getting ECONNREFUSED. Redis is down! -e trace=network filtered to network calls only. Without strace, you'd see "worker not processing" — with it, you see exactly why.

Example 2: Count System Calls

Scenario: Alice profiles which syscalls a Django request makes most.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

strace -c python -c "import django; print('ok')" 2>&1

Output:

% time seconds usecs/call calls errors syscall 45.23 0.023456 12 1954 read 23.12 0.012000 8 1500 write 12.34 0.006400 64 100 23 open

📝 What happened: -c counted syscalls. 1,954 read() calls consumed 45% of time. This profiles which operations dominate. If open() has many errors, paths might be wrong. The summary helps identify performance bottlenecks at the system call level.

Example 3: Trace Child Processes

Scenario: Carol traces a shell script AND all commands it spawns.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log

    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

strace -f /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh 2>&1 | grep -E "execve|clone" | head -5

Output:

clone(child_stack=0, ...) = 2842 [pid 2842] execve("/usr/bin/git", ["git", "pull"], ...) = 0 [pid 2843] execve("/usr/bin/python", ["python", "manage.py", "migrate"], ...) = 0

📝 What happened: -f followed forks/clones. The script spawned git then python. Each child process appeared with its PID. This reveals the full process tree — essential for understanding complex deployment scripts that spawn many subprocesses.

Example 4: Filter File Operations

Scenario: Alice sees which config files Django reads on startup.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL

        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

strace -e trace=open,openat,stat python manage.py check 2>&1 | grep settings | head -5

Output:

openat(AT_FDCWD, "/lpj/anihpj/settings.py", O_RDONLY) = 3 stat("/lpj/anihpj/settings.py", {st_mode=S_IFREG|0644, ...}) = 0

📝 What happened: Django opened and stat'd settings.py. This confirms which settings file is being used. If a config isn't being picked up, strace reveals the actual paths the process is trying to access — including paths that don't exist (errors).

Example 5: Timestamp Every Call

Scenario: Carol measures exactly how long each syscall takes to find the bottleneck.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

strace -tt -T -p $(pgrep -f "gunicorn") 2>&1 | head -3

Output:

10:30:00.123456 read(5, "GET /api/jobs HTTP/1.1\r\n...", 4096) = 256 <0.000045> 10:30:00.234567 write(5, "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n...", 2048) = 2048 <0.000089>

📝 What happened: -tt printed microseconds timestamps, -T showed syscall duration in . The read took 45µs, the write took 89µs. If a read takes 3 seconds, you've found the bottleneck. This precision debugging is impossible without strace.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: strace CMD traces new process. -p PID attaches to running. -c summary counts. -e trace=FILE filters. -f follows children. -tt -T timestamps+durations. -o FILE output to file. Performance overhead: 10-30% — don't run in production.

ltrace

TRACEMonitoringLFCS Domain 5

Trace library calls — see which shared library functions a process invokes

ltrace intercepts and records dynamic library calls. Where strace shows kernel-level syscalls, ltrace shows user-space library calls like malloc(), printf(), fopen(). Useful for debugging application-level behavior without source code.

Syntax

ltrace [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]
ltrace [OPTIONS] -p PID

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Library Call Trace

Daily Workflow: Carol uses ltrace to trace library calls when debugging dynamic linking issues. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

carol@prod-api-01:~$ ltrace -p $(pgrep gunicorn | head -1) 2>&1 | head -20
carol@prod-api-01:~$ ltrace -e malloc+free python3 /lpj/manage.py

Examples

# Log & monitoring in anihpj:
#  /lpj/ops/logs/         — Application logs
#  journalctl -u jobpost  — Service logs
#  monitoring-01:9090     — Prometheus metrics
Example 1: Trace Library Calls

Scenario: Alice sees what C library calls the Python process makes.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

ltrace -p $(pgrep -f "manage.py") 2>&1 | head -5

Output:

malloc(1024) = 0x7f8a2c001000

Parameters

FlagDescription
-p PIDAttach to running process
-e EXPRFilter — show only calls matching EXPR (e.g. malloc+free)
-o FILEWrite output to FILE
-cSummary count of all calls on exit
-SAlso trace system calls
-rShow relative timestamps between calls
-tShow absolute timestamps

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error attaching or invalid PID
free(0x7f8a2c001000) = fopen("/lpj/anihpj/settings.py", "r") = 0x7f8a2c002000

📝 What happened: Python called malloc (allocated 1024 bytes), then free (released it), then fopen (opened settings.py). This is C-library-level visibility — strace would show brk() and openat() syscalls; ltrace shows the higher-level malloc/fopen wrappers.

Scenario: Alice traces only memory allocation calls in a Django process.

sudo ltrace -e malloc+free -p $(pgrep -f "manage.py") 2>&1 | head -5

Output:

malloc(4096) = 0x7f8a2c001000 free(0x7f8a2c001000) = malloc(8192) = 0x7f8a2c002000

📝 What happened: Only malloc/free traced. + adds functions; - excludes: -e '!strlen*' excludes all strlen variants. Use -e 'signal*' for signal-related calls. This focused approach reduces output 100x compared to unfiltered ltrace.

Example 4: Timestamp Every Call

📄 Context — Performance Measurement:

# -t shows wall-clock timestamp per call
# -T shows duration spent in each call (in angle brackets)
# -tt shows microseconds precision
# Identify slow library calls at a glance

Scenario: Carol measures duration of each fopen call to find slow file access.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

sudo ltrace -t -T -e fopen -p $(pgrep -f "manage.py") 2>&1 | head -3

Output:

10:30:00.123456 fopen("/lpj/anihpj/settings.py", "r") = 0x7f8a2c003000 <0.000234> 10:30:01.234567 fopen("/etc/localtime", "r") = 0x7f8a2c004000 <0.000089>

📝 What happened: settings.py open took 234µs, localtime 89µs — both fast (cached). If a call shows <2.345678> (seconds not microseconds), that's a bottleneck. -r shows relative timestamps (time since previous call) for inter-call latency analysis.

Example 5: Output to File

📄 Context — Offline Analysis:

# Offline Analysis

Scenario: Alice saves ltrace output for later review.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

sudo ltrace -o /tmp/ltrace.log -p $(pgrep -f "manage.py") 2>&1 & sleep 5 && sudo kill %1 && head -5 /tmp/ltrace.log

Output:

malloc(4096) = 0x7f8a2c001000 free(0x7f8a2c001000) = fopen("/lpj/anihpj/settings.py", "r") = 0x7f8a2c002000

📝 What happened: -o writes to file instead of stderr. Run in background, capture for 5 seconds, then analyze. No terminal clutter — clean trace for post-mortem.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: ltrace CMD traces library calls. -p PID attaches. -c summary. -e EXPR filters. -f follows children. strace = syscalls (kernel); ltrace = library calls (user-space). Use strace for I/O/debugging; ltrace for app-level profiling.

vmstat

MONITORMonitoringLFCS Domain 5

Report virtual memory statistics — CPU, memory, I/O, and system overview

vmstat provides a snapshot of system performance: CPU, memory, swap, I/O, and processes. One of the oldest and most reliable monitoring tools. The first number is average since boot; subsequent numbers are per-interval.

Syntax

vmstat [OPTIONS] [DELAY [COUNT]]
# Common: vmstat 2 5 | vmstat -s | vmstat -d

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

carol@prod-api-01:~$ vmstat 1 5
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa

Examples

# Log & monitoring in anihpj:
#  /lpj/ops/logs/         — Application logs

Example 1: Real-Time Monitoring

Scenario: Carol monitors system performance every 2 seconds during a load test.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

vmstat 2 5

Output:

procs ---------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----

Parameters

FlagDescription
DELAY COUNTRun COUNT times with DELAY seconds interval
-aShow active/inactive memory instead of buffer/cache
-sShow event counters and memory statistics as a table
-dShow disk statistics
-S UNITUnit: k, K, m, M (default: K=1024 bytes)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error reading /proc
r b swpd free buff cache si so bi bo in cs us sy id wa 2 0 0 45678 12345 234567 0 0 12 45 123 456 12 5 80 3 3 0 0 44678 12345 234789 0 0 85 12 234 789 25 8 65 2

📝 What happened: Key columns: r=runnable processes (CPU queue), b=blocked, si/so=swap in/out (0=good), us/sy/id/wa=CPU user/system/idle/wait. First line is average since boot — ignore it. Wa > 10% = I/O bottleneck; r > CPU cores = CPU bottleneck.

Scenario: Alice gets a one-time memory overview during a memory leak investigation.

Output:

8167948 K total memory 4523456 K used memory 2345678 K active memory 1234567 K inactive memory 3644492 K free memory

📝 What happened: -s displayed a one-time detailed memory report. Total 8GB, 4.5GB used, 3.6GB free. Active memory is recently used; inactive is cached but reclaimable. If free+buffer+cache is low, the system may start swapping.

Example 3: Filter Specific Library Calls

📄 Context — Targeted Tracing:

# -e filters library calls by pattern (like strace -e)
# Show only malloc/free calls to find memory leaks
# Show only file operations (fopen, fread, fwrite)
# Reduces noise when tracing complex programs

Scenario: Alice traces only memory allocation calls in a process.

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs

    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log

    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

sudo ltrace -e malloc+free -p $(pgrep -f "manage.py") 2>&1 | head -5

Output:

malloc(1024) = 0x7f8a2c001000 free(0x7f8a2c001000) = malloc(4096) = 0x7f8a2c002000

📝 What happened: Only malloc/free calls shown — all other library calls filtered out. -e malloc+free traces both. Use -e '!malloc' to exclude malloc. Combine with -c for a count summary. Much cleaner than full ltrace output for targeted debugging.

Example 4: Timestamp Every Call

📄 Context — Performance Profiling:

# -t adds timestamps to each library call
# -tt adds microseconds, -ttt adds Unix epoch
# Identify which library calls take the most time
# Combine with -c for time-per-call statistics

Scenario: Carol times library calls to find the slowest operations.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

sudo ltrace -tt -e malloc -p $(pgrep -f "manage.py") 2>&1 | head -5

Output:

10:30:00.123456 malloc(1024) = 0x7f8a2c001000 <0.000045> 10:30:00.234567 malloc(4096) = 0x7f8a2c002000 <0.000089>

📝 What happened: Microsecond timestamps show each call's exact timing. The <0.000045> in angle brackets is the call duration. malloc(1024) took 45µs; malloc(4096) took 89µs. This precision is invaluable for identifying which library calls are performance bottlenecks.

Example 5: Trace Child Processes

📄 Context — Full Process Tree:

# -f follows forked child processes
# Without -f, only the parent process is traced
# Django spawns worker processes — need -f to trace all
# Each child output is prefixed with [pid]

Scenario: Alice traces all Django worker processes simultaneously.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

sudo ltrace -f -e malloc -p $(pgrep -f "manage.py") 2>&1 | head -5

Output:

[pid 2841] malloc(1024) = 0x7f8a2c001000 [pid 2845] malloc(512) = 0x7f8a2d001000 [pid 2841] free(0x7f8a2c001000) =

📝 What happened: Both parent [pid 2841] and worker [pid 2845] calls are traced. Each line is prefixed with the PID. This reveals how library calls are distributed across the process tree. Without -f, only the parent's calls would appear.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: vmstat N M every N seconds, M times. -s memory summary. -d disk stats. Key: r queue, b blocked, si/so swap, wa I/O wait. First line = since boot (ignore). vmstat 1 = real-time. free -h is simpler for just memory.

sar

MONITORMonitoringLFCS Domain 5

System Activity Reporter — collect and report historical performance data

sar collects and reports system activity: CPU, memory, I/O, network, and more. Part of sysstat. Unlike vmstat (real-time only), sar stores historical data, enabling retrospective analysis. Data is collected every 10 minutes by default.

Syntax

sar [OPTIONS] [INTERVAL [COUNT]]
# Common: sar | sar -u 2 5 | sar -r | sar -n DEV | sar -f /var/log/sa/sa04

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📄 Context — anihpj/jobpost Daily Operations:

# The anihpj team uses this command during daily operations
# Real-world context with the /lpj/ directory structure
# Servers: prod-web-01, prod-api-01, prod-db-01, etc.
# See Directory Skeleton section for full project layout

Parameters

FlagDescription
-uCPU utilization (default)
-rMemory utilization
-n DEVNetwork device statistics
-n EDEVNetwork error statistics
-o FILESave to binary FILE for later analysis
-f FILERead from previously saved binary FILE
INTERVAL COUNTRun COUNT times with INTERVAL seconds
-s HH:MM:SSStart time for historical data
-e HH:MM:SSEnd time for historical data

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error accessing sysstat data

# --output FILE writes all stats to CSV

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: dstat unified resource monitor. -c/-d/-n/-m/-g select resources. --top-cpu/mem process lists. dstat N M interval/iterations. Modern replacement for vmstat+iostat+netstat. Output to CSV: dstat --output report.csv.

mpstat

MONITORMonitoringLFCS Domain 5

Report per-CPU statistics — see individual core utilization

mpstat shows CPU usage broken down by individual processor/core. Where top/vmstat show aggregate, mpstat reveals imbalances — one core at 100% while others idle means single-threaded bottleneck.

Syntax

mpstat [OPTIONS] [INTERVAL [COUNT]]
# Common: mpstat | mpstat -P ALL 2 5 | mpstat -P 0 1

Parameters

FlagDescription
-P ALLShow all CPUs individually
-P NShow only CPU N

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — CPU Stats Per Core

Daily Workflow: Carol uses mpstat to check per-CPU utilization and identify uneven load distribution. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical mpstat usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ mpstat -P ALL 1 3
CPU  %usr  %nice  %sys  %iowait  %irq  %soft  %steal  %idle
all  12.34  0.00   3.21    0.15    0.00   0.10    0.00   84.20

Examples

# Log & monitoring in anihpj:
#  /lpj/ops/logs/         — Application logs
#  journalctl -u jobpost  — Service logs
#  monitoring-01:9090     — Prometheus metrics

    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs

    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units

CPU %usr %sys %iowait %idle all 45.2 8.1 2.3 44.4 0 98.2 1.5 0.2 0.1 ← Core 0 is PEgged! 1 12.3 3.2 1.2 83.3 2 34.5 5.1 2.3 58.1 3 35.8 7.2 1.8 55.2

📝 What happened: Core 0 is at 99.7% utilization while others are 17-44%. This is a classic single-threaded bottleneck — Python's GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) is limiting parallelism. Multi-process (gunicorn workers) would distribute across cores.

LOGMonitoringLFCS Domain 5

Monitor multiple log files simultaneously — tail -f for multiple files at once

multitail displays multiple log files in split windows, each with independent scrolling and color filtering. Like running multiple tail -f commands in tmux panes, but purpose-built for log monitoring.

Syntax

multitail [OPTIONS] FILE1 FILE2...
# Common: multitail /var/log/syslog /var/log/nginx/error.log

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Parameters

FlagDescription

perf

PROFILEMonitoringLFCS Domain 5

Performance profiling — CPU sampling, cache misses, and kernel tracepoints

perf is Linux's built-in profiler. It samples CPU usage at the function level, counts cache misses, and traces kernel events. The definitive tool for answering "where is my CPU time going?" without code instrumentation.

Syntax

perf COMMAND [ARGS]
# Common: sudo perf top | sudo perf record CMD | sudo perf report | perf stat CMD

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Performance Profiler

Daily Workflow: Carol uses perf to profile CPU usage and identify performance bottlenecks in jobpost. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical perf usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo perf top -p $(pgrep gunicorn | head -1)
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo perf stat python3 /lpj/manage.py test

Examples

# Log & monitoring in anihpj:
#  /lpj/ops/logs/         — Application logs
#  journalctl -u jobpost  — Service logs
#  monitoring-01:9090     — Prometheus metrics
Example 1: Live Function Profile

Scenario: Carol profiles a running Python process to see where CPU is spent.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

sudo perf top -p $(pgrep -f "gunicorn")

Output:

Samples: 12K of event 'cycles', 4000 Hz

Parameters

FlagDescription
stat CMDCount performance events for CMD
record CMDProfile and save to perf.data
reportAnalyze perf.data and show report
topLive system-wide profiling (like top for perf counters)
listList all available perf event types
-p PIDProfile specific PID
-aSystem-wide profiling (all CPUs)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error (perf_event_paranoid restriction or not installed)
Overhead Shared Object Symbol 23.45% python3 [.] _PyEval_EvalFrameDefault 12.34% python3 [.] PyUnicode_FromFormat 8.90% libc.so.6 [.] __memcpy_avx_unaligned

📝 What happened: perf top showed live function-level CPU usage. 23% of CPU is in _PyEval_EvalFrameDefault (Python's main interpreter loop). 12% in string formatting, 9% in memory copy. This is profiler-level insight without modifying any code.

sudo perf record -g -p $(pgrep -f "manage.py") -- sleep 10 && sudo perf report

Output:

📝 What happened: record -g captured call graphs for 10 seconds. report displayed the interactive analysis. -g is critical — it shows the full call chain, not just leaf functions. The data is saved in perf.data for later analysis.

📁 Directory Snippet:

45,234,567,890 cycles # 3.2 GHz 12,345,678,901 instructions # 0.27 insn per cycle 234,567,890 cache-misses # 15.2% of all cache refs

📝 What happened: perf stat counted hardware events. 45B CPU cycles, 0.27 IPC (instructions per cycle — low means memory-bound). 15% cache miss rate is high — investigate data layout or indexing. This is hardware-level performance analysis.

Scenario: Carol records CPU profiles for offline analysis.

sudo perf record -g -p $(pgrep -f "manage.py") -- sleep 10 && sudo perf report --stdio | head -10
