timeout

CONTROLMonitoringLFCS Domain 5

Run a command with a time limit — kill it if it runs too long

timeout executes a command and kills it if it exceeds the specified duration. Essential for: network timeouts, preventing hung scripts, and resource limits. Sends SIGTERM first, then SIGKILL after a grace period.

Syntax

timeout [OPTIONS] DURATION COMMAND [ARGS]
# Common: timeout 5s curl api.com | timeout 10m python script.py

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Command completed within timeout
124Timed out (killed by timeout)

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Command Timeout

Daily Workflow: Carol uses timeout to limit execution time of health checks and prevent hung scripts. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical timeout usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ timeout 5 curl -s http://prod-api-01:8000/health/
carol@prod-api-01:~$ timeout 30 python3 /lpj/manage.py migrate

Examples

# Log & monitoring in anihpj:
#  /lpj/ops/logs/         — Application logs
#  journalctl -u jobpost  — Service logs
#  monitoring-01:9090     — Prometheus metrics
Example 1: Network Timeout

Scenario: Carol adds a timeout to curl so a health check doesn't hang forever.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

timeout 5s curl -s http://localhost:8000/health && echo "UP" || echo "DOWN or timeout"

Output:

UP

📝 What happened: Curl responded within 5 seconds. If it didn't, timeout would kill it (exit 124) and "DOWN or timeout" would print. Always add timeouts to network commands. Use 124 exit code to distinguish timeout from actual failure.

Parameters

FlagDescription
-s SIGNALSignal to send on timeout (default: TERM)
-k DURATIONKill-after duration — send KILL if still running
-vVerbose — print diagnostic message on timeout
DURATIONTimeout value: NUMBER[smhd] (default: seconds)
--preserve-statusExit with same status as the command

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
124Command timed out
125timeout itself failed
126Command not executable
127Command not found
137Command killed by SIGKILL (from -k)
Example 2: Script Safety Net

Scenario: Alice prevents a migration script from running longer than 10 minutes.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

timeout 10m python manage.py migrate || echo "Migration timed out after 10 minutes"

Output:

Migration timed out after 10 minutes

📝 What happened: The migration exceeded 10 minutes and was killed. This is a safety net — prevents a stuck migration from holding up the deployment pipeline. Timeout sends SIGTERM, giving the process a chance to clean up before SIGKILL (2s later by default).

Example 3: Custom Kill Signal

Scenario: Carol uses SIGHUP for a process that should reload config on timeout.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

timeout -s HUP 30s long_running_task

Output:

# After 30 seconds, SIGHUP is sent instead of SIGTERM. # The process may reload and continue, or exit gracefully.

📝 What happened: -s HUP sent SIGHUP instead of the default SIGTERM. Useful for daemons that reload on HUP. Other signals: -s INT (Ctrl+C), -s KILL (immediate kill). -s 0 checks if the command can even start without running it.

Example 4: Send Specific Signal on Timeout

📄 Context — Graceful Termination:

# -s SIGNAL sends a specific signal instead of SIGTERM
# SIGKILL (9) forcefully kills; SIGINT (2) is polite
# Default is SIGTERM (15)
# Use SIGKILL for stubborn processes

Scenario: Carol forcibly kills a process after 5 seconds with SIGKILL.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

timeout -s 9 5 ping -c 100 anihpj.com && echo "Ping completed" || echo "Ping killed after 5s"

Output:

PING anihpj.com (10.0.0.45) 56(84) bytes of data. 64 bytes from 10.0.0.45: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.123 ms ... Ping killed after 5s

📝 What happened: -s 9 sent SIGKILL after 5 seconds — immediate termination, no cleanup. Exit code 124 means timeout occurred. -s 15 (SIGTERM, default) allows graceful shutdown. -s INT (Ctrl+C equivalent) for interactive programs. -s KILL for unresponsive ones.

Example 5: Preserve Exit Status

📄 Context — Exit Code Propagation:

# --preserve-status returns the command's exit code (not 124)
# Without it, timeout always exits 124 on timeout
# With it, you can distinguish "real failure" from "timeout"
# Essential for scripts that need accurate exit codes

Scenario: Alice needs the actual exit code from a command, not the timeout signal.

📁 Directory Snippet:

# Relevant portion of the anihpj directory tree:
lpj/
└── 📁 ops/
    ├── 📁 logs/                        # Application & system logs
    │   ├── 📄 app.log                  # Application log (all levels)
    │   ├── 📄 error.log                # ERROR and CRITICAL
    │   └── 📄 access.log               # HTTP access log
    ├── 📁 backups/                     # Backup archives
    └── 📁 systemd/                     # Service units
        ├── 📄 jobpost.service
        └── 📄 celery.service

Command:

timeout --preserve-status 30 /lpj/scripts/deploy.sh && echo "Deploy OK (exit $?)" || echo "Deploy FAILED or timed out (exit $?)"

Output:

Deploy FAILED or timed out (exit 1)

📝 What happened: Exit code 1 came from deploy.sh (real failure), NOT from timeout. Without --preserve-status, timeout returns 124 regardless. Use this when you need to know: did it fail, or did it time out? Exit 124 = timeout; any other code = from the command.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: timeout DUR CMD time-limited execution. Duration suffixes: s/m/h/d. Exit 124 = timeout. -s SIGNAL custom kill signal. -k DUR SIGKILL after grace period. --preserve-status exit with CMD's status. Always use for network operations.

script

LOGMonitoringLFCS Domain 5

Record terminal sessions — capture everything printed to the terminal

script records an entire terminal session to a file (default: typescript). Captures ALL input and output — commands typed, output displayed, colors, everything. Essential for: documentation, audit trails, and reproducing complex procedures.

script [OPTIONS] [FILE]
# Common: script session.log | script -a session.log | script -q -c "ls -la"

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

⚙️ Service Management

Commands for managing systemd services, the boot process, and system configuration. The anihpj/jobpost stack runs as systemd services — jobpost, nginx, postgresql, redis, celery — all managed with these commands.

systemctl

SERVICEService MgmtCoreLFCS Domain 5

Control the systemd system and service manager — start, stop, enable, and check services

systemctl is the central management tool for systemd. It controls services (start/stop/restart), enables/disables at boot, checks status, and views logs. Every anihpj server runs systemd — this is the most important service management command.

Syntax

systemctl COMMAND [UNIT...]
# Common: systemctl status nginx | sudo systemctl restart jobpost | systemctl list-units

Parameters

CommandDescription
start/stop/restartControl service state
enable/disableStart at boot / don't start at boot
status UNITShow service status and recent logs

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Service Lifecycle

# Carol manages the jobpost Django service after a config change:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo systemctl status jobpost
● jobpost.service - Django Jobpost Application
   Active: active (running) since Tue 2025-06-03 08:00:00 UTC
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo systemctl restart jobpost
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo systemctl status jobpost
   Active: active (running) since Tue 2025-06-04 10:30:00 UTC  # Restarted!

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Systemd Control

Daily Workflow: Carol manages the anihpj service fleet — gunicorn (Django), celery, nginx, postgresql, and redis. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical systemctl usage on prod-api-01:

carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo systemctl restart gunicorn

📝 What happened: All four services are running. --no-pager prevented interactive paging; -l showed full log lines. The status output includes: loaded state, active state, PID, memory, and last 10 log lines. Quickest post-reboot health check.

Example 2: Enable at Boot

Created symlink /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/jobpost.service → /etc/systemd/system/jobpost.service enabled

📝 What happened: enable created a symlink in the multi-user.target.wants directory. is-enabled confirmed. The service will now start automatically at boot. disable removes the symlink. mask makes it impossible to start (even manually).

UNIT LOAD ACTIVE SUB DESCRIPTION jobpost.service loaded active running Django Jobpost nginx.service loaded active running A high performance web server postgresql.service loaded active running PostgreSQL RDBMS

📝 What happened: --type=service filtered to services only, --state=running,failed showed active and problematic ones. Other states: exited, dead, inactive. Use --state=failed alone to find crashed services.

Scenario: Carol applies a config change without dropping connections.

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

Output:

Active: active (running) since Tue 2025-06-03 08:00:00 UTC

📝 What happened: reload told nginx to re-read its config without restarting. The service stayed running — no connection drops. Not all services support reload (it's optional). restart stops and starts (drops connections); reload is graceful.

Example 5: View Service Logs

Scenario: Alice checks why a service failed to start.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

systemctl status jobpost --lines=20

Output:

● jobpost.service - Django Jobpost Application Active: failed (Result: exit-code) Process: 2841 ExecStart=/lpj/venv/bin/python manage.py runserver (code=exited, status=1) Main PID: 2841 (code=exited, status=1) Jun 04 10:30:00 python[2841]: ImportError: No module named 'django'

📝 What happened: --lines=20 showed the last 20 log lines. The service failed because Django wasn't installed in the virtualenv. The exit code (1) and error message are visible directly in the status output — no need to check journalctl separately.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: systemctl status UNIT quick check. start/stop/restart/reload control. enable/disable boot control. list-units --state=failed find crashes. daemon-reload after editing unit files. is-active/is-enabled script checks.

SERVICEService MgmtLegacyLFCS Domain 5

Run System V init scripts — legacy service management, compatible with systemd

service runs SysV init scripts. On modern systems, it redirects to systemctl. Still commonly used in scripts for cross-distribution compatibility and muscle memory. Supports fewer features than systemctl but works everywhere.

Exit CodeDescription

Example 1: Quick Status Check

lpj/

Example 2: Restart Service

Scenario: Alice restarts jobpost after a code deployment.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo service jobpost restart && service jobpost status | grep Active

Output:

Active: active (running) since Tue 2025-06-04 10:35:00 UTC

📝 What happened: Jobpost restarted successfully. The service command accepts the same verbs as SysV init: start, stop, restart, status, reload. On systemd, service UNIT reload calls systemctl reload UNIT.

Example 3: List All Services

Scenario: Carol gets a quick list of all services and their states.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

service --status-all 2>&1 | head -10

[ + ] jobpost [ + ] nginx [ + ] postgresql [ - ] bluetooth [ ? ] console-setup.sh

Example 4: Service Reload

📄 Context — Graceful Config Reload:

# Carol updates nginx config and needs a graceful reload:
# /lpj/ops/systemd/nginx.conf was updated
# reload reads new config WITHOUT dropping connections
# restart would drop all active user connections

Scenario: Carol reloads nginx after updating the proxy config.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo service nginx reload && service nginx status | grep Active

Output:

Active: active (running) since Tue 2025-06-03 08:00:00 UTC

📝 What happened: nginx re-read its config without restarting. The "since" timestamp didn't change — proving no restart occurred. Not all services support reload; if unsupported, the command fails gracefully. Always prefer reload over restart for config changes.

Example 5: Cross-Distro Scripting

📄 Context — Deploy Script Portability:

# Alice writes a deploy script that works on both Ubuntu and RHEL:
# service command exists on both SysV and systemd systems
# systemctl would fail on older RHEL 6 servers
# service is the lowest common denominator for init scripts

Scenario: Alice uses service in a deploy script for maximum compatibility.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo service jobpost stop && sleep 2 && sudo service jobpost start && service jobpost status

Output:

Stopping jobpost: [OK] Starting jobpost: [OK] jobpost (pid 12345) is running...

📝 What happened: Stop → wait 2s → start → verify. The sleep prevents race conditions where the old process hasn't released the port. Cross-distro compatible: works on Ubuntu 14.04 through 24.04 and RHEL 6 through 9.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: service NAME CMD legacy interface. --status-all lists all. On systemd, it wraps systemctl. Accepts: start/stop/restart/status/reload. Know both service AND systemctl for the exam — some questions expect service syntax.

chkconfig

SERVICEService MgmtLegacyLFCS Domain 5

Manage runlevel-based service startup — RHEL/CentOS 6 and older

chkconfig manages which services start at which runlevels on legacy SysV init systems. On RHEL 7+, it's a compatibility wrapper for systemctl. Still appears in LFCS exams for legacy system knowledge.

Syntax

chkconfig [OPTIONS]
# Common: chkconfig --list | sudo chkconfig nginx on | sudo chkconfig --add jobpost

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Service Enable

# Carol's typical chkconfig usage on prod-api-01:
carol@legacy:~$ chkconfig --list
carol@legacy:~$ sudo chkconfig nginx on

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: List Service Runlevels

Scenario: Carol checks which runlevels nginx starts in.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

chkconfig --list nginx 2>/dev/null || systemctl list-unit-files | grep nginx

Output:

nginx 0:off 1:off 2:on 3:on 4:on 5:on 6:off

📝 What happened: nginx starts in runlevels 2,3,4,5 (multi-user + graphical) and stops in 0,1,6 (halt, single, reboot). On systemd, this maps to systemctl is-enabled. chkconfig reads from /etc/rc.d/rc*.d/ symlinks.

Example 2: Enable Boot Start

Scenario: Alice enables jobpost to start on boot (legacy syntax).

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo chkconfig jobpost on && chkconfig --list jobpost

Output:

jobpost 0:off 1:off 2:on 3:on 4:on 5:on 6:off

📝 What happened: on enabled for runlevels 2-5. off disables. On systemd, this redirects to systemctl enable. Legacy equivalent of systemctl enable jobpost. Know both for the exam.

Parameters

Flag/CommandDescription
--list [NAME]List runlevel settings for all or specific service
NAME onEnable service at runlevels 2-5
NAME offDisable service at all runlevels
--add NAMEAdd service to chkconfig management
--del NAMERemove service from chkconfig management
--level 35 NAME onEnable only at specific runlevels (e.g., 3 and 5)
Example 3: Add New Service

📄 Context — Legacy Init Script Registration:

# Dave writes a custom init script for a legacy database monitor:
# /etc/init.d/dbmon contains start/stop/status functions
# Must be registered with chkconfig to appear in --list
# RHEL 6 pattern: chkconfig --add registers the service

Scenario: Dave registers a custom init script with chkconfig.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo chkconfig --add dbmon && chkconfig --list dbmon

Output:

dbmon 0:off 1:off 2:off 3:off 4:off 5:off 6:off

📝 What happened: dbmon is registered but OFF at all runlevels. Now enable it: chkconfig dbmon on. On systemd, equivalent is creating a .service file + systemctl enable. chkconfig reads LSB headers from the init script to determine defaults.

Example 4: Specific Runlevels

📄 Context — Multi-User vs Graphical Boot:

# Runlevel 3 = multi-user (text mode) — servers
# Runlevel 5 = graphical (GUI mode) — workstations
# jobpost should run in both (server boots to either)
# Some GUI-only services should only run in runlevel 5

Scenario: Carol enables a service only in server runlevels (3, not 5).

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo chkconfig --level 3 jobpost on && chkconfig --list jobpost

Output:

jobpost 0:off 1:off 2:off 3:on 4:off 5:off 6:off

📝 What happened: jobpost starts ONLY at runlevel 3. --level 35 would set multiple. On systemd, this maps to systemctl enable jobpost with WantedBy=multi-user.target in the unit file. Granular runlevel control is chkconfig's unique strength.

Example 5: Remove Service

📄 Context — Cleanup After Application Removal:

# Legacy monitoring agent was uninstalled
# Init script remains in /etc/init.d/
# chkconfig --del removes it from management
# Prevents "service not found" warnings at boot

Scenario: Carol removes a deprecated service from chkconfig management.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo chkconfig --del oldmonitor && chkconfig --list oldmonitor 2>&1 || echo "Removed"

Output:

service oldmonitor does not support chkconfig Removed

📝 What happened: oldmonitor was removed from chkconfig management. The error confirms it's no longer tracked. Equivalent to systemctl disable --now oldmonitor && systemctl mask oldmonitor on systemd. Always clean up after uninstalling services.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: chkconfig --list shows runlevel settings. on/off enables/disables. --add/--del adds/removes from management. --level 35 sets specific runlevels. Legacy RHEL 6 tool. On systemd, wraps systemctl. systemctl enable is the modern equivalent.

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Examples

#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Install Default Runlevels

Scenario: Carol adds a new init script to start at default runlevels.

📁 Environment Snippet:

lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API

└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo update-rc.d jobpost defaults

Output:

Adding system startup for /etc/init.d/jobpost ...

📝 What happened: defaults created start links for runlevels 2-5 and stop links for 0,1,6. Equivalent to chkconfig jobpost on on RHEL. On modern Ubuntu: systemctl enable jobpost achieves the same result.

Example 2: Remove Init Links

Scenario: Alice removes an old service from auto-start.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo update-rc.d -f oldservice remove

Output:

Removing any system startup links for /etc/init.d/oldservice ...

📝 What happened: -f forced removal even if the init script still exists. remove deleted the symlinks. On systemd: systemctl disable oldservice. Legacy tool, but important for Debian/Ubuntu admin history.

Parameters

Flag/CommandDescription
NAME defaultsInstall start/stop links at default runlevels (2-5)
-f NAME removeForce remove all symlinks for NAME
NAME start NN RUNLEVELSSet start priority NN at specified runlevels
NAME stop NN RUNLEVELSSet stop priority NN at specified runlevels
-nDry run — show what would be done
Example 3: Custom Priority

📄 Context — Boot Order Control:

# Start order matters: postgresql must start before jobpost
# Lower priority numbers = earlier start
# S01postgresql starts before S02jobpost
# update-rc.d controls the S/K number prefix in rc*.d symlinks

Scenario: Carol sets a custom start priority so jobpost starts after PostgreSQL.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo update-rc.d jobpost start 99 2 3 4 5 . stop 01 0 1 6 .

Output:

Adding system startup for /etc/init.d/jobpost ...

📝 What happened: jobpost starts last (priority 99) and stops first (priority 01). The dots terminate each argument list. Priority 99 = last to start (good for apps that need DB/network up). Priority 01 = first to stop (clean shutdown before infrastructure).

Example 4: Dry Run

📄 Context — Safe What-If Preview:

# Before modifying boot configuration, preview changes:
# -n shows what update-rc.d WOULD do without doing it
# Critical for production servers — no surprises at boot
# Always dry-run before modifying rc*.d symlinks

Scenario: Alice previews what update-rc.d will do before committing.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo update-rc.d -n jobpost defaults

Output:

Would create symlink /etc/rc0.d/K01jobpost -> ../init.d/jobpost Would create symlink /etc/rc2.d/S02jobpost -> ../init.d/jobpost Would create symlink /etc/rc3.d/S02jobpost -> ../init.d/jobpost

📝 What happened: -n showed what WOULD happen: K01 (kill) links for runlevels 0,1,6; S02 (start) links for 2,3,4,5. Priority 02 = starts second. The actual symlinks were NOT created. Always dry-run before modifying system boot.

Example 5: Disable Without Removing

📄 Context — Temporary Service Disable:

# Jobpost needs maintenance — stop it from starting at boot temporarily
# Don't want to delete the init script (might need it later)
# update-rc.d disable leaves the script but removes symlinks
# Equivalent to systemctl disable (not mask)

Scenario: Carol temporarily prevents jobpost from auto-starting during maintenance.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo update-rc.d jobpost disable

Output:

Disabling system startup links for /etc/init.d/jobpost ...

📝 What happened: Symlinks removed but init script preserved. Re-enable with update-rc.d jobpost defaults. On systemd, this is systemctl disable jobpost. Disable = symlinks removed; remove = init script deleted. Disable is safer for temporary changes.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: update-rc.d NAME defaults adds to boot. -f NAME remove removes. start NN . stop NN . sets priority. -n dry-runs. disable preserves script. Debian/Ubuntu equivalent of chkconfig. On systemd, use systemctl enable/disable. Init scripts in /etc/init.d/.

systemd-analyze

ANALYZEService MgmtLFCS Domain 5

Analyze systemd boot performance — find what's slowing down your boot

systemd-analyze shows boot timing and identifies slow services. Shows total boot time, per-service initialization time, and critical chain analysis. Essential for optimizing server startup after hardware upgrades.

Syntax

systemd-analyze [OPTIONS] [COMMAND]
# Common: systemd-analyze | systemd-analyze blame | systemd-analyze critical-chain

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Boot Analysis

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Total Boot Time

Scenario: Carol checks how fast the server boots after an SSD upgrade.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

systemd-analyze

Output:

Startup finished in 2.345s (kernel) + 8.912s (userspace) = 11.257s

📝 What happened: Kernel took 2.3s, userspace 8.9s, total 11.3s from power-on to login. Userspace > kernel is normal — userspace includes mounting filesystems and starting services. SDD boot should be < 15s; HDD < 60s.

Example 2: Blame Slow Services

Scenario: Alice identifies which service is slowing down boot the most.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

systemd-analyze blame | head -5

Output:

5.234s postgresql.service 3.456s docker.service 2.123s networkd-dispatcher.service 1.234s jobpost.service 0.567s nginx.service

📝 What happened: PostgreSQL takes 5.2s — the biggest boot delay. Docker takes 3.5s. If these services don't need to start at boot, disable them: systemctl disable docker. blame shows wall-clock time, not CPU time — a service waiting for network shows as slow.

Example 3: Critical Chain

Scenario: Carol traces the dependency chain to find the boot bottleneck.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

systemd-analyze critical-chain jobpost.service

Output:

jobpost.service +1.234s └─network-online.target @8.912s └─NetworkManager.service +2.123s └─basic.target @5.234s

📝 What happened: jobpost depends on network-online, which depends on NetworkManager. The longest chain determines total boot time. If jobpost doesn't need network-online (uses localhost DB), change After=network.target instead of network-online.target.

Parameters

Command/FlagDescription
blameList services sorted by init time (slowest first)
critical-chain [UNIT]Show time-critical chain of units
plot > FILEGenerate SVG graph of boot timeline
security [UNIT]Analyze security exposure level of units
timeShow total kernel + userspace boot time
verify FILECheck unit files for syntax errors

NAME DESCRIPTION EXPOSURE ✓ PrivateNetwork Service has no access to network 0.5 ✗ ProtectSystem= Service may modify system files 1.0 ✗ PrivateTmp= Service shares /tmp with others 0.5 → Overall exposure level for jobpost.service: 7.2 (MEDIUM)

📝 What happened: jobpost scores 7.2 (MEDIUM exposure). Suggestions: enable ProtectSystem=full (prevents modifying /usr, /etc), PrivateTmp=yes (isolated /tmp). Add these directives to the .service file and run systemctl daemon-reload.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: systemd-analyze shows boot time. blame lists services by time. critical-chain shows dependency path. plot > boot.svg generates a visual chart. security analyzes service hardening. Use to optimize boot speed and harden services.

Example 1: View Cgroup Tree

Control group /: -.slice ├─user.slice │ └─user-1000.slice │ ├─session-1.scope │ │ ├─1234 sshd: carol [priv] │ │ └─1235 -bash ├─system.slice │ ├─nginx.service │ │ ├─2841 nginx: master │ │ └─2842 nginx: worker

lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

systemd-cgls -l --no-pager | head -30

Output:

Control group /: -.slice ├─user.slice (/user.slice) │ └─user-1000.slice (/user.slice/user-1000.slice) │ └─session-1.scope │ ├─1234 sshd: carol [priv] │ └─1235 -bash └─system.slice (/system.slice) ├─nginx.service │ ├─2841 nginx: master process │ └─2842 nginx: worker process ├─postgresql.service │ └─1234 /usr/lib/postgresql/14/bin/postgres

📝 What happened: All processes are properly contained in their cgroups. User processes in user.slice; system services in system.slice. -l showed full paths including the leading /sys/fs/cgroup/ mount. No orphan processes found — security audit passed.

Example 4: Compare Services

📄 Context — Resource Planning:

# Carol compares process counts across services:
# More processes = more resource consumption
# Helps plan CPU/memory limits per cgroup
# nginx: 1 master + N workers (N = CPU cores)

Scenario: Carol counts processes per service to plan resource allocation.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

for svc in nginx postgresql jobpost redis; do echo -n "$svc: "; systemd-cgls -u $svc.service --no-pager 2>/dev/null | grep -c "├─"; done

Output:

nginx: 5 postgresql: 12 jobpost: 4 redis: 3

📝 What happened: PostgreSQL has the most processes (12 — connection pool workers). nginx has 5 (1 master + 4 workers). Process count ≈ parallelism capacity. Use this data to set CPUQuota= and MemoryMax= in service unit files.

Example 5: Include Kernel Threads

📄 Context — Kernel Thread Visibility:

# Kernel threads are managed by the kernel, not systemd
# They appear under the root cgroup, not system.slice
# -k flag includes them for complete system visibility
# Useful when diagnosing kernel-level issues (drivers, I/O)

Scenario: Carol includes kernel threads to see complete system process organization.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

systemd-cgls -k --no-pager | grep -A2 "kthreadd" | head -5

Output:

├─2 [kthreadd] │ ├─3 [rcu_gp] │ ├─4 [rcu_par_gp] │ ├─6 [kworker/0:0H-events_highpri]

📝 What happened: Kernel threads (PID 2 = kthreadd, the kernel thread daemon) appear with brackets (not service names). They exist outside systemd's service management. -k is needed for complete troubleshooting — without it, you'd miss kernel-level processes.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: systemd-cgls shows cgroup tree. -u UNIT filters by service. -k includes kernel threads. -l long paths. --no-pager for scripts. Each service gets its own cgroup. Cgroups enforce resource limits. systemd-cgtop shows real-time usage.

systemd-cgtop

CGROUPService MgmtLFCS Domain 5

Show top control groups by resource usage — top for cgroups

systemd-cgtop displays real-time resource usage per control group (service). Like top but organized by service rather than process. Shows CPU, memory, and I/O per service — identify which service is consuming resources.

Syntax

systemd-cgtop [OPTIONS]
# Common: systemd-cgtop | systemd-cgtop -d 2 -n 5

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Cgroup Monitor

Daily Workflow: Carol manages the anihpj service fleet — gunicorn (Django), celery, nginx, postgresql, and redis. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical systemd-cgtop usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ systemd-cgtop

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Live Service Monitoring

Scenario: Carol checks which service is using the most CPU right now.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

systemd-cgtop

Output:

Control Group Tasks %CPU Memory / 89 45.2 2.3G /system.slice 45 42.1 1.8G /system.slice/postgresql.service 12 28.3 1.2G /system.slice/jobpost.service 4 12.5 456M

📝 What happened: PostgreSQL is the top consumer: 28% CPU, 1.2GB RAM. jobpost uses 12.5% CPU, 456MB. This is service-level monitoring — much more actionable than per-process top. Optimize the hungriest service first.

Example 2: Snapshot Mode

Scenario: Alice captures one resource snapshot for a cron job.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

systemd-cgtop -b -n 1 | head -10

Output:

Control Group Tasks %CPU Memory / 89 45.2 2.3G /system.slice 45 42.1 1.8G

📝 What happened: -b batch mode, -n 1 one iteration. Perfect for periodic monitoring scripts. Append to a log file for historical service-level resource tracking. Use -d 5 for 5-second refresh intervals.

Parameters

FlagDescription
-bBatch mode — single snapshot (no interactive refresh)
-n NNumber of iterations before exit
-d SECRefresh interval in seconds (default: 1)
-pOrder by CPU usage (default: by sum of CPU+memory+IO)
-tShow tasks count instead of cgroup tree
--depth=NMaximum depth of cgroup tree to show
Example 3: CPU-Sorted Monitoring

📄 Context — CPU Spike Investigation:

# prod-api-01 CPU is pegged at 100%
# Need to find which SERVICE (not which PID) is responsible
# -p sorts by CPU% — shows the hungry service immediately
# Much faster than top + manual grouping by service name

Scenario: Carol investigates a CPU spike by sorting services by CPU usage.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

systemd-cgtop -p -b -n 1 | head -8

Output:

Control Group Tasks %CPU Memory /system.slice/postgresql.service 12 85.2 1.8G /system.slice/jobpost.service 4 8.5 456M /system.slice/nginx.service 5 3.2 123M

📝 What happened: PostgreSQL is consuming 85% CPU — a runaway query. -p sorted by CPU, putting the worst offender at the top. Without this flag, the sorting might be obscured by memory usage. Immediate action: check PostgreSQL slow query log.

Example 4: Memory Leak Detection

📄 Context — Gradual Memory Growth:

# jobpost memory usage slowly grows over days (suspected memory leak)
# Periodic snapshots track the trend: 200MB → 350MB → 500MB
# -b -n 1 captures one snapshot for logging
# Compare snapshots over time to confirm the leak

Scenario: Alice captures periodic memory snapshots to detect a leak.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

systemd-cgtop -b -n 1 2>/dev/null | grep jobpost >> /lpj/ops/logs/memory-trend.log && tail -3 /lpj/ops/logs/memory-trend.log

Output:

/system.slice/jobpost.service 4 5.2 456M /system.slice/jobpost.service 4 5.1 458M /system.slice/jobpost.service 4 5.3 462M

📝 What happened: Memory grew from 456MB → 462MB over three snapshots — confirmed leak trend. Set up a cron job to capture hourly: systemd-cgtop -b -n 1 | grep jobpost >> memory-trend.log. Alert when memory exceeds threshold.

Example 5: Controlled Depth

📄 Context — Focused Service View:

# Full cgtop output is noisy on servers with 100+ services
# --depth=2 shows only top-level slices and services
# Strips out user sessions and transient scopes
# Clean, focused view for service-level monitoring

Scenario: Carol limits cgtop output depth for a cleaner dashboard view.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

systemd-cgtop --depth=2 -b -n 1

Output:

Control Group Tasks %CPU Memory / 89 45.2 2.3G /system.slice 45 42.1 1.8G /user.slice 12 2.1 345M

📝 What happened: Only top-level slices shown — clean overview. --depth=3 would show individual services within each slice. Use higher depth for detailed investigation, lower depth for dashboards. Much cleaner than unfiltered output on busy servers.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: systemd-cgtop service-level resource monitor. -b batch mode. -n N iterations. -d N refresh interval. -p sort by CPU. --depth=N limit tree depth. Like top but per-cgroup. Shows which SERVICE is the resource hog.

📝 What happened: All servers use UTC — standard for production. NTP is active, clock is synchronized. RTC (Real-Time Clock) matches system time. If "System clock synchronized: no", check NTP with timedatectl show-timesync.

Example 2: Change Timezone

Scenario: Alice sets the timezone for a developer workstation to local time.

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

📝 What happened: Timezone changed immediately. Use timedatectl list-timezones | grep Chicago to find valid timezone names. Production servers should use UTC; developer workstations can use local time. Changes take effect instantly.

Example 3: Enable NTP Sync

Scenario: Carol enables automatic time synchronization.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests

└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo timedatectl set-ntp true && timedatectl | grep "NTP service"

Output:

NTP service: active

📝 What happened: systemd-timesyncd is now synchronizing the clock. TLS certificates, database transactions, and Kerberos all require accurate time. Always enable NTP on production servers. Check sync status: timedatectl timesync-status.

Parameters

CommandDescription
set-timezone ZONESet the system timezone
set-ntp BOOLEnable/disable NTP synchronization
set-time "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS"Set system clock manually
list-timezonesList all available timezone names
timesync-statusShow detailed NTP sync status
show-timesyncShow systemd-timesyncd properties
Example 4: NTP Sync Details

📄 Context — Certificate Expiry Prevention:

# TLS certificates fail if system clock drifts > 5 minutes
# NTP keeps clock accurate to milliseconds
# timesync-status shows: server, offset, jitter, root delay
# Offset > 100ms = time sync problem = potential TLS failures

Scenario: Carol verifies NTP sync health after a network change.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

timedatectl timesync-status

Output:

Server: 185.125.190.57 (ntp.ubuntu.com) Poll interval: 32s Offset: +2.345ms Delay: 12.456ms Jitter: 1.234ms Packets: 12345/12346

📝 What happened: NTP is synced with ntp.ubuntu.com. Offset is only +2.3ms — excellent accuracy. Only 1 lost packet out of 12,346. Poll interval 32s (auto-adjusts). If offset is seconds or minutes, NTP hasn't synced yet — check firewall allows UDP 123.

Example 5: Manual Time Set

📄 Context — Air-Gapped Server Clock:

# backup-nas has no internet access (air-gapped for security)
# NTP can't reach external servers
# Manual time set is required periodically
# Clock drift on hardware: ~1-2 seconds per day

Scenario: Carol manually sets the clock on an air-gapped backup server.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo timedatectl set-ntp false && sudo timedatectl set-time "2026-06-04 14:30:00" && timedatectl | grep "Local time"

Output:

Local time: Thu 2026-06-04 14:30:01 UTC

📝 What happened: NTP disabled first (can't set time while NTP is active), then clock set manually. The +1 second is the delay between setting and checking. For air-gapped servers, set up a local NTP server or use a hardware GPS clock. Manual setting drifts ~1-2s/day.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: timedatectl shows time settings. set-timezone ZONE changes. set-ntp true enables sync. list-timezones shows options. timesync-status NTP details. Replaces date, tzselect, ntpdate. Always use UTC on servers.

# Missing locale? Run: sudo locale-gen ja_JP.UTF-8

Scenario: Alice checks which locales are available for international users.

Command:

localectl list-locales | grep -E "ja_JP|de_DE|pt_BR"

de_DE.utf8 ja_JP.utf8 pt_BR.utf8

📝 What happened: Japanese, German, and Brazilian Portuguese locales are available. If a locale is missing, install it with locale-gen ja_JP.UTF-8 then set with localectl set-locale. Django uses locale for date formatting, number formatting, and translations.

Example 4: Set Keymap

📄 Context — Console Access for International Team:

# German developer needs German keyboard layout on console
# set-keymap changes virtual console (tty1-tty6) layout
# Different from set-x11-keymap (GUI terminal layout)
# Console keymap = /etc/vconsole.conf

Scenario: Carol sets a German keyboard layout for a developer's console access.

VC Keymap: de

📝 What happened: Virtual console keymap changed to German (de). Affects Ctrl+Alt+F1-F6 terminals only, not SSH or GUI. list-keymaps shows all options. Keymap is written to /etc/vconsole.conf — persists across reboots.

System Locale: LANG=en_US.UTF-8 LC_TIME=de_DE.UTF-8 LC_MONETARY=de_DE.UTF-8 VC Keymap: n/a

loginctl

SESSIONService MgmtLFCS Domain 5

Control the systemd login manager — list sessions, users, and seats

loginctl manages user sessions tracked by systemd-logind. Shows who is logged in, from where, and for how long. More powerful than who — can kill sessions, show per-session processes, and list seats.

Syntax

loginctl [OPTIONS] [COMMAND]
# Common: loginctl | loginctl list-sessions | loginctl session-status 1

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Login Control

Daily Workflow: Carol manages the anihpj service fleet — gunicorn (Django), celery, nginx, postgresql, and redis. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical loginctl usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ loginctl list-sessions

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: List Sessions

Scenario: Carol checks who's logged into the production server.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

loginctl list-sessions

Output:

SESSION UID USER SEAT TTY 1 1000 carol pts/0 2 1001 alice pts/1 3 1003 bob pts/2

📝 What happened: Three active sessions: Carol, Alice, Bob. Each has a session ID, UID, and TTY. More detailed than who which only shows username/terminal/time. Use session-status SESSION for detailed session info including processes.

Example 2: Kill a Session

Scenario: Carol terminates an abandoned SSH session consuming resources.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo loginctl terminate-session 3 && loginctl list-sessions

Output:

SESSION UID USER SEAT TTY 1 1000 carol pts/0 2 1001 alice pts/1

📝 What happened: Bob's session 3 was terminated. All processes in that session were killed. Unlike kill which targets one process, terminate-session kills everything belonging to that login session — clean and complete.

Example 3: Show Session Details

Scenario: Alice checks what processes are running in her session.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

loginctl session-status 2 | head -10

Output:

2 - alice (1001) Since: Tue 2025-06-04 09:15:00 UTC; 1h 15min ago State: active Leader: 2345 (sshd) Service: sshd; type tty; class user CGroup: /user.slice/user-1001.slice/session-2.scope ├─2345 sshd: alice@pts/1 ├─2346 -bash └─4567 python manage.py shell

📝 What happened: Alice's session has sshd, bash, and a Django shell. The session has been active for 1h15m. The cgroup shows all processes belonging to this session. Use user-status UID for per-user summary across all sessions.

Parameters

CommandDescription
list-sessionsList all current login sessions
list-usersList all logged-in users
list-seatsList all seats (physical consoles)
session-status IDShow detailed session information
user-status USERShow all sessions for a user
terminate-session IDKill a session and all its processes
kill-session IDSend a signal to a session
lock-session IDLock a session's screen
enable-linger USERAllow user services to run without login
Example 4: User Linger for Background Services

📄 Context — Persistent User Services:

# Bob needs his personal CI watcher to run even when logged out
# Without linger, user services stop when the user logs out
# enable-linger allows systemd --user services to persist
# Essential for per-user daemons and long-running tasks

Scenario: Carol enables linger so Bob's user services run even when he's logged out.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo loginctl enable-linger bob && loginctl user-status bob | grep Linger

Output:

Linger: yes

📝 What happened: Bob's user-level systemd services will now persist after logout. Without linger, systemctl --user services stop on last session close. Linger is enabled per-user. Check with loginctl show-user USER | grep Linger. Common for tmux/screen sessions.

Example 5: Per-User Summary

📄 Context — Security Audit of Active Users:

# Eve audits all active user sessions for security review
# user-status shows: sessions, idle time, processes, cgroup
# Identifies stale sessions left open for days
# Security policy: terminate sessions idle > 24 hours

Scenario: Eve generates a security audit of all active users.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

for uid in $(loginctl list-users --no-legend | awk '{print $1}'); do echo "=== UID $uid ==="; loginctl user-status $uid 2>/dev/null | head -5; done

Output:

=== UID 1000 === carol (1000) Sessions: 1 Since: Tue 2025-06-04 08:00:00 UTC; 2h 30min ago === UID 1001 === alice (1001) Sessions: 2 Since: Tue 2025-06-04 09:15:00 UTC; 1h 15min ago

📝 What happened: Carol has 1 session (2.5h), Alice has 2 sessions (1.25h). No sessions older than 24h — audit passed. Use loginctl kill-user --signal=TERM USER to terminate all sessions of a user. Safer than killall which might miss child processes.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: loginctl list-sessions shows sessions. session-status ID details. terminate-session ID kills session. list-users shows logged-in users. user-status USER per-user. enable-linger USER persists services. Part of systemd. Replaces/enhances who and w.

📦 Package Management

Commands for installing, updating, removing, and querying software packages. The anihpj/jobpost stack depends on Python packages (pip), system packages (apt), and container images — knowing the package manager is essential for server setup and dependency management.

apt

DEBIAN Package Management Core LFCS Domain 5

Advanced Package Tool — modern Debian/Ubuntu package management

apt is the modern frontend for APT (replacing apt-get). It combines the most common commands from apt-get and apt-cache into one simpler tool. Used on all anihpj Ubuntu servers for system package management.

For anihpj/jobpost, apt is used for:

  • Installing dependencies: nginx, postgresql-client, redis-tools
  • Updating packages during maintenance windows
  • Searching for available packages before installation
  • Removing obsolete packages to free disk space

Syntax

apt [OPTIONS] COMMAND [PACKAGE...]

# Common patterns:
sudo apt update                  # Refresh package index
sudo apt install nginx           # Install a package
sudo apt upgrade                 # Upgrade all packages
apt search python3               # Search for packages
sudo apt remove package          # Remove a package

Parameters

CommandDescription
updateRefresh package index from repositories
install PKGInstall or upgrade package(s)
upgradeUpgrade all installed packages
remove PKGRemove package (keeps config files)
purge PKGRemove package + config files
search TERMSearch package descriptions
show PKGShow package details
listList packages (--installed, --upgradable)
full-upgradeUpgrade with dependency resolution (may remove/install)
autoremoveRemove no-longer-needed dependencies
cleanClear local repository of retrieved package files

Flags

FlagDescription
-y, --yesAutomatic yes to prompts (non-interactive)
-q, --quietQuiet mode — minimal output
--no-install-recommendsDo not install recommended packages
--fix-brokenFix broken dependencies
--dry-runSimulate without making changes

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
100Error

The following NEW packages will be installed:
  nginx postgresql-client redis-tools
Need to get 12.3 MB of archives.
After this operation, 45.2 MB of additional disk space will be used.

Correcting dependencies... Done The following additional packages will be installed: libnginx-mod-stream Setting up nginx (1.18.0-0ubuntu1.4) ...

📝 What happened: apt detected the broken dependency (missing libnginx-mod-stream) and installed it automatically. The interrupted nginx installation was completed. Always run --fix-broken when you see "unmet dependencies" errors.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: apt update refreshes the index (required before install/upgrade). apt install -y auto-confirms. apt autoremove --purge cleans orphans. apt full-upgrade handles dependency removal. apt list --installed shows installed packages. apt --fix-broken install repairs broken deps. Prefer apt over apt-get for interactive use.

apt-get

DEBIANPackage ManagementLFCS Domain 5

Classic APT package handling utility — stable interface for scripts and automation

apt-get is the script-friendly backend to apt. While apt is preferred for interactive use, apt-get has a stable CLI guaranteed not to change between versions — making it the right choice for scripts and CI/CD pipelines.

Syntax

apt-get [OPTIONS] COMMAND [PACKAGE...]
# Common: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y nginx

Parameters

Flag/CommandDescription
-y, --yesAutomatic yes to prompts
-q, --quietQuiet mode
dist-upgradeUpgrade with dependency resolution (may remove)
install --reinstallReinstall package

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — CI/CD Server Provisioning

# Jenkins CI pipeline uses apt-get (not apt) for stable, parsable output:
jenkins@ci-runner-01:~$ sudo apt-get update -qq && sudo apt-get install -y -qq docker.io git
# apt-get is preferred in scripts because its CLI is stable across Ubuntu versions.
# The anihpj provisioning script uses apt-get exclusively for idempotent setups.
# /lpj/scripts/provision-server.sh (excerpt):
#!/bin/bash
set -e
echo "Provisioning anihpj server..."
sudo apt-get update -qq
sudo apt-get install -y -qq nginx postgresql-client redis-tools python3-venv
sudo apt-get autoremove -y -qq
echo "Server ready."

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
100Error

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: apt-get for scripts (stable interface), apt for interactive use. dist-upgrade handles dependency changes. -s simulates. clean vs autoclean. Know that apt-get requires update before install to refresh the index.

apt-cache

DEBIANPackage ManagementLFCS Domain 5

Query the APT package cache — search and inspect packages without installing

apt-cache performs queries on the APT package cache: searching, showing package details, checking dependencies, and listing available versions. All read-only — no root needed.

Syntax

apt-cache [OPTIONS] COMMAND [PACKAGE...]
# Common: apt-cache search nginx | apt-cache show nginx | apt-cache policy nginx

Parameters

CommandDescription
search TERMSearch package names and descriptions
show PKGShow detailed package information
policy PKGShow installed/available versions
depends PKGShow package dependencies

yum

RHELPackage ManagementLegacyLFCS Domain 5

Yellowdog Updater Modified — package manager for RHEL/CentOS 7 and older

yum is the legacy package manager for RHEL/CentOS/Fedora systems. Replaced by dnf in RHEL 8+ but still widely used in older enterprise environments. While anihpj uses Ubuntu (apt), understanding yum is critical for mixed environments.

Syntax

yum [OPTIONS] COMMAND [PACKAGE...]
# Common: sudo yum install nginx | yum search httpd | sudo yum update

Parameters

CommandDescription
install PKGInstall package(s)
update [PKG]Update all or specific package
remove PKGRemove package(s)
search TERMSearch packages
info PKGShow package details
listList packages (installed/available)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Partial error (some operations failed)
2Fatal error

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: yum is legacy (RHEL 7/older). yum install -y auto-confirms. yum check-update is scriptable (exit 100 = updates available). yum history provides audit trail. For RHEL 8+, use dnf instead.

dnf

RHELPackage ManagementModernLFCS Domain 5

Dandified YUM — modern RHEL 8+/Fedora package manager

dnf is yum's successor with better performance, native Python 3, and transaction support. Used on RHEL 8+, Fedora, and CentOS 8+. The syntax is nearly identical to yum — most yum commands work with dnf as-is.

Syntax

dnf [OPTIONS] COMMAND [PACKAGE...]
# Common: sudo dnf install nginx | dnf search python3 | sudo dnf update

Parameters

Command/FlagDescription
install PKGInstall package(s)
remove PKGRemove package(s)
autoremoveRemove unused dependencies
group listList package groups

Example 1: Install with Module Streams

Scenario: Carol downloads an RPM for offline installation on an air-gapped server.

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

Output:

nginx-1.14.1-9.module_el8.8.0.x86_64.rpm 2.1 MB/s | 586 kB 00:00

📝 What happened: nginx RPM downloaded to /tmp/offline-pkgs/ for offline transfer. Use dnf download --resolve to include all dependencies. Critical for air-gapped environments where internet access is restricted.

Example 5: Undo Last Transaction

Scenario: Carol accidentally installed a package that broke a dependency. She rolls back.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo dnf history undo last

Output:

Undoing transaction 15 Removing: bad-package-1.0-1.el8.x86_64 Complete!

📝 What happened: Last transaction rolled back — the problematic package was removed. dnf maintains a full transaction history. Use dnf history list to see transaction IDs. dnf history is more reliable than yum history for rollbacks.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: dnf replaces yum in RHEL 8+. dnf module for version streams. dnf groupinstall for package groups. dnf history for transaction rollback. dnf autoremove cleans orphans. Most yum commands are alias for dnf.

dpkg

DEBIANPackage ManagementLow-LevelLFCS Domain 5

Debian Package Manager — low-level .deb package manipulation

dpkg is the low-level package tool for Debian systems. Unlike apt (which resolves dependencies), dpkg works directly with .deb files. Use for: installing local .deb files, listing package contents, verifying installed files, and querying installed packages.

Syntax

dpkg [OPTIONS] ACTION [PACKAGE...]
# Common: sudo dpkg -i package.deb | dpkg -l | dpkg -L nginx

Parameters

Flag/ActionDescription
-i FILE.debInstall a .deb file
-r PKGRemove package (keep config files)
-P PKGPurge package (remove config files too)
-l [PATTERN]List packages matching pattern
-L PKGList files installed by package
-s PKGShow package status
-S FILEPATHFind which package owns a file
-c FILE.debList contents of a .deb file
-I FILE.debShow info about a .deb file
--configure -aConfigure all unpacked but unconfigured packages
--get-selectionsShow package selections (installed state)
--verify PKGVerify package file integrity

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Debian Package

Daily Workflow: Carol installs and updates packages for the anihpj stack — Python, Django, PostgreSQL, Redis, and K8s tools. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

Example 1: Install a Local .deb File

Scenario: Alice downloaded a nginx-module.deb and installs it manually.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo dpkg -i /tmp/nginx-module.deb

Output:

Selecting previously unselected package nginx-module. (Reading database ... 45234 files and directories currently installed.) Preparing to unpack /tmp/nginx-module.deb ... Unpacking nginx-module (1.2.3) ... Setting up nginx-module (1.2.3) ...

📝 What happened: The .deb was unpacked and configured. dpkg installed only what was in the .deb — no dependency resolution. If dependencies are missing, use apt-get install -f afterward to fix them.

Example 2: List Files in a Package

Scenario: Carol checks which files the nginx package installed.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

dpkg -L nginx | grep -E "bin|sbin|conf"

Output:

/usr/sbin/nginx /etc/nginx/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/sites-available/ /etc/logrotate.d/nginx

📝 What happened: Key nginx files: binary at /usr/sbin/nginx, config at /etc/nginx/nginx.conf. Use dpkg -L to discover what a package installed and where. Equivalent to rpm -ql on RHEL.

Example 3: Find Package Owner

Scenario: Carol finds a suspicious binary and checks which package installed it.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

dpkg -S /usr/sbin/nginx

Output:

nginx: /usr/sbin/nginx

📝 What happened: /usr/sbin/nginx belongs to the "nginx" package — legitimate. If a file has no package owner, it may be manually placed or malicious. Use dpkg -S for security audits.

Example 4: Verify Package Integrity

Scenario: After a disk error, Carol verifies nginx files haven't been corrupted.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

dpkg --verify nginx

Output:

??5?????? /etc/nginx/nginx.conf missing /var/log/nginx/error.log

📝 What happened: Two issues: nginx.conf has MD5 checksum mismatch (was manually edited), and error.log is missing (log rotation deleted it). Critical flags: ??5 = checksum mismatch, missing = file gone. Run after suspected disk corruption.

Example 5: List All Installed Packages

Scenario: Carol generates an inventory of all installed packages for audit.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

dpkg -l | grep "^ii" | wc -l

Output:

847

📝 What happened: 847 packages are in "ii" (Installed, Desired=Install) state. dpkg -l shows all known packages; prefix codes: ii=installed, rc=removed-config-files, un=unknown. Use for compliance audits and system baselines.

Example 6: Remove a Package (Keep Configs)

Scenario: Carol removes an old monitoring agent but keeps its config for reference.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo dpkg -r monitoring-agent && ls /etc/monitoring-agent/

Output:

Removing monitoring-agent (1.0.1) ... config.yaml alerts.json dashboard.conf

📝 What happened: Package binaries removed but config files preserved in /etc/. -r = remove (keeps configs). Use -P (purge) to remove everything. This is useful for temporary removals where you plan to reinstall later.

Example 7: Purge a Package

Scenario: Carol completely removes nginx including all configs before a clean reinstall.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo dpkg -P nginx && ls /etc/nginx/ 2>&1

Output:

Purging configuration files for nginx (1.18.0) ... ls: cannot access '/etc/nginx/': No such file or directory

📝 What happened: -P (purge) removed binaries AND configs. The /etc/nginx/ directory is gone. Use purge when you want a truly clean slate. Contrast with -r which leaves configs behind.

Example 8: Inspect a .deb File

Scenario: Alice inspects a downloaded .deb before installing it to check what files it contains.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

dpkg -c /tmp/custom-package.deb | head -8

Output:

drwxr-xr-x root/root 0 2025-01-15 02:00 ./ drwxr-xr-x root/root 0 2025-01-15 02:00 ./usr/ drwxr-xr-x root/root 0 2025-01-15 02:00 ./usr/bin/ -rwxr-xr-x root/root 45678 2025-01-15 02:00 ./usr/bin/custom-tool drwxr-xr-x root/root 0 2025-01-15 02:00 ./etc/ -rw-r--r-- root/root 1234 2025-01-15 02:00 ./etc/custom.conf

📝 What happened: -c lists the archive contents without installing. Shows files, permissions, sizes, and timestamps. Always inspect .deb contents before installing from untrusted sources. Equivalent to tar -tvf for archives.

Example 9: Show .deb Metadata

Scenario: Carol checks the control info of a vendor-provided .deb before deployment.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

dpkg -I /tmp/vendor-tool.deb | grep -E "Package|Version|Depends|Maintainer"

Output:

Package: vendor-tool Version: 3.2.1-1 Depends: libssl3, python3 (>= 3.8), systemd Maintainer: VendorCorp

📝 What happened: -I shows the package control file (metadata). Dependencies: libssl3, python3, systemd. Always check Depends before installing with dpkg — if deps are missing, the install will fail. Use apt to resolve dependencies automatically.

Example 10: Configure Unpacked Packages

Scenario: After a power failure interrupted an installation, Carol configures all pending packages.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo dpkg --configure -a

Output:

Setting up nginx (1.18.0-0ubuntu1.4) ... Setting up postgresql-client (14+238) ... Processing triggers for man-db (2.10.2) ...

📝 What happened: Two packages that were unpacked but not configured are now fully set up. --configure -a is a rescue command — use it when dpkg was interrupted (power loss, killed process). It completes all pending configurations.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: dpkg -i file.deb installs locally (no deps). dpkg -r PKG removes (keep configs). dpkg -P PKG purges (remove all). dpkg -c file.deb lists contents. dpkg -I file.deb shows metadata. dpkg --configure -a rescues interrupted installs. dpkg --get-selections for package inventory. Use apt for dependency resolution; dpkg for low-level operations.

kernel-4.18.0-513.el8 Wed 15 Jan 2025 02:00:00 AM UTC nginx-1.14.1-9.el8 Wed 15 Jan 2025 02:00:05 AM UTC openssl-1.1.1k-9.el8 Tue 14 Jan 2025 11:00:00 PM UTC

Example 3: Find Owning Package

Scenario: Carol finds an unknown binary and traces it back to its package.

📁 Environment Snippet:

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

Output:

curl-7.61.1-30.el8.x86_64

📝 What happened: /usr/bin/curl belongs to curl-7.61.1. rpm -qf works even if the file was deleted — it queries the RPM database, not the filesystem. Use for forensic analysis of compromised systems.

Example 4: Verify Package

Scenario: Carol checks if any installed files have been tampered with.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

rpm -Va nginx

Output:

S.5....T. /etc/nginx/nginx.conf .M....... /var/log/nginx/access.log

📝 What happened: S=size changed, 5=MD5 changed, T=mtime changed (nginx.conf was edited). M=mode/permissions changed (access.log). Empty output = no changes. Use for intrusion detection and configuration management verification.

Example 5: Query Package Scripts

Scenario: Carol inspects the pre/post install scripts of a suspicious RPM before installing.

├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

rpm -qp --scripts suspicious-package.rpm

Output:

postinstall scriptlet: #!/bin/sh systemctl enable suspicious-service systemctl start suspicious-service

📝 What happened: The RPM has a post-install script that enables and starts a service. Always inspect RPM scripts before installing from untrusted sources. --scripts reveals what the package will do beyond just copying files.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: rpm -ivh installs RPMs. rpm -e removes. rpm -qa lists all packages. rpm -qf finds owning package. rpm -Va verifies integrity. rpm -qp --scripts inspects scripts. Use yum/dnf for dependency resolution; rpm for low-level queries.

Example 1: Full System Update

Scenario: Carol updates all packages on an Arch-based container.

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

:: Synchronizing package databases... core is up to date extra 1850.2 KiB 2.5M/s 00:00 :: Starting full system upgrade... there is nothing to do

📝 What happened: -Syu = Sync + refresh + sysupgrade (three operations combined). Database synced, no upgrades available. Arch is rolling-release — no version upgrades like Ubuntu, just continuous updates. Always -Syu before installing.

Scenario: Carol removes an old monitoring agent and its unused deps.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: pacman -Syu updates everything. -S PKG installs. -Rs PKG removes with deps. -Ss TERM searches. -Q queries local DB. pacman uses single letters (-S = sync, -Q = query) — memorize the flags.

pip installs Python packages from PyPI (Python Package Index). This is the most critical package manager for anihpj/jobpost — Django, DRF, gunicorn, and all Python dependencies are managed via pip.

  • Alice manages dev deps, Carol audits production deps
