Example 1: Allow Custom Service Port

📄 Context — Non-Standard Port Access:

# Django dev server runs on port 8000
# SELinux only allows http_port_t on specific ports (80, 443, 8008, etc.)
# nginx proxy_pass to port 8000 gets "Permission denied" in Enforcing
# Solution: add 8000 to http_port_t with semanage

Scenario: Alice adds port 8000 to the allowed HTTP ports for nginx proxying.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8000 && sudo semanage port -l | grep http_port_t

Output:

http_port_t tcp 80, 81, 443, 488, 8000, 8008, 8009, 8443, 9000

📝 What happened: Port 8000 is now an allowed HTTP port. nginx can proxy to it without SELinux blocking. Without this, proxy_pass http://localhost:8000 triggers AVC denials even though iptables and file permissions are correct. Remove: semanage port -d -t http_port_t -p tcp 8000.

Example 2: Set Custom File Context

📄 Context — Non-Standard Web Root:

# nginx serves static files from /lpj/jobpost/static/
# SELinux only allows httpd to read files labeled httpd_sys_content_t
# Custom paths need custom file context mappings
# Without this, nginx returns 403 Forbidden despite correct Unix perms

Scenario: Carol sets SELinux context so nginx can serve static files from the project directory.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/lpj/jobpost/static(/.*)?" && sudo restorecon -Rv /lpj/jobpost/static && ls -lZ /lpj/jobpost/static/style.css

Output:

Relabeled /lpj/jobpost/static from unconfined_u:object_r:default_t to unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t -rw-r--r-- 1 alice developers unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t 1234 Jun 4 10:30 style.css

📝 What happened: semanage fcontext -a created a persistent mapping. restorecon -Rv applied it recursively with verbose output. The file now has httpd_sys_content_t context — nginx can read it. The (/.*)? regex matches the directory AND all contents recursively.

Example 3: List and Toggle Booleans

📄 Context — Feature Toggle:

# SELinux booleans toggle specific behaviors
# httpd_can_network_connect = allow web server to make outbound connections
# Needed for nginx → Django proxy_pass
# Without this, nginx can listen but can't connect upstream

Scenario: Alice enables the boolean allowing nginx to connect to backend services.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo semanage boolean -m --on httpd_can_network_connect && getsebool httpd_can_network_connect

Output:

httpd_can_network_connect --> on

📝 What happened: nginx can now make outbound TCP connections (proxy_pass to Django). Without this boolean, even with correct ports and contexts, nginx can't connect to backend services. Common booleans to know: httpd_can_network_connect, httpd_enable_cgi, httpd_use_nfs.

Example 4: Check SELinux User Mappings

📄 Context — User Role Assignment:

# SELinux maps Linux users to SELinux users
# SELinux users have defined roles and access levels
# root → unconfined_u (full access)
# Regular users → user_u (restricted)
# Service accounts → system_u

Scenario: Eve audits SELinux user mappings during a security review.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo semanage login -l

Output:

Login Name SELinux User MLS/MCS Range __default__ unconfined_u s0-s0:c0.c1023 root unconfined_u s0-s0:c0.c1023 system_u system_u s0-s0:c0.c1023

📝 What happened: Default mapping is unconfined_u (full access). system_u is for system processes. To restrict a user: semanage login -a -s user_u alice maps alice to the restricted user_u role. semanage user -l lists all SELinux users and their roles.

Example 5: Remove a Port Mapping

📄 Context — Cleanup After Service Removal:

# When a service is decommissioned, remove its SELinux port mappings
# Keeps the policy clean and prevents port reuse confusion
# Always verify with -l before and after deletion
# semanage changes are persistent across reboots

Scenario: Carol removes the port 8000 mapping after decommissioning the dev server.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo semanage port -d -t http_port_t -p tcp 8000 && sudo semanage port -l | grep http_port_t

Output:

http_port_t tcp 80, 81, 443, 488, 8008, 8009, 8443, 9000

📝 What happened: Port 8000 removed from http_port_t. -d deletes the mapping. The change is permanent and immediate — no reload needed. Always verify with -l after changes. semanage is the authoritative tool for SELinux policy management — changes made here persist across reboots and policy updates.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: semanage port -a -t TYPE -p PROTO PORT allows port. fcontext -a -t TYPE PATH sets file context. boolean -m --on BOOL toggles features. login -l shows user mappings. Changes are permanent — no reload needed. Use restorecon after fcontext changes. -l lists current state. -d deletes mappings.

restorecon

SELINUXSecurityRHELLFCS Domain 5

Restore default SELinux file contexts — fix mislabeled files

restorecon resets file SELinux contexts to their defaults based on semanage fcontext mappings. Essential after semanage fcontext -a to apply the new mapping to existing files. Also fixes contexts after moving/copying files.

Syntax

restorecon [OPTIONS] PATH...
# Common: sudo restorecon -Rv /lpj/jobpost/static | sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www

Parameters

FlagDescription
-RRecursive — process all files under directories
-vVerbose — show each file's context change
-nDry run — show what WOULD change, don't change
-FForce reset (even if context appears correct)
-iIgnore files that don't exist

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — After File Operations

# Alice moved static files with cp (preserves original context on some systems):
alice@prod-web-01:~$ sudo cp -r /tmp/deploy/static /lpj/jobpost/
alice@prod-web-01:~$ ls -lZ /lpj/jobpost/static/style.css
unconfined_u:object_r:user_tmp_t style.css   # Wrong context!
alice@prod-web-01:~$ sudo restorecon -Rv /lpj/jobpost/static
Relabeled /lpj/jobpost/static/style.css from user_tmp_t to httpd_sys_content_t
# Now nginx can serve the file — context is correct

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Restore Context

Daily Workflow: Carol and Eve manage encryption, SSH, firewalls, and SELinux for production security. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical restorecon usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo restorecon -Rv /lpj/

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Fix Contexts After File Copy

📄 Context — Deployment Relabeling:

# cp preserves the source file's SELinux context
# Files from /tmp get user_tmp_t — nginx can't read them
# mv preserves context too (within same filesystem)
# restorecon fixes: reads semanage fcontext DB, applies correct label

Scenario: Alice fixes file contexts after deploying static files.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo restorecon -Rv /lpj/jobpost/static/

Output:

Relabeled /lpj/jobpost/static/ from unconfined_u:object_r:user_tmp_t to unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t Relabeled /lpj/jobpost/static/style.css from unconfined_u:object_r:user_tmp_t to unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t Relabeled /lpj/jobpost/static/main.js from unconfined_u:object_r:user_tmp_t to unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t

📝 What happened: -R recursively processed the directory, -v showed each change. All files went from user_tmp_t (wrong — from /tmp) to httpd_sys_content_t (correct — nginx readable). After restorecon, nginx returns 200 instead of 403.

Example 2: Dry Run Before Change

📄 Context — Safe Preview:

# -n shows what WOULD change without actually changing
# Always preview before bulk relabeling
# Large directory trees can take time to relabel
# Preview confirms the scope is correct

Scenario: Carol previews which files would be relabeled before running restorecon.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo restorecon -Rnv /lpj/

Output:

Would relabel /lpj/jobpost/static/style.css from unconfined_u:object_r:user_tmp_t to unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t Would relabel /lpj/ops/logs/access.log from unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t to unconfined_u:object_r:var_log_t

📝 What happened: -n showed what files would change but made no changes. The files still have their old contexts. This is crucial for verifying the scope — you don't want restorecon accidentally relabeling system files. If the preview looks correct, run without -n.

Example 3: Relabel After semanage fcontext

📄 Context — Complete the Two-Step Process:

# Step 1: semanage fcontext -a creates the mapping (persistent)
# Step 2: restorecon applies it to existing files
# Without step 2, new mapping only affects future file creation
# Always run restorecon after semanage fcontext -a

Scenario: Alice completes the two-step process after adding a new SELinux fcontext mapping.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/lpj/jobpost/templates(/.*)?" && sudo restorecon -Rv /lpj/jobpost/templates/

Output:

Relabeled /lpj/jobpost/templates from unconfined_u:object_r:default_t to unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t Relabeled /lpj/jobpost/templates/base.html from unconfined_u:object_r:default_t to unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t

📝 What happened: The semanage fcontext -a → restorecon two-step pattern is complete. Step 1 added the mapping to the policy database (persistent). Step 2 applied it to existing files. New files created in this directory will automatically get the correct context.

Example 4: Force Reset All Contexts

📄 Context — Full System Relabel:

# After disabling and re-enabling SELinux, full relabel is needed
# touch /.autorelabel + reboot is the standard method
# restorecon -RF / applies contexts without reboot
# Use with caution — affects the entire filesystem

Scenario: Carol force-resets SELinux contexts on a single directory.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo restorecon -RFv /lpj/jobpost/ && echo "Force reset complete"

Output:

Relabeled /lpj/jobpost/models.py from unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t to unconfined_u:object_r:default_t Relabeled /lpj/jobpost/views.py from unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t to unconfined_u:object_r:default_t Force reset complete

📝 What happened: -F forced reset even for files that already had a context. Python files were incorrectly labeled httpd_sys_content_t — reset to default_t. Use -F sparingly: it resets ALL files regardless of current context. Without -F, restorecon only fixes mismatched contexts.

Example 5: System-Wide Relabel on Boot

📄 Context — Post-Disaster Recovery:

# After major SELinux policy changes or filesystem corruption
# /.autorelabel triggers full relabel on next boot
# System reboots, relabels EVERYTHING, reboots again
# The nuclear option — but sometimes necessary

Scenario: Carol schedules a full SELinux relabel for the next reboot.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo touch /.autorelabel && echo "Full relabel scheduled for next boot" && ls -la /.autorelabel

Output:

Full relabel scheduled for next boot -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 0 Jun 4 10:30 /.autorelabel

📝 What happened: The /.autorelabel flag file tells the system to relabel all filesystems on next boot. After relabeling, the file is automatically removed. The boot takes much longer (minutes to hours depending on disk size). Equivalent to restorecon -RFv / but done during early boot for safety.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: restorecon -Rv PATH fixes contexts recursively. -n dry run. -F force reset. Always run after semanage fcontext -a. /.autorelabel triggers full relabel on boot. cp/mv preserve source contexts — use restorecon after. Use matchpathcon PATH to check what context a file SHOULD have.

🔧 Boot & Kernel Management

Commands for managing the bootloader, kernel modules, and initial RAM disk. The anihpj/jobpost team uses these for kernel tuning, boot repair, and module management across all production servers.

grub-mkconfig

BOOTBoot & KernelCoreLFCS Domain 2

Generate GRUB bootloader configuration — rebuild /boot/grub/grub.cfg

grub-mkconfig generates the GRUB2 bootloader configuration file from templates in /etc/grub.d/ and settings in /etc/default/grub. Run after kernel updates, boot parameter changes, or disk reconfiguration. On most systems, update-grub is a wrapper for this command.

Syntax

sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg
# Debian/Ubuntu shortcut: sudo update-grub
# Generated config: /boot/grub/grub.cfg (DO NOT edit directly)

Parameters

FlagDescription
-o FILEOutput to FILE (usually /boot/grub/grub.cfg)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Post-Kernel Update

# Carol rebuilds GRUB config after a kernel update on prod-db-01:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg
Generating grub configuration file ...
Found linux image: /boot/vmlinuz-6.5.0-41-generic
Found initrd image: /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-41-generic
Found linux image: /boot/vmlinuz-6.5.0-35-generic
Found initrd image: /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-35-generic
done
# Now the new kernel (6.5.0-41) will be the default at next boot

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — GRUB Config

Daily Workflow: Carol manages the boot process and kernel modules on Ubuntu 24.04 with Cilium networking. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical grub-mkconfig usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg

Example 1: Rebuild After Kernel Install

📄 Context — Kernel Upgrade Workflow:

# apt install linux-image-6.5.0-41 installs the kernel
# grub-mkconfig adds it to the boot menu
# Without this step, GRUB doesn't know about the new kernel
# Always run after kernel updates

Scenario: Carol regenerates GRUB config after a kernel security patch.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg 2>&1 | grep -E "Found|done"

Output:

Found linux image: /boot/vmlinuz-6.5.0-41-generic Found initrd image: /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-41-generic Found linux image: /boot/vmlinuz-6.5.0-35-generic done

📝 What happened: GRUB found two kernels: the new 6.5.0-41 and the old 6.5.0-35. The new kernel becomes the default (first in the list). The old kernel remains as a fallback option in the boot menu. Always keep at least one known-good kernel for recovery.

Example 2: Debian/Ubuntu Shortcut

📄 Context — Distribution-Specific Wrapper:

# update-grub is a Debian/Ubuntu wrapper script
# Internally calls: grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg
# Same effect, fewer keystrokes
# RHEL uses: grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg

Scenario: Alice uses the shortcut command after installing a new kernel.

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

Sourcing file `/etc/default/grub' Sourcing file `/etc/default/grub.d/init-select.cfg' Generating grub configuration file ... Found linux image: /boot/vmlinuz-6.5.0-41-generic Found initrd image: /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-41-generic done

📝 What happened: update-grub automatically found the correct output path. It sources /etc/default/grub for boot parameters (console, timeout, default kernel). On RHEL: grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg. The boot config path differs by distro.

# Edit /etc/default/grub to add kernel boot parameters
# GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="cgroup_memory=1 swapaccount=1"
# Then regenerate config to apply
# Essential for enabling cgroup v1 on older kernels for Docker

Scenario: Carol adds kernel parameters for container support then rebuilds GRUB.

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

📝 What happened: cgroup_memory=1 enables memory cgroup accounting (needed for Docker resource limits). swapaccount=1 enables swap accounting. Changes take effect on next reboot. Always verify with cat /proc/cmdline after reboot to confirm parameters were applied.

Example 4: Change Default Boot Entry

📄 Context — Kernel Rollback:

# New kernel causes issues → boot the old one by default
# GRUB_DEFAULT=0 means first entry (newest)
# GRUB_DEFAULT="1>2" means second menu, third entry (submenu)
# Change to "Advanced options > old kernel"

Scenario: Alice sets the previous kernel as default after a problematic update.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo sed -i 's/^GRUB_DEFAULT=.*/GRUB_DEFAULT="1>2"/' /etc/default/grub && sudo update-grub && grep GRUB_DEFAULT /etc/default/grub

Output:

GRUB_DEFAULT="1>2" done

📝 What happened: 1>2 selects submenu 1, entry 2 (typically the second kernel in "Advanced options"). After reboot, the older kernel boots by default. The problematic kernel is still available for manual selection. This is the safest rollback — no files deleted, just default changed.

📄 Context — Configuration Audit:

# grub.cfg is auto-generated — don't edit directly
# But you can inspect it to verify what was generated

Scenario: Carol verifies the generated GRUB config contains both kernels.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

grep -E "menuentry |linux |initrd " /boot/grub/grub.cfg | head -8

Output:

menuentry 'Ubuntu' ... linux /boot/vmlinuz-6.5.0-41-generic root=UUID=abc123 ro initrd /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-41-generic menuentry 'Ubuntu, with Linux 6.5.0-35-generic' ... linux /boot/vmlinuz-6.5.0-35-generic root=UUID=abc123 ro initrd /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-35-generic

📝 What happened: Two menu entries confirmed: the new 6.5.0-41 kernel (default) and the old 6.5.0-35 (fallback). Both point to the same root filesystem (UUID abc123). The config is syntactically correct. NEVER hand-edit grub.cfg — always regenerate with grub-mkconfig.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg generates config. update-grub is the Debian/Ubuntu shortcut. Edit /etc/default/grub for boot parameters. RHEL uses grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg. Never hand-edit grub.cfg. GRUB_DEFAULT sets default entry. Run after every kernel update.

grub-install

BOOTBoot & KernelCoreLFCS Domain 2

Install GRUB bootloader to a device — write boot code to MBR or ESP

grub-install writes the GRUB bootloader to a disk's Master Boot Record (BIOS) or EFI System Partition (UEFI). Needed after disk replacement, boot corruption, or when moving a system to new hardware. Different from grub-mkconfig (which only updates the menu).

Syntax

sudo grub-install [OPTIONS] DEVICE
# BIOS: sudo grub-install /dev/sda
# UEFI: sudo grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --efi-directory=/boot/efi

Parameters

FlagDescription
--target=PLATFORMTarget platform: x86_64-efi, i386-pc (BIOS), arm64-efi
--efi-directory=DIREFI System Partition mount point (UEFI only)
--boot-directory=DIRBoot directory (default: /boot)
--recheckRe-probe device map before installing
--forceForce installation even if problems detected

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Boot Repair After Disk Failure

# Carol repairs GRUB after replacing a failed boot disk on prod-db-01:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo grub-install /dev/sda
Installing for i386-pc platform.
Installation finished. No error reported.
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo update-grub
# Now the server can boot from the new disk

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — GRUB Install

Daily Workflow: Carol manages the boot process and kernel modules on Ubuntu 24.04 with Cilium networking. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical grub-install usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo grub-install /dev/sda

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: BIOS System Install

📄 Context — Legacy Boot Repair:

# Older servers use BIOS/MBR boot
# grub-install writes stage1 to the MBR (first 446 bytes of disk)
# stage2 is in /boot/grub/ (reads filesystem)
# BIOS systems use /dev/sda (whole disk, not partition)

Scenario: Carol reinstalls GRUB on a BIOS-based server after disk replacement.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo grub-install /dev/sda && echo "GRUB reinstalled on MBR"

Output:

Installing for i386-pc platform. Installation finished. No error reported. GRUB reinstalled on MBR

📝 What happened: GRUB was written to the Master Boot Record of /dev/sda. Note: it's /dev/sda (the whole disk), NOT /dev/sda1 (a partition). The MBR is in the first 512 bytes of the disk, before any partition. BIOS reads the MBR at boot time to find GRUB.

Example 2: UEFI System Install

📄 Context — Modern Boot Standard:

# All modern servers use UEFI (not BIOS)
# GRUB is installed to the EFI System Partition (ESP)
# ESP is mounted at /boot/efi (VFAT filesystem)
# UEFI boots from .efi files, not MBR sectors

Scenario: Alice installs GRUB on a UEFI-based server after a firmware update.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --efi-directory=/boot/efi --bootloader-id=Ubuntu && ls /boot/efi/EFI/ubuntu/grubx64.efi

Output:

Installing for x86_64-efi platform. Installation finished. No error reported. /boot/efi/EFI/ubuntu/grubx64.efi

📝 What happened: --target=x86_64-efi selected UEFI mode. --efi-directory pointed to the ESP. --bootloader-id created the directory name under ESP. The .efi file is now registered with the UEFI firmware. Use efibootmgr -v to verify the UEFI boot entry.

Example 3: Force Reinstall

📄 Context — Corrupted Bootloader:

# Bootloader corruption: "GRUB error: no such partition"
# --force overrides GRUB's safety checks
# --recheck rescans device mappings
# Use when GRUB refuses to install on a valid configuration

Scenario: Carol forces GRUB reinstallation after boot sector corruption.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo grub-install --force --recheck /dev/sda

Output:

Installing for i386-pc platform. /dev/sda appears to contain a partition table (dos). Proceeding anyway. Installation finished. No error reported.

📝 What happened: --force bypassed the warning about the existing partition table (normal for MBR disks — GRUB warns but it's fine). --recheck rebuilt the device map. After this, run update-grub to regenerate the menu. The server now boots normally.

Example 4: Specify Custom Boot Directory

📄 Context — Separate /boot Partition:

# Some setups have /boot on a separate partition
# --boot-directory tells GRUB where to find its files
# Useful during system rescue when /boot is mounted elsewhere
# Default is /boot (relative to root)

Scenario: Carol reinstalls GRUB from a rescue environment with /boot mounted at /mnt/boot.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo grub-install --boot-directory=/mnt/boot /dev/sda && ls /mnt/boot/grub/

Output:

Installing for i386-pc platform. Installation finished. No error reported. fonts grub.cfg grubenv i386-pc locale unicode.pf2

📝 What happened: GRUB was installed using files from /mnt/boot (the mounted rescue target). This is the standard rescue workflow: mount the target system's / and /boot, chroot if needed, then grub-install with --boot-directory pointing to the mounted /boot.

Example 5: Verify Installation

📄 Context — Post-Install Validation:

# After grub-install, verify the bootloader was written correctly
# BIOS: check MBR signature (last 2 bytes = 0x55AA)
# UEFI: check efibootmgr for the boot entry
# GRUB files should exist in /boot/grub/

Scenario: Alice verifies the GRUB installation was successful.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo dd if=/dev/sda bs=512 count=1 2>/dev/null | od -An -tx1 | tail -1 | grep "55 aa" && echo "MBR signature OK" || echo "MBR check failed"

Output:

00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 55 aa MBR signature OK

📝 What happened: The MBR ends with 55 aa — the magic boot signature. This confirms GRUB's stage1 was written correctly. For UEFI: efibootmgr -v shows the boot order. Always verify after grub-install before rebooting — a botched installation means an unbootable system.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: grub-install /dev/sda for BIOS. grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --efi-directory=/boot/efi for UEFI. --force bypasses warnings. --boot-directory for rescue scenarios. Always run update-grub after. Combine grub-install + grub-mkconfig for complete boot repair.

lsmod

KERNELBoot & KernelCoreLFCS Domain 2

List loaded kernel modules — see what's currently in the running kernel

lsmod displays all currently loaded Linux kernel modules (drivers). Shows module name, size, and which other modules depend on it. Reads from /proc/modules. Essential for checking if a driver loaded correctly after boot or module installation.

Syntax

lsmod
# Common: lsmod | grep nfs | lsmod | sort -k2 -rn | head -10

Parameters

NoteDescription
No flagslsmod takes no options — just displays all loaded modules

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Driver Verification

# Carol checks if the Cilium-related kernel modules loaded correctly:
carol@prod-web-01:~$ lsmod | grep -E "bpffs|xt_bpf|cls_bpf"
bpffs                  20480  2
xt_bpf                 16384  32
cls_bpf                24576  0

Examples

Example 1: List All Loaded Modules

📄 Context — System Inventory:

# lsmod gives a quick overview of the kernel's driver state
# Three columns: Module, Size (bytes), Used by (dependency count + names)
# Module count varies: ~50 for minimal, ~200 for full server
# More modules = more kernel memory used

Scenario: Carol gets a quick inventory of all loaded kernel modules.

Command:

lsmod | head -10 && echo "---" && lsmod | wc -l

Output:

Module Size Used by xt_bpf 16384 32 bpffs 20480 2 nf_tables 282624 0 x_tables 53248 2 ext4 933888 1 ... --- 124

📝 What happened: 124 modules loaded. The "Used by" column shows dependency count — xt_bpf is used by 32 other modules (Cilium heavily uses BPF). A module with "Used by 0" is loaded but not actively referenced. This is the kernel's equivalent of ps aux for drivers.

Example 2: Check Specific Driver

📄 Context — Hardware Troubleshooting:

# After installing a new NIC, check if the driver loaded
# If missing, the hardware won't work
# lsmod | grep DRIVER quickly confirms or denies
# Missing driver → modprobe DRIVER to load it

Scenario: Alice verifies the network driver loaded after installing a new NIC.

Command:

lsmod | grep -E "e1000|igb|ixgbe|r8169|tg3"

Output:

igb 249856 0

📝 What happened: The igb driver (Intel Gigabit Ethernet) is loaded. 249KB module size, 0 dependent modules. If no output appeared, the driver wasn't loaded — check lspci -k to see which driver the kernel assigned to the NIC, then modprobe to load it.

Example 3: Find Largest Modules

📄 Context — Memory Usage Audit:

# Kernel modules consume non-pageable kernel memory
# Largest modules are candidates for blacklisting if unused
# Sort by size to find memory hogs
# GPU and filesystem drivers are typically the largest

Scenario: Carol identifies the most memory-hungry kernel modules.

Command:

lsmod | sort -k2 -rn | head -6

Output:

Module Size Used by ext4 933888 1 nf_tables 282624 0 igb 249856 0 x_tables 53248 2 bpffs 20480 2

📝 What happened: ext4 (filesystem driver) is the largest at 933KB. nf_tables (firewall) at 282KB is loaded but unused (Used by 0) — could be blacklisted to save memory. igb at 249KB is the network driver. sort -k2 -rn sorts column 2 numerically, reversed (largest first).

Example 4: Find Module Dependencies

📄 Context — Dependency Analysis:

# "Used by" shows which modules depend on this one
# High dependency count = critical module
# Removing a module with dependents requires removing those first
# Helps understand why a module won't unload (rmmod fails)

Scenario: Alice checks why she can't unload a module — it has dependents.

Command:

lsmod | grep x_tables

Output:

x_tables 53248 2 xt_bpf,iptable_filter

📝 What happened: x_tables is used by 2 modules: xt_bpf and iptable_filter. You can't rmmod x_tables until those dependents are removed first: sudo rmmod xt_bpf iptable_filter && sudo rmmod x_tables. modprobe -r handles dependency removal automatically (unlike rmmod).

Example 5: Compare with modinfo

📄 Context — Deep Driver Inspection:

# lsmod shows WHAT is loaded; modinfo shows details ABOUT it
# Pipe lsmod output to modinfo for detailed driver information
# Useful for checking module version, author, license, parameters
# modinfo reads from /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/

Scenario: Carol checks detailed info about the loaded network driver.

Command:

lsmod | awk '/igb/ {print $1}' | xargs modinfo | grep -E "filename|version|author|description"

Output:

filename: /lib/modules/6.5.0-41-generic/kernel/drivers/net/ethernet/intel/igb/igb.ko version: 5.11.0-rc2 author: Intel Corporation, description: Intel(R) Gigabit Ethernet Network Driver

📝 What happened: The igb driver version 5.11.0-rc2, from Intel, located in the standard kernel module tree. lsmod → modinfo is the standard workflow: find the module name with lsmod, then inspect it with modinfo. The .ko extension = kernel object (compiled module).

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: lsmod lists loaded modules (no options). Reads /proc/modules. Three columns: Module, Size, Used by. lsmod | grep NAME checks if driver loaded. sort -k2 -rn finds largest modules. "Used by 0" = loaded but unused. Combine with modinfo for details.

modprobe

KERNELBoot & KernelCoreLFCS Domain 2

Add/remove kernel modules with dependency resolution — smarter than insmod/rmmod

modprobe loads and unloads kernel modules with automatic dependency handling. When you modprobe e1000, it loads e1000 AND all modules it depends on. Smart, safe, and the preferred tool over the lower-level insmod/rmmod.

Syntax

sudo modprobe [OPTIONS] MODULE
# Common: sudo modprobe e1000 | sudo modprobe -r e1000 | modprobe -c | modprobe --show-depends e1000

Parameters

FlagDescription
-rRemove module (and unused dependencies)
-cShow complete module configuration
--show-dependsShow what modules would be loaded (dry run)
-vVerbose — show each step
-fForce — load even if version mismatch
-nDry run — show what WOULD be done

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Module not found or error

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Load Cilium BPF Modules

# Carol loads BPF kernel modules required by Cilium on prod-web-01:
carol@prod-web-01:~$ sudo modprobe bpffs
carol@prod-web-01:~$ lsmod | grep bpffs
bpffs                  20480  0
carol@prod-web-01:~$ modprobe --show-depends bpffs
insmod /lib/modules/6.5.0-41-generic/kernel/fs/bpf/bpffs.ko

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Load Module

Daily Workflow: Carol manages the boot process and kernel modules on Ubuntu 24.04 with Cilium networking. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical modprobe usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo modprobe overlay

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Load a Module

📄 Context — On-Demand Driver Loading:

# Some drivers aren't auto-loaded at boot
# modprobe loads the module AND all its dependencies
# Unlike insmod, you don't need the full .ko path
# Reads module database: /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/modules.dep

Scenario: Alice loads a kernel module needed for a new hardware device.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo modprobe e1000 && lsmod | grep e1000

Output:

e1000 159744 0

📝 What happened: The e1000 module and all its dependencies were loaded. Just the module name is enough — no path needed. If the module doesn't exist, modprobe returns "modprobe: FATAL: Module e1000 not found." Check /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/ for available modules.

Example 2: Remove a Module

📄 Context — Driver Cleanup:

# -r removes the module AND unused dependencies
# Safer than rmmod (which removes only the named module)
# If dependents are in use, modprobe -r fails gracefully
# rmmod would succeed but leave dependents orphaned

Scenario: Carol removes an unused network driver module.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo modprobe -r e1000 && lsmod | grep e1000 || echo "Module removed"

Output:

Module removed

📝 What happened: e1000 and its unused dependencies were removed. If the module is in use (Used by > 0), modprobe -r fails with "modprobe: FATAL: Module e1000 is in use." Check with lsmod | grep e1000 to see what's using it first. modprobe -r --force overrides but is dangerous.

Example 3: Dry Run Dependencies

📄 Context — Pre-Load Analysis:

# Before loading, see what would be loaded
# --show-depends lists ALL modules that would be installed
# Shows the chain: module → dep1 → dep2
# Helps troubleshoot "why is this module loading that one?"

Scenario: Alice checks what modules will be loaded before committing.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

modprobe --show-depends xt_bpf

Output:

insmod /lib/modules/6.5.0-41-generic/kernel/net/netfilter/x_tables.ko insmod /lib/modules/6.5.0-41-generic/kernel/net/netfilter/xt_bpf.ko

📝 What happened: Loading xt_bpf would also load x_tables (its dependency). The order matters: x_tables first, then xt_bpf. This is a dry run — no modules were actually loaded. Use this before loading unfamiliar modules to understand the dependency chain.

Example 4: Module Configuration

📄 Context — Module Aliases and Blacklists:

# modprobe -c shows the complete module configuration
# Includes aliases (e.g., "pci:v00008086..." maps to e1000)
# Blacklists prevent auto-loading
# Options set module parameters at load time

Scenario: Carol checks if a module is blacklisted before troubleshooting.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

modprobe -c | grep -E "blacklist|^alias.*e1000" | head -5

Output:

blacklist nouveau blacklist floppy alias pci:v00008086d000010D3sv*sd*bc*sc*i* e1000 alias pci:v00008086d000010D9sv*sd*bc*sc*i* e1000

📝 What happened: nouveau and floppy are blacklisted (won't auto-load). The alias lines map PCI device IDs to the e1000 driver — when the kernel detects a matching PCI device, it knows to load e1000. Blacklists are in /etc/modprobe.d/*.conf. Add blacklist MODULE to prevent loading.

Example 5: Load with Parameters

📄 Context — Driver Tuning:

# Some modules accept parameters at load time
# Parameters control driver behavior (debug, buffer sizes, etc.)
# modprobe MODULE param=value sets parameters
# Check available params with: modinfo -p MODULE

Scenario: Alice loads a network driver with debug logging enabled.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo modprobe e1000 debug=16 && cat /sys/module/e1000/parameters/debug

Output:

16

📝 What happened: The e1000 module loaded with debug level 16 (verbose logging). /sys/module/MODULE/parameters/ shows current parameter values. Persistent parameters go in /etc/modprobe.d/e1000.conf: options e1000 debug=16. After changing, reload with modprobe -r e1000 && modprobe e1000.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: modprobe MODULE loads with deps. modprobe -r MODULE removes. --show-depends previews. -c shows config. -v verbose. -n dry run. -f force. Reads /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/modules.dep. Blacklists in /etc/modprobe.d/. Prefer over insmod/rmmod for dependency safety.

modinfo

KERNELBoot & KernelLFCS Domain 2

Display kernel module information — version, author, parameters, dependencies

modinfo shows detailed metadata about a kernel module: its description, author, license, version, dependencies, and available parameters. Reads from the module's .ko file in /lib/modules/. Essential for understanding what a module does before loading it.

Syntax

modinfo [OPTIONS] MODULE
# Common: modinfo e1000 | modinfo -p e1000 | modinfo -F description e1000

Parameters

FlagDescription
-p, --parametersShow only module parameters
-F FIELD, --field=FIELDShow only a specific field (author, description, etc.)
-n, --nullUse null byte separator (script-friendly)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Module found
1Module not found

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — BPF Module Inspection

# Carol inspects the xt_bpf module before loading it for Cilium:
carol@prod-web-01:~$ modinfo xt_bpf
filename:       /lib/modules/6.5.0-41-generic/kernel/net/netfilter/xt_bpf.ko
license:        GPL
description:    Xtables: BPF match module
author:         Willem de Bruijn 
depends:        x_tables
name:           xt_bpf
# xt_bpf depends on x_tables — modprobe will load both automatically

Examples

Example 1: Full Module Info

📄 Context — Module Vetting:

# Before loading a module, inspect its metadata
# Verify it's from a trusted source (author, license)
# Check dependencies to understand what else gets loaded
# Version mismatch = potential instability

Scenario: Alice vets a kernel module before loading it on a production server.

Command:

modinfo e1000

Output:

filename: /lib/modules/6.5.0-41-generic/kernel/drivers/net/ethernet/intel/e1000/e1000.ko license: GPL v2 description: Intel(R) PRO/1000 Network Driver author: Intel Corporation, srcversion: A1B2C3D4E5F6 depends: retpoline: Y name: e1000 vermagic: 6.5.0-41-generic SMP preempt mod_unload

📝 What happened: The e1000 module is from Intel, GPL licensed, with no dependencies. vermagic shows the kernel version it was built for — must match the running kernel. retpoline: Y means it has Spectre mitigation. srcversion is a hash of the source — changes when the module is rebuilt.

Example 2: List Module Parameters

📄 Context — Driver Tuning Options:

# -p shows all tunable parameters for a module
# Parameters control driver behavior at load time
# Set with: modprobe MODULE param=value
# Or persistently in /etc/modprobe.d/MODULE.conf

Scenario: Carol checks what parameters are available for the network driver.

Command:

modinfo -p e1000

Output:

debug:Debug level (0=none,...,16=all) (int) copybreak:Maximum size of packet that is copied to a new buffer on receive (uint) SmartPowerDownEnable:Enable PHY smart power down (array of int) InterruptThrottleRate:Interrupt Throttle Rate (array of int)

📝 What happened: Four tunable parameters: debug level, copybreak buffer size, power management, and interrupt throttling. (int) = integer type. To load with debug: modprobe e1000 debug=16. Persistent: echo "options e1000 debug=16" > /etc/modprobe.d/e1000.conf.

Example 3: Extract Single Field

📄 Context — Scripting and Automation:

# -F extracts a single field for use in scripts
# Much cleaner than grep/cut on full modinfo output
# Available fields: author, description, license, depends, version
# Returns empty string if field doesn't exist

Scenario: Alice's deploy script checks module versions programmatically.

Command:

echo "Driver: $(modinfo -F description e1000)" && echo "License: $(modinfo -F license e1000)"

Output:

Driver: Intel(R) PRO/1000 Network Driver License: GPL v2

📝 What happened: -F description extracted just the description. Much better than modinfo e1000 | grep description | cut -d: -f2. Use -F in scripts for reliable field extraction. Available fields vary by module — -F version may be empty if the module doesn't set it.

Example 4: Check Module Dependencies

📄 Context — Dependency Mapping:

# "depends" shows what other modules must be loaded first
# Helps understand the module loading order
# Empty depends = standalone module (no prerequisites)
# Chain: modprobe loads deps first, then the requested module

Scenario: Carol checks what xt_bpf depends on before loading it.

Command:

modinfo -F depends xt_bpf && modinfo -F depends x_tables

Output:

x_tables

📝 What happened: xt_bpf depends on x_tables. x_tables has no depends (empty output). The loading order: x_tables first, then xt_bpf. modprobe xt_bpf handles this automatically. insmod would NOT — it would fail if x_tables isn't already loaded. This is why modprobe is preferred.

Example 5: Module Not Found

📄 Context — Troubleshooting Missing Drivers:

# "modinfo: ERROR: Module not found" means the module isn't installed
# Check: ls /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/kernel/drivers/
# The module might need: apt install linux-modules-extra-$(uname -r)
# Or the driver name is different from what you expected

Scenario: Alice troubleshoots why a module isn't found on the system.

Command:

modinfo nonexistent-driver 2>&1 || echo "Module missing — search: apt search $(uname -r) | grep modules"

Output:

modinfo: ERROR: Module nonexistent-driver not found. Module missing — search: apt search $(uname -r) | grep modules

📝 What happened: The module doesn't exist. Solutions: (1) Install linux-modules-extra-$(uname -r) for additional drivers. (2) The driver may be built into the kernel (not a module) — check grep DRIVER /boot/config-$(uname -r). (3) The driver name may differ — search /lib/modules/ for similar names.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: modinfo MODULE shows metadata. -p lists parameters. -F FIELD extracts field. depends shows dependencies. Reads from /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/. Module must be installed (not just loaded). Built-in modules (not .ko files) have no modinfo output.

rmmod

KERNELBoot & KernelLFCS Domain 2

Remove a kernel module — simple unload without dependency handling

rmmod unloads a single kernel module. Unlike modprobe -r, it does NOT handle dependencies — if other modules depend on it, rmmod fails. Use modprobe -r for safe removal; use rmmod when you need precise single-module control.

Syntax

sudo rmmod [OPTIONS] MODULE
# Common: sudo rmmod e1000 | sudo rmmod -f e1000 | sudo rmmod -w e1000

Parameters

FlagDescription
-f, --forceForce removal (dangerous — can crash system)
-w, --waitWait until module is no longer in use
-v, --verboseVerbose output

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Module in use or not loaded

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Precise Module Unload

# Carol removes a specific module without touching its dependencies:
carol@prod-web-01:~$ lsmod | grep e1000
e1000                 159744  0
carol@prod-web-01:~$ sudo rmmod e1000
carol@prod-web-01:~$ lsmod | grep e1000 || echo "Module removed"

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Remove Module

Daily Workflow: Carol manages the boot process and kernel modules on Ubuntu 24.04 with Cilium networking. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical rmmod usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo rmmod old_driver

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Simple Unload

📄 Context — Clean Module Removal:

# Module has "Used by 0" — safe to remove
# rmmod only removes the named module
# Dependencies stay loaded (unlike modprobe -r)
# Useful when you want to keep dependency modules

Scenario: Alice removes an unused module without affecting its dependencies.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo rmmod e1000 && lsmod | grep e1000 || echo "e1000 removed"

Output:

e1000 removed

📝 What happened: Only e1000 was removed. Any modules it depends on stay loaded. If the module is in use (Used by > 0): "rmmod: ERROR: Module e1000 is in use." Check with lsmod before attempting. modprobe -r would also remove unused dependencies — rmmod is more surgical.

Example 2: Wait for Module to Be Free

📄 Context — Graceful Unload:

# -w waits until the module's reference count drops to 0
# Useful when a process is about to release the module
# Without -w, rmmod immediately fails if in use
# Blocks indefinitely — Ctrl+C to cancel

Scenario: Carol waits for a module to become free before removing it.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo rmmod -w e1000 && echo "Module unloaded"

Output:

# (blocks until module refcount reaches 0, then:) Module unloaded

📝 What happened: rmmod waited until no process was using e1000, then removed it. Use this when you know a process is about to stop using the module. Timeout: none — it waits forever. Safer than -f which forces removal even if in use (can crash the kernel).

Example 3: Force Removal

📄 Context — Emergency Unload:

# -f forces removal even if module is in use
# Dangerous — can cause kernel panic or data loss
# Only use when module is malfunctioning and system is unstable
# Last resort before reboot

Scenario: Carol force-removes a malfunctioning driver before it crashes the system.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo rmmod -f faulty_driver 2>&1 && echo "Force-removed" || echo "Force removal failed — reboot needed"

Output:

Force-removed

📝 What happened: The faulty driver was forcibly removed. Warning: processes using the module will crash. Kernel memory may be inconsistent. Always try modprobe -r first, then rmmod -w, and only use rmmod -f as a last resort. After force-removal, reboot at the earliest opportunity.

Example 4: Verbose Removal

📄 Context — Debugging Module Unload:

# -v shows what rmmod is doing step by step
# Helps debug "module in use" errors
# Shows reference count and dependent modules
# Combine with lsmod to cross-reference

Scenario: Alice debugs why a module won't unload using verbose mode.

└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo rmmod -v e1000 2>&1

Output:

rmmod: removing module 'e1000' rmmod: module 'e1000' has refcnt 0 rmmod: module 'e1000' successfully removed

📝 What happened: -v showed: module name, reference count (0 = no users), success. If refcnt > 0: "rmmod: ERROR: Module e1000 is in use." Then use lsmod | grep e1000 to see what's using it. If stuck, use rmmod -w to wait until refcnt drops to 0.

Example 5: Remove by Dependency Order

📄 Context — Manual Dependency Chain Removal:

# rmmod fails if dependents exist — must remove in reverse order
# lsmod "Used by" column shows the dependency chain
# Remove dependents first, then the target module
# modprobe -r MODULE does this automatically (preferred)

Scenario: Carol manually removes a module AND its dependents in correct order.

Command:

Output:

Both removed

📝 What happened: xt_bpf (dependent) removed first, then x_tables (dependency). Order matters: removing x_tables first would fail because xt_bpf uses it. This manual approach works but modprobe -r x_tables would handle the order automatically. Use rmmod when you need precise control; modprobe -r for convenience.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: rmmod MODULE removes single module. -f force (dangerous). -w waits until free. -v verbose debugging. Fails if module is in use. No dependency handling — remove dependents first, then the module. Use modprobe -r for safe automatic removal. lsmod check before attempting.

insmod

KERNELBoot & KernelLFCS Domain 2

Insert a kernel module — low-level load with full path, no dependency resolution

insmod loads a kernel module from a specific .ko file path. Unlike modprobe, it does NOT resolve dependencies — all prerequisite modules must already be loaded. Used for testing custom modules before installing them to the standard module tree.

Syntax

sudo insmod [OPTIONS] MODULE_PATH
# Common: sudo insmod /path/to/module.ko | sudo insmod ./my-custom-driver.ko

Parameters

FlagDescription
-fForce load even if kernel version mismatch
-vVerbose output

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success
1Error (missing dependency, invalid module)

Example 1: Load Module by Path

📄 Context — Custom Module Development:

Example 2: Dependency Error

📄 Context — Why modprobe Is Better:

# insmod fails if dependencies aren't loaded
# Error: "Unknown symbol in module" means a required function isn't available
# Fix: load the dependency module first, or use modprobe
# This is the #1 reason to prefer modprobe over insmod

Scenario: Alice tries to load a module without its dependency and gets an error.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo insmod /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/kernel/net/netfilter/xt_bpf.ko 2>&1

Output:

insmod: ERROR: could not insert module xt_bpf.ko: Unknown symbol in module

📝 What happened: xt_bpf depends on x_tables, but x_tables isn't loaded. Unknown symbol = a function xt_bpf needs (from x_tables) isn't available. Fix: sudo modprobe x_tables && sudo insmod xt_bpf.ko. Or simply: sudo modprobe xt_bpf (handles deps automatically).

Example 3: Force Load with Version Mismatch

📄 Context — Emergency Compatibility:

# -f forces loading even with kernel version mismatch
# " disagrees about version of symbol" errors

Scenario: Carol force-loads an older module during an emergency.

old_driver: disagrees about version of symbol module_layout old_driver: module verification failed: signature and/or required key missing old_driver: tainting kernel with non-GPL module

📝 What happened: The module loaded despite version mismatch and missing signature. The kernel is now "tainted" — marked as running non-standard code. Tainted kernels won't receive support from kernel developers. Rebuild the module for the correct kernel version as soon as possible.

Output:

3

📝 What happened: The custom network module loaded with debug level 3 and 4096 RX buffers. /sys/module/MODULE/parameters/ shows current parameter values. Unlike modprobe, insmod doesn't read /etc/modprobe.d/ — parameters must be passed explicitly on the command line. For production, install the module properly and use modprobe with config files.

Example 5: Verify Module Loaded Correctly

📄 Context — Post-Load Validation:

# If the module printed errors, it may be loaded but non-functional

Scenario: Carol verifies a newly loaded module is working correctly.

lpj/

Command:

sudo insmod /tmp/test-driver.ko && lsmod | grep test_driver && dmesg | tail -3

Output:

test_driver 16384 0 [ 1234.567] test_driver: loading out-of-tree module taints kernel. [ 1234.568] test_driver: module loaded successfully. version=1.0.0 [ 1234.569] test_driver: device registered as /dev/test0

📝 What happened: The module loaded and registered a device. dmesg shows: (1) kernel taint warning (out-of-tree = not from kernel source), (2) successful load with version, (3) device registration. The "taints kernel" warning is normal for custom modules — it just means the kernel is no longer in a supported state. Remove with sudo rmmod test_driver when done testing.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: insmod /path/to/module.ko loads from path. insmod module.ko param=val passes parameters. No dependency resolution — use modprobe instead. Requires full .ko path. -f forces version mismatch. Used for testing custom modules. "Unknown symbol" = missing dependency. Verify with lsmod + dmesg.

depmod

KERNELBoot & KernelLFCS Domain 2

Generate kernel module dependency database — rebuild modules.dep

depmod scans all installed kernel modules and builds the dependency database (modules.dep). modprobe reads this database to know which modules depend on which others. Run after installing new kernel modules or after make modules_install.

Syntax

sudo depmod [OPTIONS] [KERNEL_VERSION]
# Common: sudo depmod -a | sudo depmod 6.5.0-41-generic

Parameters

FlagDescription
-aProcess all kernels (default if no version given)
-AQuick mode — only update if newer modules found
-nDry run — show what would be written to stdout
-vVerbose — show each module being processed
-eReport unresolved symbols as errors

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — After Kernel Update

# Carol rebuilds the module dependency database after a kernel update:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo depmod -a
carol@prod-db-01:~$ ls -l /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/modules.dep
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 123456 Jun  4 10:30 modules.dep
# modprobe now correctly resolves dependencies for the new kernel

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Module Deps

Example 1: Rebuild All Dependencies

📄 Context — Standard Maintenance:

# depmod -a scans /lib/modules/ for all installed kernels
# Generates: modules.dep, modules.dep.bin, modules.alias, modules.symbols
# modprobe reads these files to resolve dependencies
# Run after any module installation or kernel update

Scenario: Alice rebuilds the module dependency database after installing extra modules.

lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

sudo depmod -a && ls -lh /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/modules.* | head -5

Output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 45K Jun 4 10:30 modules.alias -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 12K Jun 4 10:30 modules.alias.bin -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 123K Jun 4 10:30 modules.dep -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 34K Jun 4 10:30 modules.dep.bin -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 56K Jun 4 10:30 modules.symbols

📝 What happened: The dependency database was regenerated. modules.dep (123KB) lists dependencies; modules.alias maps hardware IDs to module names; modules.symbols maps kernel symbols to modules. Without this, modprobe would fail to find or resolve modules.

# Specify kernel version to rebuild only that version's database

Fix: export the symbol from another module or compile custom_helper_func into custom.ko. Without -e, this warning would be silent.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: depmod -a rebuilds all. -A quick update (changed only). -n dry run to stdout. depmod VERSION specific kernel. -e reports unresolved symbols. Generates modules.dep, modules.alias. Run after kernel/module installs. Required for modprobe to work correctly.

dracut

BOOTBoot & KernelRHELLFCS Domain 2

Create initial RAM disk image — build initramfs for booting

dracut generates an initramfs (initial RAM filesystem) image. This temporary root filesystem is loaded by the bootloader before the real root is mounted. Contains kernel modules, udev, and scripts needed to mount the real root. RHEL/CentOS standard; Debian/Ubuntu uses update-initramfs.

Syntax

sudo dracut [OPTIONS] [OUTPUT_IMAGE] [KERNEL_VERSION]
# Common: sudo dracut --force /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r).img $(uname -r)

Parameters

FlagDescription
--forceOverwrite existing initramfs image
--kver VERSIONBuild for specific kernel version
--add "MODULES"Include additional kernel modules
--no-hostonlyBuild generic image (portable, not host-specific)
--regenerate-allRebuild initramfs for all installed kernels

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — RHEL Server Kernel Update

# On RHEL-based monitoring-01, Carol rebuilds initramfs after a kernel update:
carol@monitoring-01:~$ sudo dracut --force --kver 6.5.0-41-generic
carol@monitoring-01:~$ ls -lh /boot/initramfs-6.5.0-41-generic.img
-rw------- 1 root root 34M Jun  4 10:30 /boot/initramfs-6.5.0-41-generic.img

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Initramfs

Example 1: Build Initramfs for Current Kernel

Scenario: Carol rebuilds initramfs after a kernel update on a RHEL server.

Scenario: Carol verifies the initramfs contains the correct storage drivers before rebooting.

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

lsinitrd /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r).img | grep -E "megaraid|nvme|ext4|xfs" | head -5

Output:

drwxr-xr-x root/root usr/lib/modules/6.5.0-41-generic/kernel/drivers/scsi/megaraid/ -rw-r--r-- root/root usr/lib/modules/6.5.0-41-generic/kernel/drivers/nvme/host/nvme.ko -rw-r--r-- root/root usr/lib/modules/6.5.0-41-generic/kernel/fs/ext4/ext4.ko

📝 What happened: All critical drivers confirmed present. lsinitrd is the RHEL equivalent of Debian's lsinitramfs. Always run this before rebooting after initramfs changes. If a driver is missing, rebuild with --add MODULE to include it. Never reboot without verifying.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: dracut --force IMG VER builds initramfs. --add MODULES includes extras. --regenerate-all all kernels. --no-hostonly generic image. lsinitrd inspects contents. Rebuild after kernel or storage changes. Without initramfs: kernel panic ("Unable to mount root"). RHEL/CentOS tool.

update-initramfs

BOOTBoot & KernelDebianLFCS Domain 2

Generate initramfs for Debian/Ubuntu — update the initial RAM filesystem

update-initramfs is the Debian/Ubuntu equivalent of dracut. Generates or updates the initramfs image for the current or specified kernel. Automatically runs during kernel package installation via DKMS hooks. Essential to run manually after custom module changes.

Syntax

sudo update-initramfs [OPTIONS]
# Common: sudo update-initramfs -u | sudo update-initramfs -u -k all

Parameters

FlagDescription
-uUpdate existing initramfs for current kernel
-cCreate new initramfs (if none exists)
-dDelete initramfs for a kernel
-k VERSIONTarget specific kernel version (or "all")
-vVerbose output

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

carol@prod-web-01:~$ sudo update-initramfs -u -k all
update-initramfs: Generating /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-41-generic
update-initramfs: Generating /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-35-generic
carol@prod-web-01:~$ ls -lh /boot/initrd.img-*
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 32M Jun  4 10:30 /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-35-generic
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 34M Jun  4 10:30 /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-41-generic

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Update Initramfs

Daily Workflow: Carol manages the boot process and kernel modules on Ubuntu 24.04 with Cilium networking. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
