Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Update Current Kernel

📄 Context — Standard Post-Kernel Workflow:

# -u updates the initramfs for the currently running kernel
# Automatically detects needed modules (host-only by default)
# Run after: kernel updates, custom module install, storage changes
# Equivalent to: dracut --force on RHEL

Scenario: Alice updates the initramfs after installing a new kernel module.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo update-initramfs -u -v 2>&1 | tail -5

Output:

Building cpio /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-41-generic.new Adding module megaraid_sas Adding module nvme Adding binary /usr/sbin/mdadm done.

📝 What happened: -v showed each module and binary added to the initramfs. The existing initrd.img was overwritten. Note: Ubuntu uses initrd.img naming (not initramfs-*.img). The initramfs is a gzipped cpio archive — inspect with lsinitramfs /boot/initrd.img-$(uname -r).

Example 2: Update All Kernels

📄 Context — Multi-Kernel Maintenance:

# -k all updates initramfs for every installed kernel
# Ensures all kernels have working initramfs
# Useful after installing kernel modules that apply to all versions
# Takes longer — processes each kernel sequentially

Scenario: Carol updates initramfs for all installed kernels after a storage driver change.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo update-initramfs -u -k all 2>&1 | grep Generating

Output:

update-initramfs: Generating /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-35-generic update-initramfs: Generating /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-41-generic update-initramfs: Generating /boot/initrd.img-5.15.0-91-generic

📝 What happened: Three kernels updated: two 6.5 variants and an older 5.15 LTS kernel. Each got a fresh initramfs. This is the safest approach — ensures you can boot any installed kernel after a driver change. Without this, only the current kernel's initramfs is updated.

Example 3: Create Fresh (Not Update)

📄 Context — Corrupted Initramfs Recovery:

# -c creates a NEW initramfs (fails if one already exists)
# First delete the old one with -d, then create fresh with -c
# Alternative: -u --force (or just use -u which does both)
# Used when initramfs is corrupted or missing

Scenario: Alice recreates a corrupted initramfs from scratch.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo update-initramfs -d -k $(uname -r) && sudo update-initramfs -c -k $(uname -r) && ls -lh /boot/initrd.img-$(uname -r)

Output:

update-initramfs: Deleting /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-41-generic update-initramfs: Generating /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-41-generic -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 34M Jun 4 10:30 /boot/initrd.img-6.5.0-41-generic

📝 What happened: Old initramfs deleted, fresh one created. This resolves corruption issues that -u can't fix. In practice, -u is usually sufficient (it recreates if needed). The -d && -c pattern is for stubborn corruption where -u fails. After this, run update-grub to ensure the boot entry points to the new file.

Example 4: Inspect Initramfs Contents

📄 Context — Verify Contents:

# lsinitramfs lists all files inside the initramfs
# Verify critical modules are included before rebooting
# Check: storage driver, filesystem driver, LVM/LUKS tools
# Missing driver = unbootable system

Scenario: Carol verifies the storage driver is in the initramfs before rebooting.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

lsinitramfs /boot/initrd.img-$(uname -r) | grep -E "megaraid|nvme|ext4"

Output:

usr/lib/modules/6.5.0-41-generic/kernel/drivers/scsi/megaraid/megaraid_sas.ko usr/lib/modules/6.5.0-41-generic/kernel/drivers/nvme/host/nvme.ko usr/lib/modules/6.5.0-41-generic/kernel/fs/ext4/ext4.ko

📝 What happened: All critical drivers confirmed: RAID controller (megaraid_sas), NVMe driver, and ext4 filesystem. If any were missing, the system would fail to mount root and kernel panic. Always run lsinitramfs after update-initramfs to verify critical modules before rebooting.

Example 5: Remove Old Kernel Initramfs

📄 Context — Cleanup After Kernel Removal:

# After uninstalling an old kernel, remove its initramfs
# -d deletes the initramfs for a specific kernel version
# Frees disk space in /boot (can fill up with old images)
# Run after: apt remove linux-image-OLD-VERSION

Scenario: Alice cleans up initramfs for a removed kernel.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo update-initramfs -d -k 5.15.0-91-generic && ls /boot/initrd.img-5.15.0-91-generic 2>&1 || echo "Cleaned up"

Output:

update-initramfs: Deleting /boot/initrd.img-5.15.0-91-generic ls: cannot access '/boot/initrd.img-5.15.0-91-generic': No such file or directory Cleaned up

📝 What happened: The old initramfs was deleted, freeing ~30MB in /boot. Always ensure at least one known-good kernel + initramfs remains. /boot often has limited space (separate partition, ~500MB). Old images can accumulate and prevent kernel updates. Clean up periodically.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: update-initramfs -u updates current. -u -k all all kernels. -c creates new. -d deletes. -v verbose. Debian/Ubuntu only. Equivalent to dracut on RHEL. Run after kernel/module changes. lsinitramfs inspects contents. update-grub afterwards for complete boot update.

💾 LVM Management

Commands for managing Logical Volume Manager (LVM) — physical volumes, volume groups, and logical volumes. The anihpj/jobpost team uses LVM on database and backup servers for flexible storage allocation, snapshots, and online resizing.

pvcreate

LVMStorageCoreLFCS Domain 3

Initialize a disk or partition for use by LVM — create a Physical Volume

pvcreate prepares a block device (disk or partition) for LVM. Writes LVM metadata to the device so it can be added to a Volume Group. The first step in any LVM setup — nothing else works until you pvcreate.

Syntax

sudo pvcreate [OPTIONS] DEVICE...
# Common: sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb | sudo pvcreate /dev/sdc1 /dev/sdd1

Parameters

FlagDescription
-f, --forceForce creation (override existing signatures)
-y, --yesAnswer yes to all prompts
--dataalignment=SIZEAlign data to SIZE boundary (SSD optimization)
-v, --verboseVerbose output

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — New Backup Disk Setup

# Carol initializes a new disk for the backup NAS server:
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb
  Physical volume "/dev/sdb" successfully created.
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo pvs
  PV         VG   Fmt  Attr PSize  PFree
  /dev/sdb        lvm2 ---  500.00g 500.00g

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — PV Create

Daily Workflow: Carol manages LVM volumes for database storage, backup partitions, and log directories. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical pvcreate usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb /dev/sdc

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Initialize a New Disk

📄 Context — Fresh Storage Setup:

# New server with empty /dev/sdb for LVM storage
# pvcreate writes LVM metadata header to the disk
# Without this, vgcreate will fail with "device not found"
# Works on whole disks (/dev/sdb) or partitions (/dev/sdb1)

Scenario: Carol prepares a new disk for LVM on the backup server.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb && sudo pvs /dev/sdb

Output:

Physical volume "/dev/sdb" successfully created. PV VG Fmt Attr PSize PFree /dev/sdb lvm2 --- 500.00g 500.00g

📝 What happened: /dev/sdb is now an LVM Physical Volume. Format: lvm2. Attributes: --- (no volume group assigned yet). PSize = 500GB, PFree = all 500GB available. The disk is ready to be added to a Volume Group with vgcreate.

Example 2: Initialize Multiple Disks

📄 Context — Multi-Disk Storage Pool:

# LVM pools multiple physical disks into one logical storage
# Initialize all disks at once for efficiency
# All disks will join the same Volume Group later
# More disks = more performance (striping) and capacity

Scenario: Alice initializes three new SSDs for a database storage pool.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvcreate /dev/sdc /dev/sdd /dev/sde && sudo pvs

Output:

Physical volume "/dev/sdc" successfully created. Physical volume "/dev/sdd" successfully created. Physical volume "/dev/sde" successfully created. PV VG Fmt Attr PSize PFree /dev/sdb lvm2 --- 500.00g 500.00g /dev/sdc lvm2 --- 200.00g 200.00g /dev/sdd lvm2 --- 200.00g 200.00g /dev/sde lvm2 --- 200.00g 200.00g

📝 What happened: Three 200GB SSDs initialized alongside the existing 500GB disk. All marked with "---" (no VG assigned). Ready for vgcreate anihpj_vg /dev/sdb /dev/sdc /dev/sdd /dev/sde to create a 1.1TB combined storage pool.

Example 3: Force Overwrite Existing Data

📄 Context — Disk Reuse:

# Disk previously used for other purposes (partition table, filesystem)
# pvcreate refuses to overwrite: "Can't open /dev/sdb exclusively"
# -f forces pvcreate to wipe existing signatures
# WARNING: all data on the disk will be lost

Scenario: Carol forces pvcreate on a disk that was previously partitioned.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvcreate -ff /dev/sdb 2>&1 && echo "PV created (forced)"

Output:

WARNING: ext4 signature detected on /dev/sdb at offset 1080. Wipe it? [y/n]: y Wiping ext4 signature on /dev/sdb. Physical volume "/dev/sdb" successfully created. PV created (forced)

📝 What happened: -ff (double force) wiped the ext4 signature automatically and created the PV. Single -f prompts for confirmation; -ff skips prompts. ALWAYS verify the correct device before using -ff — no undo. Use lsblk to double-check device names.

Example 4: SSD Alignment

📄 Context — Performance Optimization:

# SSDs need aligned I/O for optimal performance and longevity
# --dataalignment matches SSD erase block size (typically 1MiB)
# Misaligned = reduced performance and increased wear
# Modern pvcreate auto-detects optimal alignment on SSDs

Scenario: Alice creates a PV with optimal alignment for SSD performance.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvcreate --dataalignment 1M /dev/sdc && sudo pvs -o pv_name,pe_start /dev/sdc

Output:

Physical volume "/dev/sdc" successfully created. PV 1st PE /dev/sdc 1.00m

📝 What happened: The first Physical Extent starts at 1.00MiB — aligned to the SSD's native block boundary. pe_start shows where data begins. If PE start were at 192K (old default), every I/O would cross SSD block boundaries, halving throughput. Always use --dataalignment 1M on SSDs.

Example 5: Verify PV Metadata

📄 Context — Disk Inventory:

# pvdisplay shows detailed PV information
# UUID uniquely identifies the PV (survives disk moves)
# PE Size = smallest allocatable unit (default 4MiB)
# Total PE = how many PEs the PV contains

Scenario: Carol verifies the PV metadata after creation.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvdisplay /dev/sdb | grep -E "PV Name|PV UUID|PV Size|PE Size|Total PE"

Output:

PV Name /dev/sdb PV UUID abc123-def456-ghi789 PV Size 500.00 GiB PE Size 4.00 MiB Total PE 127999

📝 What happened: UUID uniquely identifies this PV (used by LVM internally). PE Size = 4MiB (default — each allocation unit is 4MiB). Total PE = 127,999 × 4MiB ≈ 500GB. The UUID is how LVM tracks PVs even if the device name changes (/dev/sdb → /dev/sdf after reboot).

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: pvcreate /dev/sdX initializes for LVM. -ff force overwrites existing data. --dataalignment 1M for SSDs. pvs lists all PVs. pvdisplay shows details. First step in LVM setup. Use whole disks or partitions. UUID survives device name changes.

pvdisplay

LVMStorageLFCS Domain 3

Display detailed Physical Volume information — size, UUID, PE count, allocation

pvdisplay shows comprehensive metadata about LVM Physical Volumes. Includes PV name, UUID, size, PE size, free space, and Volume Group membership. More detailed than pvs — use pvs for quick lists, pvdisplay for deep inspection.

Syntax

pvdisplay [OPTIONS] [PV...]
# Common: sudo pvdisplay | sudo pvdisplay /dev/sdb | sudo pvdisplay -m

Parameters

FlagDescription
-m, --mapsShow mapping of physical extents to logical volumes
-c, --colonColon-separated output (script-friendly)
-s, --shortOne-line summary per PV

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo pvdisplay /dev/sdb

  PV Name               /dev/sdb
  VG Name               anihpj_vg
  PV Size               500.00 GiB
  Allocatable           yes
  PE Size               4.00 MiB
  Total PE              127999

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — PV Display

Daily Workflow: Carol manages LVM volumes for database storage, backup partitions, and log directories. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical pvdisplay usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo pvdisplay

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Full PV Details

📄 Context — Capacity Planning:

# Before extending logical volumes, check free space on PVs
# Free PE tells you how many extents are available for allocation
# PE Size × Free PE = free space in bytes
# Allocated PE × PE Size = space already used

Scenario: Alice checks how much free space is available on the PVs.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvdisplay | grep -E "PV Name|VG Name|Free PE|Allocated PE|PV Size"

Output:

PV Name /dev/sdb VG Name anihpj_vg PV Size 500.00 GiB Allocated PE 77999 Free PE 50000

📝 What happened: Free PE = 50,000 × 4MiB = 195GB available. Allocated PE = 77,999 × 4MiB = 305GB used. The PV is 61% utilized. This PV has room for LV expansion. If Free PE approaches 0, add a new PV to the VG or extend an existing disk.

Example 2: Show Extent Mapping

📄 Context — Layout Visualization:

# -m maps physical extents to logical volumes
# Shows which LV uses which disk regions
# Useful for: identifying fragmented LVs, planning defrag
# Each PE range shows start-end and which LV owns it

Scenario: Carol visualizes how LVs are laid out across the physical disk.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvdisplay -m /dev/sdb | head -15

Output:

--- Physical volume --- PV Name /dev/sdb VG Name anihpj_vg --- Physical Segments --- Physical extent 0 to 19999: Logical volume /dev/anihpj_vg/db_lv Logical extents 0 to 19999 Physical extent 20000 to 39999: Logical volume /dev/anihpj_vg/backup_lv Logical extents 0 to 19999

📝 What happened: PE 0-19999 → db_lv (database storage). PE 20000-39999 → backup_lv (backup storage). The disk is split between two LVs — no interleaving, no fragmentation. If PEs were scattered (0-100 → db_lv, 101-200 → backup_lv, 201-300 → db_lv), the LV would be fragmented — slower sequential I/O.

Example 3: Script-Friendly Output

📄 Context — Monitoring Integration:

# -c produces colon-separated output for parsing
# Easier for scripts than parsing human-readable format
# Fields: pv_name:vg_name:pv_size:pv_free:...
# Use cut or awk to extract specific fields

Scenario: Alice's monitoring script parses PV free space from colon output.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvdisplay -c | cut -d: -f1,2,3,12 | column -s: -t

Output:

/dev/sdb anihpj_vg 500.00g 195.31g /dev/sdc anihpj_vg 200.00g 200.00g

📝 What happened: Field 1=PV name, 2=VG, 3=total size, 12=free space. /dev/sdb has 195GB free; /dev/sdc is completely empty. This format is stable across LVM versions — safer than parsing pvdisplay's human-readable output which may change format. Use pvs --noheadings -o pv_name,vg_name,pv_free as an alternative.

Example 3: Check PV Allocation Status

📄 Context — Storage Audit:

# pvdisplay shows which PVs are allocatable vs full
# Allocatable = yes means space available for new LVs
# Allocatable = no means PV is full
# Use before lvcreate to verify available PVs

Scenario: Carol checks which PVs have free space before creating a new LV.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvdisplay | grep -E "PV Name|Allocatable|Free PE|PV Size"

Output:

PV Name /dev/sdb PV Size 500.00 GiB Allocatable yes Free PE 50000 PV Name /dev/sdc PV Size 200.00 GiB Allocatable no Free PE 0

📝 What happened: /dev/sdb has 50,000 free PEs (195GB) — usable. /dev/sdc is full (Allocatable=no, Free PE=0). When Allocatable=no AND Free PE=0, the PV is fully allocated. When Allocatable=no but Free PE>0, the PV may be outside a VG or have issues.

Example 4: Check PE Size for Planning

📄 Context — Capacity Math:

# PE Size × Total PE = PV Size
# PE Size × Free PE = Available space
# 4MiB PE = 4,194,304 bytes per extent
# Larger PE = fewer total extents (65535 max)

Scenario: Alice calculates available space from PE count.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvdisplay /dev/sdb | grep -E "PE Size|Total PE|Free PE" && echo "Free: $(sudo pvdisplay -c /dev/sdb | cut -d: -f12)"

Output:

PE Size 4.00 MiB Total PE 127999 Free PE 50000 Free: 195.31g

📝 What happened: 50,000 × 4MiB = 200,000 MiB = 195.31 GiB free. -c colon output is easier to parse. Field 12 = free space. Always verify PE Size when capacity planning — it's set at VG creation and cannot be changed without recreating the VG.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: pvdisplay detailed PV info. -m shows PE-to-LV mapping. -c colon output for scripts. PV UUID survives device rename. Free PE × PE Size = free space. Equivalent quick command: pvs for summary, pvdisplay for details.

pvs

LVMStorageLFCS Domain 3

List Physical Volumes — quick summary of all LVM physical volumes

pvs provides a concise table of all Physical Volumes. Shows PV name, Volume Group, format, attributes, size, and free space. The quick-lookup counterpart to pvdisplay's detailed view. Ideal for daily health checks and scripts.

Syntax

pvs [OPTIONS] [PV...]
# Common: pvs | pvs -o pv_name,vg_name,pv_size,pv_free | pvs --noheadings

Parameters

FlagDescription
-o FIELDSCustom output columns
--noheadingsOmit header line (script-friendly)
--units UNITDisplay in specific units (g, m, t)
-vVerbose

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Daily Storage Check

# Carol checks PV status during morning health review:
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo pvs
  PV         VG         Fmt  Attr PSize   PFree
  /dev/sdb   anihpj_vg  lvm2 a--  500.00g 195.31g
  /dev/sdc   anihpj_vg  lvm2 a--  200.00g      0
  /dev/sdd              lvm2 ---  200.00g 200.00g

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — PV Scan

Daily Workflow: Carol manages LVM volumes for database storage, backup partitions, and log directories. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

Example 1: Quick PV Overview

📄 Context — Morning Health Check:

# pvs is the fastest way to check LVM storage health
# One line per PV — scan 100 disks in seconds
# Attr shows status: a=allocatable, -- = normal
# PFree approaching 0 = time to add more storage

Scenario: Carol checks all PVs during the morning review.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvs

Output:

PV VG Fmt Attr PSize PFree /dev/sdb anihpj_vg lvm2 a-- 500.00g 195.00g /dev/sdc anihpj_vg lvm2 a-- 200.00g 0 /dev/sdd anihpj_vg lvm2 a-- 200.00g 50.00g

📝 What happened: Three PVs in anihpj_vg. /dev/sdc is FULL (PFree=0) — needs attention. /dev/sdd has 50GB free. /dev/sdb has 195GB free. Attribute "a--" = allocatable, no export, no missing. Total VG free: 245GB. This is every sysadmin's first LVM command of the day.

Example 2: Custom Columns

📄 Context — Targeted Information:

# -o selects specific columns to display
# Available columns: pv_name, vg_name, pv_size, pv_free, pv_uuid, dev_size
# Use pvs -o help for full column list
# Combine with --noheadings for scripting

Scenario: Alice generates a custom PV report with only relevant fields.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvs -o pv_name,vg_name,pv_size,pv_free,pv_uuid

Output:

PV VG PSize PFree PV UUID /dev/sdb anihpj_vg 500.00g 195.00g abc123-def456 /dev/sdc anihpj_vg 200.00g 0 ghi789-jkl012

📝 What happened: Only the requested 5 columns displayed. UUID is included for tracking PVs across reboots. pvs -o help lists all 30+ available columns. Much cleaner than pvdisplay | grep for extracting specific fields.

Example 3: Script-Ready Output

📄 Context — Monitoring Automation:

# --noheadings removes the column header line
# --units g forces gigabyte units for consistent parsing
# Pipe to awk for alerting: if free < threshold, send alert
# Perfect for cron-based storage monitoring

Scenario: Alice creates a cron job that alerts when PV free space drops below 10GB.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvs --noheadings --units g -o pv_name,pv_free | awk '$2 < 10 {print "WARNING: "$1" has only "$2"G free"}'

Output:

WARNING: /dev/sdc has only 0G free

📝 What happened: /dev/sdc triggered the alert with 0GB free. --noheadings made awk parsing clean (no header line). --units g standardized output to gigabytes. This is a production-ready monitoring one-liner. Add to crontab: 0 * * * * /path/to/pv-check.sh.

Example 3: Show PV UUIDs

📄 Context — Persistent Identification:

# -o pv_uuid shows unique PV identifiers
# UUIDs survive device name changes (/dev/sdb → /dev/sdf)
# LVM uses UUIDs internally, not device names
# Essential for identifying PVs after hardware changes

Scenario: Carol looks up PV UUIDs for a storage migration.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo pvs -o pv_name,pv_uuid,vg_name,pv_size

Output:

PV PV UUID VG PSize /dev/sdb abc123-def456-ghi789-jkl012-mno345 anihpj_vg 500.00g /dev/sdc pqr678-stu901-vwx234-yza567-bcd890 anihpj_vg 200.00g

📝 What happened: UUIDs uniquely identify each PV. After moving disks between servers, UUIDs remain the same even if /dev/sdb becomes /dev/sdf. LVM scans all block devices at boot and matches UUIDs — device names don't matter. Use UUIDs in scripts for reliability.

📝 What happened: Attr "a--" = allocatable, not exported, not missing. Attr "m--" = PV missing (disk removed). Check attrs after hardware changes.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: pvs quick PV summary. -o FIELDS custom columns. --noheadings for scripts. --units g force units. Attributes: a=allocatable, x=exported, m=missing. pvs -o help lists all columns. Preferred over pvdisplay for daily use and scripts.

vgcreate

LVMStorageCoreLFCS Domain 3

Create a Volume Group — pool physical volumes into a shared storage container

vgcreate combines one or more Physical Volumes into a Volume Group. The VG acts as a storage pool from which Logical Volumes are allocated. Create a VG after initializing PVs with pvcreate. The central abstraction in LVM.

Syntax

sudo vgcreate [OPTIONS] VG_NAME PV...
# Common: sudo vgcreate anihpj_vg /dev/sdb | sudo vgcreate -s 8M db_vg /dev/sdc /dev/sdd

Parameters

FlagDescription
-s SIZESet Physical Extent size (default: 4MiB)
-l MAX_LVMaximum number of Logical Volumes in this VG
-p MAX_PVMaximum number of Physical Volumes in this VG
-v, --verboseVerbose output

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Storage Pool Creation

# Carol creates the anihpj Volume Group for database and backup storage:
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo vgcreate anihpj_vg /dev/sdb /dev/sdc
  Volume group "anihpj_vg" successfully created
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo vgs anihpj_vg
  VG         #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize   VFree
  anihpj_vg    2   0   0 wz--n- 700.00g 700.00g

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — VG Create

Daily Workflow: Carol manages LVM volumes for database storage, backup partitions, and log directories. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

Examples

#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Basic Volume Group

📄 Context — Standard LVM Setup Step 2:

# After pvcreate, pool PVs into a VG
# VG name should be descriptive: anihpj_vg, db_vg, backup_vg
# All PVs contribute their full capacity to the pool
# #PV = how many disks in the pool

Scenario: Alice creates a VG for the database server from two SSDs.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo vgcreate db_vg /dev/sdc /dev/sdd && sudo vgs db_vg

Output:

Volume group "db_vg" successfully created VG #PV #LV #SN Attr VSize VFree db_vg 2 0 0 wz--n- 400.00g 400.00g

📝 What happened: db_vg created from two 200GB SSDs = 400GB pool. #PV=2, #LV=0 (no logical volumes yet), #SN=0 (no snapshots). Attr "wz--n-" = writable, no resize, no export, normal allocation. Now create LVs with lvcreate from this 400GB pool.

Example 2: Custom Extent Size

📄 Context — Large Volume Optimization:

# -s sets PE size (default 4MiB)
# Larger PE = fewer extents = faster LVM operations
# Max 65535 PEs per PV with default tools
# For multi-TB volumes, use larger PE to stay under limit

Scenario: Carol creates a VG with larger extents for a 10TB archive volume.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo vgcreate -s 16M archive_vg /dev/sdb && sudo vgdisplay archive_vg | grep "PE Size"

Output:

Volume group "archive_vg" successfully created PE Size 16.00 MiB

📝 What happened: PE size set to 16MiB (4× default). Trade-off: less granular allocation (minimum LV size = 16MiB instead of 4MiB) but better performance for large volumes. 500GB / 16MiB = 32,000 PEs (well under the 65,535 limit). Use 4MiB for general purpose, 16-64MiB for large archive/backup VGs.

Example 3: Add PV to Existing VG

📄 Context — Storage Expansion:

# vgextend adds a new PV to an existing VG
# Increases the storage pool without downtime
# No need to unmount or stop services
# LVs can be extended into the new space immediately

Scenario: Alice adds a new disk to expand the database volume group.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo vgextend db_vg /dev/sde && sudo vgs db_vg

Output:

Volume group "db_vg" successfully extended VG #PV #LV #SN Attr VSize VFree db_vg 3 1 0 wz--n- 600.00g 200.00g

📝 What happened: #PV went from 2→3. VSize: 400G→600G. VFree: gained 200GB. The existing LV can now be extended into the new space. vgextend is the expansion command (vs vgcreate for new). Online operation — no service interruption. This is LVM's killer feature: grow storage without downtime.

Example 3: Set Maximum LV Count

📄 Context — Resource Governance:

# -l N limits the maximum number of LVs in this VG
# Prevents uncontrolled LV proliferation
# Default: unlimited (0)
# Useful in multi-tenant environments

Scenario: Alice creates a VG with a limit of 10 logical volumes.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo vgcreate -l 10 limited_vg /dev/sdd && sudo vgs limited_vg -o vg_name,max_lv,lv_count

Output:

Volume group "limited_vg" successfully created VG MaxLV #LV limited_vg 10 0

📝 What happened: MaxLV set to 10 — no more than 10 LVs can be created. Attempting to create the 11th LV will fail. -p N similarly limits the maximum number of PVs. These limits can be changed later with vgchange -l N VG. Good for preventing resource exhaustion in shared environments.

Example 4: Verify After Creation

📄 Context — Post-Creation Audit:

# Post-Creation Audit

Scenario: Carol verifies VG creation.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo vgs limited_vg -o vg_name,vg_size,vg_free,pv_count

Output:

VG VSize VFree #PV limited_vg 200.00g 200.00g 1

📝 What happened: #PV=1 confirms the VG has one physical volume. VFree=VSize means no LVs created yet. All parameters match creation intent.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: vgcreate NAME PVs... creates VG. -s SIZE sets PE size. vgextend NAME PV adds PV to existing VG. VG = storage pool. #PV = disk count. VFree = available for new LVs or extensions. vgs for quick view. PE size fixed at creation — plan carefully for large volumes.

vgdisplay

LVMStorageLFCS Domain 3

Display Volume Group details — size, PE count, free space, UUID

vgdisplay shows comprehensive Volume Group metadata: VG name, UUID, size, PE size, total/free PEs, and LV count. The detailed counterpart to vgs. Use before creating or extending logical volumes to confirm available space.

Syntax

vgdisplay [OPTIONS] [VG...]
# Common: sudo vgdisplay | sudo vgdisplay anihpj_vg | sudo vgdisplay -v

Parameters

FlagDescription
-v, --verboseShow PV and LV mapping within the VG
-c, --colonColon-separated for scripts
-s, --shortOne-line summary

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Example 1: Full VG Details

📄 Context — Capacity Planning:

# Before extending LVs, check VG free space
# Free PE / Size = how much you can extend by
# Alloc PE = already assigned to LVs
# Total PE = Alloc + Free + Unavailable

Scenario: Alice checks if the VG has enough free space for a planned LV extension.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo vgdisplay db_vg | grep -E "VG Size|PE Size|Free|Alloc"

Output:

VG Size 600.00 GiB PE Size 4.00 MiB Alloc PE / Size 102400 / 400.00 GiB Free PE / Size 51200 / 200.00 GiB

📝 What happened: 200GB free (51,200 PEs). Need to extend the LV by 50GB? 50GB / 4MiB = 12,800 PEs needed. 51,200 available — plenty of room. If Free PE approaches 0, either add a new PV with vgextend or shrink another LV to free space.

📝 What happened: Two PVs in db_vg: /dev/sdc (full — 0 free PEs), /dev/sdd (25,600 free PEs = 100GB). -v also shows LV mappings below this. This is the most comprehensive VG view — equivalent to pvs + vgs + lvs in one command.

Example 3: Check VG Metadata Status

📄 Context — VG Health Check:

# Metadata Areas = number of PVs holding VG config
# More metadata areas = better redundancy
# Metadata Sequence = number of changes since creation
# If sequence differs between PVs, VG may need repair

└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Output:

Format lvm2 Metadata Areas 2 Metadata Sequence No 15

📝 What happened: Two metadata areas (one per PV) = good redundancy. Sequence No 15 means 15 changes since VG creation. If one PV fails, the surviving PV still has the complete VG configuration. vgcfgbackup backs up metadata to /etc/lvm/backup/ for extra safety. vgcfgrestore recovers from backup.

LVMStorageLFCS Domain 3

List Volume Groups — quick summary of all LVM volume groups

vgs provides a concise table of all Volume Groups. Shows VG name, PV count, LV count, snapshot count, attributes, size, and free space. The quick counterpart to vgdisplay — use for daily checks and scripts.

Syntax

vgs [OPTIONS] [VG...]
# Common: vgs | vgs -o vg_name,vg_size,vg_free | vgs --noheadings

-o FIELDSCustom output columns
--noheadingsOmit header for scripts
--units UNITDisplay units (g, m, t)

0Success

Output:

VG VSize VFree anihpj_vg 900.00g 295.00g db_vg 400.00g 100.00g old_vg 50.00g 0

📝 What happened: anihpj_vg has the most free space (295GB) — best choice for new LVs. db_vg has 100GB — adequate. old_vg has 0GB — don't create LVs here. --sort -vg_free puts the most free at the top. Combine with --noheadings for scripts that auto-select the best VG.

Example 3: Show VG Permissions and Allocation

📄 Context — VG Attribute Decoding:

# -o vg_attr shows the VG attributes flag
# wz--n- = writeable, resizeable, normal allocation
# r = read-only, R = clustered read-only
# c = clustered (shared storage)

Scenario: Alice decodes VG attributes to understand allocation policy.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo vgs -o vg_name,vg_attr,vg_size,vg_free

Output:

VG Attr VSize VFree anihpj_vg wz--n- 900.00g 295.00g db_vg wz--n- 400.00g 100.00g

📝 What happened: Both VGs are writable, resizeable, normal allocation (wz--n-). Position 1: w=writable. Position 2: z=resizeable. Position 5: n=normal allocation (c=contiguous, l=cling). If Attr shows "r", the VG is read-only — no changes allowed. vgchange -a y VG activates a VG.

Example 4: Show VG UUIDs

# UUID-Based Scripting

lvcreate

LVMStorageCoreLFCS Domain 3

Create a Logical Volume — allocate storage from a Volume Group

lvcreate creates a Logical Volume from free space in a Volume Group. The LV appears as a block device (/dev/VG/LV) that can be formatted and mounted like a regular partition. Supports linear, striped, and mirrored allocation.

Syntax

sudo lvcreate [OPTIONS] -n LV_NAME VG_NAME
# Common: sudo lvcreate -L 50G -n db_lv db_vg | sudo lvcreate -l 100%FREE -n backup_lv anihpj_vg

Parameters

FlagDescription
-L SIZESize in bytes/K/M/G/T (e.g., -L 50G)
-l EXTENTSSize in extents or % of VG (e.g., -l 100%FREE)
-n NAMEName of the new Logical Volume
-i STRIPESNumber of stripes (for performance)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Database Volume

# Carol creates an LV for PostgreSQL data on prod-db-01:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo lvcreate -L 100G -n db_lv db_vg
  Logical volume "db_lv" created.
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/db_vg/db_lv
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo mount /dev/db_vg/db_lv /var/lib/postgresql/data

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — LV Create

Daily Workflow: Carol manages LVM volumes for database storage, backup partitions, and log directories. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical lvcreate usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo lvcreate -L 50G -n db_lv db_vg

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Create a Sized LV

📄 Context — Database Storage Allocation:

# -L creates an LV with exact size
# LV appears as /dev/VG_NAME/LV_NAME
# Format with mkfs, then mount like any partition
# Can be extended later with lvextend (no unmount needed)

Scenario: Alice creates a 50GB LV for the database.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo lvcreate -L 50G -n db_lv db_vg && sudo lvs db_vg/db_lv

Output:

Logical volume "db_lv" created. LV VG Attr LSize Pool Origin Data% Meta% db_lv db_vg -wi-a----- 50.00g

📝 What happened: 50GB LV created in db_vg. Attribute "-wi-a-----" = writable, inherited, active, no snapshot origin. The device path is /dev/db_vg/db_lv (also symlinked at /dev/mapper/db_vg-db_lv). Format: mkfs.ext4 /dev/db_vg/db_lv, mount: mount /dev/db_vg/db_lv /data.

Example 2: Use All Free Space

📄 Context — Bulk Allocation:

# -l 100%FREE allocates ALL remaining VG space
# Useful when you want one LV per VG (simple setup)
# %FREE, %VG, %PVS are all valid extent specs
# Leaves no wasted space in the VG

Scenario: Carol creates an LV consuming all remaining space for backups.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo lvcreate -l 100%FREE -n backup_lv anihpj_vg && sudo vgs anihpj_vg

Output:

Logical volume "backup_lv" created. VG #PV #LV #SN Attr VSize VFree anihpj_vg 3 2 0 wz--n- 900.00g 0

📝 What happened: VFree = 0 — all space allocated. -l 100%FREE is safer than calculating exact extents. Other extent specs: -l 50%VG (half the VG), -l 1000 (exactly 1000 extents). The LV can still be extended if more PVs are added to the VG with vgextend.

Example 3: Striped LV for Performance

📄 Context — I/O Throughput:

# -i N stripes data across N PVs (like RAID 0)
# Increases sequential read/write throughput
# Requires at least N PVs in the VG
# Trade-off: if any PV fails, ALL data is lost

Scenario: Alice creates a striped LV for high-performance database storage.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo lvcreate -L 100G -i 3 -n fast_lv db_vg && sudo lvdisplay -m db_vg/fast_lv | grep -A3 "Segments"

Output:

Logical volume "fast_lv" created. Segments 3 Stripe size 64.00 KiB

📝 What happened: fast_lv is striped across 3 PVs with 64KB stripe size. Sequential reads/writes are split across all 3 disks simultaneously — near 3× throughput of a single disk. Requires ≥ 3 PVs in db_vg. For database redo logs and high-I/O workloads. Add --stripesize N to tune stripe width.

Example 4: Create and Format in One Go

📄 Context — Provisioning Pipeline:

# Production workflow: lvcreate → mkfs → mount → fstab
# Chain commands for automated provisioning
# Verify at each step before proceeding
# Set permissions after mounting

Scenario: Carol provisions and formats a new LV for application data in one pipeline.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo lvcreate -L 20G -n app_lv anihpj_vg && sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/anihpj_vg/app_lv && sudo mkdir -p /lpj/ops/backups && sudo mount /dev/anihpj_vg/app_lv /lpj/ops/backups && df -h /lpj/ops/backups

Output:

Logical volume "app_lv" created. meta-data=/dev/anihpj_vg/app_lv isize=512 agcount=4, agsize=1310720 blks Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/mapper/anihpj_vg-app_lv 20G 33M 20G 1% /lpj/ops/backups

📝 What happened: Created 20GB LV → formatted XFS → mounted at /lpj/ops/backups. All in one command chain. XFS is preferred for large files and high performance; ext4 for general use. Add to /etc/fstab for persistence: /dev/anihpj_vg/app_lv /lpj/ops/backups xfs defaults 0 2.

Example 5: Thin Provisioning

📄 Context — Over-Allocation:

# Thin pools let you allocate more than physical space
# LVs only consume space as data is written (not at creation)
# Useful for VMs, containers, Snapshots
# Requires thin pool creation first

Scenario: Alice creates a thin pool and thin LV for efficient snapshot usage.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo lvcreate -L 100G -T anihpj_vg/thinpool && sudo lvcreate -V 200G -T anihpj_vg/thinpool -n thin_lv && sudo lvs anihpj_vg

Output:

Logical volume "thinpool" created. Logical volume "thin_lv" created. LV VG Attr LSize Pool Data% thin_lv anihpj_vg Vwi-a-tz-- 200.00g thinpool 0.00 thinpool anihpj_vg twi-aotz-- 100.00g 5.23

📝 What happened: thin_lv reports 200GB but the pool is only 100GB — over-allocated 2:1. Data% shows actual usage (0% for thin_lv, 5.23% for pool metadata). Thin provisioning is LVM's most advanced feature — use for VM storage, Docker volumes, and snapshot-heavy environments. Monitor pool usage carefully to avoid out-of-space errors.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: lvcreate -L SIZE -n NAME VG creates LV. -l 100%FREE uses all space. -i N stripes across N PVs. -T creates thin pool. LV path: /dev/VG/LV. Format with mkfs before mounting. lvs for quick list. lvdisplay for details.

Example 1: Full LV Details

📄 Context — Volume Audit:

# Complete LV metadata for audit or planning
# LV Size = current size (can be extended)
# Current LE = logical extents (Size / PE_Size)
# Block device = major:minor number (253:3 = dm-3)

Scenario: Alice audits all LV sizes and mappings.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo lvdisplay | grep -E "LV Path|LV Size|VG Name|Segments"

Output:

LV Path /dev/db_vg/db_lv VG Name db_vg LV Size 50.00 GiB Segments 1 LV Path /dev/anihpj_vg/backup_lv VG Name anihpj_vg LV Size 295.00 GiB Segments 1

📝 What happened: Two LVs: db_lv (50GB) and backup_lv (295GB). Segments=1 means each LV is contiguous (not fragmented). If Segments > 1, the LV is spread across non-contiguous disk regions — slight performance penalty. The block device numbers (253:3, 253:4) map to /dev/dm-3 and /dev/dm-4.

Example 2: Show Extent Mapping

📄 Context — Data Locality:

# -m shows which PVs hold the LV's data
# For striped LVs: shows stripe distribution
# For linear LVs: shows which PV the data is on
# Useful for: verifying striping, identifying slow disks

Scenario: Carol checks which physical disk holds the database LV.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo lvdisplay -m db_vg/db_lv | grep -A5 "Segments"

Output:

Segments 1 Logical extents 0 to 12799: Type linear Physical volume /dev/sdc Physical extents 0 to 12799

📝 What happened: db_lv is entirely on /dev/sdc (linear mapping). Logical extents 0-12799 map directly to physical extents 0-12799 on /dev/sdc — no fragmentation. If this were striped across 3 PVs, you'd see 3 segments with alternating PVs. For performance tuning, move LVs between PVs with pvmove.

Example 3: Snapshot Volume Display

📄 Context — Snapshot Verification:

# Snapshots appear as special LVs in lvdisplay
# LV snapshot status shows: active, % allocated from origin
# Snapshot size = max changes before snapshot becomes invalid
# Monitor snapshot % to prevent overflow

Scenario: Carol checks the status of a database backup snapshot.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo lvdisplay db_vg/db_snap | grep -E "LV snapshot|Allocated|LV Size"

Output:

LV snapshot status source of db_lv [active] LV Size 10.00 GiB Allocated to snapshot 12.34%

📝 What happened: db_snap is an active snapshot of db_lv. 12.34% of the 10GB snapshot space is used — 87.66% remaining. If Allocated reaches 100%, the snapshot becomes invalid (data lost). Monitor with lvs -o lv_name,data_percent. Snapshots let you freeze a point-in-time for backups without stopping the database.

Example 3: Check Snapshot Status

📄 Context — Snapshot Health:

# Snapshots show "LV snapshot status" in lvdisplay

📝 What happened: Snapshot is active and only 12% used — safe to take backup. If Allocated reaches 100%, the snapshot becomes invalid and the backup fails. Delete invalid snapshots: lvremove db_vg/db_snap. Create larger snapshots or use faster backups to prevent overflow.

Example 1: LV Overview

Scenario: Carol inventories all LVs across all VGs.

Attributes: -wi-ao = writable, inherited, active, open (mounted). db_lv and backup_lv are standard thick volumes. thin_lv draws from thinpool at 5.23% usage. The "o" in position 6 means the LV is currently mounted and in use.

Example 2: Decode Attributes

📄 Context — LV Status at a Glance:

# LV attributes are a compact status code: "vwt-aos--"
# Position 1: v=volume, V=thin volume, t=thin pool
# Position 5: a=active, s=suspended, I=invalid snapshot
# Position 6: o=open (mounted), x=exported
# Position 7: s=snapshot, S=invalid snapshot

Scenario: Alice decodes the attributes to understand LV status.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo lvs -o lv_name,lv_attr,lv_size

Output:

LV Attr LSize db_lv -wi-ao---- 50.00g snap_lv swi-a-s--- 10.00g

📝 What happened: db_lv = -wi-ao (normal, writable, active, open). snap_lv = swi-a-s (snapshot, writable, active, snapshot origin). The "s" in position 1 = snapshot volume. Position 7 "s" = this is a snapshot origin (the original being snapped). Knowing attributes helps quickly identify snapshot chains and problematic volumes.

# Thin pools can over-allocate — monitor Data% closely

# -o data_percent,metadata_percent shows usage
# Thin pool full = all thin LVs get I/O errors

Scenario: Alice monitors thin pool usage to prevent out-of-space errors.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations

Command:

sudo lvs -o lv_name,pool_lv,data_percent,metadata_percent anihpj_vg | grep -E "thinpool|thin_lv"

Output:

thinpool 5.23 2.10 thin_lv thinpool 0.00

📝 What happened: thinpool data usage = 5.23%, metadata = 2.10% — healthy. thin_lv is backed by thinpool at 0% data usage. This is the critical monitoring command for thin-provisioned storage. Set up alerts: sudo lvs --noheadings -o data_percent anihpj_vg/thinpool | awk '$1>80{print "WARNING"}'.

lvextend

LVMStorageCoreLFCS Domain 3

Extend a Logical Volume — increase LV size online without unmounting

lvextend grows a Logical Volume using free space in its Volume Group. Can be done while the LV is mounted and in use — no downtime. After extending the LV, the filesystem must also be resized (resize2fs for ext4, xfs_growfs for XFS).

Syntax

sudo lvextend [OPTIONS] LV
# Common: sudo lvextend -L +10G /dev/db_vg/db_lv | sudo lvextend -l +100%FREE /dev/anihpj_vg/backup_lv

Parameters

FlagDescription
-L +SIZEIncrease by SIZE (e.g., -L +10G)
-L SIZESet exact new size (e.g., -L 60G)
-l +EXTENTSIncrease by extents or % (e.g., -l +100%FREE)
-rAutomatically resize the filesystem too

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

Example 1: Extend by Amount

📄 Context — Emergency Space Addition:

# Database running out of space — extend NOW
# -L +10G adds 10GB (plus sign = relative)
# Without +: -L 60G sets to exactly 60GB (absolute)
# Online operation — no unmounting needed

Scenario: Alice adds 10GB to the database LV urgently.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo lvextend -L +10G /dev/db_vg/db_lv && sudo lvs db_vg/db_lv

Output:

Size of logical volume db_vg/db_lv changed from 50.00 GiB to 60.00 GiB. LV VG Attr LSize db_lv db_vg -wi-ao---- 60.00g

📝 What happened: LV grew from 50GB→60GB. The filesystem hasn't been resized yet — df -h still shows 50GB. Next: sudo resize2fs /dev/db_vg/db_lv (ext4) or sudo xfs_growfs /mountpoint (XFS). The -r flag does both in one step: sudo lvextend -r -L +10G /dev/db_vg/db_lv.

Example 2: Extend with Auto-Resize

📄 Context — One-Step Growth:

# -r automatically resizes the filesystem after extending
# Works with ext3/4 and XFS (if xfs_growfs is available)
# One command instead of lvextend + resize2fs
# Safer — can't forget the filesystem resize step

Scenario: Carol extends the backup LV AND the filesystem in one command.

├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Output:

Size of logical volume anihpj_vg/backup_lv changed from 295.00 GiB to 345.00 GiB. resize2fs 1.47.0 Filesystem at /dev/anihpj_vg/backup_lv is now 90439680 blocks long. Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/mapper/anihpj_vg-backup_lv 345G 200G 145G 58% /lpj/ops/backups

📝 What happened: LV extended AND filesystem resized — one step. df -h immediately shows 345GB. -r calls resize2fs (or xfs_growfs) automatically. This is the recommended way to extend LVs — eliminates the common mistake of extending the LV but forgetting the filesystem.

Example 3: Use All Remaining VG Space

📄 Context — Maximize Allocation:

# -l +100%FREE consumes all remaining VG free space
# Useful as a final extension before adding more disks
# After this: VFree = 0, need vgextend for more space
# Verify with vgs before and after

Scenario: Alice takes all remaining VG space for the growing backup volume.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project

Output:

Size of logical volume anihpj_vg/backup_lv changed from 345.00 GiB to 900.00 GiB. VG #PV #LV #SN Attr VSize VFree anihpj_vg 3 2 0 wz--n- 900.00g 0

📝 What happened: backup_lv consumed all remaining VG space (555GB → 900GB). VFree = 0 — the VG is fully allocated. Next step: vgextend anihpj_vg /dev/sdf to add another disk, then extend again. This is the standard LVM growth pattern: extend LV → VFree=0 → add PV → repeat.

📄 Context — Precise Allocation:

# -l +EXTENTS extends by number of extents
# More precise than -L (avoids rounding)

# Use vgdisplay to find PE size first

Scenario: Alice extends an LV by exactly 1000 extents.

Size of logical volume db_vg/db_lv changed from 60.00 GiB to 63.91 GiB. db_lv db_vg -wi-ao---- 63.91g

📝 What happened: 1000 × 4MiB = 4000 MiB ≈ 3.91 GB added. -l +1000 is exact — -L +4G would round to PE boundaries. Use -l for precise control when capacity planning. -l +100%FREE uses all remaining VG space.

# Absolute Sizing

Scenario: Alice sets an exact LV size instead of adding.

Size of logical volume db_vg/db_lv changed from 60.00 GiB to 80.00 GiB. db_lv db_vg -wi-ao---- 80.00g

📝 What happened: -L 80G (no + sign) sets the EXACT final size. Use +10G to add; use 80G to set. If current size > target, lvextend fails — use lvreduce first.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: lvextend -L +SIZE LV extends LV. -r auto-resizes filesystem. -l +100%FREE uses all VG space. + = relative, no + = absolute. Online operation. Filesystem must be resized separately unless using -r. ext4: resize2fs, XFS: xfs_growfs.

lvreduce

LVMStorageLFCS Domain 3

Reduce a Logical Volume — shrink LV size (filesystem must be shrunk first)

lvreduce decreases a Logical Volume's size. The filesystem MUST be shrunk BEFORE the LV — reversing the order causes data loss. Not all filesystems support shrinking (XFS does NOT). ext4 supports offline shrink only. Use with caution.

Syntax

sudo lvreduce [OPTIONS] LV
# Common: sudo lvreduce -L -10G /dev/anihpj_vg/backup_lv | sudo lvreduce -L 20G /dev/db_vg/test_lv

Parameters

FlagDescription
-L -SIZEReduce by SIZE (e.g., -L -10G)
-L SIZESet exact new size (e.g., -L 20G)
-f, --forceForce reduction (skip confirmation)
-rAuto-resize filesystem before reducing LV

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Reclaim Overallocated Space

# Carol shrinks an overallocated backup LV to free space for the database:
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo umount /lpj/ops/backups
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo e2fsck -f /dev/anihpj_vg/backup_lv  # Check filesystem first
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo resize2fs /dev/anihpj_vg/backup_lv 200G  # Shrink FS FIRST
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo lvreduce -L 200G /dev/anihpj_vg/backup_lv  # Then shrink LV
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo mount /lpj/ops/backups

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — LV Reduce

Daily Workflow: Carol manages LVM volumes for database storage, backup partitions, and log directories. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo lvreduce -L -5G /dev/db_vg/db_lv

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Safe Shrink with Auto-Resize

📄 Context — Reclaiming Space:

# -r shrinks filesystem first, then LV (safe order)
# Works with ext4 (must be unmounted)
# XFS does NOT support shrinking — can't use lvreduce
# Always verify with fsck before shrinking

Scenario: Alice safely shrinks an LV with automatic filesystem handling.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo lvreduce -r -L -50G /dev/anihpj_vg/backup_lv && sudo lvs anihpj_vg/backup_lv

Output:

fsck from util-linux 2.37.2 /dev/mapper/anihpj_vg-backup_lv: clean, 12345/567890 files resize2fs 1.47.0 Resizing the filesystem to 200G... Size of logical volume anihpj_vg/backup_lv changed from 250G to 200G. LV VG Attr LSize backup_lv anihpj_vg -wi-ao---- 200.00g

📝 What happened: -r checked the filesystem (fsck), shrunk it (resize2fs), then reduced the LV — all in correct order. 50GB returned to VG free space. Without -r: must umount → fsck → resize2fs → lvreduce → mount. XFS note: xfs_growfs only grows, never shrinks.

Example 2: Set Exact New Size

📄 Context — Precise Resizing:

# -L 30G sets exactly 30GB (absolute, no +/-)
# Filesystem must already be ≤ 30GB before LV shrink
# Without -r: umount → fsck → resize2fs → lvreduce
# Wrong order = data loss

Scenario: Carol sets a test LV to exactly 10GB to match a quota.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo umount /mnt/test && sudo e2fsck -f /dev/db_vg/test_lv && sudo resize2fs /dev/db_vg/test_lv 10G && sudo lvreduce -L 10G /dev/db_vg/test_lv && sudo mount /mnt/test && df -h /mnt/test

Output:

Resizing the filesystem to 10G... Size of logical volume db_vg/test_lv changed from 20G to 10G. Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/mapper/db_vg-test_lv 9.8G 45M 9.2G 1% /mnt/test

📝 What happened: Manual shrink workflow: unmount → check → shrink FS → shrink LV → remount. All steps required. resize2fs 10G set the filesystem to exactly 10GB before lvreduce -L 10G. If you lvreduce first (without shrinking FS), the filesystem thinks it's still 20GB — immediate data corruption on writes beyond 10GB.

Example 3: XFS Limitation

📄 Context — Know Your Filesystem:

# XFS does NOT support shrinking at all
# lvreduce on XFS LV = data loss
# Only option: backup → mkfs → restore
# This is why some admins prefer ext4 for flexible volumes

Scenario: Alice discovers an XFS LV can't be shrunk — documents the workaround.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo lvreduce -r -L -5G /dev/db_vg/xfs_lv 2>&1 || echo "XFS shrink not supported — must backup/recreate"

Output:

fsadm: Cannot shrink XFS filesystem Filesystem shrink failed. XFS shrink not supported — must backup/recreate

📝 What happened: Even with -r, XFS shrink fails. Workaround: create a new smaller LV, format XFS, copy data with rsync, swap mount points. This is the #1 reason to consider ext4 for volumes that may need shrinking. XFS = excellent for grow-only workloads (databases, logs).

Example 3: Reduce by Extents

📄 Context — Precise Shrink:

# -l -EXTENTS reduces by extent count
# More precise than -L -SIZE
# Must shrink filesystem BEFORE reducing LV
# Wrong order = data corruption

Scenario: Carol reduces an LV by exactly 500 extents.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo umount /mnt/data && sudo e2fsck -f /dev/anihpj_vg/data_lv && NEW_LE=$(( $(sudo lvs --noheadings -o lv_size --units b anihpj_vg/data_lv | tr -d ' B') / 4194304 - 500 )) && sudo resize2fs /dev/anihpj_vg/data_lv $((NEW_LE * 4))M && sudo lvreduce -l -500 /dev/anihpj_vg/data_lv && echo "Reduced by 500 extents (~1.95G)"

Output:

Resizing the filesystem...done Size of logical volume anihpj_vg/data_lv changed from 50G to 48.05G. Reduced by 500 extents (~1.95G)

📝 What happened: LV shrunk by 500 × 4MiB ≈ 1.95GB. The filesystem was shrunk FIRST (resize2fs), then the LV (lvreduce). This order is mandatory. -r flag does both in one step (safer). Always unmount and fsck before shrinking to prevent data loss.

Example 4: Verify Before Shrinking

📄 Context — Safety Check:

# Safety Check

Scenario: Carol verifies filesystem size before shrinking LV.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

df -h /mnt/data && sudo lvs anihpj_vg/data_lv

Output:

Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% /dev/mapper/anihpj_vg-data_lv 50G 30G 20G 60% data_lv anihpj_vg -wi-ao---- 50.00g

📝 What happened: FS shows 30G used of 50G — can safely shrink to 35G. Always leave ~20% headroom. Shrinking below used space = data loss. df first, then resize2fs, then lvreduce.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: lvreduce -L -SIZE LV shrinks LV. -r auto-shrinks FS first. Shrink FS BEFORE LV — wrong order corrupts data. XFS cannot shrink. ext4 shrink requires unmount. Always fsck before shrinking. Test in staging first. -f skips confirmation prompt.

lvremove / vgremove / pvremove

LVMStorageLFCS Domain 3

Remove LVM objects — delete logical volumes, volume groups, and physical volumes

These three commands remove LVM objects in descending order: lvremove deletes Logical Volumes, vgremove deletes Volume Groups, pvremove removes LVM metadata from Physical Volumes. Must remove LVs before VG, VG before PV. All operations are destructive and irreversible.

Syntax

sudo lvremove [OPTIONS] LV...     # Remove Logical Volumes
sudo vgremove [OPTIONS] VG...     # Remove Volume Groups (must be empty)
sudo pvremove [OPTIONS] PV...     # Remove LVM metadata from PVs

Parameters

FlagApplies ToDescription
-f, --forceAll threeForce removal without confirmation
-y, --yeslvremoveAnswer yes to all prompts

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Storage Decommissioning

# Carol decommissions an old backup LV and its VG:
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo umount /lpj/ops/old-backups
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo lvremove /dev/anihpj_vg/old_backup_lv
Do you really want to remove active LV anihpj_vg/old_backup_lv? [y/n]: y
  Logical volume "old_backup_lv" successfully removed.
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo vgremove old_vg
  Volume group "old_vg" successfully removed.
carol@backup-nas:~$ sudo pvremove /dev/sdf
  Labels on physical volume "/dev/sdf" successfully wiped.

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — LV Remove

Daily Workflow: Carol manages LVM volumes for database storage, backup partitions, and log directories. Here's how it looks on the production servers.

Examples

#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Remove an LV

📄 Context — LV Deletion:

# lvremove deletes the LV — ALL DATA IS LOST
# LV must not be mounted (umount first)
# Prompts for confirmation (no undo)
# Frees space back to the VG automatically

Scenario: Alice removes an old test LV to free space.

📁 Environment Snippet:

lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

Output:

Logical volume "test_lv" successfully removed. LV VG Attr LSize db_lv db_vg -wi-ao---- 60.00g

Example 2: Remove a VG

📄 Context — VG Decommissioning:

# vgremove requires the VG to be empty (no LVs)
# Remove all LVs first, then the VG
# VG metadata is deleted — PVs become unassigned
# PVs still have LVM metadata — use pvremove to fully clean

Scenario: Carol removes an empty VG after migrating all data.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

Command:
