carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo xfs_repair /dev/sdb1

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Standard XFS Repair

📄 Context — Post-Crash XFS Recovery:

# XFS uses journaling — crash recovery is usually automatic
# If mount fails: "wrong fs type, bad option, bad superblock"
# xfs_repair replays the log and checks consistency
# 7 phases scan all aspects of the filesystem

Scenario: Carol repairs an XFS volume that won't mount after a crash.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo umount /dev/anihpj_vg/db_lv 2>/dev/null; sudo xfs_repair /dev/anihpj_vg/db_lv && echo "Repair complete"

Output:

Phase 1 - find and verify superblock... Phase 2 - using internal log - zero log... Phase 3 - for each AG... Phase 4 - check for duplicate blocks... Phase 5 - rebuild AG headers and trees... Phase 6 - check inode connectivity... Phase 7 - verify link counts... done Repair complete

📝 What happened: All 7 phases completed. Phase 2 zeroed the log (replaying journal entries). Phase 3 scanned Allocation Groups (XFS divides the FS into AGs for parallelism). Phase 4-7 verified structural integrity. The filesystem is now mountable. XFS repairs are typically faster than ext4 on large volumes due to AG parallelism.

Example 2: Read-Only Scan

📄 Context — Pre-Repair Assessment:

# -n scans without writing anything
# Reports what WOULD be fixed
# Safe to run even on questionable hardware
# Always run -n first before actual repair

Scenario: Alice checks what's wrong before committing to repairs.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo xfs_repair -n /dev/sdb1 2>&1 | grep -E "would|error|Phase|cannot"

Output:

Phase 1 - find and verify superblock... Phase 2 - using internal log Phase 3 - for each AG... Phase 5 - rebuild AG headers and trees... - would have reset inode 12345 - would have corrected inode 12346 No modify flag set, skipping phase 5 Phase 6 - check inode connectivity... No modify flag set, skipping filesystem flush and exiting.

📝 What happened: Two inodes would be reset (corrupted). Phases 5 and 6 were skipped because -n prevents modifications. Now you know exactly what needs fixing. Remove -n and run again to apply the fixes. Always use -n first on important filesystems — never blindly repair.

Example 3: Force Zero Log

📄 Context — Last Resort:

# -L zeros the journal log if it's corrupted and prevents mounting
# DANGEROUS: discards pending journal entries → data loss
# Only use when mount fails AND xfs_repair (no -L) also fails
# Equivalent to "mkfs without the format" — structural repair only

Scenario: Carol uses -L as a last resort when standard repair fails.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo xfs_repair -L /dev/sdb1 2>&1 && echo "-L repair done — check for data loss"

Output:

Phase 1 - find and verify superblock... Phase 2 - zero log... ALERT: The filesystem has valuable metadata changes in the log which are being destroyed. This will likely cause data loss. Proceed? y Phase 3 - for each AG... done -L repair done — check for data loss

📝 What happened: The log was forcibly zeroed. The warning is serious — uncommitted transactions (last few seconds before crash) are permanently lost. Files being written during the crash may be corrupted or missing. After -L: mount the filesystem, check application data integrity, restore from backup if needed. -L is for "I need this filesystem mountable NOW."

Example 4: Check XFS on LVM Volume

📄 Context — LVM + XFS Workflow:

# XFS on LVM is common in production
# LV path: /dev/VG/LV (or /dev/mapper/VG-LV)
# xfs_repair works the same on LVM volumes
# LV must not be mounted (lvchange -a n if needed)

Scenario: Alice repairs an XFS filesystem on an LVM logical volume.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo umount /dev/anihpj_vg/db_lv && sudo xfs_repair -v /dev/anihpj_vg/db_lv | grep -E "Phase|done|error"

Output:

Phase 1 - find and verify superblock... Phase 2 - using internal log Phase 3 - for each AG... Phase 7 - verify link counts... done

📝 What happened: XFS repair on an LV is identical to a physical partition — the LV is just a block device to xfs_repair. -v shows progress through AGs. After repair: mount /dev/anihpj_vg/db_lv /data. If the LV shows as "NOT mounted" but mount fails, check lvdisplay to confirm the LV is active (lvchange -a y if not).

Example 5: XFS vs ext4 Repair Comparison

📄 Context — Know Your Filesystem:

# Key differences between XFS and ext4 repair:
# XFS: xfs_repair (separate tool), ext4: fsck.ext4 (via fsck wrapper)
# XFS: cannot shrink, ext4: can shrink (offline)
# XFS: faster on large FS (allocation groups parallelize)
# XFS: -L for log reset (dangerous), ext4: no equivalent needed

Scenario: Carol creates a quick reference comparing XFS and ext4 repair.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

echo "XFS:  xfs_repair DEV | ext4: fsck.ext4 -y DEV
XFS:  xfs_repair -n DEV (scan) | ext4: fsck -n DEV
XFS:  xfs_repair -L DEV (nuclear) | ext4: fsck -y DEV (safe auto)
XFS:  mount at boot via xfs_admin -U | ext4: tune2fs -c 30 DEV
XFS:  Cannot shrink | ext4: resize2fs DEV 10G (shrink)"

Output:

XFS: xfs_repair DEV | ext4: fsck.ext4 -y DEV XFS: xfs_repair -n DEV (scan) | ext4: fsck -n DEV XFS: xfs_repair -L DEV (nuclear) | ext4: fsck -y DEV (safe auto) XFS: mount at boot via xfs_admin -U | ext4: tune2fs -c 30 DEV XFS: Cannot shrink | ext4: resize2fs DEV 10G (shrink)

📝 What happened: XFS and ext4 use completely different repair tools with different philosophies. XFS repair is more manual (separate tool, phases visible). ext4 repair is more automated (fsck wrapper, e2fsck backend). Know both for the LFCS exam — XFS is the default on RHEL; ext4 is common on Ubuntu and general-purpose servers.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: xfs_repair DEVICE repairs XFS. -n scan only. -L zero log (last resort — data loss risk). 7 phases: superblock, log, AGs, duplicates, headers, connectivity, link counts. Filesystem MUST be unmounted. XFS is RHEL default. Cannot shrink XFS. xfs_db for debugging. xfs_admin for label/UUID changes.

🛡️ SELinux & AppArmor

Commands for managing Mandatory Access Control (MAC) — SELinux on RHEL/CentOS, AppArmor on Ubuntu/Debian. The anihpj/jobpost team uses SELinux booleans to enable service features, chcon for custom file contexts, and AppArmor profiles on Ubuntu servers for application confinement.

getenforce / setenforce / sestatus

SELINUXMACRHELLFCS Domain 5

Query and toggle SELinux enforcement — check mode, status, and detailed policy info

getenforce returns the current SELinux mode (Enforcing/Permissive/Disabled). setenforce toggles between Enforcing and Permissive at runtime. sestatus shows comprehensive SELinux status including policy version, MLS status, and loaded policy name. For basic enable/disable, see Security & Encryption.

Syntax

getenforce                          # Current mode
sudo setenforce [Enforcing|1|Permissive|0]  # Toggle mode
sestatus                            # Full SELinux status
sestatus -v                         # Verbose — show process and file contexts
sestatus -b                         # Show all boolean states

Parameters

FlagDescription
getenforceReturns: Enforcing, Permissive, or Disabled
setenforce 1|EnforcingEnable enforcement — deny + audit
setenforce 0|PermissivePermissive mode — audit only, no denial
sestatusFull status: mode, policy, MLS, mount point
sestatus -vShow file/path contexts for key processes
sestatus -bShow all booleans with current state

Return Value

CommandExit 0Exit 1
getenforceEnforcingPermissive

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — SELinux Troubleshooting

# Carol checks SELinux status on monitoring-01 (RHEL) before deploying Prometheus:
carol@monitoring-01:~$ sestatus
SELinux status:                 enabled
SELinuxfs mount:                /sys/fs/selinux
Current mode:                   enforcing
Mode from config file:          enforcing
Policy version:                 33
Policy from config file:        targeted
carol@monitoring-01:~$ getenforce
Enforcing

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — SELinux Status

Daily Workflow: Carol and Eve configure SELinux and AppArmor policies for the production servers. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical getenforce usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ getenforce
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo setenforce 0

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Full SELinux Status

📄 Context — Pre-Deployment Audit:

# Before deploying services, verify SELinux is in expected state
# sestatus shows: enabled/disabled, current mode, config mode, policy
# If "Mode from config file" differs from "Current mode", someone used setenforce
# Policy version must match kernel version for full functionality

Scenario: Carol audits SELinux status before deploying Prometheus on RHEL.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sestatus && echo "---" && sestatus -v | grep -E "Process|File" | head -6

Output:

SELinux status: enabled Current mode: enforcing Mode from config file: enforcing Policy version: 33 --- Process contexts: Current context: unconfined_u:unconfined_r:unconfined_t Init context: system_u:system_r:init_t File contexts: Controlling terminal: unconfined_u:object_r:user_devpts_t

📝 What happened: SELinux is enabled in Enforcing mode (active protection). Policy version 33 matches the kernel. Both config file AND current mode are Enforcing — no unauthorized changes. -v shows Carol's shell is running as unconfined_t (full access). Production services should NOT run as unconfined_t.

Example 2: Quick Mode Check in Scripts

📄 Context — Deployment Guard:

# getenforce returns a single word — perfect for script logic
# "if [ "$(getenforce)" != "Disabled" ]; then apply_contexts; fi"
# More reliable than grepping sestatus output
# Exit code behavior: getenforce always exits 0 (just prints mode)

Scenario: Alice's deploy script branches based on SELinux mode.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

MODE=$(getenforce) && if [ "$MODE" = "Enforcing" ]; then echo "SELinux: $MODE — applying contexts"; restorecon -Rv /opt/prometheus; else echo "SELinux: $MODE — skipping"; fi

Output:

SELinux: Enforcing — applying contexts Relabeled /opt/prometheus/bin/prometheus from default_t to bin_t

📝 What happened: Script detected Enforcing mode and applied file contexts. In Permissive mode, it would skip (contexts are irrelevant — no denials). This pattern makes deployment scripts SELinux-aware without hard-coding assumptions. Use selinuxenabled for boolean enabled/disabled checks.

Example 3: Temporary Permissive for Debugging

📄 Context — "Is It SELinux?" Test:

# App gets "Permission denied" but standard perms look correct
# Classic SELinux isolation test: set Permissive → retry → re-enable
# If app works in Permissive: it's definitely SELinux blocking
# NEVER leave in Permissive — fix the policy

Scenario: Carol isolates a permission issue by temporarily switching to Permissive.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

getenforce && sudo setenforce 0 && getenforce && sudo ausearch -m avc --start recent -ts recent 2>/dev/null | tail -3 && sudo setenforce 1 && getenforce

Output:

Enforcing Permissive type=AVC msg=audit(1717502400.123:456): avc: denied { name_connect } for comm="prometheus" dest=9090 Enforcing

📝 What happened: Switched to Permissive, found the AVC denial (Prometheus trying to bind port 9090), re-enabled Enforcing. The denial shows Prometheus needs semanage port -a -t prometheus_port_t -p tcp 9090. This 3-step test (Enforcing→Permissive→audit→Enforcing) is the standard SELinux troubleshooting workflow.

Example 4: Check All Booleans at Once

📄 Context — Policy Feature Audit:

# sestatus -b lists ALL SELinux booleans and their states
# Hundreds of booleans control specific features
# Filter for relevant ones: grep httpd, grep nfs, grep virt
# Off-by-default booleans must be explicitly enabled

Scenario: Eve audits all SELinux booleans for security compliance.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sestatus -b | grep -E "httpd_can|named_write|nfs_export" | head -5

Output:

httpd_can_network_connect off httpd_can_network_connect_db off httpd_can_sendmail off named_write_master_zones off nfs_export_all_ro on

📝 What happened: Most HTTP-related booleans are OFF — nginx can't connect to backends (httpd_can_network_connect off). To enable: setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on. -P makes it persistent. The boolean list reveals the server's security posture — more OFF = more locked down.

Example 5: Verify Mode Persistence

📄 Context — Configuration vs Runtime:

# setenforce changes runtime mode — lost on reboot
# /etc/selinux/config controls persistent mode
# sestatus shows both: "Current mode" vs "Mode from config file"
# If they differ: setenforce was used, config not updated

Scenario: Alice verifies the persistent SELinux configuration matches runtime.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

echo "Runtime: $(getenforce)" && echo "Config: $(grep ^SELINUX= /etc/selinux/config)" && sestatus | grep -E "Current mode|Mode from config"

Output:

Runtime: Enforcing Config: SELINUX=enforcing Current mode: enforcing Mode from config file: enforcing

📝 What happened: Runtime mode matches config — no drift. If runtime were Permissive but config says Enforcing, someone used setenforce 0; the system will revert to Enforcing on next reboot. Always sync: sed -i 's/^SELINUX=.*/SELINUX=enforcing/' /etc/selinux/config for permanent change.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: getenforce shows mode (one word). setenforce 0|1 toggles runtime only. sestatus full status. sestatus -v shows process/file contexts. sestatus -b lists all booleans. Edit /etc/selinux/config for persistence. Disabled mode requires reboot. Permissive = log only, Enforcing = log + deny.

chcon / restorecon

SELINUXMACRHELLFCS Domain 5

Change SELinux file context — set custom labels or restore defaults

chcon temporarily changes a file's SELinux context (overridden by restorecon/relabel). restorecon resets file contexts to policy defaults based on semanage fcontext mappings. chcon = quick fix; restorecon = permanent fix. Always use restorecon after semanage fcontext changes.

Syntax

chcon [OPTIONS] CONTEXT FILE...        # Temporary context change
restorecon [OPTIONS] PATH...            # Reset to policy defaults
# Common: sudo chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /web/index.html
#         sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www

Parameters

FlagToolDescription
-t TYPEchconChange only the type (most common)
-u USERchconChange SELinux user
-r ROLEchconChange SELinux role
--reference=FILEchconCopy context from another file
-RrestoreconRecursive — process directories
-vrestoreconVerbose — show each change
-nrestoreconDry run — show what WOULD change
-FrestoreconForce reset even if context appears correct

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Custom Web Directory

# Alice deploys static files to a custom directory and fixes contexts:
alice@prod-web-01:~$ ls -lZ /lpj/jobpost/static/style.css
unconfined_u:object_r:default_t /lpj/jobpost/static/style.css
# nginx can't read default_t — must change to httpd_sys_content_t
alice@prod-web-01:~$ sudo chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /lpj/jobpost/static/style.css
alice@prod-web-01:~$ ls -lZ /lpj/jobpost/static/style.css
unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t /lpj/jobpost/static/style.css
# NOTE: chcon is temporary — restorecon will revert it!
# Permanent fix: semanage fcontext -a then restorecon

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Change Context

Daily Workflow: Carol and Eve configure SELinux and AppArmor policies for the production servers. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical chcon usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /lpj/

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Quick Context Fix with chcon

📄 Context — Emergency File Access Fix:

# nginx returns 403 — file has wrong SELinux type
# chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t fixes it immediately
# TEMPORARY: restorecon or relabel will revert this
# Use only for testing — then apply permanent fix with semanage + restorecon

Scenario: Alice quickly fixes a file context so nginx can serve static files.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

ls -lZ /lpj/jobpost/static/index.html && sudo chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /lpj/jobpost/static/index.html && ls -lZ /lpj/jobpost/static/index.html

Output:

unconfined_u:object_r:default_t /lpj/jobpost/static/index.html unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t /lpj/jobpost/static/index.html

📝 What happened: Type changed from default_t (generic) to httpd_sys_content_t (nginx-readable). nginx now returns 200. Warning: restorecon or a system relabel will REVERT this change. For permanent: semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/lpj/jobpost/static(/.*)?" && restorecon -Rv /lpj/jobpost/static.

Example 2: Copy Context from Reference File

📄 Context — Match Existing Permission:

# --reference copies context from another file
# Useful when you know a file with the right context exists
# Don't need to remember the exact type name
# Also copies user and role, not just type

Scenario: Carol copies the SELinux context from a working file to a new one.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo chcon --reference=/var/www/html/index.html /lpj/jobpost/static/new-page.html && ls -lZ /lpj/jobpost/static/new-page.html

Output:

system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t /lpj/jobpost/static/new-page.html

📝 What happened: new-page.html now has the EXACT same context as the reference file (system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t). --reference copies all three parts (user, role, type). Without it, you'd need to remember: chcon -u system_u -r object_r -t httpd_sys_content_t FILE. Much simpler with --reference.

Example 3: Verify Before Restoring

📄 Context — Dry Run restorecon:

# -n shows what restorecon WOULD change, without actually changing
# Always preview before bulk relabeling
# Confirms the scope is correct before committing
# Reports mismatched files: "Would relabel X from Y to Z"

Scenario: Alice previews what restorecon would change before running it.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo restorecon -Rnv /lpj/jobpost/ 2>&1 | head -5

Output:

Would relabel /lpj/jobpost/static/index.html from unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t to unconfined_u:object_r:default_t Would relabel /lpj/jobpost/static/style.css from unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t to unconfined_u:object_r:default_t

📝 What happened: Dry run shows the chcon'd files would be REVERTED from httpd_sys_content_t back to default_t. This confirms: chcon changes are temporary — restorecon doesn't know about them. The permanent fix hasn't been applied yet (semanage fcontext -a). Cancel the restorecon and set up permanent contexts first.

Example 4: Force Reset All Contexts

📄 Context — Post-Migration Cleanup:

# After rsync/cp, files may have wrong contexts
# -F forces reset even if context looks correct to restorecon
# Useful after moving files between systems
# More aggressive than standard restorecon

Scenario: Carol force-resets contexts after migrating files from a dev server.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo restorecon -RFv /opt/prometheus/ 2>&1 | head -5

Output:

Relabeled /opt/prometheus/bin/prometheus from unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t to system_u:object_r:bin_t Relabeled /opt/prometheus/etc/prometheus.yml from unconfined_u:object_r:admin_home_t to system_u:object_r:etc_t

📝 What happened: Files from a user's home directory context were force-reset to system-appropriate contexts. -F skips the optimization that skips files with "correct-looking" contexts. Without -F, restorecon might skip files that appear correctly labeled but actually need different contexts on the new system.

Example 5: chcon for Testing Before Permanent Fix

📄 Context — Test-Then-Commit Workflow:

# 1. chcon -t DESIRED_TYPE file → test the application
# 2. If it works: semanage fcontext -a for permanence
# 3. restorecon to apply the permanent mapping
# 4. Verify with ls -lZ — context should persist across relabel

Scenario: Alice tests whether a new context fixes the issue, then makes it permanent.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /lpj/jobpost/static/*.js && curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" localhost/static/main.js && echo " — Test passed" && sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/lpj/jobpost/static(/.*)?" && sudo restorecon -Rv /lpj/jobpost/static/

Output:

200 — Test passed Relabeled /lpj/jobpost/static/main.js

📝 What happened: chcon tested the fix (200 OK). semanage made it permanent. restorecon applied the permanent mapping. The context now survives relabels. This test-then-commit pattern is the safest SELinux workflow — chcon for quick testing, semanage+restorecon for permanent fixes.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: chcon -t TYPE FILE temporary context (overridden by restorecon). chcon --reference=REF FILE copies context. restorecon -Rv PATH resets to policy defaults. -n dry run. -F force. chcon = test, semanage+restorecon = permanent fix. Always check with ls -lZ.

semanage — Advanced Policy Management

SELINUXMACRHELLFCS Domain 5

SELinux policy management — ports, fcontexts, booleans, permissive domains, network

semanage is the Swiss Army knife of SELinux policy management. Beyond basic port and fcontext changes, it manages permissive domains (selectively disable SELinux for one service), network labels, and user mappings. All changes are persistent across reboots and relabels.

Syntax

semanage SUBCOMMAND [OPTIONS]
# Advanced: semanage permissive -a httpd_t | semanage node -a -t node_t -M 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.0

Parameters

SubcommandDescription
permissive -a DOMAINMake a specific domain permissive (not whole system)
permissive -d DOMAINRemove permissive domain exception
node -a -t TYPE -M MASK IPLabel network nodes with SELinux context
dontaudit on|offToggle dontaudit rules (show hidden denials)
exportExport local customizations for backup
importImport policy customizations from file

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Debugging Hidden Denials

# Carol debugs a mysterious service failure with no AVC denials visible:
carol@monitoring-01:~$ sudo semanage dontaudit off
carol@monitoring-01:~$ sudo systemctl restart prometheus
carol@monitoring-01:~$ sudo ausearch -m avc --start recent | grep prometheus
type=AVC msg=audit(...): avc: denied { search } for comm="prometheus" name="net"
# Hidden denial found! Now fix it, then re-enable dontaudit:
carol@monitoring-01:~$ sudo semanage dontaudit on

Example 1: Permissive Domain (Selective Debugging)

📄 Context — Targeted Relaxation:

# Other services remain protected while you debug this one
# semanage permissive -a httpd_t — only nginx runs unconfined
# Much safer than setenforce 0 for production debugging

Scenario: Carol puts only the nginx domain in permissive mode to debug an issue.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app

├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo semanage permissive -a httpd_t && sudo semanage permissive -l

Output:

httpd_t Customized Permissive Types: 1 Builtin Permissive Types: 0

📝 What happened: Only httpd_t is permissive — all other domains remain Enforcing. nginx can now do anything without SELinux blocking (still logged). Once the issue is fixed: semanage permissive -d httpd_t. This is FAR safer than setenforce 0 which puts the entire system at risk.

Example 2: Reveal Hidden Denials

📄 Context — dontaudit Rules:

# Policy has "dontaudit" rules that suppress noisy but harmless denials
# These hidden denials don't appear in audit logs
# semanage dontaudit off reveals ALL denials
# Essential when "there are no denials but it still doesn't work"

Scenario: Alice reveals hidden SELinux denials that dontaudit rules suppress.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo semanage dontaudit off && sudo ausearch -m avc --start recent -ts recent | wc -l && echo "hidden denials visible" && sudo semanage dontaudit on

Output:

47 hidden denials visible

📝 What happened: 47 previously hidden denials appeared. Review with ausearch -m avc --start recent | audit2why to understand them. Most dontaudit denials are harmless (by design), but some may explain your issue. ALWAYS re-enable dontaudit after debugging — leaving it off generates massive audit noise.

Example 3: Label Network Nodes

📄 Context — Network-Level Access Control:

# SELinux can label network nodes (IPs/subnets) with contexts
# Enables network-level access control (e.g., only "internal_net_t" can connect)
# Used with SECMARK and labeled networking
# Advanced feature — rarely tested but powerful

Scenario: Carol labels the internal network with a custom SELinux context.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo semanage node -a -t internal_net_t -M 255.255.255.0 -p ipv4 10.0.0.0 && sudo semanage node -l

Output:

10.0.0.0 255.255.255.0 internal_net_t ipv4

📝 What happened: The 10.0.0.0/24 subnet is now labeled internal_net_t. SELinux policies can now distinguish internal vs external traffic. Remove: semanage node -d -M 255.255.255.0 -p ipv4 10.0.0.0. This is used with network_peer_controls for fine-grained network access control beyond iptables.

Example 4: Export Policy Customizations

📄 Context — Policy Backup and Replication:

# semanage export saves all local customizations
# Includes: fcontexts, ports, booleans, permissive domains, logins
# Use for: backup, disaster recovery, replicating config to new servers
# Output can be piped to semanage import on another system

Scenario: Alice backs up SELinux customizations before a major system upgrade.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo semanage export -f /tmp/selinux-customizations.txt && wc -l /tmp/selinux-customizations.txt && head -5 /tmp/selinux-customizations.txt

Output:

23 /tmp/selinux-customizations.txt boolean -m -1 httpd_can_network_connect fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/lpj/jobpost/static(/.*)?" port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8000 permissive -a httpd_t login -a -s user_u alice

📝 What happened: 23 customizations exported. The file contains semanage commands that can be replayed: sudo semanage import -f /tmp/selinux-customizations.txt. This is essential for disaster recovery — rebuild a server and reapply all SELinux customizations from backup.

Example 5: Check Port Mappings

📄 Context — Port Allocation Audit:

# semanage port -l lists all port-to-type mappings
# Shows which types can bind to which ports
# Useful for: finding available ports, avoiding conflicts
# Each type can have multiple port ranges

Scenario: Carol finds which ports are available for a new service.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo semanage port -l | grep -E "http_port_t|ssh_port_t|prometheus_port_t"

Output:

http_port_t tcp 80, 81, 443, 488, 8000, 8008, 8009, 8443, 9000 ssh_port_t tcp 22

📝 What happened: http_port_t allows HTTP on many ports (including custom 8000). ssh_port_t only on 22. If a custom service needs port 9090, it must be added: semanage port -a -t prometheus_port_t -p tcp 9090. Without this, the service will be denied even if iptables allows it. Port contexts are a second layer of access control.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: semanage permissive -a DOMAIN selective debugging. semanage dontaudit off reveals hidden denials (re-enable after!). semanage node -l network labels. semanage export/import backup/restore customizations. All changes persistent. semanage port -l | grep TYPE check port mappings.

getsebool / setsebool

SELINUXMACRHELLFCS Domain 5

Query and toggle SELinux booleans — enable/disable policy features without rewriting policy

getsebool shows the current state of SELinux booleans. setsebool toggles them on/off. Booleans are feature flags in SELinux policy — they allow/disallow specific behaviors without modifying policy source. Use -P flag with setsebool to make changes persistent across reboots.

Syntax

getsebool [BOOLEAN]                          # Show state (on/off)
getsebool -a                                  # List ALL booleans
sudo setsebool [OPTIONS] BOOLEAN VALUE        # Toggle on/off
# Common: getsebool httpd_can_network_connect
#         sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on

Parameters

FlagToolDescription
-agetseboolList all booleans
BOOLEANgetseboolShow one boolean's state
BOOLEAN on|off|1|0setseboolSet boolean value
-PsetseboolPersistent — survive reboots
-NsetseboolOnly change pending policy (not runtime)

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — Enabling nginx Features

# Carol enables the boolean that allows nginx to proxy to Django on port 8000:
carol@prod-web-01:~$ getsebool httpd_can_network_connect
httpd_can_network_connect --> off
carol@prod-web-01:~$ sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on
carol@prod-web-01:~$ getsebool httpd_can_network_connect
httpd_can_network_connect --> on
# Now nginx can proxy_pass to http://localhost:8000 without SELinux denials

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — SELinux Booleans

Daily Workflow: Carol and Eve configure SELinux and AppArmor policies for the production servers. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical getsebool usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ getsebool -a | grep http

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Check a Boolean

📄 Context — Pre-Deployment Verification:

# Before deploying, verify required booleans are enabled
# httpd_can_network_connect = nginx can proxy to backends
# Without this: "Permission denied" on proxy_pass
# One of the most commonly needed booleans

Scenario: Alice checks if nginx is allowed to make outbound connections.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

getsebool httpd_can_network_connect httpd_can_network_connect_db httpd_enable_cgi

Output:

httpd_can_network_connect --> on httpd_can_network_connect_db --> off httpd_enable_cgi --> off

📝 What happened: nginx CAN make network connections (proxy_pass to Django works). nginx CANNOT connect to databases directly (off) — Django handles DB, not nginx. CGI is disabled — modern practice, no CGI scripts. Each boolean controls a specific capability — enable only what's needed.

Example 2: Make Boolean Persistent

📄 Context — Survival Across Reboots:

# Without -P: boolean changes are runtime-only (lost on reboot)
# With -P: written to policy store, survives reboots
# Always use -P for production changes
# Without -P is useful for testing — just reboot to revert

Scenario: Carol permanently enables a boolean for production use.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on && getsebool httpd_can_network_connect && echo "Persistent change applied"

Output:

httpd_can_network_connect --> on Persistent change applied

📝 What happened: -P wrote the change to /etc/selinux/targeted/active/booleans.local. The boolean will remain ON after reboot. Without -P: change is in-memory only, lost on reboot. Test with setsebool (no -P) first, verify functionality, then apply setsebool -P for permanence.

Example 3: Search for Relevant Booleans

📄 Context — Finding the Right Boolean:

# Hundreds of booleans exist — how to find the right one?
# getsebool -a | grep KEYWORD filters by service name
# Common prefixes: httpd_, named_, nfs_, virt_, samba_, ftp_
# semanage boolean -l also works (shows descriptions too)

Scenario: Alice searches for all booleans related to NFS.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

getsebool -a | grep nfs

Output:

cdrecord_read_content --> off nfs_export_all_ro --> on nfs_export_all_rw --> on nfsd_anon_write --> off samba_share_nfs --> off

📝 What happened: Five NFS-related booleans. nfs_export_all_ro and _rw are both ON — NFS exports work. nfsd_anon_write is OFF — anonymous users can't write. Use semanage boolean -l | grep nfs to see descriptions: it shows what each boolean controls. Much more informative for unfamiliar booleans.

Example 4: Toggle Multiple Booleans

📄 Context — Service Configuration Bundle:

# Some services need multiple booleans enabled
# nginx reverse proxy needs: httpd_can_network_connect
# nginx + NFS static files needs: httpd_use_nfs
# nginx + CGI needs: httpd_enable_cgi
# Enable all at once for clean configuration

Scenario: Carol enables all booleans needed for nginx reverse proxy with NFS.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on httpd_use_nfs on httpd_can_network_connect_db off && getsebool -a | grep httpd_

Output:

httpd_can_network_connect --> on httpd_can_network_connect_db --> off httpd_use_nfs --> on

📝 What happened: Three booleans set in one command. Network connect: ON (proxy works), NFS: ON (serves from NFS mount), DB connect: OFF (security — nginx doesn't need direct DB access). Multiple booleans can be set in one setsebool command — more efficient than separate calls.

Example 5: Boolean Descriptions via semanage

📄 Context — Understanding What a Boolean Does:

# getsebool shows state but NOT description
# semanage boolean -l shows name, state, AND description
# Read descriptions before toggling — understand the impact
# Default state shows what the policy author recommended

Scenario: Alice reads boolean descriptions before deciding what to enable.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo semanage boolean -l | grep httpd_can_network_connect

Output:

httpd_can_network_connect (on , on) Allow HTTPD scripts and modules to connect to the network using TCP. httpd_can_network_connect_db (off , off) Allow HTTPD scripts and modules to connect to databases over the network.

📝 What happened: The descriptions clarify: httpd_can_network_connect controls TCP connections (needed for proxy_pass). httpd_can_network_connect_db is specifically for database connections. The (on, on) shows (Current state, Default state). Always read descriptions with semanage boolean -l before toggling unfamiliar booleans.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: getsebool BOOL checks one. getsebool -a lists all. setsebool BOOL on|off toggles (runtime only — use -P for persistent). semanage boolean -l shows descriptions. Booleans = feature flags — no policy rewrite needed. -P writes to policy store. Test without -P first, then commit with -P.

AppArmor (aa-status / aa-complain / aa-enforce)

APPARMORMACUbuntuLFCS Domain 5

AppArmor Mandatory Access Control — Ubuntu/Debian's answer to SELinux

AppArmor confines programs to a limited set of resources using path-based profiles. aa-status shows loaded profiles and enforcement mode. aa-complain puts a profile in complain mode (log only). aa-enforce puts a profile in enforce mode (block violations). Simpler than SELinux — path-based, not label-based.

Syntax

sudo aa-status                         # Show all profiles and modes
sudo aa-complain /path/to/profile       # Set to complain (log only)
sudo aa-enforce /path/to/profile        # Set to enforce (log + deny)
# Profiles: /etc/apparmor.d/
# Common: sudo aa-status | grep -E "enforce|complain"

Parameters

CommandDescription
aa-statusShow loaded profiles, modes, and process confinement
aa-complain PROFILESet to complain mode (violations logged, not blocked)
aa-enforce PROFILESet to enforce mode (violations logged AND blocked)
aa-disable PROFILEDisable a profile (unload from kernel)
aa-logprofScan logs and suggest profile updates
apparmor_parser -r PROFILEReload a profile after editing

Return Value

Exit CodeDescription
0Success

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — MySQL AppArmor Profile

# Carol checks AppArmor status on prod-db-01 (Ubuntu):
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo aa-status
apparmor module is loaded.
45 profiles are loaded.
42 profiles are in enforce mode.
3 profiles are in complain mode.
4 processes have profiles defined.
carol@prod-db-01:~$ sudo aa-status | grep -E "mysql|postgres"
   /usr/sbin/mysqld (enforce)

📁 Context: anihpj/jobpost — AppArmor

Daily Workflow: Carol and Eve configure SELinux and AppArmor policies for the production servers. Here's how it looks on the production servers.
# Carol's typical apparmor usage on prod-api-01:
carol@prod-api-01:~$ sudo aa-status

Examples

# anihpj production context:
#  prod-api-01 / prod-web-01 — Application servers
#  prod-db-01                — Database server
#  prod-redis-01             — Cache server
Example 1: Full AppArmor Status

📄 Context — Security Audit on Ubuntu:

# aa-status shows: loaded profiles, modes, confined processes
# Enforce mode = violations blocked (like SELinux Enforcing)
# Complain mode = violations logged only (like SELinux Permissive)
# Process list shows which running programs are confined

Scenario: Eve audits AppArmor status on all Ubuntu production servers.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo aa-status | head -15

Output:

apparmor module is loaded. 45 profiles are loaded. 42 profiles are in enforce mode. 3 profiles are in complain mode. 4 processes have profiles defined. 4 processes are in enforce mode. /usr/sbin/mysqld (2100) /usr/sbin/nginx (2101) nginx /usr/sbin/nginx (2102) nginx /usr/sbin/php-fpm8.1 (2103)

📝 What happened: 45 profiles loaded, 42 enforcing (active protection). Only 3 in complain mode — could be tightened. 4 processes (mysqld, nginx ×2, php-fpm) are actively confined. AppArmor works by applying profiles to executable paths — no file labeling like SELinux. Simpler model, less granular.

Example 2: Switch to Complain Mode

📄 Context — Debugging AppArmor Denials:

# AppArmor blocking a service? Put it in complain mode temporarily
# aa-complain = log violations but don't block (like SELinux Permissive)
# Check logs: /var/log/syslog or dmesg for apparmor="DENIED"
# Fix the profile, then switch back to enforce

Scenario: Alice debugs why MySQL is being blocked by AppArmor.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo aa-complain /usr/sbin/mysqld && sudo aa-status | grep mysqld && echo "--- Check logs ---" && sudo dmesg | grep -i apparmor | tail -3

Output:

/usr/sbin/mysqld (complain) --- Check logs --- audit: type=1400 apparmor="ALLOWED" operation="open" profile="/usr/sbin/mysqld" name="/data/mysql/" requested_mask="r" denied_mask="r"

📝 What happened: MySQL is now in complain mode. The audit log shows it needs read access to /data/mysql/ — the profile doesn't allow this path. Fix: add /data/mysql/ r to /etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.mysqld, then sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.mysqld, then sudo aa-enforce /usr/sbin/mysqld.

Example 3: Generate Profile Updates from Logs

📄 Context — Profile Learning Mode:

# aa-logprof scans audit logs and suggests profile updates
# Interactive: shows each denial, asks if you want to allow
# Builds profiles by observing actual application behavior
# The AppArmor way to create profiles — learn, don't hand-write

Scenario: Carol uses aa-logprof to update a profile based on logged denials.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo aa-logprof

Output:

Reading log entries from /var/log/syslog. Updating AppArmor profiles in /etc/apparmor.d. Profile: /usr/sbin/mysqld Path: /data/mysql/ Mode: r Severity: 4 [1 - /data/mysql/ r] (A)llow / [(D)eny] / (N)ew / (G)lob / Glob w/Ext / (A)bt / (F)inish

📝 What happened: aa-logprof found the MySQL denial and suggests adding /data/mysql/ r to the profile. Press 'A' to allow. This interactive learning mode is AppArmor's killer feature — it builds profiles by watching what the application actually does. Much easier than hand-writing SELinux policies.

Example 4: Disable a Profile

📄 Context — Emergency Unblock:

# aa-disable completely unloads a profile from the kernel
# More drastic than aa-complain (which keeps the profile loaded)
# Use when: profile is broken, blocking critical service, emergency
# Re-enable with aa-enforce to reload the profile

Scenario: Alice temporarily disables a broken profile during an incident.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo aa-disable /usr/sbin/mysqld && sudo aa-status | grep mysqld || echo "MySQL profile disabled" && sudo aa-enforce /usr/sbin/mysqld && echo "MySQL profile re-enabled"

Output:

Disabling '/usr/sbin/mysqld'. MySQL profile disabled Setting '/usr/sbin/mysqld' to enforce mode. MySQL profile re-enabled

📝 What happened: Profile was completely removed from kernel, then reloaded in enforce mode. aa-disable is the nuclear option — the process runs completely unconfined. aa-complain is safer (still confined, just not blocked). Use aa-complain for debugging; aa-disable only for emergencies. Always re-enable as soon as possible.

Example 5: Reload a Modified Profile

📄 Context — Profile Editing Workflow:

# Edit profile file in /etc/apparmor.d/
# apparmor_parser -r reloads the edited profile
# No need to restart the service
# Profile changes take effect immediately

Scenario: Carol edits a profile and reloads it without restarting the service.

📁 Environment Snippet:

# anihpj infrastructure context:
lpj/
├── 📁 anihpj/                          # Django project
├── 📁 jobpost/                         # Main Django app
├── 📁 api/                             # REST API
├── 📁 k8s/                             # Kubernetes manifests
├── 📁 ops/                             # Operations
└── 📁 scripts/                         # Deployment scripts

Command:

sudo nano /etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.mysqld && sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.mysqld && sudo aa-status | grep mysqld

Output:

/usr/sbin/mysqld (enforce)

📝 What happened: Profile edited and reloaded — MySQL is now running under the updated profile. apparmor_parser -r replaces the in-kernel profile with the edited version. No service restart needed. To reload ALL profiles: sudo systemctl reload apparmor or sudo aa-teardown && sudo aa-start. Always test with aa-complain before enforcing a new profile.

💡 LFCS Exam Tip: aa-status shows loaded profiles and modes. aa-complain PROFILE log-only debugging. aa-enforce PROFILE full enforcement. aa-disable PROFILE emergency unload. aa-logprof interactive profile builder. Profiles in /etc/apparmor.d/. apparmor_parser -r reloads profiles. AppArmor = Ubuntu default. SELinux = RHEL default. Path-based vs label-based.
